s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Daily record highs likely to be set at some locations Wednesday.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Strong dome of high pressure centered over southern WI per 18Z RAOBs with -3C 500 mb temperature and 6000-meter heights measured at Davenport IA will build east southeastward next 48 hrs. Bubble of very hot 850 mb air with 26C measured at Green Bay, WI and 25C air over MI and WI per NUCAPS data will advect southward into the area Wed and Thu. This will promote very hot temperatures over the local area tomorrow and Thu with air temperatures likely to reach or exceed 100F. Even with dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s, this will result in heat indices around 105F east of the Blue Ridge and 100F west of the Blue Ridge Mountains. So, Heat Advisories have been issued for Wed and will likely need to be reissued for Thu. Some daily records are likely to fall for some locations Wednesday. The atmosphere looks to remain strongly capped Wed, but on Thu, a few CAMs suggest risk of isolated thunderstorms.

GeoColor imagery has also been showing a layer of moderately dense smoke aloft overhead originitating from large fire complexes in western Ontario, CA. Over the next couple of days, the smoke may circulate across the area around the periphery of the upper high over the Midwest. So, expect gradually deteriorating air quality conditions across the local area through the end of the work week.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Chances for thunderstorms increase this weekend.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Temperatures are expected to run a few degrees cooler but remain hot on Friday with forecast highs in the 90s. So far today, temperatures have been a bit slower to rise and dew points a bit slower to fall, resulting in heat index values around where they were expected to be. s.key:
- 1) Heat continues through Friday.

- 2) Thunderstorm chances increase this weekend and could potentially linger into early next week as a front drops into the region.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Heat continues through Friday.

Although temperatures will likely peak this afternoon, above normal temperatures will persist through Friday.

The 12Z KIAD RAOB showed 850 hPa temps around 23 C, a pinch higher than they were during the heat wave earlier this month. Recent NUCAPS data from 18Z shows 925 hPa temps around 30 C which if mixed dry adiabatically to the surface would result in temps in the lower 100s. Mixing has been a bit subdued so far today due to thin smoke aloft, similar to how mixing is limited in the presence of a Saharan Air (Dust) Layer. This has also held dew points up in the upper 60s to lower 70s, highest northeast of the Potomac River where latest NUCAPS data shows a relative max in 850 hPa Tds. It is possible that areas of even slightly deeper mixing could see sfc temps jump several degrees through late afternoon (with a corresponding drop in dew points). Either way, the heat index values will remain the same - generally 100 to 105 (slightly higher east of I-95).

There is uncertainty in just how high temperatures get both Thursday and especially Friday as smoke from wildfires over Canada continues to trek toward the Mid-Atlantic. There are also questions around how much dew points mix out Thursday afternoon in particular, so have held off on any additional headlines. Of note, the RRFS-A may be onto something in how it resolves the incoming smoke with slightly lower air temps and higher dew points the next few days when compared to other guidance.

After similar temperatures Thursday, lowering thicknesses and increasing smoke aloft support the idea of temperatures being several degrees lower on Friday. The forecast may need to be lowered further if smoke is thicker, or a passing weak cold front is a bit stronger/pushes further south.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Thunderstorm chances increase this weekend and could potentially linger into early next week as a front drops into the region.

Ample subsidence and dry air aloft are expected to start the day on Thursday. Height falls/PVA will be negligible as most forcing for ascent will be associated with shortwaves in cyclonic flow passing to the north and northeast. However, a halt in height rises paired with a slowly southward sagging cold front and potentially bay breezes in areas where low-level flow goes weak in the vicinity of the front, may be enough when coupled with heating to result in a couple of isolated thunderstorms. There is further uncertainty given continued smoke aloft, as that could hamper heating and instability/convective initiation. Upstream over NE PA into NJ and the NYC tri-state area may offer a clue this afternoon as we will be in a similar environment across the MD/PA border tomorrow afternoon. Any storms that manage to develop will have ample MLCAPE (2000-3000 J/kg) and DCAPE (1000-1500 J/kg) to work with, as well as notable flow in the mid and upper levels for mid July (40-50+ kts). If any storms manage to develop by late afternoon, they could at least briefly congeal into a small cluster and propagate south/ southeast toward and across the Chesapeake Bay during the evening hours. Damaging winds would be the primary (conditional) risk, but large hail is also possible given ample CAPE, shear, and low seasonably low wet-bulb zero heights around 11.5 kft.

The surface front will drop further southward Friday. Additional smoke likely mixes into the region. Any convection on Friday will likely be limited to the higher terrain as the front washes out and pairs with orographic lift. Again, any storm that does form could be on the strong side.

Friday night, the aforementioned front will begin to lift north ahead of a wave of low pressure and stout shortwave approaching from the Upper Midwest/Great Lakes. Increasing MLCAPE late at night with some moisture advection and modest low-level flow overtop the front may result in a few thunderstorms heading into early Saturday morning, especially east of the Blue Ridge where a bit richer low-level theta-e ridge looks to pivot through.

Forcing and shear will be ample on Saturday, but the amount of instability is in question due to potential morning precip. Should enough instability develop, severe weather is certainly possible with all hazards (damaging straight-line winds, large hail, a few tornadoes, and isolated instances of flash flooding) on the table.

If the front does not make it entirely through the area, repeated strong storms will be possible on Sunday.

After a brief lull possible on Monday, another strong wave may approach by mid week next week.

If the front does not make it entirely through the area, repeated strong storms will be possible on Sun.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Hot and hazy conditions persist through Friday with a chance of a couple strong storms through this evening.

Humidity has remained very elevated this afternoon, resulting in widespread heat indices of 100 to 109. Expect reduced mixing due to smoke aloft. Heat Advisories are in effect until 8pm for much of the area, with only a slow drop in temperatures this evening.

Satellite data has started flowing again as of early this afternoon. This reveals a large and rather thick plume of smoke emanating from wildfires in Canada. The thickest smoke is on the cool side of a front draped over PA to NJ, with a secondary weak boundary dangling down the west side of the Chesapeake Bay (enhanced by the bay breeze).

This conglomerate of boundaries, accentuated by differential heating along the edge of the thicker smoke, may be enough to ignite a few thunderstorms over northern to central MD heading into this evening. Given strong instability (MLCAPE 3000-4000 J/kg), DCAPE (1000-1500 J/kg), and ~40 kts effective bulk shear, any storms that form could produce very gusty winds. Large hail can't be ruled out given ample CAPE, sufficient shear, and mid- level lapse rates around 7 C/km.

The front looks to stall near/south of I-64. - 1) Poor air quality due to smoke can be expected today along with a few showers and thunderstorms in the Allegheny Highlands and central Shenandoah Valley.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Poor air quality due to smoke can be expected today along with a few showers and thunderstorms in the Allegheny Highlands and central Shenandoah Valley.

A weak cold front is drifting south through the area early this morning, with thicker near-surface smoke originating from Canadian wildfires advecting southward in its wake. Regional observations show visibilities as low as 1-2 SM, and computer models suggest similar values could persist through much of the day, especially in the northern portions of the area. Air quality will be poor as a result through the day and possibly through tonight. Visit airnow.gov for the latest air quality forecasts from the subject matter experts at state environmental agencies.

The front will stall roughly from Pendleton County toward the SE Virginia tidewater by this afternoon. A few showers and thunderstorms may try to pop up this afternoon across the Allegheny Highlands and central Shenandoah Valley aided by instability near/south of the stalled front and orographic lift. While models indicate high temperatures in the upper 80s to mid 90s, locations that have thicker smoke may remain in the mid 80s. Humidity will be a touch lower behind the front however.

The front will begin to push back northward tonight in response to low pressure moving through the Great Lakes. While the low levels will likely be stable, elevated instability will advect northward with the front, especially closer to the Chesapeake Bay. The main question is whether there is a strong enough trigger aloft to produce convection. Most guidance has isolated to scattered coverage, if anything at all. Should a storm tap into the instability, there is enough shear to result in a stronger storm, although most of that potential holds off until after sunrise Saturday.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A strong cold front brings the threat of severe weather Saturday, possibly lingering into Sunday to the south.

An unseasonably strong upper trough and embedded shortwave/jet streak will pivot near and north of the area Saturday. Strong height falls associated with this trough, coupled with high low-level moisture content and modest mid-level lapse rates will likely result in strong instability, perhaps even if cloud breaks are muted by early day precip. The other question mark is whether smoke could have any lingering effects, though the shift in wind direction should lead to noticeable improvements in that regard. The strong deep layer flow will lead to effective shear magnitudes of 30-40 kts, helping to organize storms that develop in the vicinity of a pre-frontal surface trough in the wake of any morning activity. Low-level flow will be a bit weaker during the day, so although transient supercell structures are possible, the main risk should be damaging wind gusts and perhaps large hail as opposed to tornadoes. This could change if the effective warm front lingers overhead or mesoscale boundaries back the low level flow.

Depending on storm coverage, temps could reach well into the 90s Saturday, especially along the I-95 corridor. With high humidity, heat indices may reach 100-105 east of the Blue Ridge.

Heading into Saturday evening, low-level flow increases again ahead of the approaching synoptic cold front associated with the aforementioned upper trough. This sends PWATs hurdling to over 2.2" and keeps CAPE elevated well into the evening. The expectation is for a strongly forced line of storms to develop in the unstable airmass from the eastern Great Lakes into the upper Ohio Valley (i.e. western NY/PA into OH/WV). This line of storms may be slow to weaken as it treks into the area from the northwest through the evening, especially if there is moderate to strong instability left (depends on earlier activity). The main threat at this point would appear to be gusty to damaging winds and heavy rain due to multiple rounds of storms. High instantaneous/sub-hourly rain rates would be plausible in this setup. If any discrete activity develops in the evening ahead of the line as the LLJ increases, there may be a risk for large hail as well as a couple tornadoes, particularly in areas for surface flow is backed. With that said, much of the 00Z guidance shows this upstream convection weakening as it reaches the CWA during the evening.

Activity should wane during the overnight hours Saturday as the front and associated convection drop south and the atmosphere gradually stabilizes. The front will probably end up near or south of I-64 Sunday, with any remaining severe threat being near and south of the effective frontal boundary. Expect cooler temperatures in the wake of the front.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Brief high pressure Monday before another strong front crosses midweek.

The front continues to sag south and east of the area Monday as high pressure briefly builds in. Most of the area will remain dry with a leftover shower or thunderstorm, mainly south of I-64 where the front looks to reside. Temperatures will cool back to more seasonable levels with highs in the 80s (70s mountains).

Beyond Monday, uncertainty remains in regards to the timing of a strong upper level trough and it's associated cold frontal boundary. Some of the guidance has a leading shortwave trough crossing the area Tuesday with the cold front to follow Tuesday night into Wednesday. Depending on how this is timed with the diurnal cycle, as well as any impacts from the lingering frontal zone offshore (which could cause some sinking motion to its west locally), additional strong to severe storms are possible mid next week.

A secondary cold front will follow Wednesday into Thursday before broad high pressure over the upper Midwest expands into the region. This series of fronts will flip the airmass over to more seasonable norms if not below normal temperatures and lower humidity for the end of next week.
s.avn:
A weak front is pushing south through the area early this morning, with thick smoke from Canadian wildfires moving across the region in its wake. MVFR to intermittent IFR conditions are expected through today in smoke, although CHO may have relatively higher visibility overall. Given that modeling of visibility in smoke is far from perfect, the TAFs represent a combination of what has been happening upstream with anticipated changes due to daytime mixing and wind shifts as the front lifts back north tonight. While a shower or storm could approach CHO this afternoon or evening, and across the rest of the area late tonight, the probability is currently too low to include in the TAF. Light north winds will shift southerly tonight as the front lifts north.

Smoke should disperse by Saturday, but multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms are possible between Saturday morning and Saturday evening. Some of these could be strong to severe.

Thunderstorms are possible Sunday near CHO depending on how far south the front makes it. Prevailing VFR conditions are expected Monday with additional sub-VFR reductions Tuesday and Wednesday pending thunderstorm development.
s.mar:
Northerly winds in the wake of a cold front are lower than previously forecast, so part of the Small Craft Advisory were cancelled early, and it's questionable whether the remainder is needed. Lowered visibility in smoke can be anticipated through Friday. Winds flip to southerly tonight as the front lifts back north. Advisories may be needed for portions of the waters starting tonight, but are more likely Saturday into Saturday evening. Strong storms are possible Saturday into Saturday evening as well, which may prompt Special Marine Warnings.

Leftover storms on Sunday would probably be limited to areas around southern MD, but there is uncertainty in just how far south the front gets. Otherwise winds become northerly in the front's wake.

Expect sub-SCA level conditions Monday before SCA level channeling returns Tuesday as the gradient tightens ahead of an associated upper level trough/cold frontal boundary.
s.tide: Increasing southerly flow on Saturday and again on Tuesday could lead to water levels approaching minor flood stage, especially at Annapolis.

s.chg: Current AQI values are teetering between Code Red and Code Purple. Will be in touch with partners at state environmental departments to see if any alert level changes are needed. Either way, air quality is poor and avoiding prolonged time or strenuous activity outdoors is advised.

MVFR to intermittent IFR conditions are expected through today in smoke, although CHO may have relatively higher visibility overall. Given that modeling of visibility in smoke is far from perfect, the TAFs represent a combination of what has been happening upstream with anticipated changes due to daytime mixing and wind shifts as the front lifts back north tonight. While a shower or storm could approach CHO this afternoon or evening, and across the rest of the area late tonight, the probability is currently too low to include in the TAF. Light north winds will shift southerly tonight as the front lifts north.

Smoke should disperse by Saturday, but multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms are possible between Saturday morning and Saturday evening. Some of these could be strong to severe.

Thunderstorms are possible Sunday near CHO depending on how far south the front makes it. Prevailing VFR conditions are expected Monday with additional sub-VFR reductions Tuesday and Wednesday pending thunderstorm development.
s.mar:
Lowered visibility in smoke can be anticipated through Friday. Winds flip to southerly tonight as the front lifts back north. Advisories may be needed for portions of the waters starting tonight, but are more likely Saturday into Saturday evening. Strong storms are possible Saturday into Saturday evening as well, which may prompt Special Marine Warnings.

Leftover storms on Sunday would probably be limited to areas around southern MD, but there is uncertainty in just how far south the front gets. Otherwise winds become northerly in the front's wake.

Expect sub-SCA level conditions Monday before SCA level channeling returns Tuesday as the gradient tightens ahead of an associated upper level trough/cold frontal boundary.
s.tide: Increasing southerly flow on Saturday and again on Tuesday could lead to water levels approaching minor flood stage, especially at Annapolis.

s.chg: Other than refining the times of highest storm chances through Saturday, no changes have been made to the forecast.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Poor air quality due to smoke can be expected through tonight along with a few showers and thunderstorms.

A few showers and thunderstorms may try to develop by early this evening near the central Shenandoah Valley before drifting east and northeast as a stalled front begins to lift north. This frontal zone may be enhanced a bit on the gradient of thicker smoke to its northeast.

The front will continue to push back northward tonight in response to low pressure moving through the Great Lakes. While the low levels will likely be stable for most, instability will advect northward with the front, especially closer to the Chesapeake Bay where even surface-based parcels may become conditionally unstable by daybreak Saturday. The main question is whether there is a strong enough trigger to produce any convection. Most guidance has storms on the nose of moisture advection focused to our north, with limited coverage locally. Should a storm tap into the instability, there is enough shear to result in an organized stronger storm, although most of that potential holds off until after sunrise Saturday.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A strong cold front brings the threat of severe weather Saturday, possibly lingering into Sunday to the south.

An unseasonably strong upper trough and embedded shortwave/jet streak will pivot near and north of the area Saturday. Strong height falls associated with this trough, coupled with high low-level moisture content and modest mid-level lapse rates will likely result in strong instability, perhaps even if cloud breaks are muted by early day clouds. The other question mark is whether smoke could have any lingering effects, though the shift in wind direction should lead to noticeable improvements in that regard by afternoon. The strong deep layer flow will lead to effective shear magnitudes of 30-40 kts, helping to organize storms that develop in the vicinity of a pre-frontal surface trough. Low-level flow will be a bit weaker during the day, so although transient supercell structures are possible, the main risk should be damaging wind gusts and perhaps large hail as opposed to tornadoes. This could change if the effective warm front lingers overhead or mesoscale boundaries back the low-level flow.

Depending on storm coverage, temps could reach well into the 90s Saturday, especially along the I-95 corridor. With high humidity, heat indices may reach 100-105 east of the Blue Ridge.

Heading into Saturday evening, low-level flow increases again ahead of the approaching synoptic cold front associated with the aforementioned upper trough. This sends PWATs hurdling to over 2.2" and keeps CAPE elevated well into the evening. The expectation is for a strongly forced line of storms to develop in the unstable airmass from the eastern Great Lakes into the upper Ohio Valley (i.e. western NY/PA into OH/WV). This line of storms may be slow to weaken as it treks into the area from the northwest through the evening, especially if there is moderate to strong instability left (depends on earlier activity). The main threat at this point would appear to be gusty to damaging winds and heavy rain due to multiple rounds of storms. High instantaneous/sub-hourly rain rates would be plausible in this setup. If any discrete activity develops in the evening ahead of the line as the LLJ increases, there may be a risk for large hail as well as a couple tornadoes, particularly in areas for surface flow is backed. With that said, much of the guidance shows this upstream convection weakening as it reaches the CWA during the evening. Some training is possible on the western slopes which may raise the flood concerns there.

Activity should wane during the overnight hours Saturday as the front and associated convection drop south and the atmosphere gradually stabilizes. The front will probably end up near or south of I-64 Sunday, with any remaining severe threat being near and south of the effective frontal boundary. Expect cooler temperatures in the wake of the front.


KEY MESSAGE 3...A strong cold front and trough of low pressure may bring severe weather Tuesday and/or Wednesday.

After a quiet start to the workweek, the threat of hazardous weather returns as a strong upper-level trough and cold front crosses the region.

Some uncertainty remains in regards to the timing/placement of this system, but broadly it looks to cross during the Tuesday and Wednesday timeframe. Currently, most of the guidance has a warm front lifting through the area late Monday into Tuesday, with a pre-frontal shortwave trough ejecting eastward ahead of the boundary Tuesday afternoon and evening. The synoptic cold front looks to cross the region Tuesday night into Wednesday with the mean upper-level trough axis and possibly a secondary cold front to follow Wednesday afternoon and evening.

As a result, there is a threat of severe thunderstorms Tuesday and Wednesday, especially during the typical diurnal period. Some linear organization to the storms is likely given the high shear environment, although confidence this far out is limited.

SPC outlooks denote roughly at 15% risk Tuesday into Wednesday from west to east, with various ML/AI guidance a tick or two higher than that. Damaging winds will likely be the primary threat with storms, although other hazards cannot be ruled out pending the placement of the trough and ingredients at play.

Behind this system will be lower humidity and cooler than normal temperatures for the second half of next week with high pressure returning to the region.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Hot and humid conditions with a risk of severe thunderstorms today.

Scattered showers and thunderstorms have been rapidly forming early this morning as a warm front lifts northward. These storms will likely remain mostly elevated with stabilized low levels. They're also on the leading edge on the higher instability, but there is some shear present. The main threat may be some small hail, although gusty winds may be more likely to reach the surface closer to the Chesapeake Bay. This activity is likely mostly north and east of the area by 8 AM, which may leave the rest of the morning dry.

Regional visibility observations show the lingering effects of the wildfire smoke. With surface winds turning southerly and winds aloft turning southwesterly, there should be an improvement in these conditions from south to north through the midday hours.

Skies may not become completely sunny, but it won't take much to warm up. It will also be very humid with dew points in the lower to mid 70s. Heat index values will likely range from 100-105 east of the Blue Ridge and mid to upper 90s in the lower elevations to the west. A Heat Advisory has been issued for the I-95 corridor from Baltimore southward. This area is expected to have the most heating before storms arrive, and higher dew points will likely remain pooled east of a developing lee trough in this area.

With 30+ kt of deep layer shear, the hot and humid airmass will result in substantial instability and a favorable environment for severe thunderstorm development. A primary focus for storm initiation and/or intensification will be the lee trough east of the Blue Ridge. Most CAMs have storms developing in this area by early to mid afternoon. Storms will likely also develop well upstream in the Great Lakes closer to the surface front. What happens in between these features is a bit more uncertain, though additional thunderstorms are certainly possible given the strong upper trough and deepening surface low to the north. Some areas could see multiple rounds. The primary hazard will be damaging winds, with some considerable swaths of damage possible in any sustained supercells or linear segments. Some isolated large hail is possible, but modest mid level lapse rates will be a limiting factor. A tornado is also possible, with the greatest chances in northeast Maryland where low level flow will be more favorable. Frequent lightning and heavy rainfall are likely with any storm. Precipitable water values surge to greater than 2 inches. The flash flood threat appears to be isolated and limited to any areas with localized training or repeating storms, as overall storm motions should be progressive. The QPF signal is highest in northeast MD.

A secondary concentration of thunderstorms will develop closer to the cold front near the Great Lakes. Most guidance shows this activity rapidly weakening as it approaches the area during the late evening, with some stronger storms potentially reaching the Allegheny Front. The REFS does show a bit more persistence to these storms however. Either way, there will be a drying trend the second half of the night.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Thunderstorm chances may linger across southern portions of the area as the front stalls to the south Sunday and Monday.

The cold front will push south through the area Sunday. By the time convection initiates, it may largely be south of the forecast area. However, there is enough uncertainty in the frontal position that the I-64 corridor in central VA could see some thunderstorms on Sunday. The greatest risk for severe thunderstorms remains south of the area.

High pressure briefly building to the north will bring cooler temperatures Sunday and Monday. The front will stall temporarily but begin to lift back north Monday into Monday night. Depending how quickly this occurs, some showers and thunderstorms could move back into the area.


KEY MESSAGE 3...A strong cold front and trough of low pressure may bring severe weather Tuesday and/or Wednesday.

A strong upper trough and cold front will cross the region Tuesday into Wednesday. There still remains uncertainty in timing and placement of upper trough and front, along with coverage of convection each day. It looks as if there will be secondary cold front to follow the first front sometime midday Wednesday into the afternoon. As we get closer in time each day, we will have a better feel for this convective period of time in the middle of the week.

SPC outlooks denote roughly at 15% risk Tuesday into Wednesday from west to east, with various ML/AI guidance a tick or two higher than that. Damaging winds will likely be the primary threat with storms, although other hazards cannot be ruled out pending the placement of the trough and ingredients at play.

Behind this system will be lower humidity and cooler than normal temperatures for the second half of next week with high pressure returning to the region.
s.avn:
A warm front is lifting north across the area early this morning, with scattered showers and thunderstorms developing along it. Looks like most of these should be north/east of the terminals by 12Z. Smoke continues to reduce visibilities, though largely in the MVFR category now. These conditions should improve from south to north through midday as southerly winds pick up, which could potentially gust to 20 kt this afternoon.

Additional thunderstorms are likely this afternoon, especially for the metro terminals. Coverage is a bit more uncertain for CHO and MRB. Timing is also a bit uncertain, and it's not out of the question there could be multiple rounds. Thunderstorms may be strong to severe with strong winds, hail, frequent lightning, and very heavy rain. A possibly weakening line of storms may approach during the late evening as it drops in from the northwest, but it may largely fall apart first. Winds will shift back to the N and NW behind the cold front heading into Sunday. CHO may remain close enough to the front to see more thunderstorms Sunday afternoon.

Prevailing VFR conditions are expected Monday, though some guidance has showers and thunderstorms working back northward with a warm front by afternoon or Monday night.

Possible sub-VFR conditions on Tuesday into Wednesday. Showers and thunderstorms could push through multiple times. We will monitor the set up as we get past this weekend. Winds southeast to south 5 to 10 knots Tuesday. Winds south to southwest 10 to 15 knots Wednesday.
s.mar:
Scattered thunderstorms along a warm front may produce gusty winds and heavy rain early this morning. Lowered visibility in smoke will improve by this afternoon. Southerly winds strengthen by this afternoon in the wake of the warm front. Advisories have been issued from 11 AM to 11 PM for all waters, and lingering for the mid bay through the night. Strong to severe storms are possible this afternoon and evening as well, which may prompt Special Marine Warnings.

Leftover storms on Sunday would probably be limited to areas around southern MD, but trends suggest they will form farther to the south. Otherwise winds become northerly in the front's wake, and could result in marginal advisory conditions.

Expect sub-SCA level conditions Sunday night into Monday as high pressure builds to the north. Southerly channeling may increase winds by Monday night.

SCA conditions due to southerly channeling could occur Tuesday into Wednesday as a storm system and two possible cold fronts push across the region. Winds southeast 10 to 15 knots Tuesday. Winds south 10 to 20 knots gusts higher Wednesday.
s.tide: Increasing southerly flow today and again on Tuesday could lead to water levels approaching minor flood stage, especially at Annapolis. However, current trends suggest levels should fall short of flood stage today/tonight.

s.chg: Early morning thunderstorms have weakened and departed. A zone of subtle lift has been left in its wake. Thunderstorms may develop as early as midday in the vicinity of western Maryland.
s.key:
- 1) Hot and humid conditions with a risk of severe thunderstorms today.

- 2) Thunderstorm chances may linger across southern portions of the area as the front stalls to the south Sunday and Monday.

- 3) A strong cold front and trough of low pressure may bring severe weather Tuesday and/or Wednesday.

12Z KIAD RAOB shows plentiful elevated instability in the wake of a warm front. Will have to see where this effective warm front ends up later this morning. Differential heating in the wake of the warm front and earlier storms coupled with the onset of height falls aloft could prompt storms to fire as early as midday in the vicinity of western MD. If that's the case, storms could reach the metros by mid afternoon (3-4pm).

Despite the presence of clouds, it won't take much heating to reach convective temperatures given high (and increasing) low- level theta-e.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Hot and humid conditions with a risk of severe thunderstorms today.

15Z mesoanalysis indicates a corridor of (even higher) theta-e air at 925-850 hpa approaching the Appalachian crest. A surface trough roughly along I-81 is evident in surface analysis. As the low-level moist plume approaches from the west and interacts with the surface trough, anticipate steady to rapid expansion of thunderstorms in the vicinity of the Blue Ridge by 1-2pm.

Upstream convective development is already widespread over SW PA, OH and WV. See no reason given the environment that this won't continue to expand as it presses eastward given the very humid and unstable airmass in place.

Regarding the flood threat, individual storm cells will likely be moving given flow aloft, but the flow is oriented parallel to the lifting mechanism (nearby warm front). Back-building cells or clusters (possibly transient HP supercells) as well as multiple rounds are possible. Areas with lower FFG and in complex terrain around western MD would be of particular concern, and a watch is in effect there until 2am. To the east, there may be a hint downsloping/rain shadow, with most model QPFs showing a relative min between the Alleghenies and I-81. Farther to the east, the metro areas are typically more vulnerable to begin with. KEY MESSAGE 1...Thunderstorm chances may linger across southern portions of the area as a front stalls to the south today and Monday.

A cold front will continue to ease southward through the area this morning. Several corridors of isolated to scattered showers have formed in the broader frontal zone as a shortwave trough approaches. While models are struggling with the specific coverage, showers will remain possible through mid morning or so (shifting south with time), when the trough departs and deeper moisture pushes south.

It does appear that the wind shift will make it through a large part of the area by this afternoon, but there will be some lingering convergence and moisture near and south of I-64 in central Virginia as a wave of low pressure passes to the south. Most guidance shows scattered showers and thunderstorms developing in this corridor through the afternoon before drifting south. Since greater instability will be south of the forecast area and shear is modest, the severe weather threat is limited.

The front will stall out near North Carolina tonight and Monday as high pressure crosses the northern Mid Atlantic. This high will depart to the east by Monday evening, with return flow at 850mb beginning a bit earlier. This will allow moisture, and eventually the front, to return northward. Any rain risk will likely remain limited to the southern tier of the CWA Monday afternoon. Stronger moisture return Monday night could result in some showers and thunderstorms spreading northward with time.

Near to below normal temperatures can be expected in the wake of the front, with the largest negative anomaly tonight into Monday.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A strong cold front brings the potential for severe thunderstorms and localized flash flooding Tuesday, possibly lingering into Wednesday depending on the front's progress.

A strong upper trough and cold front will cross the region Tuesday into Wednesday. A secondary cold front may follow the first front sometime midday Wednesday into the afternoon. There's still some uncertainty with how Tuesday unfolds as there could be ongoing showers and thunderstorms in the warm advection regime that limits heating. In addition, the trough and front will likely remain northwest of the area through peak heating. However, height falls, prefrontal troughing, and the terrain will provide a lifting mechanism. Even though instability may not become too large, there will be increasing wind fields ahead of the trough. Damaging winds will likely be the primary threat with storms, although other hazards cannot be ruled out pending the placement of the trough and ingredients at play. A flash flood threat may also develop as precipitable water increases above 2 inches and a low level jet develops that may be nearly parallel to storm motions and the approaching front. Both threats may linger after sunset as the best forcing (and possibly existing organized convection) arrives from the northwest.

More uncertainty exists for Wednesday due to the timing and placement of the secondary front and trough axis. Strong wind fields will remain in place, so a severe weather threat could linger east of this front. At this time, the greatest potential, should it occur, would be east of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

Longwave troughing remains over the eastern US for the end of the week. The front will remain south of the area (though how far south is in question) as high pressure builds to the north. The main story will be below normal temperatures and lower humidity. While dry weather is most likely, uncertainty in more subtle synoptic forcing features increases toward the end of the week.

- A strong cold front and trough of low pressure will likely bring strong to severe storms Tuesday, and possibly Wednesday.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Smoke concentrations will continue through this evening before diminishing late tonight; quiet weather expected Monday; showers and thunderstorms return Monday night into Tue morning.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Isolated to scattered showers across the VA Piedmont will continue to dwindle as instability wanes and dry air advection continues on NW wind. Smoke will continue to impact skies and air quality across the region through this evening with smoke concentrations diminishing per HRRR forecasts.

High pressure builds over the area tonight supporting dry and cooler conditions.

Strong moisture return Monday night could result in some showers and thunderstorms spreading northward with time.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A strong cold front and trough of low pressure will likely bring strong to severe storms Tuesday, and possibly Wednesday.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Guidance continues to show an anomalous upper-level trough building over the area, and the cold front associated with this system will approach Tuesday before passing through the area Wednesday.

There still remains uncertainty in timing and placement of upper trough and front, but hot and humid air ahead of the front along with lower heights and a strong wind field aloft increases the threat for severe thunderstorms.

SPC outlooks already have our area in a slight to enhanced risk Tuesday, and a 15% near and east of Interstate 95 for Wednesday. ML guidance highlights Tuesday as well, with some even showing higher probabilities. Damaging winds will likely be the primary threat with storms, although other hazards cannot be ruled out if supercells develop.

Behind this system will be lower humidity and cooler than normal temperatures for the second half of next week with high pressure returning to the region.
s.avn: VFR conditions are expected most of the time Tuesday through Thursday, but strong to severe thunderstorms are likely Tuesday and possible Wednesday, especially in the afternoon and evening.
s.mar:
Strengthening southerly flow Monday evening into Wednesday morning will result in SCA conditions.

A southwest flow is expected ahead of a cold front Tuesday into Wednesday. An SCA will likely be needed since there will be a stronger gradient for this time of year. Strong to severe storms are likely Tuesday afternoon/evening and possible Wednesday afternoon/evening. High pressure will build in behind the cold front for Thursday with a northerly flow. Winds may approach SCA criteria, but confidence is low.
s.tide: Increasing southerly flow from Monday evening into Tuesday will lead to water levels reaching Action stages, but minor flooding is not expected at this time.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong to severe thunderstorms are likely Tuesday, with some thunderstorm risk lingering into Wednesday.

High pressure positioned over the northern Mid Atlantic/eastern Great Lakes will provide below normal temperatures today. Most convection should remain suppressed to the south until late afternoon or early evening. There may be a notable cumulus field however.

As the high departs this evening, a front stalled near the Virginia/North Carolina border will begin to lift northward, with moisture and elevated instability increasing from south to north through the night. Therefore, some scattered showers and thunderstorms are possible, especially the second half of the night. Central Virginia and the central Shenandoah Valley could see activity earlier this evening, and there are some indications of higher rain totals from storms becoming locked along the terrain.

Tuesday is the greatest day of concern this week. The warm front will likely lift north of the area Tuesday morning, allowing a warm and humid airmass to overspread the area. A seasonably strong trough will be approaching from the west, providing forcing and at least 30 to 40 kt of shear. This combination provides a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms, and it appears the typical afternoon and evening time frame will be favored for the strongest storms. Some details remain unresolved, especially the effects of today's upstream convection, any lingering local showers and clouds, and if there will be any focal points for greater storm coverage. Thunderstorms are also likely across the Ohio Valley, and the progression of this activity could be in the mix as well. Damaging winds will be the primary hazard, although large hail and a tornado or two are possible if supercells develop. Relatively speaking, the tornado threat is higher to the north (and north of the CWA) closer to the warm front.

With precipitable water values increasing (over 2 inches east of the Blue Ridge), any storm mergers and training could result in localized flash flooding. There are many mesoscale details that need to unfold, but additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms may continue through the night as the cold front approaches and a low level jet overspreads the area. While severe weather steadily becomes less likely, I could see a lingering flash flood threat, as the ingredients may be in place for slow moving or training heavy rainers.

There is some uncertainty with the cold frontal position by Wednesday. With the upper trough overhead, additional showers and thunderstorms are likely, especially east of the Blue Ridge. While some additional strong to severe thunderstorms can't be ruled out if things trend slower, it's beginning to appear the best parameters for that to occur will be shunted toward southeast Virginia.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Cooler than average with mainly dry conditions for the end of the week as high pressure builds into the region.

An upper level trough of low pressure will pivot its axis through the region Thursday. This will allow for an area of high pressure to build in from the west late Thursday through early Sunday. The result will be mainly dry conditions in most areas with temperatures 5 to 10 degrees below average for the third week of July. It does look as if the high will begin to break down this weekend. The result will be an increase in humidity and daytime temperatures approaching average for July by Sunday. Model spread increases during this time in regards when the next chance for rain could be.
s.avn:
High pressure passes north of the area today, with light NE winds becoming SE by this afternoon. A warm front will approach from the south tonight. This will result in MVFR to possibly IFR ceilings spreading south to north. There will also be a chance of showers and thunderstorms, but coverage uncertainties result in PROB30 TAFs for now.

Ceilings will lift Tuesday with gusty south winds developing. Showers and thunderstorms will become likely by afternoon, some of which may be severe. Additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms may linger into the evening/night with potential for locally heavy rain. Low clouds or fog could form in the wake. Additional thunderstorms are possible Wednesday afternoon for the metros and CHO depending on how quickly the cold front sweeps through.

VFR conditions Thursday and Friday. Winds north 5 to 10 knots Thursday, becoming easterly Friday.
s.mar:
NE winds become SE by this afternoon. Winds strengthen tonight, with channeling occurring along the bay. A Small Craft Advisory has been issued for favored portions of the bay from 8 PM until 5 AM. A warm front may bring a few thunderstorms late tonight.

There may be a lull in the winds Tuesday morning, before southerly winds increase during the afternoon. Small Craft Advisories will be likely through Wednesday morning. Some strong to severe thunderstorms are also likely Tuesday afternoon and evening. The cold front will cross on Wednesday and could spark a few more strong thunderstorms. Winds will shift to the NW then N, with additional advisories likely needed through Thursday morning.

Winds should decrease through Thursday as high pressure builds toward the area. Winds north becoming east 5 to 10 knots Friday.
s.tide: Increasing SE to S flow from this evening into Tuesday will lead to water levels reaching Action stages. Annapolis could approach minor flood stage.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong to severe thunderstorms are likely Tuesday, with some thunderstorm risk lingering into Wednesday.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Moisture is expected to return in earnest tonight in strengthening srly flow. Elevated showers and thunderstorms are possible overnight into Tue morning as a front returns northward. Morning low clouds and a cap will likely delay convective initiation until the mid afternoon, but afternoon temps in the low 90s combined with at least low 70s dewpoints should result in strong instability with 1500-2000 J/kg CAPE progged. This combined with approaching anomalous upper level trough and associated strong wind speeds aloft, particularly for the peak of summer should provide ample forcing and shear to result in a significant severe wx episode Tue. Scattered significant wind damage reports seem likely, with the potential for isolated tornadoes, and perhaps flash flooding. Flash flood threat does not appear significant enough for a watch given anticipated fast storm motions of 30kt or more.

By Wednesday, there is some uncertainty with the cold frontal position. With the upper trough overhead, additional showers and thunderstorms are likely, especially across southern Maryland. While some additional strong to severe thunderstorms can't be ruled out if things trend slower, it's beginning to appear the best parameters for that to occur will be shunted toward southeast Virginia.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Cooler than average temperatures anticipated beginning Thursday through the end of the week.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

An upper-level trough centered over southeastern Canada will track towards the northeast on Thursday, allowing high pressure to slide into the region from the west. This resulting high pressure could persist through early Sunday. Dewpoints will also trend lower during this period, resulting in relatively dry conditions. Temperatures range in the low-to-mid 80s, trending slightly below average for July. This high pressure could begin to break down late this weekend as a strong upper-level trough begins to form over the Great Lakes region. As the trailing cold front transitions east, humidity and precipitation chances could begin to increase again at the start of next week as this system moves through.
s.avn:
Multiple rounds of thunderstorms seem likely Tue, one in the morning between 08Z-12Z, another one between 19Z-21Z, and third one in the evening. Storms could linger well into the overnight. More storms are possible Wed, particularly eastern terminals. Severe wind gusts of 50-kt or greater are the main threat.

Prevailing VFR conditions are likely across terminals Friday and Saturday. Light northeast winds begin to shift southerly late Saturday night.
s.mar:
Strengthening srly flow tonight is expected to result in SCA conditions. Gusty SSW winds expected Tue through Tue night with likelihood of strong gusts over 33 kt, which will likely require SMWs. SCAs have been extended through Tue night into Wed morning.

Winds stay below SCA thresholds Friday and through the weekend. 5-10 knot winds flow northeast before shifting southerly late Saturday night.
s.tide: Increasing SE to S flow from this evening into Tuesday will lead to water levels reaching Action stages.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong to severe thunderstorms are likely today, with some thunderstorm risk lingering into Wednesday.

Higher dew points have been advecting into the area with moisture and instability increasing in S/SW flow. So far shower activity has been isolated and short lived. However, a subtle shortwave is approaching, and some of the convection currently across WV and SW VA could persist or redevelop across the area through the early morning hours. Areas of stratus are also forming. Both of these features could inhibit surface heating this morning, although it does appear we should have some partial sun by midday as the warm front continues to lift to the north. This should be enough to allow temperatures to rise into the mid 80s to lower 90s. Combined with dew points in the 70s, at least moderate surface based instability should develop, highest east of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

A seasonably strong trough will be approaching from the west, providing forcing and anywhere between 30 and 50 kt of flow in the cloud bearing layer. This will provide a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms, with supercells and clusters both possible. One initiation region will likely be along the prefrontal/lee trough near or just east of the Blue Ridge. These storms will likely affect the I-95 corridor between mid afternoon and early evening. While these storms will certainly carry severe potential, it is interesting to note on average the 850-700 mb wind fields will be greater to our south and west until late afternoon or early evening. Other details remain unresolved, especially the effects of upstream convection that moved through the upper Great Lakes and mid Mississippi Valley. This could have some impact on how thunderstorms develop across the Ohio Valley this afternoon and what subsequently moves into western areas. If stronger/more widespread convection does not move in from the Ohio Valley, there is some potential there is a relative minimum in coverage between the Blue Ridge and Alleghenies.

The coverage of afternoon storms and upstream effects will determine what happens this evening as the strongest forcing overspread the area along with increasing low level wind fields. A second round of showers and thunderstorms will be possible for some areas, though increasing low level stability may limit the severe weather threat. It appears the evening/overnight coverage could gradually shift to southern parts of the forecast area, or even mostly to our south, potentially focusing on outflow from earlier activity.

Damaging winds will be the primary severe hazard, although large hail and a tornado or two are possible if supercells develop. Some localized swaths of more considerable wind damage are possible. Relatively speaking, the tornado threat is higher to the north (and north of the CWA) closer to the warm front and possibly closer to the Chesapeake Bay where low level winds could be backed. With that said, forecast hodographs vary quite a bit between models and also throughout time, so any relatively higher threat will depend on the mesoscale details.

With precipitable water values increasing (over 2 inches east of the Blue Ridge), any storm mergers and training along mesoscale boundaries could result in localized flash flooding. Overall storm motions will be progressive though, so this threat appears too localized for a Flood Watch at the moment and will continue to be evaluated. Additional areas to monitor will be the Ohio Valley low level jet potentially leading to training (looks to be mostly west of the area), and the evening low level jet leading to backbuilding along any residual outflow/convergence feature (best QPF signal is currently mostly south of the forecast area).

Dry air should start working in from the northwest during the second half of the night, and the surface cold front should reach the Appalachians by 8 AM Wednesday. There is still plenty of uncertainty regarding the front's progress by afternoon, and more specifically, how far south and east the deeper moisture and instability reach. Some models do show convection firing east of the Blue Ridge mountains in the afternoon, with shear sufficient for severe thunderstorms. SPC has expanded severe weather probabilities farther north and west compared to the previous outlook. However, it's also still possible most storms are across SE Virginia. Western parts of the CWA will start feeling post frontal effects with falling dew points and highs in the upper 70s/lower 80s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Below average temps Thursday through the weekend with only small rain chances.

UL trofing will prevail over NE US with sfc high pressure building in settling overhead Fri into Sat. Canadian high pressure will result in lower Tds, allowing for a pleasant airmass in the Mid Atlantic for late July. Overnight lows in the 50 for most, low 60s metros and near waters. Would not be surprised with a few pockets of mid to upper 40s Thu and Fri night in sheltered valleys. Daily highs only 60s in higher terrain, 70s to low 80s elsewhere. Rain chances possible Sat into Sun from either the stalled front over the SE state buckling northward or a cold front approaching from the NW. Confidence remains low.
s.avn:
So far showers have been isolated, but a weak approaching disturbance could increase chances toward sunrise (currently sct storms in WV and SW VA). MRB has the lowest chance, with the metro terminals probably sitting around a 40% chance, but kept PROB30s until coverage becomes more obvious. MVFR ceilings are also quickly advancing northward, but have been rather patchy. With models backing off a bit on IFR coverage, am not sure how well these clouds fill in through sunrise. Nevertheless, VFR conditions will prevail by mid to late morning (last at MTN). Gusty south winds will develop by early afternoon.

Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms are likely after this initial activity, one between 18Z-00Z, and the other one coming (or lingering) into the evening. Right now, the greatest evening precipitation chances are from IAD/DCA to the south. Only included PROB30s for thunder since coverage and timing becomes much more uncertain. Especially with the afternoon storms, severe wind gusts are possible, along with the potential for some large hail and very heavy rain. Some low clouds could try to form overnight, but confidence is low.

More storms are possible Wed, particularly eastern terminals, though the initiation point could be mostly south/east. Any storms could be strong to severe again though. Winds will then shift to the northwest as a cold front passes through.

Prevailing VFR Thu through Sun. Light NE winds become S'ly Sat night.
s.mar:
SCA continues along the bay through this morning, though channeling effects likely decrease for a time. Gusty SSW winds expected by this afternoon for all waters, which will linger into the night. Some gusts around 30 kt are possible on the bay. Strong to severe thunderstorms are also likely this afternoon and evening, so Special Marine Warnings are likely. Winds will gradually taper off from north to south late tonight into Wednesday. Have extended SCAs to account for this timing. However, a cold front will quickly follow Wednesday afternoon, shifting winds to the NW, then a N surge will push across the area Wednesday night. This will likely warrant additional SCAs through early Thursday. Another round of strong to severe thunderstorms are possible Wednesday afternoon as the front crosses.

Winds expected to remain below SCA levels Thu aftn through Sun. NE winds become S'ly Sat night.
s.tide: Elevated southerly flow continues through this evening, pushing anomalies close to one foot. No tidal flooding is forecast at this time, but Annapolis and Havre de Grace will be close. Water levels will drop as a cold front passes Wednesday.

This will likely cut down on heating, especially across northern areas with temperatures struggling to reach 90F based on current trends. Central and southern VA seems like it will see the most heating and the highest probabilities of severe weather. Many CAMs show a minima in QPF between the Alleghenies and the Blue Ridge Mountains. Also, HRRR forecasts are likely overdone as it has temperatures reaching into the mid and upper 90s, which ain't happening based on 24-hr model and current trends. While the potential still exists for severe wx, there are still many unknowns at this time.

KEY MESSAGE 1...A few strong to severe thunderstorms are possible from central Virginia to southern Maryland this afternoon.

The cold front appears to be just southeast of Lake Erie as of 3 AM with the upper level trough axis across the eastern Great Lakes down into the Ohio Valley. The heaviest rain has exited the area. Convection that has been developing west of the Appalachians has been dissipating as it crosses the ridge into more stability and encounters downsloping flow. A few areas of light showers/sprinkles still exist though. With clearing skies and relatively light winds, a few patches of fog could form, but it is unlikely to be widespread.

A prefrontal trough will switch winds to westerly through much of the day before northerly winds bring the true airmass change tonight. The cold front likely overtakes the trough at some point but will temporarily stall this afternoon, likely extending across central Virginia to southern Maryland. Dew points will remain in the 70s in this area, supporting some instability to go along with the wind shear provided by the upper trough. Scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms are forecast along and southeast of the front, although there remains some uncertainty in coverage and intensity. Given the shear in place, there is some potential for severe thunderstorms, with damaging winds being the primary threat. Thunderstorms may also be repetitive along the slow moving front, but the expected fast individual storm motions will likely preclude any flood threat.

The front will drop south of the area this evening, but an area of low pressure may ride along it. This could result in additional showers spreading across central Virginia and southern Maryland through the night.

In terms of temperatures, highs today will be in the 70s to lower 80s west of I-81 and mid to upper 80s to the east. Lows tonight will drop into the 50s and 60s, and some of the sheltered high elevation valleys could reach the 40s.

There has been a lot of variation between models whether any fog or low clouds form through dawn, so did not forecast anything below MVFR for now. Should anything develop, it should clear quickly after sunrise as winds turn westerly. The front sags slowly across the area today. Some showers and thunderstorms may form ahead of the front this afternoon, potentially affecting CHO and DCA. The greatest coverage may be just to the south though. A wave of low pressure may ride along the front this evening and could push some additional showers toward CHO and DCA, but most of the lower ceilings will likely remain to the south. Winds will turn northerly this evening.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...A few strong to severe thunderstorms are possible from Central Virginia to Southern Maryland this afternoon.

Surface observations and visible satellite show surface convergence becoming maximized from Central Virginia to Southern Maryland as a cold front overtakes a pre-frontal trough that was already in place. Thus far, showers have struggled to mature, with very few, if any, producing lightning. This is likely due to ample dry air present in the mid-upper levels evident on both the 12z IAD sounding and model soundings. As low-level convergence continues to increase from Central Virginia to Southern Maryland, it may eventually be enough to overcome the dry air and sustain the development of thunderstorms. If a more robust storm were to develop, there could be a conditional threat for it to become severe, with damaging winds being the primary threat. Parameter-wise the environment is impressive, with around 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, 50-60 knots of effective bulk shear, and DCAPE over 1000 J/kg. However, this could be a case where the high DCAPE, highly sheared environment is also proving unfavorable for maintaining deeper updrafts. So there's a conditional severe thunderstorm threat late this afternoon into this evening, with damaging winds being the primary threat. SPC has far southern Maryland outlooked in a Slight (level 2 of 5) Risk for severe thunderstorms, with a Marginal (level 1 of 5) Risk extending a bit further north and west. Any showers or storms should gradually wind down through the evening, with drier conditions expected during the second half of the night. Cooler, drier air will start to filter in behind the front, with overnight lows dropping back into the 50s to the west of the Blue Ridge, with low-mid 60s further east.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Below average temperatures and mainly dry conditions are expected Thursday through Saturday.

A sprawling area of high pressure will build to our north for Thursday and Friday, before shifting off the New England Coastline on Saturday. Northerly flow ahead of the approaching high will advect a much cooler and drier airmass into the region for Thursday. Well below normal temperatures and dewpoints are forecast for late July, with high temperatures only in the upper 70s/low 80s. Dewpoints in the 50s will also make it feel much less humid than is typical for July. Mostly sunny skies will accompany the well below normal temperatures/dewpoints. Temperatures will stay well below normal for Friday and Saturday within easterly flow. Some moisture could be drawn northward from the stalled frontal zone across the southeastern states during this time. The current forecast has some low rain chances both days, mainly in southern portions of the CWA and along the Allegheny Mountains.

KEY MESSAGE 3... Gradual increase in moisture & precipitation chances early next week.

Broad high pressure will continue to shift northeast over the weekend, with low pressure building over northeastern Canada and a stemming trough potentially forming over the Mid-Atlantic late Sunday and into Monday. Dewpoints start to increase during this time, so shower & thunderstorm chances could increase during the afternoon & evening hours Sunday and Monday as this perturbation moves through. Machine-learning algorithms show some lower-end probabilities for severe occurrence during this time, although ensembles still show uncertainty in timing of the overall synoptic setup. As this trough approaches, temperatures gradually begin to increase back into the upper 80s.

Dewpoints could remain elevated within the region as this system moves through, with the upper-level low to the north slowly tracking to the south before shifting to the northeast midweek. This could overall re-introduce chances for rain within the region after a brief dry spell.
s.avn:
Prevailing VFR conditions are expected at the terminals today. We continue to monitor the development of showers and thunderstorms especially to the south of DCA. PROB30s have been maintained in the TAF for both DCA and CHO, but coverage of storms appears to be lesser than has been advertised by most guidance thus far. Any threat for showers and storms should gradually wind down this evening. Thereafter, predominantly VFR conditions are expected at the terminals through Saturday. Lower ceilings could briefly be possible in easterly flow on Friday or Saturday. Winds will predominantly be out of the west to northwest today, north later tonight into tomorrow, and then east to southeast on Friday and Saturday.

Predominantly VFR conditions are anticipated across terminals Sunday and Monday, although a few scattered showers and thunderstorms in the afternoon/evening hours could temporarily cause reduced conditions during this period. Light southeasterly winds briefly shift southwesterly by Monday evening.

KEY MESSAGE 1...A few showers and thunderstorms are possible from Central Virginia to Southern Maryland tonight.

00Z surface analysis places a cold front from near Wilmington DE to Annapolis MD to Culpeper VA to Staunton VA. Moderate amounts of instability and flow remain along and south of this front, which is intersecting a northward-moving outflow boundary from earlier convection that impacted the Fredericksburg to southern MD area. This corridor may continue to see activity tonight, but with decreasing severity especially beyond late evening as the front continues to push south and diurnal instability wanes.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Below average temperatures and mainly dry conditions are expected Thursday through Saturday.

A sprawling area of high pressure will build to our north for Thursday and Friday, before shifting off the New England Coastline on Saturday. Northerly flow ahead of the approaching high will advect a much cooler and drier airmass into the region for Thursday. Well below normal temperatures and dewpoints are forecast for late July, with high temperatures only in the upper 70s/low 80s. Dewpoints in the 50s will also make it feel much less humid than is typical for July. Mostly sunny skies will accompany the well below normal temperatures/dewpoints. Temperatures will stay well below normal for Friday and Saturday within easterly flow. Some moisture could be drawn northward from the stalled frontal zone across the southeastern states during this time. The current forecast has some low rain chances both days, mainly in southern portions of the CWA and along the Allegheny Mountains.

KEY MESSAGE 3... Gradual increase in moisture & precipitation chances early next week.

Broad high pressure will continue to shift northeast over the weekend, with low pressure building over northeastern Canada and a stemming trough potentially forming over the Mid-Atlantic late Sunday and into Monday. Dewpoints start to increase during this time, so shower & thunderstorm chances could increase during the afternoon & evening hours Sunday and Monday as this perturbation moves through. Machine-learning algorithms show some lower-end probabilities for severe occurrence during this time, although ensembles still show uncertainty in timing of the overall synoptic setup. As this trough approaches, temperatures gradually begin to increase back into the upper 80s.

Dewpoints could remain elevated within the region as this system moves through, with the upper-level low to the north slowly tracking to the south before shifting to the northeast midweek. This could overall re-introduce chances for rain within the region after a brief dry spell.
s.avn:

Winds will predominantly be out of the west to northwest today, north later tonight into tomorrow, and then east to southeast on Friday and Saturday.

Predominantly VFR conditions are anticipated across terminals Sunday and Monday, although a few scattered showers and thunderstorms in the afternoon/evening hours could temporarily cause reduced conditions during this period. Light southeasterly winds briefly shift southwesterly by Monday evening.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Below average temperatures and mainly dry conditions are expected into the weekend.

The cold front has pushed south of the forecast area, and 50s dew points are steadily spreading southward. Any rain should stay south of the area today, although clouds may not clear the southern tier until later this afternoon. High pressure of Canadian origin will build from the upper Great Lakes today to New England by Friday night. The cold advection on northerly winds will support below normal highs in the upper 70s and lower 80s. Humidity will also be low, with dew points potentially dropping into the 40s today across the northern half of the CWA. Tonight will be the coolest for most areas with calm winds and mostly clear skies. Any rural areas could drop into the 50s, while the urban centers and bayshore remain in the mid 60s. Friday will feature more mid and high level cloud cover.

As the high becomes positioned to the northeast, an inverted trough will develop along the Appalachian Mountains. This will help draw some moisture back northward from the stalled frontal zone across the southeastern states. Shortwave troughs in the northwest flow aloft could combine with the convergence in the surface trough to produce a few showers at times Friday afternoon through Saturday night. This rain is most probable west of I-81, but a few showers across the southern tier can't be ruled out depending on how the stationary front to our south buckles. While low temperatures will start creeping up in response to higher dew points, Saturday's high temperatures should remain below normal.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Returning to a summer-like pattern next week.

UL troffing will persist through much of next week over the NE US. S/WVs will move through the broad NW H5 flow with some guidance developing a cut-off low over NE towards the middle of next week. Regardless of UL evolution, a return to a summer-like pattern is favored with a notable increase in PWs/sfc RH. Heat builds gradually as well, but nothing near headline levels at this time. The increase in heat and moisture will increase instability and t-storm chances. Rain chances increase gradually each day through Tue (when there is some consensus a cdfnt could approach), but admittedly varies which day is highest between guidance. ML guidance highlights Tue as the highest day for SVR wx, though low probs exist almost daily.
s.avn:
Cold front is south of the area now, with northerly winds and clearing skies expected through the day. Little to no weather impacts are expected through Saturday as high pressure passes by to the north. Winds become easterly Friday and southeasterly Saturday but remain light. While low confidence at this time, increasing low level moisture could bring some low clouds or fog to CHO by Saturday night.

Low chance of thunderstorms Sunday afternoon with an upper level disturbance, with the greatest chance currently at MRB and CHO.

Prevailing VFR conditions Mon/Tue with any restrictions likely confined to diurnal t-storms. Light SE'ly winds Mon become SW'ly Mon eve and eventually N of W by Tue.
s.mar:
Small Craft Advisory conditions will continue early this morning, especially on waters open to the northerly winds. Winds will gradually decline through midday as high pressure builds to the north. That high will remain in control of the weather through the weekend, with easterly winds Friday and southeasterly Saturday and Sunday. While there could be some localized or brief enhancements, advisories are unlikely at this time.

Winds likely become southerly Monday and possibly into Tuesday depending on the timing of the next front. Channeling could enhance winds along the bay Monday night. Could have SMWs for any stronger storms each afternoon/eve.
s.tide: Water levels should reach a minimum today in northerly flow before snapping back tonight. Anomalies will rebound within onshore flow this weekend, with more sensitive locations potentially reaching Action Stage. Annapolis could approach minor flood thresholds by Saturday night.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Below average temperatures and mainly dry conditions are expected into the weekend.

Surface high pressure, originating from Canada, remains overhead today before slowly shifting towards New England. Below normal temperatures are expected today and tomorrow with highs in the 70s to low 80s. Southerly winds bring increased cloud cover today with an upper level trough yielding a slight chance of rain showers in the southern portions of the forecast area. Precipitation chances continue Saturday afternoon, mainly along the I-81 corridor in the afternoon before conditions dry out overnight. Sunday will be the warmest day of the weekend with highs in the 70s to upper 80s with dry conditions expected.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Returning to a summer-like pattern next week.

Coming off of the weekend, an upper-level trough begins to dig into the northeastern U.S. This will usher in the potential for organized convection early to mid week. In spite of multiple frontal passages during the period, next week could carry a return to summer-like conditions with heat indices in the mid 90s to near 100 degrees.

The key players will be a longstanding upper ridge across the southwestern U.S. into the southern/central Great Plains, a deep upper low near Hudson Bay, and longwave trough over the eastern U.S. While ensemble solutions do not show a more formidable shortwave tracking across the area, the setup certainly lends itself to a more active pattern. A series of "ridge rollers" are likely to cross the northern tier of the country before crossing the Great Lakes and northeastern states. At this juncture, the machine-learning algorithms favor an uptick in convection on Monday into Tuesday. This would present the most likely opportunity for any severe thunderstorms. A progressive pattern aloft will bring a cold front through the region on Tuesday evening/night, with a secondary boundary on its heels. While temperatures remain seasonable in this mid/late week pattern shift, dew points slowly come down to finish out the month of July.
s.avn:
VFR conditions and light winds are expected today and through the weekend as high pressure remains over the mid atlantic. Southeast winds today and Saturday become north/northeasterly Sunday.

With the shift toward a more active pattern, expect an increase in convective-driven restrictions on Monday into Tuesday. Between the pair of days, the arrival of a cold front on Tuesday would aid in a better shot for severe storms. Outside of convection, expect VFR conditions to largely remain. Overall winds generally waver between southwest to westerly, with afternoon gusts to around 15 to 20 knots.
s.mar:
No hazardous conditions are expected over the waters today through the weekend. Light winds and dry conditions continue through Sunday with winds expected to stay below Small Craft Advisory criteria.

There is an increasing signal of southerly channeling for Monday evening into the night. If this continues, Small Craft Advisories may be needed for portions of the Chesapeake Bay. This could linger a bit longer into Tuesday morning over southern portions of the bay waters. Otherwise, the bigger story is the increasing convective threats for early next week. Special Marine Warnings may be needed for any of the stronger thunderstorms, particularly on Tuesday as a cold front moves through.
s.tide: Tidal anomalies rebound within onshore flow this weekend, with more sensitive locations potentially reaching Action Stage this morning and through the weekend. Annapolis could approach minor flood thresholds by Sat night.
