s.key:
- Warming temperatures into the weekend with mainly hit and miss showers or thunderstorms.

- Returning to a summer-like pattern next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Warming temperatures into the weekend with mainly hit and miss showers or thunderstorms.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Several shortwave-troughs will traverse the region over the weekend, while at the surface, light southeasterly flow around retreating New England surface high will allow for moisture return into the area. Isolated showers are possible tonight across southwest areas as low-level moisture returns into the area. Warming temperatures and increasing instability may result in isold to sct showers and thunderstorms Sat into Sun, mainly west of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Moisture and instability increase further on Monday with greater coverage and convection spreading east of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Returning to a summer-like pattern next week.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Ensemble model guidance continues to favor a highly amplified pattern across the country next week. Mid/upper heights should continue to build across the Desert Southwest into the Great Plains region. At the same time, below average heights persist near Hudson Bay while extending down along the Eastern Seaboard as an elongated trough. This would support a mainly northwesterly flow regime as impulses track up and over the sprawling upper ridge across the middle of the U.S. These often have a tendency to produce convective complexes, some of which result in mesoscale convective systems (MCS). Thus, expect some uptick in convective chances during early portions of next week.

One more formidable shortwave emerges on Tuesday which will be characterized by falling heights/pressures as well as increasing moisture advection. This coincides with ample instability rising into the 1,500 to 2,500 J/kg range. With enough vertical shear and height falls, global models support an active day of thunderstorm activity. Ensembles show some sagging of the surface isobaric pattern with its position indicative of a lee-side trough. This will likely be one focus for convection along with terrain circulations and the upstream cold front. Damaging wind gusts and torrential downpours are possible with any such storm. Given the later arrival of the front, the threat for storms may persist beyond the core diurnal heating hours.

Models show this frontal zone sagging southward to near the Virginia- North Carolina border by mid-week. A shift to post-frontal northwesterlies should gradually quell the threat for thunderstorms. Dew points begin to fall with temperatures remaining seasonable. High temperatures largely top out in the upper 80s to low 90s which is close to climatology for late July. Overnight lows fall into the 60s most nights.
s.avn:
Isolated showers or thunderstoms will be possible west of the Blue Ridge Mountains, potentially impacting Charlottesville, particularly Sat and Sun afternoons.

The pattern shift will bring a return of convection to the forecast. Conditions should stay VFR much of the day on Monday as most thunderstorms likely stay back in the higher terrain. However, Tuesday is looking like a much more active weather day ahead of a notable cold front. Convective-related restrictions become increasingly likely, particularly during the afternoon/evening hours. Some showers may linger into Wednesday which could be accompanied by low ceilings. Gradual improvements take place thereafter as winds shift to northwesterly. Before this wind shift occurs, expect mainly south to southwesterly winds with afternoon gusts to around 15 to 20 knots.
s.mar:
Light onshore flow 10 kt or less through the weekend. Overall, great boating weather through the weekend into early next week.

Southerly winds pick up in intensity on Monday evening/night into Tuesday. Channeling effects could bring gusts to around 20 knots or so, which would be supportive of Small Craft Advisories, particularly across wider waters of the Chesapeake Bay. A convective threat increases through the day on Tuesday which would support the need of some Special Marine Warnings. Winds shift to northwesterly by Wednesday with gusts to around 10 to 15 knots.
s.tide: Tidal anomalies rebound within onshore flow this weekend, with more sensitive locations potentially reaching Action Stage through the weekend. Annapolis could approach minor flood thresholds early next week.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Gradually warming temperatures through Monday with increasing precipitation chances each day.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Multiple shortwave-troughs will traverse the region during the first half of next week bringing increasing chances of precip.

Air mass remains pretty stable this afternoon per NUCAPS data from 1744Z. Really don't see much developing today, except for a spotty shower here and there west of I-81.

Atmosphere becomes a bit more unstable Sunday and Monday aided by mid-level cooling and increasing warmth and instability and forcing from an approaching shortwave-trough. Should see a gradual uptick in convection each afternoon through Tuesday.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Returning to a summer-like pattern next week.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Global ensemble models agree on a highly amplified pattern across the continent. In particular, a sprawling upper ridge is likely to dominate the Desert Southwest into the Great Plains. At the same time, below average heights will persist along eastern sections of North America. While the core of lower heights stays in close proximity to Hudson Bay, an elongated longwave trough maintains its presence along the Eastern Seaboard. This configuration would support a mainly northwesterly flow regime aloft with embedded disturbances sweeping up and over the prominent central U.S. ridge.

Tuesday still presents itself as the most active day of the period as the calendar closes on the month of July. Although ensembles somewhat wash out the signal of this shortwave, deterministic solutions depict this sharpening system encroaching on the area by Tuesday into Tuesday night. Aided by modest height/pressure falls, a deep wave of low pressure is expected to track from the Ohio Valley toward the Delmarva region. Ample instability and vertical shear are in play for an active day of severe weather, but at the same time is accompanied by many of the usual question marks. Many global solutions indicate some ongoing showers on Tuesday morning. How quickly these showers and residual clouds scour out will determine whether instability is fully realized during the core heating hours. As it stands now, damaging wind gusts and torrential downpours capable of flash flooding are the main threats Tuesday into Tuesday night.

During the mid to late week period, the Mid-Atlantic region sits in a post-frontal environment as the earlier boundary lingers near the southeastern U.S. Expect reduced shower chances and less humidity as the week progresses. The warmest conditions are likely to be early in the week as highs push to near 90 degrees. However, this is simply close to climatology for late July.

Primary hazard type each day will be damaging wind gusts.

The associated warm front lifts through the forecast area early Tuesday morning ahead of the potent cold front pushing through later Tuesday afternoon and into the evening. Despite morning rain showers with the warm front, guidance continues to show plenty of instability. Combined with ample shear, strong to severe thunderstorms are expected. Currently primary hazard type looks to be damaging wind gusts with heavy rainfall capable of Flash Flooding. SPC has the entire forecast area with the exception for western MD, in a slight risk for severe weather. The rest of the forecast area is in a marginal risk.

Damaging wind gusts appear to be primary risk due to expected fast storm motions, but isolated tornadoes can't never be ruled out in NW flow. With mid-level lapse rates in the 6-7 C/km range, 30-40 kts of 0-6 km shear, and cold advection occurring at 500mb, a decent hail setup is taking place right now. Central VA will see the best chance for severe hail, as shear drops off markedly to the NW, as does the instability. A few severe thunderstorms have already occurred, and we could see a few more before the night is done. Can't even rule out a few 60 mph wind gusts with DCAPE values in the 600-800 J/kg range, which is sufficient for some severe downdrafts.

Warmer and slightly more unstable conditions are expected Monday, but shortwave ridging aloft may limit thunderstorm coverage. Overall, it looks like less coverage Monday afternoon than today.

A deepening shortwave-trough will drop from the eastern Great Lakes into our area Tue afternoon pushing a strong cold front through the area Tue evening. Strong height falls coupled with strengthening winds aloft will lead to greater thunderstorm coverage and storm organization with a much greater risk of severe thunderstorms. Damaging wind gusts appear to be primary risk due to expected fast storm motions, but isolated tornadoes can't never be ruled out in NW flow. Convection should start exiting the area quickly after 00Z Wed.

One caveat is potential for showers and thunderstorms early Tue morning, which may leave behind plenty of clouds and limit instability through the day Tue.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier conditions return mid to late week.

In the wake of Tuesday's frontal boundary, the associated low will slowly meander towards the northeast over the next couple of days. This should reduce rain chances overall, but spotty showers and thunderstorms remain possible as this low slowly slides offshore of New England late in the week. High pressure moves in overhead towards the end of the week bringing drier air and similar conditions overall as the week prior, with highs in the low to mid 80s.

Heading into next weekend, a broad area of low pressure begins to form over the Midwest and track eastward. As temperatures gradually rise towards more normal July averages, this could bring additional shower and thunderstorm chances to the region.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms are possible through this evening, along with a local flash flood risk.

MCV over central PA and cold front approaching from NW PA (and general height falls within the upper trough) will serve as forcing to continue the development of widespread showers and thunderstorms this afternoon. Shear will be sufficient for supercells, but cluster and bowing segments may eventually dominate, presenting a risk of damaging winds. Discrete storms will have potential for hail as well. A tornado threat may evolve later this afternoon/early evening as a low level jet pivots into the area and the trough takes on a negative tilt. The axis of storms will likely be closer to the I-95 corridor by this time, where winds could also be backed a little more closer to the bay. At the moment, this threat appears a little more isolated and uncertain, but discussion was had with SPC that some areas could be upgraded to a Tornado Watch should discrete storm modes dominate. The forcing features listed above could also lead to some upscale growth or training as the storms get closer to the bay. This might lead to a few instances of flash flooding, especially from Baltimore to the northeast, as precipitable water values approach 2 inches. A Flood Watch remains in effect for this area. Thunderstorms will likely clear off to the east by 10 PM, although there may be a few lingering showers, especially along the Alleghenies.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A few chances for rain through the weekend, but no hazardous weather expected between Wednesday and Monday at this time.

The upper-low over the northeast CONUS will linger through Friday before finally pulling off to the northeast. As a result, there will be non-zero shower and thunderstorm chances each day, primarily areas further north and east. KEY MESSAGE 1...Increasing shower and thunderstorm chances Sunday through early next week as low pressure and a series of fronts cross the region.

Back toward the typical summertime regime Sunday into the first half of next week with daily chances for showers and thunderstorms. The greatest coverage of showers and thunderstorms appears to be Sunday into Monday as a potent upper level trough ejects eastward from the Great Lakes into the Ohio River Valley. The incumbent upper level trough looks to be pinched off as it dives south and east yielding a cut low pressure system which looks to cross the area late Sunday into Monday. The cutoff low and associated cold front will bring widespread shower and thunderstorm chances to the region both days along with abundant cloud cover. Shear and instability values look to remain low due to weak winds aloft and widespread cloudiness. Even with that said, GoogleWxNext2 and NSSL probabilities have 10 to 30 percent contours over the region during the Sunday and Monday timeframe. This will be dictated by the placement and timing of the low/associated front as it crosses the region. Moisture will be ample ahead of the boundary on southerly flow although instability will be lacking with modeled CAPE values less than a few hundred j/kg given the extra cloud cover and timing of the system beyond the peak heating window.

Beneficial rainfall is likely given the coverage of showers and thunderstorms. Overall looking at half an inch to one inch of rain Sunday through the middle of next week. Locally higher totals are possible under heavier thunderstorms and across portions of the Alleghenies/Shenandoah Valley where the low looks to track through. The flooding threat remains lo, but not zero given repetitive rounds of thunderstorms (especially over urban/poor drainage areas).

Beyond Monday, diurnal chances for showers and thunderstorms look to continue as the front stalls near or just south of the area. The next cold front and upper level trough will follow with another round of widespread thunderstorm chances later in the workweek. High temperatures will remain at or just above normal through the period. Sunday and Monday look to be the coolest with highs in the upper 70s and mid 80s. Highs get back close to 90 Tuesday through Thursday next week. Overnight lows will fall back into the mid to upper 60s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Primarily dry conditions through Saturday.

Southerly flow may become gusty Saturday afternoon. Showers along with sub-VFR ceilings may reach CHO and MRB late Saturday night, but confidence is low.

More widespread sub-VFR conditions are expected Sunday as showers and thunderstorms return to the terminals due to a front crossing the region. The severe weather threat appears low, but not zero at this time. Expect temporary restrictions at times due to thunderstorms. Gusts will remain out of the south/southeast at less than 20 kts.

Expect sub-VFR conditions to continue at times Monday as the front and low pressure system slowly exit the region. The front will stall nearby or just to the south of the region Tuesday and Wednesday keeping temporary restrictions in place, especially at terminals south of the corridor. Winds will blow out of the northeast Monday before becoming light and variable midweek.

The current frontal analysis places a stalled boundary near Savannah, Georgia while stretching back into the Ozarks. At the same time, an occluded frontal system continues to spin off the coast of Nova Scotia. In between, the Mid-Atlantic region up into New England remains under the influence of surface high pressure. This is providing continued tranquil weather underneath a mixture of sunshine and shallow fair weather cumulus. Plenty of daytime solar insolation has helped push early afternoon temperatures into the low/mid 80s, accompanied by dew points mainly in the upper 50s to mid 60s. Winds remain light and somewhat variable owing to the anticyclone over the region. Expect minimal change through the remainder of the afternoon and evening. Heading into the overnight hours, low temperatures will fall into the 60s to low 70s, with upper 50s along the Allegheny Front. Clouds begin to increase late in the night, but conditions are to remain dry.

The primary feature of interest for the weekend into early next week is a slow moving upper low currently spinning near southern Minnesota into Iowa. Aside from a few isolated showers across higher elevations of the Potomac Highlands, Saturday will be another dry day for the Mid-Atlantic region. The most notable change will be the shift to southerly flow which slowly increases humidity levels. This becomes even more noticeable by Sunday into the first full week of August. Additionally, expect another uptick in temperatures with highs reaching the upper 80s to low 90s. Afternoon wind gusts push into the 20 to 25 mph range depending on how mixed the boundary layer becomes. A milder night lies ahead given mostly cloudy skies and warm advection flow. Many spots should see lows in the upper 60s to low 70s, with spotty mid 70s across the urban hubs.

Sunday and Monday present a more active pattern as the upstream closed low slowly moves across the Ohio Valley. There is some potential for severe thunderstorms across areas west of I-95. Areas to the east largely stay under residual ridging aloft which should limit the convective potential. The Storm Prediction Center currently places the former region in a Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5). Precipitable water values rise into the 2 to 2.25 inch range which will enhance the potential for heavy rainfall in any thunderstorm cores. The overall setup changes little into Monday, albeit with the upper low in closer proximity to the Appalachians. A modified tropical air mass remains in place which comes with a weakly defined west-east oriented frontal zone. Current limitations from a discernible flood risk would include (1) Weak low-level convergence, (2) Limited instability, and (3) Ongoing drought conditions. Will continue to monitor as additional model guidance arrives. Overall temperatures remain near to slightly below average owing to showers and cloud cover.

Shower and thunderstorm chances continue each afternoon and evening beyond Monday as we enter more of a typical Summertime pattern. The mean upper level trough and cutoff low will shift north and east with a residual boundary leftover near the coast Tuesday into Wednesday. As the low pulls further away several weak pieces of shortwave energy will pivot around it adding extra lift for dally shower and thunderstorm development. The greatest concentration of storms will likely be over the terrain and in/around where the bay/river breeze sets up. Overall coverage will remain scattered, but likely amplified during the peak heating period given the high PWATS (1.5-2"+) sitting over the region. With that said, any flood threat would remain relegated to poor drainage areas pending repetitive rounds of storms or if storm track/sit over an urban location. Highs get back close to 90 Tuesday through Friday next week. Overnight lows will fall back into the mid to upper 60s.

High pressure departing east over the Atlantic today will bring the return of a warm southerly breeze across the region. Highs are forecast to reach the mid 80s to low 90s, and there is going to be a noticeable increase in humidity. Still, brief mid-level ridging aloft is going to keep a cap on convection today as only a few stray showers are possible this afternoon.

Attention turns to the low pressure system and its associated cold front over the Midwest that slowly moves east across the OH Valley this weekend into early next week. The base of the mid-level trough is forecast to pinch off over the lower OH Valley tonight, though still remain attached to the parent upper trough. Through the start of next week the lobes of energy along the upper trough become more elongated, stretching south into the TN Valley, then stall near the central Appalachians during the early to middle part of next week. The cold front also stalls over the area sometime early next week. To our east, the Bermuda High builds into the western Atlantic and likely remains in place through the end of next week.

The Mid-Atlantic, sandwiched between these two nearly stationary synoptic features, will see a steady stream of deep tropical moisture advecting into the region. Ample heat and humidity is going to produce rounds of showers and thunderstorms each day starting Sunday, and possibly continuing through all of next week.

There is some potential for a few strong to severe thunderstorms Sunday afternoon/evening, with SPC maintaining the Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5) across most of the area. Damaging wind gusts look to be the primary threat with any severe storm that develops. Precipitable water values rise into the 2 to 2.25" range, which will enhance the potential for heavy rainfall in any thunderstorm. The 7/31 12Z and early 8/1 00Z ensemble guidance remain in flux regarding high-end rainfall amounts, so the rainfall forecast remains uncertain. Widespread amounts of 0.5" to 1" are most likely Sunday into Monday, but a stripe of localized higher rain amounts are possible. It is hard to point to any specific area that is most at risk at this moment, so be sure to keep up with future forecast updates. Since storm motion will be fast, any flood threat is going to come from repeated rounds of showers/thunderstorms. Flood Watches may be needed if confidence increases, but does not seem likely at this time.

Beyond Monday, the greatest concentration of thunderstorms is likely be over the terrain and in/around where the bay/river breeze sets up. Overall coverage remain scattered, but likely amplified during the peak heating period given the high PWATS (1.5-2"+) sitting over the region. Any flood threat would remain relegated to poor drainage areas pending repetitive rounds of storms or if storm track/sit over an urban location. Highs in the upper 80s to 90F.

The main system of interest is an expansive upper low spinning across western Illinois. This broad cyclonic circulation is forecast to push eastward over the next few days which will lend itself toward an increasingly active convective pattern into next week.

The initial surface pattern has not changed a whole lot in the past 24 hours. A frontal zone remains stalled near Savannah, Georgia while evolving into a warm front across the Mid-South. This frontal system extends into an occluded low which accompanies the vertically stacked upper low over Illinois. High pressure over the Mid-Atlantic region has largely filled, although gradients still remain weak. Winds have shifted over to south to southeasterly which has aided in an uptick in dew points/humidity levels. Overall winds are largely under 10 mph, but this should pick up in strength with higher winds noted above 3,000 feet per the KLWX VAD wind profiler.

As mid/upper-level moisture streams northeastward ahead of the cyclone over the Midwest, clouds will continue to increase through the afternoon and evening. Although the local radar is mainly devoid of any activity, a cluster of showers is lifting northward from the Richmond, Virginia metro area. Consequently, have added isolated thunderstorms along the I-95 corridor in central Virginia as well as southern Maryland. Otherwise, subsidence from the upper ridge should mostly squash any notable shower/thunderstorm threat. The other exception would be along the Allegheny Front where the 12Z HREF ensemble 40 dBZ paintball plots show isolated cells capable of brief heavy showers. Any threat should subside by nightfall with the loss of diurnal heating. Overall high temperatures are expected to peak in the upper 80s to low 90s, with 70s to low 80s across mountain locales. While high clouds are thick at times, there are enough cloud breaks to bring solar insolation down to the ground. For tonight, showers increase in coverage for the Blue Ridge westward. Forecast lows fall into the 60s to low 70s (mid 70s for the metro hubs).

By Sunday, the influence of the upstream closed low begins to enter the picture as it pushes along the Ohio River. While evolving into more of an open wave, this eventual positively- tilted trough will begin to lower heights across areas west of I-95. As these modest height falls move in during peak heating, these locations would offer the most likely opportunity for strong to severe thunderstorms. The increasingly moist environment will favor abundant low clouds which would curb instability levels. Any cloud breaks would offer the best opportunity for destabilization. Although downdraft CAPE levels are unimpressive, the fact precipitable water values rise to 2 to 2.50 inches will favor water-loaded downdrafts capable of strong and gusty winds. With this tropical air mass entering the picture, cannot fully rule out the threat for flash flooding despite the ongoing drought. A number of 12Z high-resolution models show north/south oriented patches of 3 to 5 inches, albeit in different spots from one another. With abundant clouds and showers in the area, highs will drop down into the upper 70s to mid 80s.

Models agree on a bit more eastward acceleration of the upper trough on Monday. A meridionally (north/south) oriented frontal zone sits off to the west as abundant modified tropical moisture streams poleward. This generally focuses the upper-echilon moisture content to east of the Blue Ridge. Models still favor precipitable water values on the order of the 95th to 99th percentile based on early August climatology. Numerical guidance is all over the place in terms of precipitation placement. However, the environment certainly supports torrential downpours. Any flash flood threat will be dependent on: (1) Which areas see heavy rainfall the day before, (2) If repeat convection occurs, and (3) Whether vulnerable urbanized/poor drainage locations are impacted. A large upper trough over the western OH Valley this morning is progged to slowly move east toward the Mid-Atlantic through the early part of this week. While the main mid-level energy of this system will pass by north of our area on Monday, a trailing wave of vorticity will stretch south along the Appalachians into the Deep South. A weaker cutoff mid-level low develops somewhere near the southern Appalachians Monday night. An associated surface boundary moves into the northern half of the area tonight, then stalls nearby through at least Tuesday before possibly lifting north as a warm front. To our east the Bermuda High remains squarely in place across the western Atlantic. Southerly flow is advecting deep tropical moisture into the Mid-Atlantic today, with PWATs well over 2".

Light to moderate showers have already started moving into the area early this morning. A heavier line of showers over West Virginia is likely to reach the Alleghenies after sunrise. Many additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms are expected to develop through tonight. The very moist environment will favor abundant low clouds which result in lower instability values, though cloud breaks could produce some areas of additional destabilization. SPC has maintained the Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) for severe thunderstorms today. Given the saturated environment, water-loaded downdrafts capable of strong winds are going to be the main severe threat.

The likely higher threat is going to be the potential for flash flooding. Areas that see multiple rounds of heavy showers and thunderstorms will be most at risk, especially urban and poor drainage areas. A Flood Watch has been coordinated with the surrounding offices for areas along the Blue Ridge, central Shenandoah Valley, and Alleghenies.

For the Alleghenies, the time period of highest concern is likely this afternoon as the frontal boundary moves into the area. Given the orientation of the boundary and how storms will progress along it (from southwest to northeast), there is the potential for training thunderstorms. A similar, though lower confidence scenario, could play out in the central Shenandoah Valley and along the Blue Ridge. Terrain enhanced convection could produce localized higher rain amounts on the eastern slopes of the ridge. Overall, rain amounts of 1-2" are likely, with localized higher amounts of 3-4" possible.

For the DC and Baltimore Metro areas, there is concern for flooding as multiple rounds of showers/thunderstorms move through late this afternoon into tonight. However, confidence remains low regarding exactly where any heavier thunderstorms develop. We will continue to analyze new model data this morning, so it is possible the Flood Watch is extended east into the metro areas. Showers and a few thunderstorms likely persist well into tonight, especially east of the Blue Ridge.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Sustained shower and thunderstorm chances continue through the end of the week.

For the start of the work week shower and thunderstorm chances continue each afternoon and evening as we sit within the warm sector. Meanwhile, waves of low pressure will continue to pivot through as a stalled boundary sits just south and east of the area. Additional concerns for flooding may develop as the week progresses.

Daily shower and thunderstorm chances continue through the end of the week as an upper level low stalls over the Appalachians before slowly tracking eastward. As this system finally pushes offshore towards the end of next week, the lingering frontal boundary could produce potentially increased chances for severe weather. Medium- range machine learning outputs show an enhanced possibility between Thursday and Saturday as this system transitions offshore. As PWATs will remain elevated during this period (ranging between 1.5-2.1 inches), heavy rainfall as well as gusty to damaging winds will be likely hazards with any severe storms that do form. Given persistent ongoing drought within the region, flood threats will likely be isolated to poor drainage areas during any periods of sustained heavy rain.

As this system stalls just south of the region during the week, temperatures will slowly increase and, combined with increased humidity during this period, could bring back elevated heat indices in the upper 90s across the metros beginning Wednesday. High pressure moves in overhead once any lingering frontal boundaries push offshore.

Relative to high-resolution model guidance, convection has filled out the region much earlier than anticipated. As of the mid-afternoon hours, a swath of heavier showers and thunderstorms are currently working their way across southern Maryland up toward the Baltimore metro area. A number of mesoscale circulations continue to form along this wavy line; however, none have warranted any convective-based warnings at this time. This activity should reach the Chesapeake Bay and north of the Mason-Dixon Line within the next hour.

As this complex of showers and thunderstorms exit off to the east, the upstream environment will need to continue to be monitored. The 17Z RAP objective analysis indicates instability has not been fully exhausted as 1,000 to 2,000 J/kg of surface- based CAPE (uncapped) remains. In fact, the KLWX radar shows additional cells percolating just north of I-64 in central Virginia. These are largely forming within breaks in the low clouds where instability has been maximized. Expect these to follow a similar north to north-northeastward path over the next couple of hours. For the Blue Ridge westward, overall conditions have been quieter for the most part. Flood Watches remain in effect for the threat of flash flooding through much of this evening. While high-resolution models have struggled with this event, there is a signal for convection to fill in where the Flood Watch exists.

Today's thunderstorms will all carry a risk for heavy rainfall given precipitable water (PWAT) values ranging from 2 to 2.25 inches. Sitting near record numbers certainly supports the torrential downpour potential. Earlier activity which moved across I-95 in Virginia produced 2 to 2.50 inches in about 90 minutes. This may warrant an expansion of the current Flood Watch depending on whether locations experience additional rounds of storms. Besides the convective threats, it will be a warm and humid day with highs topping out in the low/mid 80s. Did bring temperatures down a tad given the dense low clouds over much of the region. Off and on again showers continue into the night with forecast lows in the mid 60s to low 70s. Despite thick cloud cover overnight, some patchy fog may develop in areas that see winds go calm or feature plenty of ground water from earlier rainfall.

The upper low/trough responsible to the shift to active weather will track from the Ohio Valley toward the northeastern U.S. through Monday. Relative to previous days of model runs, there has been a shift to a more progressive regime. The accompanying cold front works its way to near the I-95 corridor on Monday afternoon. This system will continue to have access to highly anomalous tropical moisture with similar PWATs to today. A flash flood risk exists along/east of I-95, particularly for areas impacted by recent heavy rainfall. Forecast highs on Monday should again reach the low/mid 80s, with mainly 70s across mountain locales. While post-frontal winds become northwesterly, humidity levels remain elevated into the night with lows in the 60s to low 70s (mid/upper 50s across the higher terrain).


KEY MESSAGE 2...Additional shower and thunderstorm chances Tuesday into the upcoming weekend ahead.

It's a typical summertime regime for remainder of the workweek into the upcoming weekend as we sit within the warm sector. Synoptically, we are still monitoring the progression of an upper level low pressure system over the Ohio River Valley/central Appalachians. This system will be slow to push eastward heading into the upcoming weekend. At the surface, is a stalled boundary that will act as a catalyst for several pieces of shortwave energy to move along yielding increased chances for showers and thunderstorms during the diurnal periods each day.

Tuesday appears to be the driest day of the next 7 days as the front stalls down across central and southeast Virginia with weak high pressure building over north-central PA. Storm chances look to increase Wednesday through late week as pieces of shortwave energy pivot across the trough with mid level flow increasing to 30-40 kts between the stalled front over the Great Lakes and stalled front to our south. The warm and moist airmass combined with these passing waves of energy will yield greater thunderstorm coverage especially during the afternoon and evening periods Wednesday through Sunday. Right now, confidence remains low for severe weather based on coverage, magnitude, and timing during the period. SPC does have a mention for severe weather during the Thursday through Sunday period due to increased instability and mid level flow (30-40kts). This aligns with 15-30 percent probabilities from medium range machine learning outputs during the same timeframe. Based on current 6z/12z outputs, any focus for severe weather would be on Thursday west of the Blue Ridge and again Friday into Saturday as a weak front slides through. Main threats with storms would be damaging winds and locally heavy rainfall leading to instances of flash flooding given PWATs around 2 inches. Current drought conditions should help us avoid widespread flooding woes although poor drainage and urban areas will be the most susceptible over the coming days ahead.

Expect oppressive humidity with seasonable temperatures in the mid 80s and low 90s. The increased humidity combined with some sunshine Wednesday through Saturday will yield heat indices in the mid 90s to low 100s each afternoon east of the mountains.
s.avn:
With convection migrating further east than expected, convection has impacted the D.C. and Baltimore terminals much earlier in the day. Aside from KBWI and KMTN, any nearby lightning has waned. While convection has weakened across northeastern Maryland, will keep the convective TEMPO groups through 20Z. Otherwise, have shifted from TEMPO back to PROB30 groups for later this afternoon given a more questionable setup in the wake. Low clouds also remain a fixture in the forecast with TAF sites teetering between VFR and MVFR. Some showers linger into the night with IFR ceilings possible as the boundary layer stabilizes.

For Monday, low ceilings continue in the morning before another round of storms look likely during the afternoon/evening hours. This is especially the case for areas along/east of U.S. 15. Have placed PROB30 groups for the threat of restrictions due to thunderstorms. Winds shift from southerly over to northwesterly on Monday evening behind the associated cold front.

Expect periods of sub-VFR conditions to continue at times Tuesday through the upcoming weekend given increased chances for showers and thunderstorms. The greatest coverage storms will be during the afternoon and evening hours each day. North to northeast winds Tuesday switching to the south and southeast for the remainder of the workweek.
s.mar:
Given southerly channeling effects, Small Craft Advisories remain in effect across all waters. Aside from the upper/middle tidal Potomac, these remain in place through the overnight hours. Aside from gradient wind gusts, convection has become rather widespread this afternoon. Stronger storms will require Special Marine Warnings through this evening, some of which could include the threat for waterspouts given some low-level wind shear. A stabilizing boundary layer should limit convective gusts into the overnight hours.

Southerly gusts decrease to around 10 to 15 knots for much of Monday, although some upticks could approach advisory levels at times. Otherwise, another round of stronger storms are possible during the afternoon/evening hours. Further Special Marine Warnings may be necessary which would lend itself to hazardous boating/swimming conditions.

Sub-SCA level winds are expected out of the north and northeast Tuesday. SCA level southerly channeling is expected Wednesday through Friday for portions of the waters. A few showers & thunderstorms are possible over the waters during this period due to a stalled front nearby. SMWs may be needed to encompass this threat during the afternoon and evening hours.
s.tide: Tidal anomalies will continue to remain elevated through much of the Monday before dropping Tuesday due to a wind shift. Additional coastal flooding is possible at times of high tide as sensitive locations as a result. Anomalies climb again mid to late week.

A Coastal Flood Advisory was also issued for Anne Arundel County.

This aligns with 15-30 percent probabilities from medium range machine learning outputs during the same timeframe. Based on current 6z/12z outputs, any focus for severe weather would be on Thursday west of the Blue Ridge and again Friday into Saturday as a weak front slides through. Main threats with storms would be damaging winds and locally heavy rainfall leading to instances of flash flooding given PWATs around 2 inches. Current drought conditions should help us avoid widespread flooding woes although poor drainage and urban areas will be the most susceptible over the coming days ahead.

Expect oppressive humidity with seasonable temperatures in the mid 80s and low 90s. The increased humidity combined with some sunshine Wednesday through Saturday will yield heat indices in the mid 90s to low 100s each afternoon east of the mountains.
s.avn:
Widespread showers and intermittent heavier downpours and thunderstorms continue to affect all the terminals except MRB, with the most intense activity possible through 03Z or so, though showers may continue after that. Showers and storms to the west may eventually reach MRB by late evening if they hold together, with models having various signals on what coverage will be like overnight. Even in a more widespread scenario, there should be a downward trend toward dawn.

Ceilings will gradually lower through the night, with most terminals likely experiencing a period of IFR late tonight into Monday morning. Fog/mist may also reduce visibility in some locations.

For Monday, low ceilings continue in the morning before another round of storms look likely during the afternoon/evening hours. The latest models have storm initiation from MTN to DCA to CHO, but coverage remains uncertain. Have placed PROB30 groups for the threat of restrictions due to thunderstorms. Winds shift from southerly over to northwesterly on Monday evening behind the associated cold front.

Expect periods of sub-VFR conditions to continue at times Tuesday through the upcoming weekend given increased chances for showers and thunderstorms. The greatest coverage storms will be during the afternoon and evening hours each day. North to northeast winds Tuesday switching to the south and southeast for the remainder of the workweek.
s.mar:
Given southerly channeling effects, Small Craft Advisories remain in effect across all waters. Aside from the upper/middle tidal Potomac, these remain in place through the overnight hours. While a strong thunderstorm can't be ruled out through the night, recent radar trends suggest activity will mainly consist of showers and perhaps a few lightning strikes.

Southerly gusts decrease to around 10 to 15 knots for much of Monday, although some upticks could approach advisory levels at times. Otherwise, another round of stronger storms are possible during the afternoon/evening hours. Further Special Marine Warnings may be necessary which would lend itself to hazardous boating/swimming conditions.

Sub-SCA level winds are expected out of the north and northeast Tuesday. SCA level southerly channeling is expected Wednesday through Friday for portions of the waters. A few showers & thunderstorms are possible over the waters during this period due to a stalled front nearby. SMWs may be needed to encompass this threat during the afternoon and evening hours.
s.tide: Tidal anomalies will continue to remain elevated through much of the Monday before dropping Tuesday due to a wind shift. Additional coastal flooding is possible at times of high tide as sensitive locations as a result. Annapolis is in minor flood this evening and will be close again Monday morning. Anomalies climb again mid to late week.

s.chg: Stronger convection has mostly moved out of the area early this morning, with light showers lingering. Flood Watch was dropped earlier in the night.
s.key:
- 1) Additional rounds of locally heavy thunderstorms could lead to instances of flash flooding through this afternoon.

- 2) Additional shower and thunderstorm chances persist through this weekend.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE...Additional rounds of locally heavy thunderstorms could lead to instances of flash flooding through this afternoon.

The upper level low previously over the upper OH Valley continues to elongate/weaken as it moves northeast and away from our area this morning. The associated frontal boundary over eastern OH / western PA early this morning is going to slowly drop south into our area by this afternoon. The front is going to be the main focus for another round of showers and thunderstorms. The main uncertainty is the exact placement of this boundary, with most high res guidance showing it from Baltimore to Staunton by 18Z this afternoon. Along and south/east of this line is where most of the rain chances (50-70 pct) will be for today, with mostly dry conditions to the north/west.

It is still going to be warm and muggy areawide as highs reach the mid to upper 80s. Thunderstorms once again are going to be efficient rain makers with a deep warm cloud layer and PWATs above 2". A few instances of flash flooding are possible if any heavy thunderstorm develops and moves slowly over an urban or poor drainage area. The frontal boundary completely crosses the area this evening, ushering in drier conditions for tonight. Slightly lower dew points allow temps to drop to the 60s for most locations (upper 50s in the mountains).

The boundary attempts to lift north as a warm front Tuesday, but only makes it to around I-64. This means most of the area remains dry. Isolated showers and thunderstorms are possible in the afternoon along and south of a line from Staunton to Fredericksburg. The dry spell is going to be short lived as the warm front lifts north across the entire area on Wednesday, bringing the return of an active weather pattern that persists through the weekend.


KEY MESSAGE 2: Additional shower and thunderstorm chances persist through this weekend.

Showers and thunderstorms will focus in the afternoon & evening hours each day. Increasing humidity will allow for PWATs ranging from the 75th-90th percentile, indicating potentially increased flooding concerns with any thunderstorms that do materialize. Severe thunderstorm probabilities continue to indicate the potential for severe thunderstorms during the Thursday-Sunday timeframe, with machine learning outputs remaining in the 15%-30% range. Still, that remains uncertain given the lack of defined synoptic support and abundant cloud cover over the region that limits instability.

As this synoptic pattern persists, temperatures gradually increase back to summertime normals, with elevated humidity contributing towards heat indices that will approach 100F across the metros late into the week. Looking ahead, deterministic models do show some signal for this front transitioning offshore towards the start of next week with drier air moving in from the west, potentially providing some relief from the humidity. For now, the primary weather feature remains as humid & rainy, along with increasing heat.
s.avn:
Clusters of showers and thunderstorms continue tracking across the area early this morning, and these could reach the IAD/DCA/BWI terminals during the early morning hours. A mix of MVFR-IFR CIGs is impacting some terminals, but that is going to vary through the morning hours as showers/storms move through.

VFR conditions return this afternoon as a front slowly moves south across the area. Another round of showers/thunderstorms are likely this afternoon, except at MRB that will be north of the boundary. Dry and VFR conditions tonight through Wednesday morning. Daily shower and thunderstorm chances return Wednesday afternoon as that frontal boundary lifts back north across the area as a warm front.

Sub-VFR conditions will likely continue to be intermittent at terminals throughout the week as daily shower and thunderstorm chances persist, particularly in the afternoon & evening timeframes. South to southwesterly winds flow Wednesday through the end of the week.
s.mar:

A weak front slowly moves south across the waters today, though not before another round of showers and thunderstorms develop this afternoon. Special Marine Warnings are likely needed again today, especially south of the Bay Bridge and over the lower Tidal Potomac. Wind gusts in excess of 35 knots are the primary threat to mariners, in addition to lightning strikes.

The front pushes south of the waters this evening. Dry conditions and sub-SCA winds expected Tuesday into Wednesday morning. The stalled boundary lifts back north over the area as a warm front by Wednesday afternoon. Southerly flow returns, and could approach SCA levels over the central Chesapeake Bay. Wednesday also brings with it the return of daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms.

Southerly channeling over the waters are anticipated to produce SCA conditions Thursday afternoon through Friday. Showers & thunderstorms remain possible over the waters during this period (especially in the afternoon/evening hours) due to a stalled front nearby.
s.tide: Elevated tidal levels will lead to additional minor tidal flooding at Annapolis during this morning's high tide. As a result, the Coastal Flood Advisory was extended to cover that high tide as well. Other sensitive locations will approach or reach Action Stage. A brief period of lighter winds is expected Tuesday and that should prevent minor tidal flooding at all locations. Southerly flow returns Wednesday through the end of the week, bringing the possibility of additional periods of coastal flooding.

s.chg: With the expectation of decreasing coverage of heavy rainfall, have shifted wording to mention south of I-66. Any flash flooding threat likely focuses closer to the I-64 corridor.
s.key:
- 1) Additional heavy rainfall is possible this afternoon and evening, mainly south of I-66.

- 2) Additional shower and thunderstorm chances persist through this weekend.

s.chg: With an uptick in convective potential this afternoon, a few Special Marine Warnings and Severe Thunderstorm Warnings have been issued in the last hour or two. However, these storms are still on track to exit the forecast area by the early evening.
s.key:
- 1) Heavy rainfall is possible this afternoon and evening, mainly south of I-66, before turning quieter into Tuesday.

- 2) Increased shower and thunderstorm chances Thursday into early next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Heavy rainfall is possible this afternoon and evening, mainly south of I-66, before turning quieter into Tuesday.

A cold front is currently on the move as it edges south of I-66/U.S. 50. The latest KLWX WSR-88 radar imagery shows a broken line of storms moving well south/east of the Capital Beltway back down toward the central Virginia Piedmont and I-64 corridor. Although some of these cells continue to pulse up, the overall severe risk appears on the lower end as multiple gust fronts/outflows race out ahead. As of the mid-afternoon hours, the most consolidated area of showers and embedded thunderstorms continues over Albemarle, Orange, and Spotsylvania counties in central Virginia. With a bulk of this area in a severe/extreme (D2-D3) drought, it will likely take quite a bit of torrential rainfall to flood. All of this convection is forecast to continue nosing south and east before exiting the entire forecast area by the early evening.

For areas to the north of the convection, skies have cleared out rather quickly. A few local exceptions are noted as anvil cirrus lift northeastward to near the metro areas. This drying effect is evident on the multi-channel water vapor imagery as the mean longwave trough axis passes through. While the stronger forcing is displaced well to the north into upstate New York and southern Quebec, enough height falls cross the local area to push this front through. By late this evening, the cold front is expected to span southeastern Virginia back across interior North Carolina. The post-frontal air mass will remain dry with decreasing cloud cover.

After spending much of the day in the low/mid 80s, expect temperatures and dew points to fall into tonight. With high pressure building in from the upper Ohio Valley, forecast lows are to fall into the upper 50s to 60s. For the Alleghenies, some locations could even push into the mid 50s. The Shenandoah Valley westward may see some patchy fog for locations that fully decouple overnight under clear skies and light winds.

During subsequent days through mid-week, expect more tranquil weather to arrive on Tuesday. High pressure remains in charge as the stalled front sticks closer to the Virginia Tidewater region. Clouds increase from the south as moisture overruns the frontal system to the south. Despite the clouds, forecast highs push back into the 80s, but with lower humidity levels. Seasonable conditions persist into Tuesday night while a few showers approach from central Virginia and the Northern Neck of Virginia.

Wednesday yields the next shot for showers and thunderstorms. At the synoptic level, a cut-off low over the southeastern U.S. weakens/shears while subtropical ridging retrogrades toward the Atlantic coast. As this occurs, mid-level winds begin to increase along the western flank of the offshore anticyclone. A series of perturbations in the flow will lift across the area at the same time the surface front returns to the I-95 corridor. Precipitable water values shift back to over 2 inches which will not only increase humidity levels, but also bring heavy rainfall back to the forecast. A Marginal Risk for excessive rainfall exists on Wednesday as this pattern shift unfolds. Highs remain in the 80s with afternoon heat indices into the mid 90s.


KEY MESSAGE 2: Increased shower and thunderstorm chances Thursday into early next week.

Synoptically, we are still monitoring the progression of an upper level low pressure system over the Ohio River Valley/central Appalachians. This system will be slow to push eastward heading into the weekend and early next week. At the surface, is a stalled/washed out boundary that will act as a catalyst for several pieces of shortwave energy to move along yielding increased chances for showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening periods each day.

Additional showers and thunderstorms are likely Thursday through Sunday given the boundary washing out over the area. The warm/moist airmass combined with the washed out boundary and ripples of shortwave energy will aid in scattered to numerous diurnal thunderstorm development. Severe weather could be a concern each day, but overall confidence remains uncertain due to abundant cloud cover and no real forcing mechanisms. Expect much of the convection to be driven by terrain circulations or bay/river breeze interactions. Current machine learning probabilities remain between 15-30 percent Thursday through Monday with 30-45 percent probabilities east of the Blue Ridge Friday. Friday may be the day where we have a more pronounced severe threat due to a lee side trough combined with 30-40kt mid level flow driving convection eastward. Locally damaging wind gusts will be the primary threat with storms along with isolated instances of flash flooding.

Expect PWATS to remain between the 75th-90th percentile right on through early next week. This is due to the lack of any real airmass changing cold front holding off until the (beyond Tuesday) middle or end of next week per latest long range guidance. As a result expect increased humidity and above average temperatures across the region. Highs will range from the mid to upper 80s and low 90s each afternoon with heat indices up around 100 degrees east of the Blue Ridge and over the I-95 metros late week. Once again it won't be raining all the time with plenty of dry time in between. Plan for seasonable summer temperatures and oppressive humidity through the extended period.
s.avn:
With frontal convection now well south of the D.C. and Baltimore terminals, the only TAF site with restrictions is KCHO. A cluster of slow moving strong to severe thunderstorms remains around the terminal this afternoon. Have maintained a TEMPO group until 20Z to account for this convective threat. Otherwise, VFR conditions should prevail for all sites through Tuesday as the front sags off toward the south. Multiple wind shifts will occur during this time as initial post-frontal northwesterlies turn more northeast to easterly in time. A shift to southerlies is expected by Wednesday as the system returns northward as a warm front. This brings shower and thunderstorm chances which carries the potential for a few restrictions.

Expect periods of sub-VFR conditions to continue at times Thursday through the upcoming weekend given increased chances for showers and thunderstorms. The greatest coverage storms will be during the afternoon and evening hours each day. Winds switch back to the south and southwest Wednesday through the remainder of the workweek. Speeds generally less than 15 kts.
s.mar:
As frontal convection slowly pushes toward the south and east, the threat for Special Marine Warnings exists over southern portions of the tidal Potomac and Chesapeake Bay. This all should wind down by the early evening at the latest. Post- frontal northwesterlies are expected into the night before shifting to northeasterly early Tuesday. Some uptick in gusts to around 15 knots are possible as this wind shift occurs. Otherwise, wind speeds do not really pick up until Wednesday as southerly flow returns. Channeling effects across the wider waters of the Chesapeake Bay could again reach 15 knots or so. Convective chances return with the warm front which could yield frequent lightning strikes and gusty marine winds.

SCA level southerly channeling is expected Thursday afternoon through Saturday for portions of the waters. A few showers & thunderstorms are possible over the waters during this period due to a stalled front nearby. SMWs may be needed to encompass this threat during the afternoon and evening hours.
s.tide: Tidal anomalies will continue to remain elevated through much of the day before dropping Tuesday due to a wind shift. Additional coastal flooding is possible at times of high tide as sensitive locations as a result. Anomalies climb again mid to late week in response to return southerly flow.

s.chg: Risk of showers and thunderstorms is pushing south. Small Craft Advisory issued for late tonight/Tuesday morning.
s.key:
- 1) A relative break in rain chances is expected through Tuesday.

- 2) Increased shower and thunderstorm chances Thursday into early next week.

A cold front will continue to push south across the waters through this evening, shifting winds to the northwest. A few thunderstorms remain possible across southern Maryland through mid or late evening, but the risk for strong storms is decreasing. After midnight, a surge of northeasterly winds will spread across the area. Given the warm water temperatures, these winds should easily mix down on the wider waters along the bay, so a Small Craft Advisory has been issued from late tonight into Tuesday morning. Winds will turn easterly then southeasterly later Tuesday.

Wind speeds do not really pick up again until Wednesday as southerly flow returns. Channeling effects across the wider waters of the Chesapeake Bay could again reach 15 knots or so. Convective chances return with the warm front which could yield frequent lightning strikes and gusty marine winds.

s.chg: A few showers have developed early this morning over the Chesapeake Bay and central VA. This is where additional showers are possible this afternoon, with other areas remaining dry. As a warm front lifts north across the area tonight, there is the potential for flash flooding due to slow moving convection.
s.key:
- 1) Monitoring potential for localized urban flooding tonight as a warm front lifts north.

- 2) Daily shower and thunderstorm chances Wednesday through early next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Monitoring potential for localized urban flooding tonight as a warm front lifts north.

A stalled frontal boundary is located over southern Virginia early this morning where slow moving showers are ongoing. Looking at dry conditions for most of the area today as the boundary remains nearly stationary through this morning. However, the boundary is going to start lifting north as a warm front this afternoon, then make steadier progress through the area tonight. Showers and some thunderstorms push into parts of Central Virginia this afternoon.

A cutoff mid-level low over the Deep South today retrogrades north this evening, and that is what will push the warm front into our area. As the front presses north, expect additional slow moving shower and thunderstorms to develop across central VA, then up toward the Washington DC and Baltimore Metro areas overnight tonight into Wednesday morning.

There is a concerning signal in some of the high res guidance that indicate potential for flash flooding in the metro areas tonight. Convection appears to be enhanced from the development of a broad wave of surface low pressure, or an MCV that develops in the aftermath of diurnal convection. Either way, any slow moving shower or thunderstorm tonight is going to be cable of producing heavy rainfall in a short period of time. Tropical moisture returns as PWATs surge to over 2" once again. This likely yields high rain rates of 1-3" per hour in the heaviest showers/thunderstorms. A Flood Watch may be needed for parts of the area, but confidence is too low at this time. Will need to carefully analyze the 12Z and later guidance to determine if the threat for urban flash flooding is there tonight.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Daily shower and thunderstorm chances Wednesday through early next week.

Ongoing showers and thunderstorms continue into Wednesday morning as the warm front remains somewhere north of I-66. The cut-off low over the southeastern U.S. weakens/shears while subtropical ridging retrogrades toward the Atlantic coast. Increasing warmth and humidity around the west side of the subtropical Atlantic ridge, coupled with weak disturbances aloft will lead to afternoon and evening showers and thunderstorms each day Thursday into early next week. Mid-level flow appears strongest Thursday through the weekend. Given the degree of instability with temps in the 90s and 70s dewpoints, there could be a risk for severe thunderstorms each day. Locally heavy rainfall is going to be possible each day, as well. Increasing warmth and humidity yield heat indices around 100 Thursday through Sunday.
s.avn:
VFR conditions are expected through this evening for most of the area. A stalled boundary south of the area is going to lift north as warm front this afternoon into tomorrow. Sub-VFR conditions quickly arrive at CHO early this evening, then at IAD/DCA late this evening, and BWI/MTN/MRB late tonight. A period of moderate to heavy showers, and possibly some thunderstorms, is likely to move across the area tonight. IFR CIGs are becoming increasingly likely, with reductions in visibility from heavy rainfall possible.

Sub-VFR conditions persist into Wednesday, though there is likely to be a return to VFR conditions during the afternoon. Beyond that, expect an active weather pattern through the weekend with daily chances for showers and thunderstorms.
s.mar: A stalled boundary south of the waters will lift north as a warm front tonight. Southerly channeling is expected to develop at times Wednesday through Friday, with Small Craft Advisories likely needed for most of the waters. Additionally, daily chances for showers and thunderstorms return to the forecast Wednesday through the weekend. Any thunderstorm will be capable of producing wind gusts over 35 knots, in addition to lightning strikes.
s.tide: Tidal anomalies continue to decrease today as north winds continue. Southerly winds will return tonight behind a warm front that lifts north through the area. Anomalies climb again mid to late week in response to return southerly flow. Additional periods of coastal flooding are possible at times of high tide at sensitive locations.

s.chg: No significant changes were made to the forecast, but will continue to monitor the threat of heavy rainfall for tonight as 12Z models come in this morning.

- 1) Monitoring potential for localized urban flooding tonight as a warm front lifts north.

- 2) Daily shower and thunderstorm chances Wednesday through early next week.

A stalled frontal boundary is currently located over the Virginia Tidewater region while extending back into central North Carolina. Any associated shower activity remains well south of the local area this morning. However, clouds do continue to lift up from southern Virginia, with further expansion of cloud cover expected through the day. Looking at dry conditions for most of the area today as the boundary remains nearly stationary through the remainder of the morning. However, the boundary is going to start lifting north as a warm front this afternoon, then make steadier progress through the area tonight. Showers and some thunderstorms push into parts of Central Virginia this afternoon.

A cutoff mid-level low over the Deep South today retrogrades north this evening, and that is what will push the warm front into our area. As the front presses north, expect additional slow moving shower and thunderstorms to develop across central VA, then up toward the Washington DC and Baltimore Metro areas overnight tonight into Wednesday morning.

There is a concerning signal in some of the high res guidance that indicate potential for flash flooding in the metro areas tonight. Convection appears to be enhanced from the development of a broad wave of surface low pressure, or an MCV that develops in the aftermath of diurnal convection. Either way, any slow moving shower or thunderstorm tonight is going to be cable of producing heavy rainfall in a short period of time. Tropical moisture returns as PWATs surge to over 2" once again. This likely yields high rain rates of 1-3" per hour in the heaviest showers/thunderstorms. A Flood Watch may be needed for parts of the area, but confidence is too low at this time. Mid-level flow appears strongest Thursday through the weekend. Given the degree of instability with temps in the 90s and 70s dewpoints, there could be a risk for severe thunderstorms each day. s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Monitoring potential for localized urban flooding tonight into Wednesday morning as a warm front lifts north.

While the earlier frontal boundary is currently down in southern Virginia, broad ascent atop this frontal zone is yielding multiple areas of convection. The latest KLWX WSR-88D radar imagery depicts one such wave bringing some light showers to areas just north of I-64 in central Virginia. Being at the leading edge of the instability gradient, this storm cluster is not terribly organized and has continued to weaken. However, in the wake of these storms, a more concentrated axis of heavier showers and thunderstorms have begun to develop around the Richmond metro area. These are slow moving and already yielding Flash Flood Warnings in central Virginia. Looking further south, additional slow moving cells are forming over the Virginia Tidewater region. As the warm front lifts northward in time, all of this convection shifts focus toward the local area by tonight into early Wednesday morning. How this evolves over the next 6 to 12 hours will dictate the degree of impact to the region.

Besides the showers moving near/just east of Charlottesville, the weather has been tranquil across the remainder of the area. Aside from some shallow fair weather cumulus fields, skies remain mostly sunny this afternoon. Being north of the frontal zone, mean surface winds are largely out of the east to northeasterly direction. Overall temperatures are holding steady in the low/mid 80s, with mainly 70s across mountain locales. This comes with dew points in the 60s which are supporting heat indices in the mid 80s to low 90s. Expect clouds to increase into tonight as the warm front lifts poleward. Forecast lows will be in the 60s to low 70s, with increasing shower chances.

Looking a bit more closely at the threat for overnight heavy rainfall, the 12Z high-resolution models are not showing the strongest of signals. However, there are a number of meteorological conditions which warrant this situation to bear watching. This includes: (1) Precipitable water values (PWAT) increasing from 1.50 to around 2 to 2.25 inches, (2) An uptick in warm advection with the approaching front, and (3) Enhanced lift with vorticity swinging northward from an upper low across the Mid-South. Where the heavy rainfall sets up will dictate the degree of impact. If this impacts the urban sprawl around the D.C. metro, poor drainage will support a risk of flash flooding. Will continue to monitor the situation and 00Z/18Z guidance to determine if any Flood Watches will be needed.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Daily shower and thunderstorm chances are expected Wednesday into early next week.

In the wake of what morning convection materializes, the models do show a brief lull in the action. The northward pushing warm front eventually stalls nearby before shearing out. Likewise, the upper low across the Mid-South region begins to fill although the reflection of this circulation still shows up across southern West Virginia on Wednesday. Remaining perturbations around this mid/upper low should help fire off some afternoon/evening thunderstorms. A number of models depict anomalous moisture lingering across the region with PWATs over 2 inches for those of the Blue Ridge. While no clear signal exists, slow moving cells could produce a few instances of flash flooding. However, the longstanding drought conditions could easily curb that threat.

Seasonably warm temperatures and typical early August humidity remain a fixture in the forecast for the foreseeable future. A broad subtropical ridge in the mid/upper levels will continue retrograding from the western Atlantic back toward the Eastern Seaboard. At the same time, while the strongest jet energy remains tied to the northern tier states, the quasi-zonal flow aloft will steer a myriad from weak to modest shortwaves toward the northeastern U.S. As usual, these types of features are of low confidence given the mesoscale nature of the convective elements. As such, will continue to maintain a risk of strong to severe thunderstorms as well as isolated instances of flash flooding each day. At this point, Friday presents the most active looking day of the period. However, this could easily change as global models continue to waver from run to run.
s.avn:
Showers continue to weaken while pushing to the vicinity of KCHO. Given closer proximity to the frontal zone, activity near Richmond is likely to impact the Charlottesville area first. This TAF site should bring the most likely period for restrictions as storms move in from the southeast. Elsewhere, VFR conditions continue through the evening and early overnight hours. This is accompanied by mainly light easterly winds. However, lowering ceilings will support restrictions across all terminals tonight into Wednesday morning. Locally heavier rainfall could impact the D.C. metro area terminals. Some improvements are expected by midday before another round of storms could impact the area. PROB30 groups accompany this threat, particularly in the 20Z-00Z window on Wednesday.

Winds shift to mainly south to southwesterly for the foreseeable future as a Bermuda high pressure system persists across the western Atlantic. Daily convective chances each afternoon and evening will support convective-driven restrictions. With little change in the upcoming pattern, this sort of forecast will likely hold for the next several days.

KEY MESSAGE...Localized urban flash flooding possible this morning as warm front lifts north.

A stalled frontal boundary over Southern Virginia is lifting north across our area as a warm front. A slug of deep tropical moisture is already surging northward into the Mid-Atlantic, with PWATs analyzed at or over 2" early this morning. Several of the 00Z high res models indicate the potential for heavy rain amounts of 1-3" across the I- 95 metro area from Fredericksburg up to Washington DC. It will be hard for models to show consensus on any given location since convection will be driven by warm advection along the front, and aided by forcing for ascent from an upper low lover the Mid-South. If any of this heavy rain occurs over the urban sprawl around the D.C. metro, poor drainage will support a risk of flash flooding. A Flood Watch is in effect through 11 AM this morning for the previously mentioned areas along I-95.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Daily shower and thunderstorm chances are expected through early next week.

In the wake of what morning convection materializes, the models do show a brief lull in the action. The northward pushing warm front eventually stalls nearby before shearing out. Likewise, the upper low across the Mid-South region begins to fill although the reflection of this circulation still shows up across southern West Virginia.

A deep southerly flow will continue around high pressure over the Atlantic, ushering plenty of moisture. PWATS will be near or greater than 2" in the valleys with 1-2" in the mountains, which is about 1- 2 SD above climo. A surface trough and shortwave energy will trigger scattered showers/thunderstorms, but it should not be a washout during the afternoon/evening. The main threat will be brief heavy downpours and gusty winds. However, DCAPE and shear are on the lower side, so the probability of severe storms is lower. If some storms train over the same area, localized flash flooding can occur. The pattern does favor the possibility for training convection (cloud layer winds nearly parallel to low-level wind), but the coverage should be isolated.

A similar pattern will hold on for Thursday and Friday while the subtropical jet strengthens to the north and west. Therefore, more showers and thunderstorms are likely along with the threat for isolated instances of flash flooding and locally damaging wind gusts. Hotter conditions may cause relatively steeper low-level lapse rates and the wind field strengthens a bit (especially Friday).

A quasi-zonal flow aloft will develop for the weekend into next week, bringing more seasonably hot and humid conditions along with daily chances for showers and thunderstorms.

A warm front is lifting across the Mid-Atlantic this morning. 12Z analysis shows a small meso-low feature near Madison VA, and this feature will likely drift northeastward just northwest of US-29 toward Baltimore's northwest suburbs through midday.

On radar and satellite, this feature has the appearance of an occluded low. The pseudo "triple point" east of DC toward Annapolis is where convergence is strongest on the mesoscale, outside of the low moving from near Madison to Culpeper.

The highest PW axis is overhead this morning, so anything that develops as subtle daytime heating commences will be capable of very heavy rainfall rates. Slow storm motions/training are possible as this weak low moves overhead. Forcing for ascent via moisture flux has ceased, so further development will rely on subtle convergence axes and/or heating of an extremely humid airmass through limited cloud breaks.

Gave some thought to both canceling the existing watch early, and expanding to Anne Arundel/Baltimore. But, given ongoing heavy showers and potential for further development until the mesolow moves through, felt it best to leave the watch in place for at least a little while longer. Meanwhile, just outside the current watch, heavy rain would have to place itself directly over the urbanized areas of Baltimore or Annapolis to result in flooding given ongoing drought. Given the conditional threat, held off on a watch for now, but the last few runs of the HRRR have rather stubborn recurring activity in this area into the afternoon, so that will need to be monitored closely.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Hot, humid conditions persist into next week, along with daily chances for shower and thunderstorms.

A very repetitive weather pattern has set up for the next several days, characterized by warm and humid air from offshore high pressure and continued impulses of upper level energy. This will yield showers and storms each day through at least early next week, and likely even beyond.

Starting with today, numerous storms are developing along the lee trough, as well as a few along the Chesapeake Bay Breeze. The environment is characterized by around 2000-3000 J/kg of MLCAPE, but very weak shear (around 20 knots). This is yielding a few strong storms, but very few that are able to maintain themselves for very long. This is also likely due to meager mid-level lapse rates around 5 C/km. This will continue to be the story through this evening. Latest mesoanalysis also depicts around 400-600 J/kg of DCAPE, which coincides with max downdraft velocities around 60 mph or so, which is about what is being seen in the strongest of storms. Expect this threat to remain pretty isolated, with most storms through the evening producing primarily heavy rainfall, frequent lightning, and gusts around 40 mph. Torrential rainfall rates can be expected at times, with PWATs in excess of two inches currently across much of the area. Storms will gradually come to an end this evening as they rain themselves out after sunset.

Friday looks somewhat similar to what we are seeing today, albeit with slightly more shear/forcing. A slightly more potent piece of energy looks to move across the area during peak heating. This should yield deep-layer shear values closer to 30 knots perhaps. There will be a similar thermodynamic environment in place, with high amounts of CAPE, but DCAPE values similar or even a bit less than today. One thing to watch for though is that, thanks to the shortwave, mid-level lapse rates will be in the 6-7 C/km range tomorrow afternoon, which could lead to a higher coverage of stronger updrafts. This would then allow more storms to potentially tap into that peak downdraft potential and yield a few more severe storms than we see this afternoon. Would also expect to see some large hail as well, given the higher lapse rates aloft. A Marginal Risk is maintained from the Storm Prediction Center.

Beyond Friday, this pattern likely continues through at least the early and middle portions of next week. South to southwesterly flow is maintained over the Mid-Atlantic. Hot and humid conditions each afternoon, with highs reaching the upper 80s to low 90s, and heat indices in the low 100s each of the Blue Ridge. Scattered showers and thunderstorms each afternoon. Deep layer shear is forecast to increase through the weekend as the subtropical jet stream strengthens. On Saturday, a more potent shortwave trough is forecast to move overhead that could aid in stronger, more organized severe convection. Damaging wind gusts will be the main threat.

A quasi-zonal flow aloft will develop Sunday into into next week. Sunday could bring a short reprieve as dry conditions prevail. However, seasonably hot and humid conditions continue, and should quickly bring showers and storms back into the forecast Monday through most of next week.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Patchy dense fog will be possible over the next several mornings.

With daily showers and thunderstorms, and warm/humid overnights, patchy dense fog can be expected each morning. The location will be difficult to pinpoint, with areas that receive rain the day prior the likely candidates.


KEY MESSAGE 3...A cold front could arrive late in the week, potentially bringing a pattern change into next weekend.

While this is very far out in the forecast period, there is some signal that a more potent frontal system could push through the region late in the week. The details are murky at this stage of the forecast, with timing very uncertain, as well as potential impacts. Guidance is generally between Thursday/Friday right now, with improvement in the weather pattern possible thereafter. Any decent frontal passage in the summer time should be watched closely for potential severe weather, so we will keep monitoring this in the coming days to see if that potential is there, and try to narrow down the timeframe a bit more.
