s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms expected this afternoon through this evening across portions of the area.

Shower and thunderstorms are beginning to develop over the higher terrain and in the lee of the Blue Ridge as of 2 PM EDT. Not seeing much of anything developing on the Bay/River breezes, so seems like the main threat will be with storms along the lee trough and leading edge of the incoming shortwave this afternoon/evening. Mostly sunny to partly cloudy skies throughout the day have lead to MLCAPE values on the order of 1500-3000 J/kg with lowest amounts SW and higher amounts towards the Chesapeake Bay into northeast MD. DCAPE values range from 500-800 J/kg, which is sufficient to produce some damaging wind gusts with the strongest storms. The highest shear is along the MD/PA border, with values around 20-25 knots. As a result of all of this, a Severe Thunderstorm Watch was issued from areas along/east of I-81 and north of US-50. Storms thus far have had trouble really getting organized, which is likely due to weaker lapse rates out west, and not quite having the strongest shear we expect later in the afternoon. As storms move east, as well as the subsequent outflows from said storms, expect them to grow upscale and become stronger the closer we get to the I-95 corridor into northeast MD. This is where it seems like all of the ingredients have the best chance of coming together for the highest severe weather threat. That being said, any storms in this environment could become severe and produce locally damaging winds even outside of more organized clusters. Frequent cloud-to-ground lightning can be expected with storms today, likely well ahead of and behind storms. Use extreme caution if outdoors later this afternoon and remember that when thunder roars to head indoors!

The severe threat should wane into the evenining as we lose daytime heating. However, storms today will produce very heavy rainfall rates, perhaps as high as 3-4 inches/hour for short periods. Should this find the wrong area, and/or if an area sees a couple back-to-back, a flash flooding threat isn't out of the question. This threat is highest in northeast MD, which is where the best chance for colliding outflow boundaries and/or Bay Breeze interactions is. This could cause some localized training effects, which brough a few areas a quick 3 to 4 inches yesterday, so can't completely rule that out. WPC has this area in a SLGT risk excessive rainfall outlook as a result.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Patchy morning fog, high humidity, hot temperatures, and daily thunderstorm chances continue through early next week.

Somewhat similar conditions are expected Saturday as another potent shortwave passes through. The main difference is that mid-level flow turns a bit more W to WSW versus the SW'ly flow we have had in recent days. As a result, coverage of storms is likely to be less than what we see today. However, shear values increase a bit, reaching 30 to 35 kts as the subtropical jet stream begins to strengthen. Mid-level lapse rates are also impressive, similar to today's event. Instability will be a bit less tomorrow, owing to the westerly mid-level flow. Thermodynamic profiles depict skinnier CAPE profiles, but inverted-V signatures towards the surface. All of this to say, while our area is not currently highlighted in a severe weather risk area from SPC, it bears watching. Our thoughts are that the coverage should be less tomorrow, but the ceiling could be higher in terms of damaging wind potential, should storms be able to develop and get organized. Current machine learning guidance which suggest 15-30 percent probabilities for damaging wind gusts Saturday afternoon and evening. With that said, guidance continues to focus on areas along and north of I-66/US-50 for both Friday and Saturday.

Convection begins to wane a bit Sunday into Monday given quasi-zonal flow aloft. A few storms may develop over the higher elevations, but coverage will be much less than in recent days. This will be short-lived however, with storm chances increasing once again Tuesday through the end of the week as a series of shortwave disturbances passing through.

Outside of the storm chances expect highs in the upper 80s and low 90s with heat indices east of the BLue Ridge up around 100 degrees. The hottest days look to be Sunday through Tuesday given the strengthened subtropical ridge over the region.


KEY MESSAGE 3...A cold front could arrive late next week and into the weekend bringing relief from the heat and humidity.

While this is very far out in the forecast period, there is some signal that a more potent frontal system could push through the region late in the week. The details are murky at this stage of the forecast, with timing very uncertain, as well as potential impacts. Deterministic and ensemble guidance is generally between Thursday/Friday right now, with improvement in the weather pattern possible into the upcoming weekend. Any decent frontal passage in the summertime should be watched closely for potential severe weather, so we will keep monitoring this in the coming days to see if that potential is there, and try to narrow down the timeframe a bit more.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1... Typical Summertime pattern continues with building heat next week. Storm chances today decreasing Sunday and Monday.

It's a typical Summertime pattern as we enter the second weekend and week of August. The forecast is on repeat with patchy morning dense fog giving way to hot and humid conditions with late day afternoon and evening thunderstorms.

Today, we'll bring another passing shortwave disturbance which will trigger an additional round of afternoon and evening strong thunderstorms. Thunderstorm coverage will be a bit less due to mid level west to west/west-southwest flow yielding some downsloping flow east of the mountains. This is a stark contrast to the southerly flow over the past few days yielding locally higher storm coverage.

Storms today will be isolated to scattered with a focus again along and north of I-66/US-50 and east of the Allegheny Mountains. Instability will remain high as a result of the high heat and humidity. Shear values will sit around 30 to 35 kts as the subtropical jet stream begins to strengthen. This could yield a more organized severe weather threat which aligns with current learning machine guidance that suggest 15-30 percent probabilities for damaging wind gusts this afternoon and evening. Thermodynamic profiles also depict this sentiment with skinnier CAPE profiles and inverted-V signatures towards the surface yielding a higher ceiling for damaging wind potential. The Storm Prediction Center continues a Marginal Risk for severe weather (Level 1 out of 5) for this afternoon and evening with wind as the primary threat. Isolated instances of flooding also cannot be ruled out, especially over the urban areas around Baltimore/DC given the repetitive heavy rains the last few days.

Convection wanes a bit Sunday into Monday given quasi-zonal flow aloft and the strengthen upper level ridge axis nearby. A few storms may develop over the higher elevations, but coverage will be much less than in recent days. This will be short-lived however, with storm chances increasing once again Tuesday through the end of the week as a series of shortwave disturbances pass through.

Outside of he storm chances expect highs in the upper 80s and low 90s with heat indices east of the Blue Ridge up around 100 degrees. The hottest days look to be Monday and Tuesday given the strengthened subtropical ridge over the region. Highs will push into the mid 90s with heat indices closer to 105 degrees east of the Blue Ridge/along the urban corridor.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A cold front could arrive late next week bringing relief from the heat and humidity into the upcoming weekend.

Daily storm chances look to continue through at least Friday as a more potent frontal system tracks toward the region. Ahead of that front will be several fast moving shortwave disturbances which will help aid in shower and thunderstorm development during the diurnal period. Storm coverage is a bit uncertain with activity remaining isolated to scattered Tuesday becoming a scattered to numerous Wednesday into late week as the front tries to push through. Speaking of the front, details remain a bit murky on it's passage. Most 00z ensemble/deterministic guidance suggests a frontal passage Thursday afternoon into Saturday. Guidance also depicts an MCS type setup during the Tuesday and Wednesday timeframe. Machine learning guidance is grabbing onto this as well with probabilities running between 15 to 30 percent for severe weather during the midweek timeframe. SPC mentions areas back toward our west on the Day 4 and 5 outlook, so something we'll continue to monitor, especially as the subtropical ridge flattens.

There is a bit more uncertainty in regards to severe weather Thursday through Saturday. Of course with any decent frontal passage will have to be monitor given machine probabilities remaining between 5-30 percent for severe weather. This will ultimately be determined by the timing of the front in regards to the peak heating period. Temperatures will cool from the 90s into the 80s late week. Weather does look to improve for the upcoming weekend as Canadian high pressure works into the region.

It's a typical Summertime pattern as we enter the second weekend and week of August. The forecast is on repeat with patchy morning dense fog giving way to hot and humid conditions with late day afternoon and evening thunderstorms.

Round one of storms has pushed across the MD/PA border this afternoon, which was very poorly handled by any model guidance. High CAPE/DCAPE values, steep low-level lapse rates, and 30-35 knots of shear yields a pretty potent organized cluster, especially in northeast MD. Watching a few clusters of storms over the Shenandoah Valley this afternoon, which is the round that was anticipated in previous forecasts. There are a few question marks now, especially since the prior storms threw an outflow boundary all the way to the I-66 corridor. As storms progress east, we will see how any storms interact with said boundary. High-end today seems to be small, organized bowing segments with the potential for 60-70 mph wind gusts. This is due to much more DCAPE today (on the order of 1000 J/kg) compared to recent days. Still, coverage is much more isolated, which was expected, so POPs remain around 40 percent the rest of the afternoon, but anyone under one of these storms could be dealing with damaging winds, torrential rainfall and frequent lightning. Flooding threat is pretty minimal at this point, as storms have been moving very quickly thus far. Again, if anything gets hung up and the intersection of boundaries, you could see some isolated issues if it is over a sensitive area, but that should be few and far between.

Convection wanes a bit Sunday given quasi-zonal flow aloft and the strengthening upper-level ridge axis nearby. A few storms may develop over the higher elevations, but coverage will be much less than in recent days. This will be short-lived however, with storm chances increasing once again Tuesday through the end of the week as a series of shortwave disturbances pass through.

Things have changed slightly on Monday, as precipitation chances have increased a bit over the past several model runs. Another piece of shortwave energy will slide across the region amidst a hot and very humid airmass yet again. Similar to what we are seeing today, coverage is a question mark at this point, but could be a couple of pretty strong to severe storms that day. Something that bears watching at this stage, but confidence is just too low for a severe weather outlook at this point.

Outside of he storm chances expect highs in the upper 80s and low 90s with heat indices east of the Blue Ridge up around 100 degrees. The hottest days look to be Monday and Tuesday given the strengthened subtropical ridge over the region. Highs will push into the mid 90s with heat indices closer to 105 degrees east of the Blue Ridge/along the urban corridor.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A cold front could arrive late next week bringing relief from the heat and humidity into the upcoming weekend.

Daily storm chances look to continue through at least Friday as a more potent frontal system tracks toward the region. Ahead of that front will be several fast moving shortwave disturbances which will help aid in shower and thunderstorm development during the diurnal period. Storm coverage is a bit uncertain with activity remaining isolated to scattered Tuesday becoming a scattered to numerous Wednesday into late week as the front tries to push through. Speaking of the front, details remain a bit murky on it's passage. Most 00z ensemble/deterministic guidance suggests a frontal passage Thursday afternoon into Saturday. Guidance also depicts an MCS type setup during the Tuesday and Wednesday timeframe. Machine learning guidance is grabbing onto this as well with probabilities running between 15 to 30 percent for severe weather during the midweek timeframe. SPC mentions areas back toward our west on the Day 4 and 5 outlook, so something we'll continue to monitor, especially as the subtropical ridge flattens.

There is a bit more uncertainty in regards to severe weather Thursday through Saturday. Of course with any decent frontal passage will have to be monitor given machine probabilities remaining between 5-30 percent for severe weather. This will ultimately be determined by the timing of the front in regards to the peak heating period. Temperatures will cool from the 90s into the 80s late week. Weather does look to improve for the upcoming weekend as Canadian high pressure works into the region.

Not much of a change in the overall synoptic and mesoscale pattern as we continue in this typical August summertime regime. It's a rinse and repeat forecast of hot temperatures, high humidity, and diurnal thunderstorms chances.

Storm coverage will be at it's lowest today and potentially lingering into Monday as we sit between shortwave impulses. The strengthening subtropical ridge offshore combined with west to southwest flow aloft should aid in the suppression of convection today outside of the usual terrain and bay breeze circulations. Current 00z guidance keeps things fairly isolated over the terrain and in locations mainly along and south of I-64. Any thunderstorms that pop up will be short-lived with gusty winds, locally heavy rainfall, and frequent lightning as the primary concerns.

As for Monday, the chances for thunderstorms have increased given another piece of shortwave energy ejecting across the region. Current 00z guidance suggests scattered to numerous thunderstorms across the region with a focus east of the Alleghenies Monday afternoon and evening. SPC currently has most of the region in a Marginal Risk (Level 1 out of 5) for severe weather with a Slight Risk (Level 2 out of 5) grazing northwest Garrett Co. MD. Machine guidance is also high on the severe threat with WxNext2 probabilities of 30-60 percent and CSU probabilities of 15 to 30 percent across the area during the Monday into Tuesday timeframe. Even with that said, coverage and timing remain the two big question marks similar to what we saw on Saturday across the region. With a hot and humid airmass in place and marginal shear this will be something to watch in the near term period.

Additional shortwave disturbances look to pass through Tuesday into Wednesday and again Wednesday into Thursday. Uncertainty remains in regards to timing and coverage which will dictate the risk for severe weather. Current machine learning guidance and day 4-8 outlooks from SPC mention at least a chance for severe weather each day mainly during the afternoon and evening hours. Ensemble and deterministic guidance put us in an MCS setup which will make it even harder to time out severe weather, especially with complexes of storms moving around the top of the ridge. Once again something that will continue to monitor in the coming days ahead.

Outside of he storm chances expect highs in the upper 80s and low 90s with heat indices east of the Blue Ridge up around 100 degrees. KEY MESSAGE 1... An active start to the new workweek with multiple chances for severe weather. Hot temperatures and high humidity continue.

Shaping up to be a fairly active weather pattern today through Wednesday as multiple pieces of shortwave energy traverse the region. This morning we continue to monitor a decaying MCS as it moves across western PA, north-central WV, and toward far western MD early this morning. Most of the guidance dissipates this activity as it continues east with just a few residual showers and mid/high level clouds along the Alleghenies and north of the PA/MD line. Residual outflows from this system combined with an additional MCS back across the central Ohio River Valley this morning and a lee side trough will set the stage for thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. Depending on how this MCS maintains itself across our forecast area today, or have its remnant outflow focus the development of new convection tomorrow afternoon. If the MCS were to totally fall apart before crossing the mountains, with no remnant cold pool making it further east, the development of thunderstorms across our area would be a bit more in question, given only weak large scale forcing for ascent and questions about where/if a lee trough would set up.

What we do know is that whatever occurs the ingredients will be there for severe weather development. This is due largely in part to strong daytime heating with highs in the upper 80s and mid 90s. Dewpoints will remain in the upper 60s to mid 70s yielding heat index values around 100 degrees east of the Blue Ridge. The heat combined with a shortwave disturbance aloft should be the kicker for at least a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Current CAM guidance suggest a mash up between scattered clusters to a linear line of storms peeling off the Alleghenies between 1-9pm. Storms will initialize over the mountains between 2-4pm before advancing east into the metros between 4-8pm. SPC has expanded the Slight Risk (Level 2 out of 5) for locations along and north of I-66/US-50 with a Marginal Risk (Level 1 out of 5) across the rest of the region (outside of locations south of I-64). Damaging winds will be the primary threat with storms along with isolated large hail and isolated instances of flash flooding. Machine guidance continues to advertise a high ceiling on the severe threat with WxNext2 probabilities of 45-70 percent and CSU probabilities of 15 to 30 percent across the area this afternoon and evening. Damaging winds will be the primary threat with storms along with isolated large hail and isolated instances of flash flooding.

Additional shortwave disturbances look to pass through Tuesday into Wednesday. Mid-level flow will increase during this time along with stronger height falls yielding more widespread convective chances. With that said, uncertainty remains in regards to timing, coverage, and location of the storms during the period. This is largely due in part to the evolution of any MCSs ejecting out of the Ohio River Valley/Great Lakes region along with the remnant outflows left behind. Outside of the background winds, expect daily shower and thunderstorm chances each afternoon and evening through upcoming Friday (though can't rule out storms overnight and in the mornings as well). Special Marine Warnings may be needed to encompass any stronger thunderstorms that may form especially today (especially as an organized line approaches) and Wednesday. Strong to severe wind gusts and frequent lightning will be the main threats.

s.chg: Monitoring the evolution of upstream thunderstorm clusters and how the environment evolves through this evening. Wednesday
s.key:
- 1) The risk of severe thunderstorms seems to be decreasing through tonight, although upstream thunderstorm complexes still need to be monitored.

- 2) Showers and thunderstorms remain possible at times Wednesday through Friday.

- 3) Drier conditions anticipated heading into next week, with a few showers & thunderstorms possible late this weekend.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...The risk of severe thunderstorms seems to be decreasing through tonight, although upstream thunderstorm complexes still need to be monitored.

The thunderstorm complex that was in Ohio earlier dove southward toward higher instability in far southwest VA, with only some stratified rain affecting western/southwestern portions of the CWA over the next couple hours. Additional thunderstorms across western Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois are now also showing signs of diving southward due to the cold pool left by the eastern Ohio storms. While some 12Z CAMs showed remnants of this convection reaching the area this evening, this is increasingly in question. East of the dense overcast, there has been some filtered heating is occurring. This will result in some instability, but it isn't clear there will be enough of a trigger to kick off any storms locally. Most recent CAMS have backed off on local development, but can't totally rule out a few isolated to scattered storms mainly east of the Blue Ridge. Shear is a bit more marginal today, but it's still possible there could be a stronger storm with gusty to damaging winds. This threat would obviously be highest if an organized complex moved in from the west.

Given the current trajectories of the storms to the west, it's possible additional heavy rain avoids Garrett County. If these trends continue, the Flood Watch may be cancelled early.

Based on current models, the second half of the night should largely be dry. There may be some patchy fog if clearing occurs. Lows will be in the 60s to lower 70s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Showers and thunderstorms remain possible at times Wednesday through Friday.

The west to east oriented cold front will remain near the area through Friday. The main question is whether we remain in west or northwest flow and more stable conditions, or if the richer moisture is able to advect back in from the southwest. Periods of cloud cover could also be an issue that affects diurnal destabilization. Many, but not all, models show a relative lull on Wednesday as the greatest instability remains south and west of the area.

One, possibly two, waves of low pressure may track along the front between Wednesday night and Friday. This could lift the front northward, or at least provide a more notable source of forcing other than subtle shortwaves aloft. It's unclear how well shear, instability, and forcing will overlap, but it is possible some stronger storms could develop if they do. ML/AI guidance has mixed signals on severe probabilities, but overall lower compared to Monday and today.

Temperatures will likely be within several degrees of normal through Friday with elevated humidity levels.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Drier conditions anticipated heading into next week, with a few showers & thunderstorms possible late this weekend.

Dry air moves in from the Great Lakes region at the start of the weekend as upper-level ridging builds over the lower Mississippi Valley by Saturday. Temperatures remain slightly cooler than average during this period with fewer precipitation chances overall. As this high pressure builds towards the south, shortwave energy forming north of the ridge over the Great Lakes will track towards the Mid-Atlantic Sunday and heading into Monday. This could produce chances for additional showers and thunderstorms, with most medium- range severe outlooks currently producing rather marginal 5-15 percent probabilities for severe thunderstorms.

Once this shortwave system passes through, zonal flow transitions over the region, reducing thunderstorm chances overall. Temperatures will start to increase during this period as surface high pressure transitions into the region.
s.avn:
VFR conditions will likely prevail through Friday outside of thunderstorms and small potential for morning fog.

Stable conditions may limit thunderstorm development or maintenance across much of the area through tonight, although some guidance still pops a few showers and thunderstorms this afternoon. Given decreasing prospects and isolated coverage if they do form, removed PROB30 groups this afternoon in the metro TAFs. An area of stratified rain from earlier thunderstorms is crossing the Appalachians, but that seems to be evaporating with little to no lightning now, so this mention may be removed at MRB/CHO.

Some earlier model runs showed upstream convection in the Ohio Valley moving into the area this evening. Left PROB30 groups in the TAFs for this potential, but current observations suggest these storms may be turning southward toward higher instability. So in the end, it's possible the TAF airports remain dry through tonight with mainly mid and high clouds.

Many (but not all) models are now showing a relatively lull in storm chances Wednesday, so am not mentioning any chances at this time.

Showers and thunderstorms remain possible Thursday and Friday but will depend on the position of a cold front and the timing of any disturbances. Outside of the thunderstorms expect patchy fog between the terminals each morning. Winds will remain light (outside of any thunderstorm outflows) between northwest and south west.

Prevailing VFR conditions are anticipated at the start of the weekend. On Sunday, a frontal boundary moves through the region that could generate showers & thunderstorms as well as periodic sub-VFR conditions at terminals. Northerly winds shift southerly as this front passes through.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Shower and thunderstorm chances decrease today before increasing Thursday and Friday as a cold front crosses.

Looking at a lull in the thunderstorm activity today with subsidence left behind the caravan of MCSs that traversed the region over the last 24 to 48 hours. Overall flow remains out of the west and northwest which is allowing slightly drier and much more stable air to advect into the region. After a few light showers (mainly Baltimore/east) and little patchy fog this morning, expect a spotty shower or thunderstorm this afternoon, mainly as a result of terrain circulations or the bay/river breeze. Skies will trend partly cloudy to mostly sunny with abundant high cloud cover and even a little wildfire smoke from fires burning over the Pacific Northwest/Canada. The suspended smoke and high clouds will help limit destabilization this afternoon with a focus, mainly south and west of our region.

The quiet weather doesn't last too long as we monitor two shortwaves set to track across the region. The first shortwave looks to cross later this evening into Thursday morning (9pm-2am) with another along the actual cold front Friday. Both of these disturbances will allow for an uptick of shower and thunderstorm chances across the region. Timing and coverage remain a bit uncertain yielding some questions in regards to the overall severe threat. Instability and shear do look to increase a bit with MLCAPE values around 1000-1500 j/kg and shear values up to 36 kts tonight into Friday. Machine learning/AI guidance remains mixed on severe probabilities generally ranging between 5-20 percent with a focus across southwestern portions of the forecast area. If severe weather were to occur, damaging winds and isolated instances of flash flooding would be the primary concerns.

Outside of thunderstorms, look for seasonable temperatures and increased humidity, especially Thursday and Friday ahead of the frontal boundary. Highs will range from the mid 80s to low 90s (70s mountains) with overnight lows in the mid 60s and low 70s (upper 50s and low 60s mountains).


KEY MESSAGE 2... Dry conditions Saturday, with chances for showers and thunderstorms Sunday and Monday.

High pressure will build to our north on Saturday. Northerly winds will usher cooler and drier air into the area, with dewpoints dropping into the 50s and lower 60s, and temperatures only making it into the upper 70s to mid 80s. Conditions will remain dry beneath mostly sunny skies.

High pressure will progress offshore on Sunday as low pressure and an associated shortwave track through the Great Lakes. Winds will turn out of the south in response, drawing deeper moisture back north into the forecast area. Depending on the track of that system and how much moisture return occurs ahead of it, showers and thunderstorms may be possible for portions of the forecast area on Sunday afternoon and evening. Additional showers and thunderstorms may be possible again on Monday, before drier air works back into the area on Tuesday.
s.avn:
VFR conditions will continue to prevail through Friday despite temporary restrictions each morning due to patchy fog and each afternoon due to thunderstorms.

Overall looking at dry/VFR conditions Wednesday given added subsidence over the region. Winds will remain light out of the west/northwest at less than 15kts. Shower chances may return tonight as a wave of low pressure ripples through. Did add PROB30s in at the corridor terminals between 03-08z/11pm-4am. Confidence remains low for the timing of the showers/thunderstorms and coverage with the bulk of guidance hinting at activity being isolated to widely scattered.

Showers and thunderstorm chances increase again Thursday and Friday pending the position of a cold front and the timing of any additional disturbances. Outside of the thunderstorms expect patchy fog between the terminals each morning. Winds will remain light (outside of any thunderstorm outflows) between northwest and south west.

Prevailing VFR conditions are forecast for both Saturday and Sunday. Winds will be light out of the north to northeast on Saturday, before turning out of the south on Sunday. An afternoon shower or thunderstorm could be possible on Sunday, potentially leading to brief restrictions at the terminals.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Decreasing storm coverage today before ramping up late in the week with a returning warm front.

The earlier frontal boundary has now settled down near the Virginia-North Carolina border. To the north, temperatures are holding steady in the low/mid 80s with mainly 60s dew points. With diurnal heating, some shallow cumulus fields have formed, but these are largely capped by the limited instability. Otherwise, filtered sunshine is noted amidst passing high clouds and elevated smoke from the western U.S. wildfires.

Upstream convection which continues to train over eastern Indiana/western Ohio should stay well west of the local area. Convective activity is likely to follow the instability gradient which ushers this convection into eastern Kentucky. Aside from this complex, a few high-resolution solutions attempt to form some cells across the Lower Great Lakes. This would carry isolated showers and embedded thunderstorms toward the Mason- Dixon Line by the mid/late evening. While not severe, these could carry a risk of brief heavy rainfall and lightning. Any such activity exits toward the Eastern Shore after around 2 AM. Some patchy fog may form west of the Blue Ridge, accompanied by area-wide lows in the 60s, with low 70s along/east of I-95.

Heights further build on Thursday into Friday as upper ridging stretches up from the Gulf of America into the central and southeastern U.S. Locally, being north of this ridge will favor continued northwesterly flow aloft which carries the risk of mesoscale convective systems (MCS) intrusions. On Thursday, the main shower and thunderstorm chances focus across the Alleghenies down into the central Virginia Piedmont and I-64 corridor. This largely ties to the front still being displaced off toward the south. Eventual northward progression is possible into Friday which introduces a better chance for storms. The latest ensembles support probabilities in the 40 to 70 percent range. While not a washout by any means, this should be heavily guided by the peak in daytime heating. High temperatures each day will be in the 80s to low 90s, with 70s for the mountains. Likewise, seasonable conditions can be expected overnight.

Ample high pressure builds to the north of the region on Saturday as the frontal zone again sags back toward the Carolinas. An onshore component to the wind could keep some additional cloud cover around. However, overall trends suggest a drop off in humidity before winds return to southerly late in the weekend.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Showers and thunderstorms possible between Sunday and Monday before becoming drier into early next week.

Upper-level ridging continues to build over the Southwest CONUS over the weekend, with multiple shortwave troughs tracking to the east offshore of New England. Beginning Sunday, an upper-level perturbation forms over the Canadian Rockies and tracks eastward, with a stemming frontal boundary tracking across the East Coast late Sunday and into Monday. This boundary will likely bring chances for scattered showers and thunderstorms here in the Mid-Atlantic, although model guidance has been somewhat marginal on the severe potential for this event. As of the 12z ensemble runs, several outputs have the highest likelihood for severe weather just south of the area towards southern VA and the Carolinas, while the GFS ensemble runs still have a 15%-30% probability for severe weather centered within the region. Should any thunderstorms become severe, the most likely hazards will likely be elevated wind gusts as well as locally heavy rainfall. As drought conditions continue to improve within the region, flooding potential becomes more of a concern with any heavy rainfall-producing thunderstorms that materialize.

Otherwise, temperatures remain near-normal for mid-August, with humid conditions as well as temperatures ranging in the 80s and lower-90s at times near the metros. High pressure moves into the region once the frontal boundary passes offshore by Tuesday, bringing drier conditions to the region.
s.avn:
While VFR conditions are expected into Thursday, have introduced a PROB30 for thunderstorm restrictions late this evening. Otherwise, winds remain somewhat variable and light given continued weak gradients. Winds on Thursday should be mainly out of the west to northwest with the frontal zone off to the south. Any afternoon/evening storms should be confined closer to I-64 around KCHO, with others to the north remaining dry. More widespread showers and thunderstorms are possible on Friday which would favor further convective-driven restrictions. High pressure builds to the north on Saturday which should favor VFR conditions amidst east to northeasterly winds.

Beginning Sunday, a cold front could bring sub-VFR conditions to terminals as scattered showers and thunderstorms are possible throughout the region. These conditions could be intermittent through Monday as the front passes through. Southeast winds shift northwest Monday evening in the wake of the front.
s.mar:
Background winds remain on the weaker side as a frontal zone sags off toward the south. Gusts will mostly be in the 5 to 10 knot range, while pushing up to 15 knots at times when southerly channeling occurs. The main threat for hazardous marine conditions would be on Friday given more widespread showers and thunderstorms. Any storm will be capable of gusty winds and frequent lightning. This front drops toward the Carolinas on Saturday as high pressure builds over the northeastern U.S. The resulting winds will mainly be out of the east to northeast.

SCAs will likely be needed by Sunday afternoon as a cold front tracks through the region. Between Sunday & Monday, gusty showers and thunderstorms are possible over the waters. Winds diminish once the front passes through late Monday. Southeast winds shift northwest by Monday evening in the wake of the front.
s.tide: Water levels will slowly elevate in the next couple of days. This brings a more sensitive location like Annapolis into Action Stage for the Thursday morning high tide. However, there is currently no discernible threat for coastal flooding this week.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Low storm chances continue today with higher humidity and hotter temperatures. More storms Friday as the front sags south.

It's another mostly dry day ahead with just a few spotty showers and t-storms across the region. Still monitoring the upper level ridge nearby over the central and southeastern U.S along with a nearby stalled front draped from the VA Tidewater westward into the TN/Ohio River Valleys. Pieces of energy will continue to traverse this boundary within west to northwest flow today through Friday. Confidence in timing and thunderstorm coverage is low for today given the heightened ridge with increasing chances Friday as the ridge flattens and front moves through.

As for today, expect any residual showers early this morning over northeast MD, southern MD, and central VA to quickly end as a weak upper level trough pushes east prior to 8z/4am. Additional spotty showers and thunderstorms may dot the area later this afternoon with a focus over the Alleghenies (due to terrain circulations) and across central VA/Shenandoah Valley where the front resides. The front will gradually lift back toward the north late tonight into Friday with another wave of low pressure set to push through. This will lead to increased chances for showers and thunderstorms across the region with a focus, especially along and south of I-66/US-50. Thunderstorm activity will likely occur during the peak heating period with locally damaging winds, frequent lightning, and isolated instances of flash flooding as the primary concerns. SPC continues to highlight areas along and south of US-33 in VA with a Marginal Risk (Level 1 out of 5) for severe weather. This aligns with machine learning/ AI guidance which suggests 5 to 15 percent probs for severe weather Friday afternoon and evening. A lot of this will be dependent upon cloud cover and any interaction from potential MCSs diving across the central and lower Ohio River Valley and into far southern WV/southwest VA. Some guidance remains aggressive like the NAMnest while the HRRR, ARW, and NSSL remain more reasonable with coverage/magnitude. No washouts are expected although chances will increase during the peak heating period, especially south and west of the I-95 metro areas.

Being along the eastern flank of the sprawling upper ridge across the southern U.S., northwesterly flow persists aloft. At the surface, a wavy stalled boundary persists along the Virginia/North Carolina border stretching back toward the Great Smoky Mountains. To the north of this frontal zone, the local area continues to see fairly tranquil weather. Although the usual summertime gradients are on the weaker side, ample boundary layer mixing is yielding some northwesterly gusts up to 15 to 20 mph. This is occurring underneath scattered fair weather cumulus and some thin high cirrus moving in from the Lower Great Lakes. With early afternoon temperatures in the 80s, expect further surface heating to carry highs into the upper 80s to low 90s. Adding dew points in the mid/upper 60s will carry afternoon heat index values into the low/mid 90s.

In terms of shower chances, while a few 12Z high-resolution models depict some convection across central Virginia, a lack of cumulus development suggests otherwise. Will maintain isolated showers toward sundown, but any activity does not appear imminent based on the GOES-19 visible satellite channel. Heading into the evening and overnight, some increase in clouds are expected with overnight lows along/east of U.S. 15 in the low/mid 70s. West of this highway, mainly 60s can be expected.

Friday still presents a mixed signal in terms of how active the weather may become. The mentioned boundary near the Virginia/North Carolina border is forecast to slowly edge northward in time. However, its northward progression likely does not carry it even past southern Virginia. As a result, the better instability likely stays off to the south which would influence overall convective chances. One other additional item to address is the nocturnal mesoscale convective system (MCS) expected to be crossing the Ohio Valley early Friday. The 12Z HREF 40 dBZ paintball plot shows most of this complex diving southeastward across eastern Kentucky into southwestern Virginia. This would largely ride along the instability gradient which would favor keeping a bulk of this activity out of the local area. Some decaying showers could impact the central Shenandoah Valley/Blue Ridge region during the mid/late morning hours. Abundant cloud cover should linger over a bulk of the area which may hinder subsequent diurnal convection. Instability is a bit higher south of U.S. 50 which likely delineates the area to see strong to severe convection. This largely matches the Marginal Risk area from the Storm Prediction Center. Damaging wind gusts would be the primary threat for any more intense cell. Otherwise, expect mostly cloudy skies with highs in the 80s (70s for the mountains), amidst likely east to northeasterly winds. Some overnight showers may linger across portions of the region. Forecast lows will be in the 60s to low 70s with continued overcast conditions.

On Saturday, surface high pressure begins to build across Ontario down into New England while the stalled front sags further south. This will favor an onshore flow regime with winds out of the east to northeast. Consequently, there should be added cloud cover across the region which will yield a mix of clouds and sun. While many stay dry on Saturday, additional perturbations in the northwesterly flow aloft should increase shower chances west of I-95. Some of this activity could edge eastward to the I-95 corridor by late Saturday night. Overall high temperatures will be in the low/mid 80s, with 70s across the higher terrain. Nighttime lows should remain very close to the previous night.

As this gradient pushes through, some severe storms are possible out of this system. Models have shifted probabilities northward to our area here over the Mid-Atlantic compared to more southward trends earlier in the week, with several machine-learning models identifying a 15%-30% probability for severe storms over our region before shifting towards the south by Monday. That being said, the recent shift in track means that there is still some uncertainty in the overall severe potential; nonetheless, some showers and thunderstorms can be anticipated as this frontal boundary pushes off the East Coast early next week.

Lingering showers & thunderstorms remain possible on Monday as the stemming cold front transitions offshore to the south. Upper-level patterns return to a more zonal flow at this point, with surface high pressure moving into the region by midweek. Humidity likely remains elevated by this time as a trough brings moisture just north of the region. However, chances for severe weather diminishes for a bit as high pressure builds over the Appalachians. Temperatures remain seasonable, with highs in the upper 80s and lower 90s each day.

Will maintain a PROB30 group at KCHO from 4-8 PM for thunderstorms, but this is looking less likely based on current visible satellite imagery.

Winds turn more northeasterly on Friday with a broader coverage of showers and thunderstorms. A decaying MCS may bring some morning restrictions to KCHO, with afternoon/evening activity possibly impacting the D.C. terminals. The uncertainty seems to increase with northward extent from the front. Friday night carries with it continued onshore flow which could favor some lower ceilings overnight. High pressure builds over Quebec into New England on Saturday which will support a return to VFR conditions. This comes with prevailing easterly flow.

Lingering showers and thunderstorms could allow intermittent sub-VFR conditions to linger into Monday. Once the front passes through by Tuesday, VFR conditions are anticipated with southwest winds shifting northwest by Tuesday.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms are possible on Sunday.

A potent shortwave by late-summer standards and an associated area of low pressure will track across Ontario toward Hudson Bay on Sunday, with a likely convectively induced disturbance and associated weak area of low pressure tracking into the Great Lakes. Low-level winds will turn out of the south in response to this disturbance, drawing a boundary that is currently stalled out to our south northeastward as a warm front. This front is expected to clear much of the area by Sunday evening, advecting in a very warm, humid, and highly unstable airmass into the region. However there are some uncertainties with regard to just how far north and east this highly unstable airmass will make it. Guidance is in good agreement that locations to the west of the Blue Ridge will destabilize, but there's greater spread in solutions further east.

An atypically strong low-level jet for late summer will accompany this system. Model soundings show large, clockwise turning hodographs, with ample streamwise vorticity and SRH at low-levels. When combined with 2000 J/kg of MLCAPE, this raises concerns for severe thunderstorms, with supercells possible. Damaging winds should be the primary threat, but a tornado or two can't be ruled out given the high SRH environment in place. As mentioned before, locations to the west of the Blue Ridge appear to have the greatest chance for severe thunderstorms, but there is plenty of time for things to change with two days of convection upstream of the event.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Seasonably warm conditions and daily chances for showers and thunderstorms are expected through Monday, with drier conditions for Tuesday and Wednesday.

A typical late summertime pattern will remain in place through early next week, with seasonable temperatures and daily chances for showers and thunderstorms. High temperatures will generally be in the mid 80s to around 90 each day, with overnight lows in the upper 60s to low 70s.

Early this morning we continue to monitor ongoing thunderstorm activity in the Mississippi/Ohio Valleys. An extensive area of thunderstorms has developed to the north of a stationary front across Illinois, Indiana, and western Ohio, with additional thunderstorm activity ongoing in West Virginia. Much of this activity is expected to eventually dissipate, but remnant mid- upper level disturbances associated with this activity will likely progress into the area later today, eventually sparking the development of showers and thunderstorms. Instability is mainly expected to be focused across southwestern portions of the forecast area, with locations to the south and west of the Potomac having the greatest chance for a thunderstorm this afternoon. A passing shower can't be ruled out anywhere, but northeastern Maryland will have the greatest chance to remain dry.

Thunderstorm activity is expected to be focused even further off toward the southwest on Saturday, with the Central Shenandoah Valley and Central Virginia having the greatest chance for a storm. The background environment both today and tomorrow has vertical profiles that are deeply saturated, with modest flow through the mid-levels (around 35 knots of 0-6 km shear). DCAPE values will be low given the saturated profiles, but a wet microburst or two can't be ruled out. SPC has southwestern portions of the forecast area outlooked in a Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms today, with damaging winds being the primary risk. On Saturday the Marginal Risk only clips Highland an Augusta Counties.

Following a greater severe thunderstorm threat on Sunday, there may be additional thunderstorms across the forecast area on Monday, but details remain highly uncertain this far out. Most guidance suggests that a cold front will move through later Monday into Monday night as high pressure builds to our north. Temperatures will change very little behind this front, but drier air will advect in from the north, with dewpoints likely dropping into the 50s on Tuesday. This drier air will suppress thunderstorm activity, most likely leading to dry conditions on both Tuesday and Wednesday.
s.avn:
Prevailing VFR conditions are expected at the terminals through early next week. Temporary drops to sub-VFR conditions may be possible at times during showers and thunderstorms. Today the greatest chance for storms will be at CHO, with chances decreasing off toward the north and east. For now, a PROB30 group for thunderstorms has been included at CHO, with mentions of showers further northeast. Additional showers and a thunderstorm or two may be possible near CHO on Saturday. More widespread chances for showers and thunderstorms are expected on Sunday, with the potential for all terminals to see impacts. Showers and thunderstorms may be possible again on Monday, with drier conditions expected on Tuesday behind a cold front.

Winds will be light and variable today, light out of the east to northeast on Saturday, out of the south on Sunday, west to northwest on Monday, and north to northwest on Tuesday.
s.mar: Light and variable winds are expected over the waters today, before turning light out of the east tomorrow. Winds become southerly and increase in magnitude on Sunday, with Small Craft Advisory conditions likely. Sub-SCA level northwesterly winds are forecast for Monday and Tuesday. An SMW associated with thunderstorms can't be ruled out any day through Monday. As it looks now, the greatest chance for an afternoon or evening storm will be on Sunday, with the lowest chance on Saturday.
s.tide: Water levels are largely expected to stay below Action Stage through Saturday. The potential exception could be Annapolis, which could reach Action Stage at the higher of the daily tides. Water levels will start to increase in southerly flow on Sunday, with Annapolis potentially approaching Minor Flood Stage.

Expect much of this activity to gradually dissipate, but remnant mid-upper level disturbances associated with this activity will likely progress into the area later today, eventually sparking the development of showers and thunderstorms. A passing shower can't be ruled out anywhere, but northeastern Maryland will have the greatest chance to remain dry.

Thunderstorm activity is expected to be focused even further off toward the southwest on Saturday, with the Central Shenandoah Valley and Central Virginia having the greatest chance for a storm. The background environment both today and tomorrow has vertical profiles that are deeply saturated, with modest flow through the mid-levels (around 35 knots of 0-6 km shear). DCAPE values will be low given the saturated profiles, but a wet microburst or two can't be ruled out. SPC has southwestern portions of the forecast area outlooked in a Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms today, with damaging winds being the primary risk. On Saturday the Marginal Risk only clips Highland an Augusta Counties.

Following a greater severe thunderstorm threat on Sunday, there may be additional thunderstorms across the forecast area on Monday, but details remain highly uncertain this far out. Most guidance suggests that a cold front will move through later Monday into Monday night as high pressure builds to our north. Temperatures will change very little behind this front, but drier air will advect in from the north, with dewpoints likely dropping into the 50s on Tuesday. This drier air will suppress thunderstorm activity, most likely leading to dry conditions on both Tuesday and Wednesday.
s.avn:
Prevailing VFR conditions are expected at the terminals through early next week. Temporary drops to sub-VFR conditions may be possible at times during showers and thunderstorms. Today the greatest chance for storms will be at CHO, with chances decreasing off toward the north and east. For now, a PROB30 group for thunderstorms has been included at CHO, with mentions of showers further northeast. Additional showers and a thunderstorm or two may be possible near CHO on Saturday. More widespread chances for showers and thunderstorms are expected on Sunday, with the potential for all terminals to see impacts. Showers and thunderstorms may be possible again on Monday, with drier conditions expected on Tuesday behind a cold front.

Winds will be light and variable today, light out of the east to northeast on Saturday, out of the south on Sunday, west to northwest on Monday, and north to northwest on Tuesday.
s.mar: Light and variable winds are expected over the waters today, before turning light out of the east tomorrow. Winds become southerly and increase in magnitude on Sunday, with Small Craft Advisory conditions likely. Sub-SCA level northwesterly winds are forecast for Monday and Tuesday. An SMW associated with thunderstorms can't be ruled out any day through Monday. As it looks now, the greatest chance for an afternoon or evening storm will be on Sunday, with the lowest chance on Saturday.
s.tide: Water levels are largely expected to stay below Action Stage through Saturday. The potential exception could be Annapolis, which could reach Action Stage at the higher of the daily tides. Water levels will start to increase in southerly flow on Sunday, with Annapolis potentially approaching Minor Flood Stage.

s.chg: Have continued to update the probability of precipitation forecast for today as the guidance has struggled with ongoing activity. Otherwise, models have trended up for a remnant MCS possibly crossing through portions of the area late Saturday night. For mid/late next week, Thursday is starting to present itself as a more active weather day, but that is still 6 to 7 days out.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms and some instances of flash flooding are possible on Sunday.

Some residual convective activity may be ongoing on Sunday morning. This remains to be seen and will be guided by the degree of overnight instability and boundary placement. How the atmosphere recovers through the day should ultimately dictate the degree of severe thunderstorm threat during the core diurnal heating hours. The ingredients are certainly present for a more impactful event if meteorological parameters all come together.

Looking a bit more closely at this event, a broad mid/upper ridge persist across the Four Corners eastward to the southwestern Atlantic. Amplified flow north of this expansive anticyclone will continue to be a conduit to active convection, many in the form of mesoscale convective systems (MCS). As mentioned above, a remnant MCS might still be ongoing early Sunday across the region. While above average heights persist, expect some non-zero height falls to cross the area in response to an approaching shortwave. Within this northwesterly flow aloft, vertical shear is ample for the time of year, generally around 30 to 35 knots. Depending on model choice, mixed-layer CAPE values approach 1,500 to 2,500 J/kg. The combination of these two will easily support a risk of severe weather. While damaging wind gusts are the most likely threat, other severe types loom if storms can remain discrete in nature.

Additionally, a Slight Risk for excessive rainfall continues along much of the Alleghenies eastward along/north of I-66/U.S. 50. Precipitable water values rise markedly, possibly into the 2 to 2.25 inch range. While a single thunderstorm will be capable of torrential downpours, the bigger threat would be for repeat and/or training convection. The latter potential exists which supports the flash flood risk. Although drought continues over much of the region, many areas have seen a one category improvement over the past week. Convection will likely be ongoing into Sunday night with the cold front not passing through until early Monday.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Seasonably warm conditions and daily shower and thunderstorm chances are expected through Monday, before another round of storms are possible on Thursday.

The local area has largely remained just north of a west-east oriented semi-stalled frontal zone. As of the early afternoon, the boundary currently stretches from the Delmarva Peninsula back across the Richmond metro area into central West Virginia.

On the local WSR-88D radar imagery, what remains of an overnight convective complex across the Ohio Valley is crossing the area. Although most of it has dissipated, the remnant mesoscale convective vortex (MCV) is currently trekking across the central Virginia Piedmont. While there are no current threats with this feature, these can notoriously be triggers toward more intense convection. This cyclonic swirl is likely to cross the I-95 corridor in central Virginia by around 4 PM before moving into the Northern Neck of Virginia. Off to the north, spotty showers remain but these are producing minimal precipitation at best. With earlier overcast skies yielding many cloud breaks, such areas of clearing will need to monitored for further convective initation. As of the writing of this discussion, nothing is imminent at this point.

For the remainder of the day, will maintain shower and thunderstorm chances across much of the area, especially south of I-66/U.S. 50. This generally follows the Marginal Risk area maintained by the Storm Prediction Center. Any taller updraft would be capable of producing pockets of damaging wind gusts. All convective threats should wane by sundown with the loss of daytime heating. Today's highs will top out in the 80s (70s for the mountains) given immense cloud cover and north to northeasterly component of the winds. Tonight remains dry with some patchy fog for those along/west of U.S. 15. Overnight low temperatures fall into the 60s to low 70s, mildest across the city metros.

High pressure building across southern Quebec down into New England will favor a mostly quiet day for the area on Saturday. An onshore component to the winds should favor a mix of clouds and sun through the day. Highs will rise into the mid/upper 80s with any shower/thunderstorm chances confined to the Potomac Highlands across the central Shenandoah Valley toward I-64. Recent high-resolution models are showing an MCS racing across the Ohio Valley late Saturday. Some of this could leak across the Alleghenies, but confidence is low given a fairly mixed model signal.

As Sunday's cold front tracks offshore, upper-level zonal flow bringing drier air from the Great Lakes persists over the Mid- Atlantic through midweek, creating a break in the rain and thunderstorms. While temperatures & dewpoints drop a few degrees by Tuesday in the wake of the front, temperatures should gradually increase again in the latter half of the week as high pressure builds overhead.

Meanwhile, an upper-level trough will begin to form over the Northern Plains and then track across the Great Lakes late in the week, with a strong cold front potentially moving through the Mid- Atlantic between Thursday and Friday. Medium-range algorithms are already highlighting a potential for severe thunderstorms with this system. However, severe probabilities currently vary widely across models, with CSU ML probabilities highlighting only a marginal 5%- 15% probability as of the 12Z model runs while the WxNext2 Mean AI outlook is already showing a 30%-45% probability. Deterministically, the GFS/EDMWF also have not quite aligned on the timing and placement of the trough 7 days out. Should this setup materalize, storms capable of heavy downpours and damaging winds would be possible. As drought conditions continue to improve area-wide, localized flooding becomes more of a concern with any thunderstorms that form in the region. For now, this will be a feature to continue to monitor as the synoptic setup becomes more defined.
s.avn:
What had initially appeared to be a more active day of convection has been more lackluster in nature. However, there are a number of cloud breaks occurring which could lead to some destabilization this afternoon, particularly around KCHO given closer proximity to the front. Will maintain a PROB30 group from 4-8 PM for this terminal given the threat of thunderstorms. Otherwise, expect VFR conditions with light winds turning more northeast to easterly into Saturday.

VFR conditions are expected for Saturday as high pressure builds over New England into southern Quebec. Any shower chances are likely confined to those west of the Blue Ridge and south of I-66. A decaying MCS could move through late Saturday night, but there is plenty of uncertainty at this point. Sunday presents itself as a much more active weather day which would include some convective-driven restrictions. Ahead of the approaching cold front, southerly winds pick up in strength with afternoon gusts to around 15 to 20 knots. Convection could loom into Sunday night and Monday morning which would support additional sub-VFR conditions. Conditions turn drier for later in the day as the cold front moves off toward the southeast.

Prevailing VFR conditions are anticipated at terminals Tuesday through Wednesday. Light northwest winds shift southerly on Wednesday.
s.mar:
The marine waters should stay mostly hazard free, although the more southern waters could see a thunderstorm or two capable of frequent lightning. Otherwise, background wind fields remain below advisory threshold through early Sunday. Ahead of a cold front, southerly winds increase in earnest which will carry gusts to around 20 to 25 knots. This likely requires Small Craft Advisories from Sunday afternoon into the overnight hours. Additionally, there will be an increasing risk of strong to severe thunderstorms, many of which may need Special Marine Warnings. Sunday likely presents itself as the most hazardous day to be on the waters, particularly from the afternoon onward. Convection may continue into Monday morning before the storm threat and winds drop off through the day.

Winds stay below SCA thresholds on Tuesday. Beginning Wednesday afternoon, wind gusts pick up to marginal SCA thresholds before diminishing overnight. Northwest winds shift southeast by Wednesday morning.
s.tide: Water levels are largely expected to stay below Action Stage through Saturday. The potential exception could be Annapolis, which could reach Action Stage at the higher of the daily tides. Water levels will start to increase in southerly flow on Sunday, with Annapolis potentially approaching Minor Flood Stage.

Have opted to continue the advisory with the expectation fog will return. But, instead of expanding the advisory further south and east, have buffered it with a Special Weather Statement for more patchy dense river valley fog.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Severe thunderstorms and some instances of flash flooding are possible on Sunday.

Overnight model guidance has come into a broad consensus regarding the synoptic evolution for Sunday.

In the upper levels, a belt of seasonably strong westerlies will persist from the upper Great Lakes across the Saint Lawrence Valley into the Northeast and Canadian Maritimes. Broad ascent on the equatorward side of this jet will persist much of the time from early Sunday morning through late Sunday night.

Meanwhile, a pair of mid-level shortwaves, likely augmented by upstream convection over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, will track across the Mid-Atlantic on Sunday. Although timing remains a bit uncertain, most guidance now agrees on an initial wave and attendant enhanced lift/flow during the morning. This initial wave may slow on its exit during the afternoon, only to be followed by another stout wave during the late afternoon and evening. W/NW flow in the 700-500 hPa layer increases to 30-40 kts, possibly higher depending on how these waves are deepened by convection that occurs today/tonight upstream.

In the low levels, flow will also increase. This will allow a sharp rise in theta-e, with PWs rising from around 1.75" at 09Z to near 2.25" by 15Z. Further increases are progged into the evening. Low-level/steering flow will lie parallel to a slowly northward lifting warm front expected to bisect the area, so despite the increased flow, backbuilding/repeating convection seems plausible. Training plus the high PW airmass yields a threat for excessive rain and flooding, perhaps mitigated a bit by ongoing drought east of the Appalachians.

Areas that have seen recent heavy rain, or typical poor drainage/urban areas would be rather susceptible to any such excessive rainfall amounts. Of note, the 00Z HREF 3-hr PMM has 50-70% chance of exceeding 1" in the vicinity of western MD early Sunday morning as a presumably weakening MCS treks into the region. s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms and some instances of flash flooding are possible on Sunday.

Sunday is shaping up to be an active weather day across the region. Showers and thunderstorms are expected to form later this afternoon across eastern Indiana/western Ohio ahead of a remnant MCV. These thunderstorms are then forecast to persist overnight as they track eastward across eastern Ohio, northern West Virginia, and western Pennsylvania. Much further to the north, a more potent shortwave and associated surface low will track toward Hudson Bay. Return flow ahead of that disturbance along with high pressure shifting eastward off the New England Coast will cause a warm front to simultaneously lift northeastward through our forecast late tonight into the day tomorrow. Guidance is in good agreement that the front will clear locations to the west of the Blue Ridge tomorrow morning, but it may slow or halt its northeastward progress somewhere between US-15 and I-95 as showers linger through much of the day. Southerly flow behind the front will advect an increasingly moist and unstable airmass northward into the forecast area, setting the stage for showers and thunderstorms to occur, especially across southwestern portions of the forecast area.

The arrival of the overnight storms from the Ohio Valley will roughly coincide with the northeastward movement of the warm front, with just limited instability available to these showers and thunderstorms as they track eastward across the forecast area. These showers and storms are forecast to reach the Allegheny Front around 3-6 AM before gradually shifting eastward through the morning. On and off showers with a few embedded thunderstorms are expected for most locations through the morning. The showers may even linger into the afternoon near/east of I-95, which will limit daytime heating and resultant destabilization in those locations.

Guidance is split on whether thunderstorms will form immediately behind the morning showers, but it likely won't take much heating for storms to refire given the uncapped and very moist airmass that will be in place. If the storms don't immediately reform on the back edge of the precipitation shield, there could be a brief lull for a few hours in the subsidence behind the departing MCV, before the next disturbance approaches from the Ohio Valley. Initial activity associated with this disturbance will likely form off to our north and west in the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and then move in from the west during the evening hours. These storms will then track eastward across the area through the first half of the overnight, with conditions finally drying out later Sunday night.

Storms on Sunday will pose a threat for both flash flooding and severe weather. Precipitable water values are forecast to climb to well in excess of 2 inches, which when when combined with increasing instability and deep warm cloud layers will make any storms capable of producing very heavy rainfall. Flow will be increasing aloft, which will keep storms progressive. However, with the potential for multiple rounds and high instantaneous rates, isolated instances of flash flooding could be possible anywhere in the forecast area. A Flood Watch was issued for Garrett County from 6 AM to Midnight, where flooding was observed a few nights ago and soils remain saturated. Further east, confidence in the placement of heavier storms was too low for a Watch to be issued at this time.

Storms may also be capable of producing damaging winds, and potentially even a tornado or two. The severe thunderstorm threat appears to be greatest to the west of the Blue Ridge/to the south of I-66 east of the Blue Ridge, where they'll have a better chance to destabilize behind the morning convection. This same area is outlooked with a Slight Risk for severe thunderstorms from SPC. Further northeast, instability will be more limited, with a Marginal Risk from SPC. As it stands now, the highest potential for severe storms may be with the later thunderstorms as they move toward the Alleghenies from the Ohio Valley in the evening. With morning convection moving through, forecast confidence in the details is low, so we'll need to monitor short term trends and adjust the forecast accordingly.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Seasonable conditions continue through the week with a break in thunderstorm chances Tuesday and Wednesday.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe weather and flash flooding are possible through tonight.

Very active weather is expected over the next 12 to 24 hours, with the threat for flash flooding, damaging wind gusts, and a few tornadoes.

As of 06Z/2AM EDT, thunderstorms containing very heavy rain had prompted several Flash Flood Warnings and water rescues in southeastern Ohio. These thunderstorms are on track to reach western Maryland (Garrett County) by daybreak/6AM EDT.

Will be closely evaluating the downstream environment into Allegany County MD, as well as Mineral, Grant, Hampshire and Hardy Counties in WV to see if the watch needs to be expanded to cover this morning round of storms that have a history of producing about 3 inches of rain in an hour.

The first shortwave of note which is the impetus for the approaching complex has an impressive swirl on radar/satellite. Given the orientation of the heaviest thunderstorms in this complex, it appears that WNW to ESE training will continue as this complex enters western MD. The signal for heavy rain becomes a bit more diffuse as these storms cross the mountains through mid to late morning, though a persistent convergence axis is noted in obs/guidance trends in the above mentioned areas (Allegany down to Hampshire/Hardy Counties).

To the east, strong moisture advection in the low levels should cause at least scattered showers to break out by around or just before day break across northern VA into central MD. Instability is not as high here, so thunder and heavy rain may old off until mid to late morning. Coverage of heavier storms looks a bit lower and of less confidence this morning, though any heavier rain could still bring about a conditional flood threat in urban/poor drainage areas.

Guidance shows a relative lull in between the wave moving in this morning and another stout shortwave (currently over IL) moving through late this afternoon and evening. Upstream trends between these waves in the Indianapolis area, however, show convection initiating even in the middle of the night. This seems indicative of sufficient WAA to result in rapidly redeveloping convection at least in an isolated sense in between these two waves at pretty much any point today.

Trends will need to be very closely monitored given the very high PW airmass and potential for repeat/training thunderstorms. Should this heavier activity train over any one area, 3 to 6 inches of rain would be possible on a localized basis. This could cause scattered to numerous instances of flash flooding, with considerable flash flooding possible in urban/poor drainage areas or areas that have seen heavy rain recently. If and when it becomes clearer where the greatest coverage of heavy rain will set up, additional Flood Watches may be issued.

Regarding the severe weather threat, strong low-level winds will boost SRH in a high moisture content environment. Wet downbursts and brief spin ups would be possible in this environment, with the tornado threat maximized along the slowly lifting warm frontal zone - especially if any cell or cluster interacts with/tracks along it. Shear is favorable for right- moving (i.e. NW to SE) supercells if enough instability is realized, and in those cases storms would be more apt to ingest streamwise vorticity along the warm front (or residual outflow).

The wave this evening, though timed a bit after peak heating, may pose the relative highest risk of damaging wind gusts due to increased low-level flow orthogonal to what will probably a linear type feature.

Convection (and corresponding severe/flood threats) may wane only gradually tonight with continued low-level moist advection beneath height falls aloft. This causes instability to remain or even increase through the night.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe weather and flash flooding are possible through tonight.

Very active weather is expected over the next 12 hours, with the threat for flash flooding, damaging wind gusts, and a few tornadoes.

As of 330 PM, regional radar shows two developing MCSs across western Pennsylvania and West Virginia, both with a history of producing damaging winds. These MCSs are expected to continue eastward into our area over the next few hours. Skies have cleared out ahead of the storms, so strong daytime heating is underway and conditions are destabilizing. MLCAPE values are forecast to increase to around 1500-2000 J/kg ahead of the line, with effective bulk shear increasing to around 30-35 knots. This parameter space should allow these storms to continue across much of the forecast area, leading to a threat for primarily damaging winds. With around 30 knots of 0-3 km shear oriented roughly perpendicular to the lines, a brief QLCS tornado also can't be ruled out. This threat could be locally maximized as the line encounters a warm front oriented from north to south extending from near Frederick to Fredericksburg. The storms should tend to weaken later tonight as they move east of this boundary into a lower instability airmass.

Storms are right on the doorstep of the Alleghenies at the moment, and should press eastward toward the I-95 corridor by around 8-10 PM. Additional storms are also in the process of developing across central Indiana to north central Ohio. Some recent CAM runs hint that those storms may develop into a secondary line that would move through a couple hours after the first round. There are also some hints of backbuilding, especially in the DC Metro area between those rounds as low- level flow picks up behind the first MCS, equaling or exceeding winds higher up in the atmosphere. This results in Corfidi upshear vectors near zero, suggesting that backbuilding and localized training could be possible in the vicinity of the warm front. Thermodynamically, the environment is extremely favorable for heavy rainfall production, with precipitable water values well in excess of 2 inches, and forecast to potentially near 2.5 inches this evening. That coupled with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and deep warm cloud layers will make any storms capable of producing very heavy instantaneous rainfall rates. That coupled with the potential for multiple rounds of storms, and/or training/backbuilding raises concerns for flash flooding this evening. A Flood Watch remains in effect for Garrett County, which had a flood event a few nights ago. Another Flood Watch may be considered for the DC Metro shortly, given the above conditions.

Storms are expected to clear the area by around 2 or 3 AM, with dry conditions later tonight. Additional thunderstorms may be possible tomorrow afternoon, but coverage of storms is expected to be much lower, and the threat for both severe thunderstorms and flash flooding is expected to be much lower, if not zero.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Thunderstorm chances return Wednesday night into Thursday.

Surface high pressure will build from the Ohio Valley into the Mid Atlantic Tuesday and Wednesday, providing dry conditions and slightly lower humidity. Temperatures may cool off a few degrees Tuesday but overall remain seasonable.

The next cold front will approach from the northwest Wednesday night, perhaps bringing some showers and thunderstorms depending on its timing. The front will slowly drift south through the area Thursday, which will result in the greatest chance of showers and thunderstorms. At this time, it's not certain if there will be enough instability, and enough overlap with higher shear values, to present a severe weather threat. It's possible the front will stall or only move just south of the area, which will play a role in precipitation chances Friday. On Saturday, a shortwave trough may cause low pressure to develop along the front, which could bring more rain, even if we are north of its track. The next cold front could approach from the Great Lakes next Sunday.
