KEY MESSAGE 1...Scattered showers and thunderstorms remain possible until a cold front crosses tonight, with a chance possibly persisting into Tuesday.

A couple of perturbations are approaching the area this afternoon while a surface cold front moves southward from the Great Lakes. Despite west to northwest winds, dew points remain in the upper 60s to mid 70s with precipitable water values near 2 inches. Scattered showers and a few thunderstorms have already developed across the northern part of the CWA and across PA in this environment. This convection will gradually drift east and southeast with time through the evening. Steepened low-level lapse rates with lingering low- level moisture could result in a few gusty thunderstorms (generally 35-50 mph), along with some downpours and lightning. Heating and instability will be a bit more pronounced across central VA to southern MD, so these areas would probably stand the highest chance at seeing anything at or near severe thresholds (which is 58 mph). DCAPE will be very marginal (400-600 J/kg) due to lingering mid- level moisture and meager lapse rates aloft, but a bit higher to the south (especially Fredericksburg to southern MD). Typically, values of at least 600-800 J/kg are needed to accelerate downdraft winds to severe levels. However, storms may not reach this area until near or after sunset, so the net effect may be strong to perhaps near severe storms.

The low-level synoptic cold front will cross the region tonight. Therefore, a few additional showers are possible, but the threat for thunderstorms should start diminishing after midnight. Areas which clear out tonight could have patchy fog. Most guidance favors the western river valleys at this time.

While the surface front will likely be south of the area Tuesday, it will be losing its definition, and some low and mid level moisture may linger, especially across the southern half of the area. With daytime heating, this will result in some weak instability. Some models have scattered showers and storms developing off the terrain and moving eastward during the afternoon across the southern quarter to half of the forecast area (mostly south of I-66 if not I-64). The weak instability will limit the strength of this activity despite shear which could approach 30 kt. Temperatures and dew points will be a touch lower today, but still seasonable with highs in the mid to upper 80s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Thunderstorm chances return Wednesday night into Thursday, and continue into next weekend.

High pressure building from the Ohio Valley will keep dry conditions Tuesday night into Wednesday. Temperatures may tick back up closer to 90. The next cold front will approach from the northwest Wednesday night, but the timing for rain chances has generally been pushed to the second half of the night, which would reduce the threat for thunderstorms. Where this cold front ends up by Thursday afternoon will have an effect on the coverage and strength of showers and thunderstorms. While everyone could see some rain, there is uncertainty with the amount of instability and how much it would overlap with shear. AI/ML guidance has been consistent the past several days showing the greatest risk for any stronger thunderstorms being across the southern or southeastern portion of the forecast area.

It's possible the front will stall or only move just south of the area, which will play a role in precipitation chances Friday. It will be far enough south to bring a cool down, with highs in the 70s and 80s by Friday.

A deepening trough of low pressure approaching from the Great Lakes (possibly even a closed low) may result in one or more areas of low pressure developing along the front between Friday and this weekend. Thus chances of rain have been trending upward, even if we are north of the low track. Expect temperatures slightly below normal given the clouds and potential rain.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...High pressure builds in through mid week.

Yesterday's cold front will slow and dissipate over the Carolinas today as high pressure builds in from the Ohio River Valley. Prior to the arrival of high pressure, some lingering moisture and very weak ascent may cause a few pop up showers and thunderstorms along the I-64 corridor in Virginia over to southern Maryland this afternoon into early this evening. Weak forcing and modest CAPE (with a notable capping inversion just above 700 hPa and poor mid-level lapse rates) should keep storm coverage and intensity low.

High pressure will build across the Mid-Atlantic Wednesday with dry conditions expected. A cold front will approach from the Great Lakes bringing an increasing chance of showers and perhaps a thunderstorm by late Wednesday night.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Daily chances for showers and thunderstorms return Thursday, then continue Friday through Sunday.

Although timing remains a bit uncertain, a cold front looks to enter the area Thursday morning, then slowly cross through Thursday night. Questions regarding early day precip and cloud cover lend to uncertainty in how much instability builds Thursday afternoon, though a few stronger storms are certainly possible given increased flow aloft and lift along the front.

Model guidance is in relatively good agreement that the longwave pattern across the CONUS will amplify significantly heading into next weekend as unseasonably deep troughing digs across the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley. While there is some spread with respect to just how deep this trough will be and its exact east/west placement, nearly all solutions place us downstream of the trough, which will keep us in southwesterly flow aloft and keep the pattern active. Daily chances for showers and thunderstorms are expected within the zone of large scale ascent downstream of the longwave trough sharpening to our west. Depending on how much instability develops, some of these storms could potentially be on the stronger side. Temperatures are forecast to run slightly below normal, with highs in the upper 70s and low 80s, and overnight lows in the 60s.

Most solutions have the longwave trough making some eastward progress by Sunday night into Monday, which should result in a cold front passing through. Continued below normal temperatures and drier conditions are forecast behind the front for Monday.
s.avn:
NW flow as a cold front crosses along with some mid/high clouds will compete with high humidity for the formation of some fog through early this morning. The most likely TAF site to see fog seems to be KCHO where recent rain plus more displacement from the light NW flow associated with the approaching cold front is.

Otherwise, VFR conditions are expected at the TAF sites through mid week (Wednesday). Added a PROB30 for -SHRA at KCHO 18-22Z, though some TS or slightly later timing are possible. Rain may approach the TAF sites ahead of a cold front late Wednesday night, with TS possible Thursday afternoon and evening. Light N/NW flow is expected through tonight, becoming SW to S Wednesday into Wednesday night before possibly returning to NW Thursday into Thursday night depending on the placement of the next cold front.

Overall, the depth of moisture has diminished in the wake of last night's cold frontal passage, so as the aforementioned short-wave traverses the region into early afternoon, its main impact should be restricted to isolated/widely scattered showers and garden variety thunderstorms for portions of VA and far southern MD. While a thunderstorm can't be ruled out, poor mid level lapse rates may cap updrafts.

Surface high pressure builds eastward from the Ohio Valley tonight. Some clearing takes place, though more uncertainty exists across southern portions of the forecast area. Where skies are clear, fog may form, especially in the river valleys. The high will slide across the area Wednesday, providing dry conditions. Temperatures will be near or slightly above average.

As a shortwave trough pivots through the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Valley, the next cold front will approach the area Wednesday night. The chance for showers, and perhaps a thunderstorm, will increase the second half of the night from the north. Although timing remains a bit uncertain, the cold front looks to enter the area Thursday morning, then slowly cross southward through Thursday night. Questions regarding early day precip and cloud cover lend to uncertainty in how much instability builds Thursday afternoon, though a few stronger storms are certainly possible given increased flow aloft and lift along the front. AI/ML severe probabilities have been consistent showing higher values across southeastern portions of the CWA. The bulk of 12Z NWP guidance is in general agreement with the strongest convective signals near or just south of the southern CWA border. Temperatures will depend on clouds and frontal position, with a range from the upper 70s to near 90 possible across the CWA.

There could be a relative break in some areas on Friday if high pressure over the St. Lawrence valley shoves the front to the south. Relatively speaking, rain chances will be higher farther south, closer to the frontal zone. Troughing will begin to amplify Friday night, with low pressure perhaps developing and/or lifting northeastward from the Carolinas. Overrunning moisture will spread northward late in the day and overnight, though there remain questions on how quickly and how far north and west the rain reaches.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Numerous showers and thunderstorms Saturday with lingering showers Sunday. Turning cooler and dry for next week.

The longwave pattern is forecast to amplify significantly this weekend into next week as trough digs across the Great Lks and OH Valley. This will drive a pair of cold fronts across the area Sat and Sun providing focus for showers and thunderstorms. Saturday looks like the more active and more unstable day as shortwave energy moves across. By Sunday, the first cold front should have pushed the deep moisture and instability to the south limiting the coverage and intensity of showers.

As trough axis shifts east of the area Sunday night or Monday, expect a cooler and drying trend to start the new work week.

- 1) Departing high pressure gives way to a cold front and increasing shower and thunderstorm chances by Thursday.

- 2) Chances for showers and thunderstorms continue through at least Saturday, before cooler and drier air moves in early next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Departing high pressure gives way to a cold front and increasing shower and thunderstorm chances by Thursday.

High pressure moving overhead will maintain dry conditions with partly to mostly sunny skies today. The high will move offshore tonight as a cold front approaches from the Great Lakes. Clouds will increase this evening, with shower chances ticking up near and west of I-81 after midnight. Shower activity is possible across much of the area by daybreak Thursday, depending on the evolution of showers and storms over the OH Valley today.

Latest guidance is a bit slower and further west/northwest with the position of a cold front on Thursday. SLP progs hint at two subtle warm front type features that will lift northeast during the day on Thursday ahead of a pair of weak surface lows (one near PA/NJ, and the other near central VA). Where this front ends up just prior to peak heating will be crucial in determining the severe weather threat locally on Thursday.

Forecast soundings show strong mid-level capping west of the front Thursday afternoon, with no capping and notably stronger CAPE approaching or exceeding 2000 J/kg east of it. The consensus is for this front to be more or less over I-95 Thursday afternoon during peak heating, though there is some variance anywhere from near the Blue Ridge to the Chesapeake Bay. Mid-level lapse rates start the day unimpressive, around 5 C/km likely due to saturation aloft associated with a weak wave of showers, but steepen slightly closer to 6 C/km by afternoon due to some cooling aloft.

The extent of any clouds and showers cast some uncertainty on the extent of heating and instability later in the day. The background environment is favorable for strong to severe updrafts and even supercells. An 80-90+ kt upper jet will pivot over the area, with its right entrance ascent positioned over the surface frontal zone in the afternoon. Mid-level heights stay relatively steady, but PVA (strongest north) will be prevalent ahead of the aforementioned mid/upper wave and jet.

Flow will increase through the column, with 25-40 kts in the 2-5 km AGL layer and effective deep layer bulk shear around 40 kts. SRH also increases to 100-200 m2/s2. Initial discrete cells in this environment may quickly grow upscale into a line capable of surges of strong to severe straight-line wind and a few embedded spin ups. Some hail can't be ruled out in the strongest storms due to cooling temps aloft. Finally, although Corfidi vectors are not too low (10-15 kts), on the mesoscale some backbuilding or training potential may exist on the tail (southwest) end of any developing line heading into the evening.

Again, the highest potential will be along and east of the front which currently appears to be near I-95 during the afternoon into the early evening hours.

Although somewhat conditional based on (1) the placement of the front, and (2) the degree of instability, Thursday's severe weather and excessive rainfall risk bears monitoring. For now, given the uncertainties listed above, the risk is more in the Marginal (level 1 out of 5) bin for severe weather (i.e. any damaging winds, large hail, tornadoes), but with a conditionally much higher ceiling than most typical late summer days. The excessive rainfall/flood risk may be even more conditional due to uncertain mesoscale factors and lingering drought.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Chances for showers and thunderstorms continue through at least Saturday, before cooler and drier air moves in early next week.

The longwave pattern across the CONUS will amplify moving into the weekend, with a shortwave disturbance and an even more potent upper-level low digging into the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes on Saturday. Downstream of the trough axis, we'll be in a favorable location for large scale ascent, with showers and thunderstorms possible Saturday afternoon. The upper trough axis will shift eastward to near our longitude by Sunday as an upper low continues to deepen to the north of Lake Ontario. Most solutions favor a cold front moving through either late Saturday night or early Sunday. Drier low-level air will filter into the region behind the front, with dewpoints dropping through the 60s on Sunday. That combined with the trough axis being located overhead (leading to less large scale ascent), leads to most solutions showing dry conditions locally. However, there still are a few solutions that produce a passing shower or storm on Sunday.

Even drier air will advect into the area for Monday and Tuesday, with dewpoints forecast to drop into the 50s. This will lead to dry conditions, and also make it feel considerably less humid. High temperatures each day Saturday through Tuesday will generally be in the low to mid 80s at lower elevations, with 70s in the mountains.

Winds will gradually turn more southwesterly by this afternoon with VFR conditions expected. Rain may approach the TAF sites ahead of a cold front late tonight, with more numerous showers and possible thunderstorms Thursday afternoon and evening. Highest TS probs are near/east of I-95 terminals Thursday PM. Some lower ceilings are possible, especially around MRB Thursday morning. Showers may linger at CHO Thursday night and Friday, along with potential lower ceilings.

Sub-VFR ceilings may be possible Saturday morning, before conditions gradually improve back to VFR Saturday afternoon. Thereafter, prevailing VFR conditions are expected through the weekend. Temporary drops to sub-VFR conditions can't be ruled out in thunderstorms on Saturday or Sunday. Winds will be light out of the southeast on Saturday, and then light out of the northwest on Sunday.

This will drive a pair of cold fronts across the area Sat and Sun providing focus for showers and thunderstorms. Saturday looks like the more unstable day as we remain in WSW flow aloft and with better forcing ahead of the trough axis. By Sunday, the first cold front should have pushed the deep moisture and instability to the south limiting the coverage and intensity of showers while the trough axis moves overhead limiting the upper level forcing.

Cloud cover and precipitation chances increase across the terminals overnight, although primarily VFR conditions are expected through early Thursday morning. Morning convection may impact MRB as showers and thunderstorms track across western MD/eastern panhandle of WV. Showers and thunderstorms impact the terminals Thursday afternoon with restrictions likely during heavy precipitation. Highest chances for strong to severe thunderstorms remains along and east of I-95 terminals. After precipitation moves out of the area, low ceilings are possible Thursday night into Friday.

Sct convection Sat through Sun.
s.mar: Winds remain below Small Craft Advisory criteria through Thursday morning. A Small Craft Advisory is in effect for the southern Chesapeake Bay Thursday afternoon. SMWs are possible Thursday afternoon as strong to severe thunderstorms track across the waters. Otherwise, non hazardous marine weather is expected through the end of the week.
s.tide: Current tidal anomalies largely range from 0.25 to 0.50 feet this evening. These may rise slightly in time, but only locations like Annapolis and perhaps Alexandria could hit Action stage during the next couple of days. This will particularly be the case during the higher of the two astronomical high tides.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe weather is possible, mainly east of the Blue Ridge this afternoon into early evening.

A slow-moving cold front arcs down the Saint Lawrence River Valley to the lower Great Lakes back into the central Great Plains. To the south, a largely stationary front was attempting to lift slowly northward as a warm front, and stretched from the Carolinas back to Oklahoma. Showers and thunderstorms were persistently trekking west to east along the northern front, with a weak surface low and MCV/shortwave crossing Illinois. This shortwave will be the impetus for convective development across the Mid-Atlantic later today as the local area sits in between the two aforementioned fronts.

Most instability this morning is rather weak and elevated in nature, but is expected to increase rapidly in the I-95 corridor from south to north as higher moisture air advects into the area, as well as near the Appalachians ahead of an approaching shortwave. For now, weak lift and CAPE is keeping the area dry outside of a few WAA showers near western MD.

Additional development, perhaps even deeper convective cores, is possible by as early as late morning given the anticipated rapid increase in CAPE and lift.

Flow aloft is seasonably strong by late August standards, with a 100+ knot 300 hPa jet streak expected to pivot over the Saint Lawrence River Valley into northern New England by evening. The tail of this upper jet may actually strengthen and persist near the Mason-Dixon Line early this evening, which could briefly enhance large scale ascent locally via RRQ dynamics.

In the mid levels, the previously mentioned shortwave has trended notably deeper and a bit slower over the last 12-24 hours. This brings the axis of the shortwave, its enhanced flow, and PVA across the Appalachians around midday, then across areas near and east of the Blue Ridge/Catoctin Mountains east to I-95 and the Chesapeake Bay during peak heating. In addition to bringing large scale ascent, this pushes effective deep layer bulk shear into the 35- to 50-knot range later today (highest north/northeast). Shear of this magnitude is favorable for sustained, organized updrafts, including line segments and supercells (discrete or line-embedded).

Thermodynamically, the atmosphere will be very moist, especially further east. Strong low-level theta-e advection is expected to persist through early evening ahead of the approaching shortwave and cold front. Widespread clouds will limit heating somewhat, especially west of the Blue Ridge where the storm threat is notably less, but with the strong low-level moisture advection and slow-but-steady cooling aloft, the net result should be about 1000-2000 J/kg MLCAPE in the moist plume east of the Blue Ridge heading into this afternoon, possibly as early as late morning. The moist low-level advection beneath cooling aloft may also result in re-generative CAPE and multiple rounds of thunderstorms in any one location. This would be most likely from near the DC metro north and east where large scale ascent is strongest, with the added component of enhanced low-level convergence along bay or river breezes (and eventually composite outflow boundaries).

Finally, PWs will approach or exceed 2 inches in the moist axis near and east of I-95 this afternoon into early evening. Deep warm cloud layers in the high PW airmass will yield heavy to extreme instantaneous and sub-hourly rainfall rates in the stronger precip cores. Individual cell motion is expected to be progressive (30-40 mph) given enhanced flow through the column and the potential for modest cold pool development with any persistent cells, clusters or line segments. However, the wavy slow-moving front approaching from the north may lie close to parallel to the mean steering flow at times, especially when modulated by outflow from potential multiple rounds of storms. This, coupled with the bay breeze which often takes on a similar orientation, plus the urban footprint that has seen heavy rain recently raises a (primarily urban/poor drainage) flash flood risk over the I-95 corridor in northeast Maryland, including the Baltimore area. The threat is a bit more conditional further south and west into areas like Annapolis and the DC/Capital Beltway region; these areas also feature urban sprawl and inherently lower FFG, but the training potential is more conditional based on favorable outflow or cell interactions given slightly further displacement from the synoptic front(s) and bay breeze.

Multiple hazards are possible today, and are outlined below.

Damaging Wind... Straight-line/downburst winds are likely the highest threat today, at least from an areal coverage standpoint. Tall, skinny CAPE profiles with modest pockets of mid-level dry air yield DCAPE of 600-800 J/kg, which would be marginally favorable for strong to severe downdrafts. Background mid-level flow may approach 40 knots around 700 hPa. With the high PW air and modest DCAPE, water-loaded downdrafts via precip drag would be possible especially with any bowing line segments or collapsing mesocyclones/mesovorticies. The lack of steeper lapse rates (hence modest DCAPE) should keep most wind gusts within the strongest storms in the 55-70 mph range, with more widespread 40-55 mph potential. Given heavy precip and late summer, leafed- up trees, would anticipate scattered to numerous instances of tree and branch falls and subsequent power outage potential. The risk is highest near and east of I-95 where storms are most likely to become linear and be a bit more intense, since they're further east in the moist axis with a little more time to heat. To the west, especially west of the Blue Ridge, less moisture and heating should keep the coverage of more intense storms low.

Tornadoes... A conditional risk for a brief spin-up is evident for most areas east of the Blue Ridge given the magnitude of low/mid-level flow and high PWs/lower LCLs. Relatively greater tornado potential may exist closer to the front near the I-70 corridor east of Frederick where surface winds will be backed and low-level SRH will be higher, especially in close proximity to the bay breeze along the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay into northeast MD. Potential would be further maximized by (1) discrete supercells occurring earlier when the synoptic low-level winds remain backed and SRH is higher on a broad scale, and (2) with any favorable QLCS surge/mesovortex interactions with residual outflow or the bay breeze. Although unlikely due to a lack of stronger 0-1 km shear/SRH and steeper lapse rates, robust 3CAPE near the bay could result in a conditional risk for a strong tornado if all of the above factors were to coalesce.

Flash Flooding... We have been in a wetter pattern recently, but the majority of the region is still in or just coming out of drought. Poor drainage and urban areas are susceptible to heavy rain, especially the intense sub-hourly rates possible today, regardless. Additionally, areas near and just northeast of Baltimore have seen multiple episodes of heavy rain over the last few weeks. Individual storms should move pretty swiftly, but the slowing southwest end of any lines or clusters would orient parallel to the nearby surface front, bay breeze, and mean steering flow. This brings a risk of flash flooding to northeast MD in particular, with a more conditional risk further south and west into the greater DC metro.

Hail... Although lapse rates aloft will be modest at best given the moist profiles, supercellular shear and modest mid-level cooling will be favorable for at least some marginal/spotty severe hail potential. Should mid-level shear/cooling be more potent or cells be more discrete, the hail risk could increase, but this seems unlikely given the otherwise tropical-esque airmass.

The threat for severe weather and flooding appears highest between 2 PM this afternoon and 8 PM this evening, progressing west to east in one or two rounds.

By later this evening, the departure of large scale lift and the loss of daytime heating should end the severe/flood threat.


KEY MESSAGE 2...After a brief lull Friday, additional showers and a few thunderstorms are possible Friday night into Saturday.

Although a stalled front will remain nearby on Friday, a lack of shortwaves aloft or other lifting mechanisms should generally keep shower and thunderstorm coverage and intensity lower.

By Friday night into Saturday, a surface low develops near the VA Tidewater and moves northeast along the coast/front. Also, another mid/upper wave approaches from the west. Depending on the exact track and strength of each of these features, and how they interact, this could bring higher potential for showers and thunderstorms to the region. Enhanced flow downstream of a deepening trough over the Midwest results in an environment conditionally favorable for strong storms if enough instability is realized.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Lingering chance for showers and thunderstorms on Sunday.

Guidance has trended a bit slower with the eastward progression of a highly amplified upper trough that will be in place across the eastern CONUS on Sunday. Most solutions now have the trough axis just to our west at peak heating, as opposed to earlier solutions which had it directly overhead. With the trough axis just upstream and the potential for a shortwave to rotate through the base of the trough and move toward our area, chances for thunderstorms on Sunday appear to be trending upward. With temperatures cooling aloft, weak low-level winds, appreciable deep layer shear, and a relatively straight hodograph shape, any stronger storms that occur may be capable of producing some hail, and potentially some locally gusty winds as well.


KEY MESSAGE 4...Drier and less humid conditions to start next week.

The upper trough will progress off to our east and high pressure will build to our north on Monday and Tuesday. Northwesterly winds ahead of the approaching high will advect drier air into the area at low levels (dewpoints falling into the 50s). This will result in dry conditions locally. Guidance begins to diverge a bit by Wednesday, but some solutions shower higher dewpoint air and associated chances for showers and thunderstorms returning again.
s.avn:
Early morning satellite and surface obs show widespread mid- level cloud cover. VFR bases should persist well into the afternoon, expect perhaps in the vicinity of convection. TS potential will increase by around 18Z and persist through 00Z especially for terminals near and northeast of the DC metro. Some storms could result in briefly very low visibility and strong, erratic winds. These is some potential for multiple rounds or backbuilding storms, especially in NE MD.

Low (IFR) ceilings or fog likely develop this evening in the wake of rain (except perhaps near KCHO which may be most removed from the higher precip coverage). A modest northerly wind in the wake of a southward pushing cold front overnight may cause conditions to lift and improve for the metros after 06Z.

Friday offers a relative lull in more widespread rain/TS probs, but sub-VFR is possible both early in the morning with low clouds or fog, and/or in the vicinity of storms. Prevailing VFR conditions and northwesterly winds are forecast for both Sunday and Monday. A stray afternoon shower or storm can't be ruled out Sunday afternoon.
s.mar:
Southerly winds are expected to increase ahead of an approaching cold front. The highest likelihood for persistent gusts around 20 knots (outside of storms) is over the wider waters of the middle Chesapeake Bay, but felt there is enough background flow to expand the SCA to cover all waters this afternoon into early evening (2PM to 8PM EDT). This also coincides with the highest thunderstorm potential and Special Marine Warnings.

A brief and marginal northerly push of wind is possible late tonight behind a cold front, but confidence was not nearly high enough in magnitude nor duration to hoist a headline. Otherwise, winds shift back to the south Friday into Saturday, though with a bit tempered confidence due to waves of low pressure and a stalled front nearby. Winds should be relatively light outside of any storms, for which the potential peaks Friday night into Saturday. Sub-SCA level northwesterly winds are forecast for \ both Sunday and Monday. A stray shower or storm can't be ruled out Sunday afternoon.

The threat for severe weather and flooding appears highest between 2 PM this afternoon and 8 PM this evening, progressing west to east in one or two rounds. However, it may start a couple hours earlier further west (or on the bay breeze), and could linger through late evening over southern Maryland.

By later this evening, the departure of large scale lift and the loss of daytime heating should end the severe/flood threat.


KEY MESSAGE 2...After a brief lull Friday, additional showers and a few thunderstorms are possible Friday night into Saturday.

Although a stalled front will remain nearby on Friday, a lack of shortwaves aloft or other lifting mechanisms should generally keep shower and thunderstorm coverage and intensity lower.

By Friday night into Saturday, a surface low develops near the VA Tidewater and moves northeast along the coast/front. Also, another mid/upper wave approaches from the west. Depending on the exact track and strength of each of these features, and how they interact, this could bring higher potential for showers and thunderstorms to the region. Enhanced flow downstream of a deepening trough over the Midwest results in an environment conditionally favorable for strong storms if enough instability is realized.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Lingering chance for showers and thunderstorms on Sunday.

Guidance has trended a bit slower with the eastward progression of a highly amplified upper trough that will be in place across the eastern CONUS on Sunday. Most solutions now have the trough axis just to our west at peak heating, as opposed to earlier solutions which had it directly overhead. With the trough axis just upstream and the potential for a shortwave to rotate through the base of the trough and move toward our area, chances for thunderstorms on Sunday appear to be trending upward. With temperatures cooling aloft, weak low-level winds, appreciable deep layer shear, and a relatively straight hodograph shape, any stronger storms that occur may be capable of producing some hail, and potentially some locally gusty winds as well.


KEY MESSAGE 4...Drier and less humid conditions to start next week.

The upper trough will progress off to our east and high pressure will build to our north on Monday and Tuesday. Northwesterly winds ahead of the approaching high will advect drier air into the area at low levels (dewpoints falling into the 50s). This will result in dry conditions locally. Guidance begins to diverge a bit by Wednesday, but some solutions shower higher dewpoint air and associated chances for showers and thunderstorms returning again.
s.avn:
VFR bases should persist well into the afternoon, expect perhaps in the vicinity of convection. TS potential will increase by around 18Z and persist through 00Z especially for terminals near and northeast of the DC metro. Some storms could result in briefly very low visibility and strong, erratic winds. These is some potential for multiple rounds or backbuilding storms, especially in NE MD.

Low (IFR) ceilings or fog likely develop this evening in the wake of rain (except perhaps near KCHO which may be most removed from the higher precip coverage). A modest northerly wind in the wake of a southward pushing cold front overnight may cause conditions to lift and improve for the metros after 06Z.

Friday offers a relative lull in more widespread rain/TS probs, but sub-VFR is possible both early in the morning with low clouds or fog, and/or in the vicinity of storms. Prevailing VFR conditions and northwesterly winds are forecast for both Sunday and Monday. A stray afternoon shower or storm can't be ruled out Sunday afternoon.
s.mar:
Southerly winds are expected to increase ahead of an approaching cold front. The highest likelihood for persistent gusts around 20 knots (outside of storms) is over the wider waters of the middle Chesapeake Bay, but felt there is enough background flow to expand the SCA to cover all waters this afternoon into early evening (2PM to 8PM EDT). This also coincides with the highest thunderstorm potential and Special Marine Warnings.

A brief and marginal northerly push of wind is possible late tonight behind a cold front, but confidence was not nearly high enough in magnitude nor duration to hoist a headline. Otherwise, winds shift back to the south Friday into Saturday, though with a bit tempered confidence due to waves of low pressure and a stalled front nearby. Winds should be relatively light outside of any storms, for which the potential peaks Friday night into Saturday. Sub-SCA level northwesterly winds are forecast for \ both Sunday and Monday. A stray shower or storm can't be ruled out Sunday afternoon.

s.chg: Severe and Tornado Watches have been issued for parts of the area until 10 PM.
s.key:
- Severe and Tornado Watches are in effect until 10 PM.

- After a brief lull Friday, additional showers and a few thunderstorms are possible Friday night into Saturday.

- Thunderstorm chances increase on Sunday before drier conditions move in early next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe and Tornado Watches are in effect until 10 PM.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Our atmosphere is characterized by 90F temps and mid 70s dewpoints with up to 3500 J/KG of MUCAPE, DCAPE of 418 J/kg, 40 kt of 0-6 km shear, and 0-3 km SRH of 220 m^2/S^2 based on our 18Z IAD sounding. Storms have already exhibited mid-level rotation, particularly the one over the eastern shore of MD. Expect discrete supercells this afternoon with a sig tornado potential, particularly along and south of I-70 where 18Z gridded NUCAPS data showed a tight low-level moisture gradient. By evening, storms may congeal into an MCS or line as shown in earlier and most recent HRRR forecasts. Flash flooding risk is expected to remain low due to progressive storm motions of around 27kt, but brief intense rainfall rates of 2"/hour are possible.


KEY MESSAGE 2...After a brief lull Friday, additional showers and a few thunderstorms are possible Friday night into Saturday.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Although a stalled front will remain nearby on Friday, a lack of shortwaves aloft or other lifting mechanisms should generally keep shower and thunderstorm coverage and intensity lower.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Thunderstorm chances increase on Sunday before drier conditions move in early next week.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...

Recent model guidance has continued with the trend of the upper trough moving through more slowly on Sunday, thus leading to the increase in chances for strong to severe thunderstorms. AI probabilities continue to trend upward with highest chances along and west of the Blue Ridge Sunday afternoon.

In the wake of potential showers and thunderstorms on Sunday, surface high pressure builds overhead through Tuesday. Temperatures Monday and Tuesday will top out in the 70s to low 80s with low relative humidity values expected. Precipitation chances return on Wednesday as a stalled boundary to the south shifts northward.
s.avn:
Main thunderstorm threat is between now and 21/00Z, but the risk may persist longer into mid evening. Low ceilings will develop behind storms and front later tonight. A lull is expected Fri with more rain and possible thunderstorms Saturday.

Northwesterly winds gust up to 25 knots on Sunday at MRB with eastward terminals blowing around 10 knots in the afternoon. Showers and thunderstorms are possible, leading to flight restrictions across all terminals. Winds shift to westerly on Monday with VFR conditions expected.
s.mar:
Numerous severe thunderstorms are expected this afternoon, mainly north of US-50. Additional SMWs may be required. More storms are expected Saturday into Sunday.

Northwest winds on Sunday shift to westerly on Monday, remaining below SCA criteria both days. There is a chance for showers and thunderstorms on Sunday, although chances are highest west of the waters. Should storms track over the waters, SMWs are possible.

s.chg: Severe Thunderstorm Watches and Tornado Watches have been allowed to expire. A few spotty showers leftover this evening with lower humidity and cooler temps tonight into Friday.
s.key:
- 1) Quieting down tonight into Friday with lowering humidity and cooler temperatures.

- 2) Thunderstorm chances increase Friday night and continue through Sunday. Lowering humidity and drier conditions early next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Quieting down tonight into Friday with lowering humidity and cooler temperatures

Severe Thunderstorm Watches and Tornado Watches have been allowed to expire early as the severe threat diminishes. The line of thunderstorms that have prompted the watches earlier this evening have since pushed south into the northern neck of VA and the lower Delmarva. Our area really dodged the brunt of the severe weather due to poor lapse rates, low DCAPE, and earlier cloud cover across the region. Locations such as southeast PA, Delaware, and the Eastern Shore of Maryland were not as lucky with multiple reports of damage due to earlier tornado warned storms.

Expect calmer conditions tonight with just a few residual showers and the cold front sags south and east into the region. Skies will trend partly to mostly cloudy with lowering ceilings east of the Blue Ridge on light north to northwest flow. Humidity will drop as well along with temperatures. Lows tonight will range from the upper 50s over the mountains to low to mid 60s in and around the Baltimore/DC metros.

Friday will bring a lull in the shower and thunderstorm activity as the front stalls south and east of the region. Expect partly to mostly cloudy skies with highs in the mid 70s and low 80s. With the front nearby expect an isolated shower or thunderstorm over terrain or down toward the I-64 corridor Friday afternoon. More scattered to numerous showers and embedded thunderstorms look to hold off until Friday night and Saturday as the front lifts north and an area of low pressure develops off the VA Tidewater/lower Delmarva region.

KEY MESSAGE 2... Thunderstorm chances increase Friday night and continue through Sunday. Lowering humidity and drier conditions early next week.

By Friday night into Saturday, a surface low develops near the VA Tidewater and moves northeast along the coast/front. Also, another mid/upper wave approaches from the west. Depending on the exact track and strength of each of these features, and how they interact, this could bring higher potential for showers and thunderstorms to the region. Enhanced flow downstream of a deepening trough over the Midwest results in an environment conditionally favorable for strong storms if enough instability is realized.

Current model guidance has continued with the trend of the upper trough moving through more slowly on Sunday, thus leading to the increased in chances for strong to severe thunderstorms since higher instability will be realized. AI probabilities (10-30 percent) continue to trend upward with highest chances along and west of the Blue Ridge Sunday afternoon.

In the wake of potential showers and thunderstorms on Sunday, surface high pressure builds overhead through Tuesday. Temperatures Monday and Tuesday will top out in the 70s to low 80s with low relative humidity values expected. Precipitation chances and humidity return on Wednesday as a stalled boundary to the south shifts northward.
s.avn:
Overall looking at quiet weather conditions overnight with pockets of SCT-BKN low ceilings, especially in areas east of the Blue Ridge and south of I-66/US-50 as the front sags south/east. Sporadic 15-20 kt gusts will continue along the front as it continues south and east through 02z/10pm. A residual shower or two cannot be ruled out, with most terminals remaining dry. Some patchy fog may be noted out toward MRB, CHO, and SHD early Friday morning prior to 12z/8am with vsbys between 3-6SM. More widespread mountain valley fog is expected west of these terminals. A period of low ceilings IFR/MVFR (1-3 kft) is possible between 03-14z across the corridor terminals as well as CHO given the front nearby. Ceilings look to improve mid to late Friday morning into the afternoon due a brief lull in the wake of the front.

Showers and thunderstorms do return to the terminals from the south beyond 3-6z/Saturday as an area of low pressure develops along the coast and pushes up along the stalled front nearby. Coverage of showers and thunderstorms will be scattered to numerous throughout the day with temporary restrictions at times. More organized severe weather is possible by Sunday. Winds will be out of the north and northwest Friday and Saturday at less than 15 kts.

Northwesterly winds gust up to 25 knots on Sunday at MRB with eastward terminals blowing around 10 knots in the afternoon. Showers and thunderstorms are possible, leading to flight restrictions across all terminals. Winds shift to westerly on Monday and Tuesday with VFR conditions expected.
s.mar:
SCAs will continue for all waters through at least 4z/12am as a cold front sags south and east. Any residual convection should exit the lower waters here prior to 130z/930pm. Expect improving marine conditions overnight with areas of fog and low clouds. Winds will be out of the north and northwest at less than 15 kts. Sub-SCA level conditions are expected Friday with winds still out of the north/northwest at less than 15 kts. Thunderstorm activity will be limited with rain chances returning from the south late Friday night into Saturday morning. More scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms are expected Saturday afternoon and evening. Winds will turn more to the northeast at less than 15 kts.


Northwest winds on Sunday shift to westerly on Monday, remaining below SCA criteria both days. There is a chance for showers and thunderstorms on Sunday, although chances are highest west of the waters. Should storms track over the waters, SMWs are possible.

s.chg:
Dense Fog Advisory is in effect for portions of western MD and eastern WV until 8 AM, primarily for the valleys.

Made substantial changes to the aviation section to account for less low clouds this morning.
s.key:
- 1) Thunderstorm chances increase Friday night and continue through Sunday.

- 2) Drier conditions anticipated early next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Thunderstorm chances increase Friday night and continue through Sunday. Lowering humidity and drier conditions early next week.

The region remains under the influence of an upper trough over the next several days. A subtle piece of shortwave energy will round the base of the trough this evening/tonight and lift through the region into Saturday. Meanwhile, the cold front that pushed through last evening will remain nearly stationary across southeastern VA through tonight. An area of low pressure will develop near the VA Tidewater as a result during this time, with rain expected for much of the region by Saturday morning.

The main axis of the upper-level trough will begin to shift slightly east late Saturday into Sunday, which will in turn push a much more potent piece of upper-level energy across the Ohio Valley into the Adirondacks. On the front end of this, there could be some lingering convection moving out of the Ohio Valley into our western zones later Saturday. This will carry a non-zero severe weather threat into the Alleghenies Saturday evening/night, with damaging winds the primary threat.

By Sunday, the actual front will push through the region, and may have enough left in the tank to spark a few more storms east of I-95 in the afternoon/evening hours. Severe threat looks rather low at this point, but will continue to monitor.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier conditions anticipated early next week.

By Monday, the weekend's frontal boundary should transition offshore, and upper-level patterns transition to zonal flow as surface high pressure builds over the Appalachians. Dewpoints could broadly get to below 60F by Tuesday morning as this high pressure builds, allowing for much drier conditions within the region. These conditions to persist until midweek, with temperatures trending a bit cooler than average to start between Monday and Tuesday but slowly creeping up later in the week as high pressure builds.

Beginning Wednesday, an upper-level trough begins to form over the Great Lakes and track southeast, with a surface low anticipated to potentially track through the Mid-Atlantic by Thursday. A few showers & thunderstorms are possible during this period as the low moves through, and humidity & temperatures rise back to late- August normals during this time.
s.avn:
Model guidance backed off significantly on lower clouds developing this morning, so removed those from almost all of the TAFs. MRB could still see some lower clouds/fog, but for now that is staying just to the west. VFR conditions are expected elsewhere today.

Showers and thunderstorms do return to the terminals from the south Saturday morning as an area of low pressure develops along the coast and pushes up along the stalled front nearby. For now, have added PROB30s into the 06z TAFs, owing to uncertainty with start time. Also, kept it SHRA for now, as thunder may be a bit more likely into the afternoon hours, but going to continue to evaluate that as we get closer in time. Coverage of showers and thunderstorms will be scattered to numerous throughout the day with temporary restrictions at times. Winds will be out of the north and northwest today and Saturday at less than 15 kts.

Northwesterly winds gust up to 25 knots on Sunday at MRB with eastward terminals blowing around 10 knots in the afternoon. Showers and thunderstorms are possible during the afternoon, leading to potential flight restrictions. Probabilities remain pretty low, with the metro terminals below 30 percent POPs.

Winds shift to westerly on Monday and Tuesday with VFR conditions expected.
s.mar:
Winds will be out of the north and northwest at less than 15 kts. Sub-SCA level conditions are expected Friday with winds still out of the north/northwest at less than 15 kts. Thunderstorm activity will be limited with rain chances returning from the south late Friday night into Saturday morning.

More scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms are expected Saturday afternoon and evening. Winds will turn more to the northeast at less than 15 kts.

Could see some storms over the waters on Sunday as well, but chances remain around 30 percent for most.

Northwest winds on Sunday shift to westerly on Monday, remaining below SCA criteria both days. There is a chance for showers and thunderstorms on Sunday, although chances are highest west of the waters. Should storms track over the waters, SMWs are possible.

s.key:
- Wet conditions expected tonight and Saturday with improving weather Sunday.

- Dry conditions anticipated early next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Wet conditions expected tonight and Saturday with improving weather Sunday.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Low pressure is expected to organize across the southern Mid- Atlantic tonight into Saturday as upper level energy digs across the OH Valley. As this low begins to lift northeast tonight, expect rain to develop across much of the area tonight into Saturday with some decent rainfall totals expected south of the Capital Beltway, particularly across St. Mary's County where most guidance show one to two inches of rain, possibly more. A few WPC/NBM QPF members show enough rain in St. Mary's County to bring the St. Marys River at Great Mills into flood stage. The steady rain will exit the area by late morning with a lull in precip expected, although a low overcast is expected to persist. By evening, another round of showers and thunderstorms will approach the Appalachian Mountains and may make to areas east of the Blue Ridge Mountains overnight Sat night into early Sunday.

By Sunday morning the cold front will be crossing the area with dry air advection ensuing in strengthening NW winds. However, there could still be enough moisture and lift to spark a few showers, but overall drying conditions are expected throughout the day.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry conditions anticipated early next week.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Behind an anticipated cold front, Monday brings drier and cooler than average conditions. With a strong upper-level low moving further into eastern Canada, subsidence increases in our region as a surface high pressure system builds over West Virginia well into Tuesday. This offers some potential relief from humid conditions with dewpoints dropping into the 50s and 60s. On Monday and Tuesday, we are expecting highs to remain in the low 70s to mid 80s.

As we head into late next week, an upper-level short wave moves into the Great Lakes region, bringing increasing chances for widespread lift across our forecast area. Depending on the location of a surface low tracking along the Mid-Atlantic, tropical moisture could reach as far north as Pennsylvania, increasing chances for showers and thunderstorms through much of Thursday. With PWATs above 1.5 inches, the hot and humid conditions return late next week. Temperatures rise back into late-August normals with highs in the 80s and 90s Thursday.
s.avn:
Rain developing tonight with cigs gradually dropping into IFR category by daybreak. Rain exits by Noon Saturday with IFR/MVFR cigs persisting all day. Isolated thunderstorms also possible. Conditions improving Saturday.

Light to gentle winds shift westerly on Monday and Tuesday. VFR conditions are expected early next week.
s.mar:
Possible SCA conditions Saturday and again Sunday in NW winds.

Sub-SCA level conditions are expected Monday and Tuesday with gentle winds out of the west/northwest. Chances for showers and thunderstorms pick back up on Wednesday,making SMWs are possible.

s.chg:
Update on the current showers developing over southern MD and the VA Piedmont. Flooding threat remains limited, but will need to be monitored closely as the axis of heavier rain sets up throughout the morning.

Also updated aviation and marine discussions substantially to add more details on today's setup.
s.key:
- 1) Showers and thunderstorms today with the potential for heavy rainfall and isolated instances of flash flooding.

- 2) Dry conditions anticipated Sunday through early next week.

- 3) Warmer and more humid conditions return mid-week, with thunderstorm chances returning by Thursday.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Showers and thunderstorms today with the potential for heavy rainfall and isolated instances of flash flooding.

Latest surface analysis still depicts a stalled frontal boundary off to our south and east. Satellite imagery depicts an influx of moisture into the region east of an approaching upper trough axis. We are starting to see some heavier showers develop in the right entrance region of a 90 knot upper-level jet. Low pressure is developing over the Carolina, but remains very loosely developed at this stage. At any rate, all of these features are expected to evolve throughout the day, giving a continuous threat for showers and thunderstorms through the afternoon hours.

The latest SPC mesoanalysis is starting to hone in on an area generally southeast of the I-95 corridor. PWATs in this region remain in the 1.6-1.8 inch range, with a decent overlap of low- level moisture convergence and PPP. Current forecast calls for 1-2" somewhere along/southeast of I-95, but could see some locally higher amounts. As it stands right now, the region of concern should fall just southeast of the metro areas. Sandy soils and antecedent low soil moisture in this region should mitigate the flooding threat. However, the one exception will be if the heaviest axis either shifts north into St. Marys county, where recent heavy rains leave that area slightly more susceptible to flooding. Additionally, if the axis does shift north into the metros, flash flooding could become an issue. No flood watch at this time, as confidence remains higher that the highest rain totals will fall in less susceptible areas. If that changes, one may be considered later this morning.

During the late morning and early afternoon hours there could be a lull, but there remains a chance for pop-up showers and storms pretty much anywhere during this period.

By evening, another round of showers and thunderstorms will approach the Appalachian Mountains and may make to areas east of the Blue Ridge Mountains overnight into early Sunday. Severe threat is low with these, as they will be running into stable surface air. However, they could bring some heavy rainfall and thunder. Some fog may then develop in the valleys and VA Piedmont, but it will have to do so prior to the arrival of the front.

By Sunday morning the cold front will be crossing the area with dry air advection ensuing in strengthening NW winds. However, there could still be enough moisture and lift to spark a few showers, but overall drying conditions are expected throughout the day.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry conditions anticipated Sunday through early next week.

Dewpoints drop sharply in the wake of the cold front Monday as dry air moves into the region from the Midwest. Surface high pressure will begin to build over the Appalachians and track east over the next couple of days, with conditions feeling briefly fall-like as temperatures range slightly below average for August. Overnight lows range largely in the 50s throughout the region by Tuesday, and sub-60F dewpoints could persist until midweek.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Warmer and more humid conditions return mid- week, with thunderstorm chances returning by Thursday.

As the week continues, a broad upper-level trough will begin to form over the Great Lakes and track towards the Mid-Atlantic by Thursday. As the associated surface low approaches the region, moist air from the south will flow into the area, bringing back an increase in humidity & temperatures back to late-August normals. As this low tracks through, expect shower & thunderstorm chances to increase as the associated cold front tracks offshore by the end of the week. Medium-range severe indices still maintain a low-end non-zero chance for stronger convection as this front moves through. Temperatures rise back into the upper 80s by Thursday.
s.avn:
Low pressure tracking along a stalled boundary to our southeast will push showers and some embedded storms into the region later this morning. Still lots of uncertainty with just how much rain falls and how intense any showers will be that reach the terminals. Low clouds will also be an issue, which makes restrictions likely. Though, if the showers and up being less intense, it is possible that conditions remain low-end MVFR rather than dropping to IFR. Latest TAFs reflect some uncertainty there, with areas further east a bit more likely than those to the west.

Another low pressure system over the Great Lakes region will push a cold front through the region later tonight. This will bring another line of shower and storms along with it, persisting through the early overnight hours. This could bring another period of restrictions. In the wake of the rain, fog is expected to develop at CHO and probably MRB as well Sunday morning. It is possible it could creep into IAD as well.

Predominantly VFR conditions are anticipated across terminals Sunday through Wednesday. Winds on Sunday through Tuesday remain out of the WNW to NW, gusting up to 20 knots during the afternoon hours (except CHO which will be 5 to 8 knots lower).

Beginning Wednesday afternoon, winds shift out of the south, but should be a bit weaker. Additionally, a few showers and thunderstorms become possible ahead of an approaching cold front that could bring temporarily reduced conditions into the evening and perhaps overnight hours.
s.mar:
Easterly winds expected today around 5 to 10 knots with gusts up to 15 knots as low pressure slides by to our southeast. SCA conditions are not expected, however any heavier showers or storms could bring down gusts around 20 to 25 knots at times throughout the day. These would likely come in short bursts, and should be few and far between. Another line of showers and storms moves in late tonight, but again should not bring any substantial wind gusts as we will be stable.

Winds turn out of the WNW Sunday through Tuesday, and should remain sub-SCA throughout that period. A few gusts near 18 knots are possible, especially further north, but not seeing a prolonged period enough to warrant an SCA at this time.

Winds shift southerly by Wednesday, with winds gusting above SCA thresholds later that evening in a classic southerly channeling event ahead of an approaching cold front.

Update on the current showers developing over southern MD and the VA Piedmont. Flooding threat remains limited, but will need to be monitored closely as the axis of heavier rain sets up throughout the morning.

Also updated aviation and marine discussions substantially to add more details on today's setup.

Locally, we are situated just downstream of the primary trough axis. Drier air should continue to advect in at low-levels within westerly flow over the course of the day, but some weak instability (around 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE) may develop by peak heating. Forecast soundings show very dry air in place at mid-levels along with a weakness/slightly warmer layer likely tied to large scale subsidence. CAMs suggest that a few showers or even a thunderstorm or two may potentially form later this afternoon, especially to the east of the Blue Ridge as the upper trough axis moves through. However, most locations are expected to remain dry. While conditions overall appear relatively hostile toward deeper convection developing, if a deeper storm were to develop, there could be a conditional threat for some small hail, given cooler, drier thermal profiles, minimal CAPE below the freezing level, and straight line hodographs with very little low-level shear, but respectable shear (around 35-40 kts 0-6 km) through the mid- upper levels. Any showers or storms should quickly dissipate with loss of daytime heating this evening.

As an upper level ridge over the midwest begins to flatten in amplitude, southwesterly mid-level winds advect tropical moisture northward into our region. As this tropical air mass moves through our region, humid conditions return through the end of the week. A weak piece of shortwave energy is also expected to approach the region Wednesday evening, which could spark a few storms in the evening/overnight hours.

As the upper trough over the northeast CONUS starts to push more offshore on Wednesday, we will see some subtle rises in 500 hPa heights. This, paired with a developing southerly surface wind pattern will yield more typical August warmth and increased humidity. Expect high temperatures in the upper 80s to near 90, along with dew points increasing into the low to mid 60s. The ridge doesn't will only be overhead during the day though, as another piece of shortwave energy rotates through late in the evening into the overnight. There won't be a lot of instability left over when this rotates through, but there may be enough to pop off a few overnight showers.

By Thursday, after a day of southerly flow ahead of an approaching cold front from the west, humidity will jump markedly. Temperatures remain in the mid 80s to low 90s, but dew points jump into the upper 60s and perhaps even into the low 70s. The aforementioned cold front will come through during the day Thursday. If timed during peak heating, there could be around 1000 to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE to work with. The shortwave is subtle, with only about 20 kts of deep layer shear showing up in most guidance. So, the threat for organized severe weather is rather low. Additionally, this is not one of the extreme heat/humidity setups, so thinking is a more isolated wind threat at this point. Latest AI medium-range guidance generally agrees, painting anywhere from 5 to 15 percent severe probs over the region depending on which one you use.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry conditions anticipated through early portions of the week.

In the wake of some morning shower activity across northeastern Maryland, any residual clouds have largely cleared out. The air mass remains seasonably dry with dew points holding steady in the mid 50s to low 60s.

High pressure will continue to slowly build toward the area through Tuesday, resulting in dry conditions and lower humidity levels. High temperatures will generally be in the upper 70s to mid 80s, with overnight lows in the 50s to lower 60s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Warmer and more humid conditions return mid- week, with thunderstorm chances returning by Thursday.

Heading into Wednesday, dry, pleasant conditions continue into much of the day and afternoon. As an upper level ridge over the midwest begins to flatten in amplitude, southwesterly mid-level winds advect tropical moisture northward into our region. As this tropical air mass moves through our region, humid conditions return through the end of the week. A weak piece of shortwave energy is also expected to approach the region Wednesday evening, which could spark a few storms in the evening/overnight hours.

As the upper trough over the northeast CONUS starts to push more offshore on Wednesday, we will see some subtle rises in 500 hPa heights. This, paired with a developing southerly surface wind pattern will yield more typical August warmth and increased humidity. Expect high temperatures in the upper 80s to near 90, along with dew points increasing into the low to mid 60s. The ridge doesn't will only be overhead during the day though, as another piece of shortwave energy rotates through late in the evening into the overnight. There won't be a lot of instability left over when this rotates through, but there may be enough to pop off a few overnight showers.

By Thursday, after a day of southerly flow ahead of an approaching cold front from the west, humidity will jump markedly. Temperatures remain in the mid 80s to low 90s, but dew points jump into the upper 60s and perhaps even into the low 70s. The aforementioned cold front will come through during the day Thursday. If timed during peak heating, there could be around 1000 to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE to work with. The shortwave is subtle, with only about 20 kts of deep layer shear showing up in most guidance. So, the threat for organized severe weather is rather low. Additionally, this is not one of the extreme heat/humidity setups, so thinking is a more isolated wind threat at this point. Latest AI medium-range guidance generally agrees, painting anywhere from 5 to 15 percent severe probs over the region depending on which one you use.

By Friday, the front should be mostly offshore. However, there is still the slight chance that it lingers somewhere near/east of I-95, which could bring renewed afternoon storm chances.

- 2) Turning more warm and humid through Thursday, with increasing thunderstorm chances, before high pressure returns for the weekend.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...High pressure will support tranquil weather through Tuesday.

A vertically stacked area of low pressure remains centered over southwestern Quebec. This ties to a occluded frontal system which extends along the New England coast into the eastern Carolinas. While characterized by 500-mb height departures on the order of 2 to 2.5 standard deviations below climatology, any direct impacts remain off to the north. For the local area, daytime heating has fostered the development of a stratocumulus deck. Although the GOES-19 visible channel does show some enhancement on satellite near I-95, there is quite a bit of dry air in the 700-500 mb layer which is limiting cloud top heights. The forecast will remain dry amidst this mix of clouds and sun. With enough boundary layer mixing, westerly winds should top out in the 15 to 20 mph range this afternoon. Forecast highs top out in the upper 70s to mid 80s, with mainly 60s to mids 70s for mountain locations.

Given dew points are in the 50s to low 60s, this dry air mass will support a decent cooling trend into the evening and overnight period. Winds remain light overnight as an anticyclone approaches from the Ohio Valley. Coupled with mainly clear skies, ample radiational cooling effects are likely which will favor 50s to low 60s.

The dome of high pressure remains in charge on Tuesday while the earlier front stays along the southeastern U.S. coast. This does come with an uptick in temperatures as the upper low lifts poleward which yields a height/thickness rise. Northwesterly gradients persist which helps maintain the lower humidity air mass. High temperatures on Tuesday are expected to top out in the low/mid 80s (upper 60s to 70s in the mountains). Tuesday night's lows will rise a bit given some added cloud cover.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Turning more warm and humid through Thursday, with increasing thunderstorm chances, before high pressure returns for the weekend.

The early week surface anticyclone begins to depart off the Atlantic coast by Wednesday. Clockwise flow around this exiting high pressure will usher in a southerly wind through the day. Some afternoon gusts up to 20 mph are possible depending on the degree of vertical mixing. High temperatures begin to approach the 90 degree mark, which comes with a gradual uptick in dew points/humidity levels. This is accompanied by the expected increase in overnight warmth.

An upper trough currently crossing southern Saskatchewan is likely to impact the local weather by Wednesday and Thursday. While much of Wednesday should be dry, some weak/modest perturbations in the flow ahead of the trough could bring some late day showers. However, the more notable forcing from this trough does not arrive until Thursday. A mixture of thermodynamic ingredients are in place for this event, but it is difficult to say if these will align or not. While instability levels increase with the uptick in low-level moisture, vertical shear generally averages around 20 to 25 knots. Some isolated severe thunderstorms are possible, but the overall setup lends itself to a number of question marks. However, Thursday does look like a typical late August day with a front encroaching on the region. This would be characterized by numerous showers and some thunderstorms, many of which will bring heavy downpours and frequent lightning. Any thunderstorm threat may linger into the night with the cold front being a late arriver.

Heading into Friday and the weekend, an upper-level trough begins to move directly over our forecast area. With highs remaining in the mid 70s to 80s, warm and humid conditions return to our region. This airmass brings with it chances for showers and thunderstorms Friday afternoon and evening.

On Saturday and Sunday, the upper air wave pattern flattens into zonal flow. Depending on whether this synoptic pattern holds, Saturday and Sunday could see a few diurnally driven showers and thunderstorms.

VFR conditions are expected to prevail through at least Tuesday, if not longer. This is in response to an approaching area of high pressure which settles over the region by Tuesday. Winds will be somewhat variable in direction at times given this ridge of high pressure. As this system pushes offshore, southerly winds return for Wednesday with afternoon gusts up to 15 to 20 knots. Some showers may impact the terminals by Wednesday evening/night, a few of which may warrant some restrictions. With a cold front impacting the area on Thursday, sub-VFR conditions are expected. A few strong to severe thunderstorms are possible that afternoon/evening. Restrictions could linger into Thursday night with the cold front moving through overnight.

Depending on the frontal timing, showers may linger into Friday which would favor a few additional restrictions. High pressure moves in for the weekend which should yield more favorable flying conditions.
s.mar:
Winds will be somewhat variable through this evening before turning more northerly tonight as the dome of high pressure pushes in from the west. Northerly channeling effects could bring a few 18 knot gusts to wider portions of the Chesapeake Bay tonight. Wind gusts drop off through Wednesday morning before another ramp up ensues for the second half of Wednesday. Southerly channeling effects will likely warrant Small Craft Advisories across portions of the waters through Wednesday night. With the cold front not arriving until late Thursday, there are some hints of some 15 to 20 knot southerly gusts on Thursday. This also comes with the risk of stronger convection, many capable of needing Special Marine Warnings.

Scattered showers & thunderstorms Friday could also create locally gusty winds over the waters, perhaps necessitating a few SMWs.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong thunderstorms are possible Thursday amidst increasingly warm and humid conditions.

A shortwave trough passing to the north has resulted in a robust cumulus and stratocumulus field (thickest north) this afternoon. Most of these clouds should dissipate with sunset due to loss of heating and local height rises. Low humidity air sticks around through tonight. Surface high pressure will be nearly overhead, with light winds allowing low temperatures to drop to the mid 50s to mid 60s. Patchy fog is possible, especially west of the Blue Ridge, although passing clouds may prevent full radiational cooling.

High pressure will depart off the coast Wednesday with surface winds turning southerly. Some afternoon gusts up to 20 mph are possible depending on the degree of vertical mixing. High temperatures will tick up into the upper 80s to near 90, which comes with an increase in dew points/humidity levels. It looks like the atmosphere will remain capped most of the day, although a pop up shower along the terrain could occur in the afternoon. Moisture return increases overnight, which could result in some scattered showers and storms. However, most of the 12Z guidance has very limited to no coverage.

More notable forcing arrives Thursday as an upper level trough and surface cold front approach from the northwest. However, these forcing features may be somewhat displaced from the local area during peak diurnal heating. The front likely lags to the northwest while the strongest forcing with the trough passes to the north. A secondary shortwave may approach but not until the evening. Thus there remains some uncertainty in the coverage and timing of any showers and thunderstorms. There is also some question on instability as there may be a fair amount of cloud cover around and perhaps some lingering morning showers. If everything were to come together though, moderate instability combined with shear of 20-30 kt could result in some strong to locally severe thunderstorms with damaging winds being the primary threat. Before and storms arrive, it will be warm and humid with highs in the mid 80s to near 90.

The cold front may bisect the area by Friday morning while the mid/upper level trough axis remains to the west. Some showers and thunderstorms will continue to be possible near and south of the front, although the risk for strong thunderstorms is lower.


KEY MESSAGE 2...After a brief cool down this weekend, hot weather will return next week.

The front may weaken or stall to the south this weekend while high pressure builds eastward from the Great Lakes to St. Lawrence Valley. Overall, the high should be strong enough to shove most of the moisture to the south, although there is some lingering potential for showers across southern areas on Saturday. The coolest temperatures are also most likely Saturday, with warming conditions expected Sunday as the high pushes off to the east. Upper level ridging also builds eastward on Sunday. Combined with return flow around the high, hotter conditions are expected early next week with high temperatures rising back into the 90s by Monday for many locations. A diurnally driven shower or thunderstorm is possible, but the ridging should suppress most precipitation.
s.avn:
VFR conditions are expected through this evening, although some cumulus/stratocumulus ceilings are possible (except CHO). Northwest winds up to 10 kt become light and variable or calm tonight. Fog/BR is possible at MRB late tonight, but dense fog appears less likely at this time.

As high pressure pushes offshore Wednesday, southerly winds return for Wednesday with afternoon gusts up to 15 to 20 knots possible. Some isolated to scattered showers may impact the terminals by Wednesday evening/night.

A cold front will approach the region on Thursday. A few strong to severe storms are possible that afternoon/evening, with gusty winds being the primary threat. As the front stalls nearby Thursday night, some MVFR to IFR ceilings or visibilities may develop.

Prevailing VFR conditions are expected on Friday and Saturday. Temporary drops to sub VFR conditions may be possible in thunderstorms on Friday. Light and variable winds are forecast for Friday. Winds shift out of the north to northeast on Saturday and are expected to remain light.
s.mar:
High pressure nearby is providing prevailing northwest winds this afternoon, although the flow is light enough that onshore winds have developed in some areas. Winds remain light and variable tonight, then become southerly Wednesday as the high departs offshore. Winds may start increasing in the afternoon, but the greatest probability for 20 kt gusts will arrive Wednesday evening and night due to channeling. An advisory has been issued for many locations along the Chesapeake.

With the next cold front not arriving until late Thursday, there are some hints of some 15 to 20 knot southerly gusts continuing on Thursday. The front will also bring the risk of strong, gusty thunderstorms, although these may not arrive until late in the day.

Sub-small craft advisory level winds are expected on Friday as a cold front moves in from the north west. Special Marine Warning could be possible as Friday's thunderstorms move over the waters. Sub-SCA level north to northeasterly winds are forecast for Saturday.
s.tide: Increasing southerly flow develops Wednesday into Wednesday night, leading to rising water levels. Most locations will only see action stages, but Annapolis could approach minor flood stage early Thursday morning.
