- 1) Increasing risk for severe thunderstorms amidst increasingly warm and humid conditions ahead of an approaching cold front.

- 2) Drier conditions heading into the weekend, with increasingly hot & humid conditions at the start of next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Increasing risk for severe thunderstorms amidst increasingly warm and humid conditions ahead of an approaching cold front.

Today marks a shift in the weather pattern from recent days as high pressure pushes offshore. This will turn winds out of the south, yielding a much more humid tropical air mass. The process of moisture transfer will just be starting today, so dew points only jump back into the mid 60s, but it will set the stage for the pre-frontal environment on Thursday. Highs today reach the mid to upper 80s for most, and the 70s in the higher elevations. It looks like the atmosphere should remain capped most of the day, although a pop up shower along the terrain could occur in the afternoon.

Moisture return increases overnight along a northward-lifting warm front, which could result in some scattered showers and storms overnight into Thursday morning. How much activity occurs overnight could have implications on the rest of the day, but probabilities remain rather low overall. At any rate, there will likely be some cloud cover at the very least. Whether or not this clears out later in the morning will have large implications on the overall severe threat.

More notable forcing arrives Thursday as an upper level trough and surface cold front approach from the northwest. However, these forcing features may be somewhat displaced from the local area during peak diurnal heating. The front will lag to our northwest, while the strongest forcing with the trough passes to the north. A secondary shortwave may approach but not until the evening. Thus there remains some uncertainty in the coverage and timing of any showers and thunderstorms. There could even be two rounds, dependent upon whether that morning cloud cover clears out early enough. If everything does come together though, moderate instability combined with deep-layer shear of around 25-35 kt could result in some severe thunderstorms. Mid- level lapse rate don't look all that unimpressive, so in addition to the primary damaging wind threat, large hail is also going to be a possibility. Wouldn't even be shocked to see a supercell or two. Some of the more aggressive model guidance, particularly the HRRR, does paint some rather impressive veering low-level wind profiles over the region in forecast soundings. If this scenario were to come to fruition, there would also be a non-zero tornado threat. Not that this is the most likely scenario, but worth mentioning at this point. It is also worth noting that the Storm Prediction Center did drop the Slight Risk area southward into our area, particularly along the MD/PA border east of the Blue Ridge. This matches the thinking here in an increased severe weather threat compared to our thinking the past few days.

The cold front may bisect the area by Friday morning while the mid/upper level trough axis remains to the west. Some showers and thunderstorms will continue to be possible near and south of the front, although the risk for strong thunderstorms is lower.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier conditions heading into the weekend, with increasingly hot & humid conditions at the start of next week.

Upper-level zonal flow returns over the Mid-Atlantic by Saturday in the wake of the cold front. A few diurnal showers & thunderstorms remain possible throughout the early weekend, but overall conditions become progressively drier as surface high pressure tracks across the Blue Ridge. Temperatures remain seasonable during this period, with daily highs ranging in the mid-to-upper 80s during the day.

Towards the start of next week, broad upper-level ridging starts to build over the Southeast. Combined with relatively moist air aloft, heat & humidity here will start to feel like peak summertime conditions once again, with dewpoints ranging in the low-70s over the metros and highs in the lower 90s by next Monday. 850 mb temp anomalies show this pattern only continuing to build in the long- term, which may lead to a warmer-than-average start to September should this pattern persist. Thunderstorm chances could gradually increase during this period as ridging transitions offshore. Regardless, anticipate a return to summertime heat & humidity here in the Mid-Atlantic should this upper-level setup persist.
s.avn:
As high pressure pushes offshore today, southerly winds will gust up to 15 to 20 knots. Some isolated to scattered showers may impact the terminals by Wednesday evening/night.

A cold front will approach the region on Thursday. A few strong to severe storms are possible that afternoon/evening, with gusty winds being the primary threat. There are even some indications that a couple of rounds of storms are possible, one in the early afternoon and one later in the evening.

As the front stalls nearby Thursday night, some MVFR to IFR ceilings or visibilities may develop. Showers and storms could even linger into Friday, but unsure if this would impact any of the terminals at this time, as the front should stall east of I-95 and focus that threat east of most of the terminals. Can't completely rule out some restrictions though.

Prevailing VFR conditions are expected Saturday. Winds shift out of the north to northeast on Saturday and are expected to remain light.
s.mar:
Winds become southerly today as high pressure pushes offshore, and will increase during the afternoon. The greatest probability for 20 kt gusts will arrive this evening/tonight due to channeling. An SCA has been issued for many locations along the Chesapeake.

With the next cold front not arriving until late Thursday, there are some hints of some 15 to 20 knot southerly gusts continuing on Thursday. The front will also bring the risk of strong, gusty thunderstorms, which would likely necessitate SMWs. There are even some indications that a couple of rounds of storms are possible, one in the early afternoon and one later in the evening.

Sub-small craft advisory level winds are expected on Friday as a cold front moves in from the north west. Special Marine Warning could be possible as Friday's thunderstorms move over the waters. Sub-SCA level north to northeasterly winds are forecast for Saturday.
s.tide: Increasing southerly flow develops through tonight, leading to rising water levels. Most locations will only see action stages, but Annapolis could approach minor flood stage early Thursday morning.

s.chg: There have been no significant changes to the forecast for this cycle.

- 1) Severe thunderstorms are possible Thursday amidst increasingly warm and humid conditions.

- 2) Drier conditions heading into the weekend, with increasingly hot & humid conditions at the start of next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms are possible Thursday amidst increasingly warm and humid conditions.

High pressure is pushing off the coast this afternoon, resulting in locally gusty southerly winds and temperatures pushing into the mid to upper 80s. Some models continue to show a few showers popping in southwestern portions of the CWA later this afternoon and evening, but so far cumulus appear shallow on satellite imagery.

Moisture return increases overnight along a northward-lifting warm front, which could result in some isolated to scattered showers and storms. There's not a lot of model agreement on where or when (or even if) this convection develops, although elevated instability does gradually advect northward. There is slightly more consensus closer to the Chesapeake Bay on either side of sunrise, so that is where the mentionable chances reside for now.

More notable forcing arrives Thursday as an upper level trough and surface cold front approach from the northwest. However, these forcing features may be somewhat displaced from the local area during peak diurnal heating. The front will lag to our northwest, while the strongest forcing with the trough passes to the north. A secondary shortwave may approach but not until the evening. Thus there remains some uncertainty in the coverage and timing of any showers and thunderstorms, although there is some model consensus on development along a surface trough between the I-95 and I-81 corridors by mid afternoon. Residual cloud cover and any leftover morning showers could put a damper on instability. Then, especially for areas near and east of I-95, convection may not arrive until after sunset, when it could be weakening. However, if everything does come together, moderate instability combined with deep-layer shear of around 25-35 kt could result in some severe thunderstorms. Damaging winds are the primary threat. Moderate mid level lapse rates, strong winds in the upper atmosphere, and relatively light low level winds could also result in some severe level hail. While there is some low level curvature to hodographs, it's unclear if there will be sufficient shear for a tornado threat. We will have to monitor heavy rain potential as well, since relatively unidirectional flow relative to the surface trough could result in some training (hinted at by splotches of higher QPF in some CAMs). At the moment, this threat appears higher to our north, and precipitable water values and warm cloud depths are relatively modest. Thus no Flood Watches are planned at this time. While some showers and storms may linger into the night, the severe weather threat should be winding down by mid to late evening.

The cold front may bisect the area by Friday morning while the mid/upper level trough axis remains to the west. Some showers and thunderstorms will continue to be possible near and south of the front, although the risk for strong thunderstorms is lower.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier conditions heading into the weekend, with increasingly hot & humid conditions at the start of next week.

Heights begin to rise Saturday as an upper level low drifts eastward into northern Quebec. Surface high pressure will build from the Great Lakes toward the northern Mid Atlantic, which should push the cold front south enough to keep most areas dry. However, some convergence along the Appalachians could result in an isolated afternoon shower. Temperatures remain seasonable during this period, with daily highs ranging in the mid-to- upper 80s during the day.

Towards the start of next week, broad upper-level ridging starts to build over the Southeast. Combined with relatively moist air aloft, heat & humidity here will start to feel like peak summertime conditions once again. Temperatures rising to the lower to mid 90s combined with increasing dew points may result in heat index values in the upper 90s to just above 100. 850 mb temp anomalies show this pattern only continuing to build in the long- term, which may lead to a warmer-than- average start to September should this pattern persist. Thunderstorm chances could gradually increase during this period as ridging transitions offshore, although forcing appears minimal through at least Tuesday. Regardless, anticipate a return to summertime heat & humidity here in the Mid- Atlantic.
s.avn:
High pressure pushing offshore is resulting in some gusts up to 20 kt this afternoon. A warm front lifting north tonight may bring some isolated to scattered showers and perhaps a thunderstorm. The greatest model consensus in closer to the Chesapeake Bay a few hours either side of sunrise. Thus included PROB30 groups for BWI and MTN.

A cold front will approach the region on Thursday. A few strong to severe storms are possible during the afternoon/evening, with gusty winds being the primary threat. Timing and coverage are still a bit uncertain, so only have PROB30 mentioned in the TAFs for now.

As the front stalls nearby Thursday night, some MVFR to IFR ceilings or visibilities may develop. Current models seem to be favoring fog, especially west of the metro areas. Showers and storms could even redevelop Friday, but unsure if this would impact any of the terminals (CHO would have the highest chance).

Prevailing VFR conditions are expected Saturday through Monday as high pressure builds across the area.
s.mar:
High pressure moving off the coast is resulting in increasing southerly winds this afternoon. While some locations are starting to near 20 kt gusts, the greatest probability will arrive this evening/tonight due to channeling. A Small Craft Advisory remains in effect from 6 PM through 6 AM for many locations along the Chesapeake Bay.

With the next cold front not arriving until late Thursday, there are some hints of some 15 to 20 knot southerly gusts continuing or renewing Thursday, especially by afternoon. Another SCA may be needed. The front will also bring the risk of strong, gusty thunderstorms, which would likely necessitate SMWs. Some thunderstorms are even possible around sunrise, but the greatest risk for severe thunderstorms will be during the late afternoon and evening.

Sub-small craft advisory level winds are expected on Friday as a cold front moves in from the northwest. While some additional thunderstorms are possible, the greater risk may be south of Maryland. Sub-SCA level north to northeasterly winds are forecast for Saturday, becoming southerly Sunday as high pressure pushes to the east.
s.tide: Increasing southerly flow continues through tonight, leading to rising water levels. Most locations will only see action stages, but Annapolis could approach minor flood stage early Thursday morning. With the latest forecast only barely reaching flood stage, will hold off on an advisory until confidence in the water level trends increases.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms are possible Thursday amidst increasingly warm and humid conditions.

Current surface analysis depicts a warm front still to our south over the VA/NC border, as well as a cold front over the Ohio Valley extending southward from the parent low in Quebec. Aloft, latest satellite imagery depicts an influx of moisture into the region this morning in response to a subtle jetlet within the main trough axis. This is producing some showers to our northeast of southeastern PA and into NJ as well. This activity is building slowly southwest this morning, and is still expected to build into northeast MD in the next several hours leading up to sunrise.

More notable forcing arrives later today as the main upper level trough and surface cold front approach from the northwest. However, these forcing features may be somewhat displaced from the local area during peak diurnal heating. The front will lag to our northwest, while the strongest forcing with the trough passes to the north. A secondary shortwave may approach but not until the evening. Thus there remains some uncertainty in the coverage and timing of any showers and thunderstorms, although there is some model consensus on development along a surface trough between the I-95 and I-81 corridors by mid afternoon. Residual cloud cover and any leftover morning showers could put a damper on instability. Then, especially for areas near and east of I-95, convection may not arrive until after sunset, when it could be weakening. However, if everything does come together, moderate instability combined with deep-layer shear of around 25-35 kt could result in some severe thunderstorms. Damaging winds are the primary threat. Moderate mid level lapse rates, strong winds in the upper atmosphere, and relatively light low level winds could also result in some severe level hail. As mentioned in previous forecasts, model guidance is still depicting some decent low-level curvature to hodographs, especially along the MD/PA border in northeast MD. The Storm Prediction Center has actually added this area in to a two- percent tornado threat today, which makes a lot of sense, should things all come together. We will have to monitor heavy rain potential as well, since relatively unidirectional flow relative to the surface trough could result in some training (hinted at by splotches of higher QPF in some CAMs). At the moment, this threat appears higher to our north, and precipitable water values and warm cloud depths are relatively modest. Thus no Flood Watches are planned at this time. While some showers and storms may linger into the night, the severe weather threat should be winding down by mid to late evening.

The cold front may bisect the area by Friday morning while the mid/upper level trough axis remains to the west. Some showers and thunderstorms will continue to be possible near and south of the front, although the risk for strong thunderstorms is lower.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Turning drier this weekend, with increasingly hot and humid conditions for early/mid next week.

The late week cold front is expected to stall along the southeastern U.S. coastline throughout the weekend. As this occurs, broad surface high pressure is likely to extend from the southern Mid-Atlantic up to New England. This configuration will support tranquil weather this weekend with seasonable temperatures. Mid-level heights (585 to 589 dm) remain slightly above average which does keep temperatures on the warmer side. Humidity levels drop a bit to start the weekend, but do begin to come up some as winds shift to southerly on the back side of the exiting surface ridge. This eventually sets up for a hot and humid period into next week which also marks the conclusion of Meteorological Summer (June 1-August 31).

A persistent mid/upper ridge across the southern tier of the country is forecast to flex northward in time. Global ensembles generally agree on this evolution, but vary with details along the northern edge of this ridge. The net result will be another round of hot temperatures along with increasing humidity. During the early to mid- week period, forecast highs rise into the low/mid 90s, with heat indices between 98 and 103 degrees. This could inch closer to the 105 degree heat index mark by Tuesday and Wednesday which is Heat Advisory criteria for locations east of the Blue Ridge. Despite all of the heat and humidity, daily thunderstorm chances could be more limited if the area is underneath the upper ridge. However, these details will likely become better resolved in a few days.

Looking a bit further ahead, the Day 6 to 10 outlook from the Climate Prediction Center favors above average chances for continued heat to linger into subsequent days.
s.avn:
A warm front lifting north tonight may bring some isolated to scattered showers and perhaps a thunderstorm later this morning, particularly at BWI and MTN, hence the PROB30s there during that timeframe.

A cold front will approach the region today and push through tonight into Friday. A few strong to severe storms are possible during the afternoon/evening, with gusty winds being the primary threat. Starting to get a little bit more clarity on timing for storms, so tried to hone in on the areas with highest confidence (MRB, IAD, MTN, and BWI). Still PROB30s at DCA and CHO. Storms could be slow to push through, so there may be some prolonged period of restrictions for those that do get storms today.

As the front stalls nearby tonight, some MVFR to IFR ceilings or visibilities may develop. Current models seem to be favoring fog, especially west of the metro areas. Showers and storms could even redevelop Friday, but unsure if this would impact any of the terminals (CHO would have the highest chance).

VFR conditions are expected Saturday through Monday Monday, which comes with a dry forecast. Initial winds will be out of the south before an eventual shift to westerly by early next week. Relatively weak gradients should support peak gusts around 5 to 10 knots.

- 1) Warm and humid conditions combined with a cold front will lead to severe thunderstorms across portions of the area later today.

- 2) Turning drier this weekend, with increasingly hot and humid conditions for early/mid next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms are possible Thursday amidst increasingly warm and humid conditions. Still dealing with a few spotty showers and thunderstorms this morning as a result of a subtle jet streak within the mean upper level trough axis. The bulk of this activity has been confined to central and northeast MD with even a few blips east of Charlottesville, VA. Expect this spotty shower and thunderstorm activity to continue over the next 2-3 hrs across these areas with a lull into the early afternoon period before better forcing arrives. Any of these thunderstorms will contain 20-30 mph of wind, small, hail, lightning, and locally heavy rainfall. Behind this jetlet/jet streak, skies have already started to clear. The warm front is now up toward the Richmond, VA area with cold front extending from the OH/PA border south to areas just west of the Ohio River.

With this clearing, expect the atmosphere to reload ahead of the incumbent cold frontal boundary. As it stands now, guidance has backed up the timing a bit heading into the late afternoon and period. This is due largely in part to the actual cold front being disjointed from the upper level trough and any KEY MESSAGE 2... additional pieces of shortwave energy ahead of the main boundary. Coverage as a result will be fairly tricky with a mashup of spotty to scattered storms during the afternoon transitioning into some organization into the evening hours as the front drops in. Latest HRRR, NAMnest, ARW, and even the HREF show a scattering of storms initiating west of Blue Ridge and along the western shore of the bay between 2-5pm before advancing east between 5-10pm. Damaging winds will be the main threat with storms today given 25-35 kts of deep layer shear and modest instability values up of 1000 j/kg. Moderate mid level lapse rates (6.5-8 C/km), strong winds in the upper atmosphere, and relatively light low level winds could also result in some severe level hail. Given relatively unidirectional flow relative to the surface trough could result in some training (hinted at by splotches of higher QPF in some CAMs from Baltimore, MD points northeast). No Flood Watches are planned at this time, but will be something to monitor given how things evolve this afternoon. While some showers and storms may linger into the night, the severe weather threat should be winding down after 9-10pm.

As a result, expect additional showers and thunderstorms during the peak heating period, especially along and south of the front. Highest probabilities for severe weather appear to be south of I-66/US-50 across southern MD, the VA Piedmont, and northern neck of VA. Damaging winds will be the main threat along with locally heavy rainfall. Coverage once again will be scattered, but highly dependent on where the front resides and if any cloud cover lingers across the region.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Turning drier this weekend, with increasingly hot and humid conditions for early/mid next week.

The late week cold front is expected to stall along the southeastern U.S. coastline throughout the weekend. As this occurs, broad surface high pressure is likely to extend from the southern Mid-Atlantic up to New England. This configuration will support tranquil weather this weekend with seasonable temperatures. Mid-level heights (585 to 589 dm) remain slightly above average which does keep temperatures on the warmer side. Humidity levels drop a bit to start the weekend, but do begin to come up some as winds shift to southerly on the back side of the exiting surface ridge. This eventually sets up for a hot and humid period into next week which also marks the conclusion of Meteorological Summer (June 1-August 31).

A persistent mid/upper ridge across the southern tier of the country is forecast to flex northward in time. Global ensembles generally agree on this evolution, but vary with details along the northern edge of this ridge. The net result will be another round of hot temperatures along with increasing humidity. During the early to mid- week period, forecast highs rise into the low/mid 90s, with heat indices between 98 and 103 degrees. This could inch closer to the 105 degree heat index mark by Tuesday and Wednesday which is Heat Advisory criteria for locations east of the Blue Ridge. Despite all of the heat and humidity, daily thunderstorm chances could be more limited if the area is underneath the upper ridge. However, these details will likely become better resolved in a few days.

Looking a bit further ahead, the Day 6 to 10 outlook from the Climate Prediction Center favors above average chances for continued heat to linger into subsequent days.

VFR conditions will continue to prevail through this evening outside of thunderstorms. Some patches of MVFR have been noted north and east of BWI/MTN toward LNS/PHL given scattered showers and thunderstorms. Biggest threat with the spotty activity this morning will be erratic winds, small hail, lightning, and locally heavy rainfall. Expect these vicinity storms/showers to continue to pull north and east of BWI/MTN over the next 2-3 hrs.

A cold front will approach the region later this afternoon and evening before pushing south of the area Friday evening. A few strong to severe storms are possible during the afternoon/evening, with gusty winds being the primary threat. Eventually activity will shift east likely in a broken line between 21-02z/5-10pm. Storms could be slow to push through, so there may be some prolonged period of restrictions for those that do get storms today.

Shower and thunderstorm activity may linger into the front half of the overnight period prior to 6z/2am as the front stalls nearby. Some MVFR and IFR cigs and vsbys may develop as a result. Current guidance seems to be favor fog, especially west of the metro areas. Showers and storms could even redevelop Friday, but unsure if this would impact any of the terminals (CHO and perhaps DCA would have the highest chances).

VFR conditions are expected Saturday through Tuesday, which comes with a mostly dry forecast. Initial winds will be out of the south before an eventual shift to the west by early next week. Relatively weak gradients should support peak gusts around 5 to 15 knots.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Warm and humid conditions combined with a front will lead to severe storms across parts of area through this evening.

Turning active this afternoon and evening as spokes of shortwave energy/outflows ahead of an incoming cold front pass through the region. A Severe Thunderstorm Watch will likely be issued for portions of Maryland, northern-central VA, and the eastern WV Panhandle. Storms look to initialize along the bay breeze toward Baltimore/northeast MD and along a spoke of shortwave energy pivoting between I-81 and the Blue Ridge between now-4pm as the capping inversion buckles. Expect scattered to broken lines or clusters of convection pushing northeast from the Blue Ridge/I-81 impacting a large chunk of the metros between 5-9pm. Not everyone will see the storms this afternoon and evening, but something to monitor; especially if you have plans outdoors.

Hi-res guidance continues to struggle a bit in the evolution of storms this afternoon given the capping inversion and a outflow boundary zipping southwest from southern NJ/DE down along the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay. The lead shortwave is up across southern/central NJ with a secondary shortwave in the vicinity of southwest and central VA, and the main cold front back toward the Ohio River. It's a matter of how these remaining pieces of energy and lifting mechanisms interact, especially through the remaining peak heating period for severe weather development.

Damaging winds will be the main threat with storms today given 30-35 kts of deep layer shear and modest instability values up of 1000 j/kg. Moderate mid level lapse rates (7-8 C/km), strong winds in the upper atmosphere, and relatively light low level winds could also result in some severe level hail. As mentioned in previous forecasts, hi-res model guidance is still depicting some decent low- level curvature to hodographs, especially along the MD/PA border in northeast MD (due to perhaps a bay breeze/outflow from decaying storms over southern NJ) which may increase low level shear. The Storm Prediction Center continues a Slight Risk (Level 2 out of 5) for severe weather through this evening.

Heavy rainfall will remain a concern given multiple rounds of convection, especially over central and northeast MD where residual outflow boundaries could slow up convection. Given relatively unidirectional flow relative to the surface trough could result in some training (hinted at by splotches of higher QPF in some CAMs from Baltimore/Annapolis, MD points northeast; a secondary area down around Fredericksburg/Stafford/Culpeper, VA). No Flood Watches are planned at this time, but will need to be monitor given PWATS over 1.5"+ and likely rain rates of 0.50-1" in a 30-45 minute period. While some showers and storms may linger into the night, the severe weather threat should be winding down after 9-10pm.

As a result, expect additional showers and thunderstorms during the peak heating period, especially along and south of the front. KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry conditions this weekend with increasingly hot and humid conditions through next week.

Surface high pressure builds south into the Mid-Atlantic as winds shift quickly from north to easterly on Saturday. The high moves offshore Sunday, bringing the return of southerly winds. While we remain under broad troughing aloft, the presence of drier air at the surface will keep rain chances out of the forecast. Lingering humidity and building heat make for a warm and muggy weekend as highs reach the 80s to around 90F.

Models are generally in good agreement that a strong mid-level ridge builds across the southern U.S. and into the Mid-Atlantic during the early to middle part of next week. This brings us well above normal temperatures for late August as highs reach the low to mid 90s. Hot and humid conditions are likely as heat indices reach to the low 100s east of the Blue Ridge.

A series of mid-level disturbances will ride along the top of the ridge from the northern High Plains to the Northeast next week. Depending on the exact position of the ridge, some of these disturbances could be near or over our area come the middle to late part of the week. For now, Monday and Tuesday look mostly dry, though cannot rule out a stray thunderstorm or two given the humid/unstable atmosphere. By Wednesday, the upper ridge begins to retreat slightly, allowing the shortwave troughs to move over our area. Several of the AI models indicate increasing severe potential at some point Wednesday to Friday of next week, which is certainly possible given the high instability that will be in place, along with substantial upper-level support from any strong disturbance.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Cooler and less humid today; warmer and more humid Sunday with isolated afternoon thunderstorms.

High pressure will pass north of the area today and then off the Mid Atlantic coast Sunday. It will be slightly cooler and less humid today on NNW winds. As a result, most areas should remain dry and seasonable today, although an inverted surface trough may result in isolated showers along the Allegheny Mountains. Southerly flow returns Sunday, bringing increasing heat and humidity. A passing shortwave trough may support a few afternoon showers and thunderstorms about anywhere.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Late summer heat returns next week.

Guidance remains steadfast on late summer heat returning to end meteorological summer (June 1-August 31) and begin meteorological autumn (September 1-November 30).

A strong mid-level ridge will build across the southern CONUS and into the Mid-Atlantic beginning on Sunday, and persist through at least the middle of the week. Some guidance has been trending towards having the ridge axis a bit further south and west, which would lower heights a bit and introduce more chances for showers and thunderstorms at times in large scale NW flow aloft. This lends to a bit of spread in the temperature forecast, especially if any back- door surface cold fronts slide into the region by mid/late week.

Despite the uncertainties, it remains likely that high temperatures will reach the lower to middle 90s for much of the region for much of the upcoming week. Depending on smaller scale details, dew points could end up a little higher or lower than currently progged which will ultimately affect how high heat index values get. Values approaching Heat Advisory criteria (100-104 west of the Blue Ridge, 105-109 east of the Blue Ridge) can't be ruled out, but the more likely scenario is for heat indices a bit below those values.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Thunderstorm chances increase next week.

Disturbances rounding a ridge to the south and west in NW flow aloft will introduce shower and thunderstorm chances at times next week. The timing and amplitude of these waves have very low predictability beyond a couple days in advance (at best). But the general theme will be enhanced lift and shear clashing with an increasingly hot and unstable airmass over or near the Mid-Atlantic. AI/ML guidance has broad elevated probabilities of severe weather much of next week, the details (including timing and magnitude/potential impact) of which will be ironed out in the coming days.

It should be noted that there is a conditional potential for one or more organized clusters of strong to severe storms at some point next week. The most likely time currently appears to be around mid week, but changes are to be expected at this time range.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Warmer and more humid this afternoon with isolated thunderstorms.

A trough of low pressure will continue to initiate showers and scattered thunderstorms through the afternoon. The main threats will be heavy downpours and damaging winds. Some hail could occur in strongest thunderstorms. Any thunderstorms should dissipate quickly as we approach sunset.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Near-record early September heat expected.

A strong mid-level ridge over the Southern Plains will build toward the Mid-South during the early to middle part of the week. The latest trend is for the ridge to build further east into the TN Valley on Tuesday and Wednesday, then break down late in the week as as strong trough digs down from southern Canada. Having the ridge build to the east is going to keep hot and mostly dry conditions over the region for longer.

Despite the uncertainties, it remains likely that high temperatures will reach the lower to middle 90s for most of the area this week. Latest guidance indicates potential for temperatures in the upper 90s to near 100 by mid week, so long as it is not disrupted by cloud cover or convection. Depending on smaller scale details, dew points could end up a little higher or lower than currently progged which will ultimately affect how high heat index values get. Values approaching Heat Advisory criteria (100-104 west of the Blue Ridge, 105-109 east of the Blue Ridge) are possible Tuesday through Thursday. Similar heat and humidity could persist into Friday, but a lot of uncertainty for the late week temperature forecast due to possible convective systems moving through the area.

Temperatures may begin to moderate by next weekend as a cold front crosses the region.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Thunderstorm chances increase this week, but timing remains highly uncertain.

Disturbances rounding a ridge to the south and west in NW flow aloft will introduce shower and thunderstorm chances at times this week. Given the latest trend bringing the ridge further east during the middle of the week that should keep most of the convective systems over NY/PA and the Northeast Tuesday and Wednesday. s.chg: The potential for thunderstorms has significantly decreased today, so have trimmed back rain and thunder chances in the forecast.
s.key:
- 1) Thunderstorm chances increase this week, but timing and intensity remain uncertain.

- 2) Near-record early September heat expected.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Thunderstorm chances increase this week, but timing and intensity remain uncertain.

The focus of showers and thunderstorms today has now trended south of our area. Abundant mid-level cloud cover really prevented a lot of instability from developing and temperatures have been several degrees below forecast. The warmest conditions in Central VA where temps are near 90F. The forecast was updated to lower rain chances, with coverage of thunderstorms now expected to be low and focused in Central VA to southern MD. Any lingering showers dissipate this evening, with muggy and mostly cloudy skies tonight.

Looking at the rest of this week, the strong mid-level ridge positioned over the Mid-South will slowly push east toward the TN Valley. Numerous shortwave troughs / disturbances will round the top of the ridge, traversing the Great Lakes to Mid-Atlantic. This is going to bring us several rounds of thunderstorms, some of which could be strong to severe. The presence of strong lift and increasing shear, along with a hot and unstable airmass will produce an environment supporting of significant severe thunderstorms. The big caveat is timing. This setup can be very tricky to forecast exactly when these complexes of storms develop, and exactly where they track. The next shortwave is forecast to arrive Tuesday afternoon/evening. SPC has the northeast part of the forecast area in a Slight Risk (level 2 of 5), and a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) down into central VA. The latest 12Z guidance today has pushed back convection to Tuesday evening, and by that time we may avoid the worst of the severe weather impacts as storms arrive after peak daytime heating.

SPC also has a Slight Risk across the area Wednesday through Friday as several additional shortwave troughs are expected to traverse the region. At some point this week, most likely toward the end when a strong upper trough digs south from Canada, we will be in a much more favorable position for the upper forcing, instability, and daytime heating to align. The latest AI/ML guidance indicates the highest chance for this is now on Thursday, but I would not discount any day for potentially strong to severe thunderstorms at this time.

A cold front begins to slide south through the area Friday night into Saturday, bringing drier conditions and seasonal temperatures. Some thunderstorm chances linger south of I-66 on Saturday, then most of the area is dry and cooler come Sunday.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Near-record early September heat expected.

A strong ridge of high pressure over the southern Plains will build toward the Mid-South throughout this week. While humidity will be up to support several rounds of showers and thunderstorms, the heat will be up as well, especially Tuesday through Thursday. High temperatures are expected to reach the lower to middle 90s Tuesday and Wednesday, while making a possible run at 100 degrees in a few spots in parts of eastern and northeastern Virginia, near the metros, and along the eastern areas of the Blue Ridge Mountains on Thursday. Heat indices, because of the humidity, will be high as well. Heat indices should reach 100 to 103 degrees in scattered places in interior parts of our region on Tuesday. Expect more widespread 100 to 105 degree heat indices on Wednesday. To round it off, Thursday will have heat indices readings more so in the 103 to 105 degree ranges. These ranges can obviously change some by a few degrees warmer or a few degrees cooler. Either way, the point we want to make is it is going to be hot and humid through much of the week. Heat headlines could be issued soon regarding this 3-day stretch of heat and humidity. For the moment, monitor information at www.weather.gov. Even Friday, although may be cooler in terms of temperatures because of convection with a front, heat indices could still reach the 95 to 100 degree range in many places.
s.avn:
Not much in the way of convection is expected now this afternoon as a thick deck of mid-level clouds have kept conditions stable. A few showers or storms possible around CHO, otherwise other terminals could see a few light showers through this evening. Some patch fog or low clouds possible tonight, but not enough confidence to include in the TAFs.

Looking at the rest of this week, while VFR conditions are expected to prevail there could be periods of sub-VFR conditions. Each morning, low clouds could develop due to a very moist environment, then lift by late morning as daytime heating strengthens. There will be complexes of thunderstorms moving across the region, but timing is uncertain. The next one could arrive Tuesday evening into Tuesday night, then several more rounds possible again sometime Wednesday through Friday. Conditions improve this weekend as cold front moves through the region.
s.mar: Favorable marine conditions are expected through the week. Thunderstorm complexes are forecast to move from the Great Lakes to the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast at times this week. While the timing of exactly when this will occur remains uncertain, it is likely that Special Marine Warnings will be needed. Wind gusts in excess of 35- 40 knots and lightning strikes are going to be the main threats to mariners.

s.key:
- 1) Severe weather risk increasing for the second half of the week.

- 2) Record high minimum temperatures likely this week, but record high maximum temperatures appear unlikely now.

- 3) Heat & thunderstorms begin to decrease towards the start of the weekend.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe weather risk increasing for the second half of the week.

The upper ridge over the TN Valley is expected to build east over the next 36 hrs with heights cresting over the local area Wed afternoon. The ridge is expected to begin losing its grip over the area during the second half of the week as upper trough amplifies across the Northeast into the Mid Atlantic. Large scale height falls are not forecast to occur over the area until Wed night or Thu, so until then, forcing for upward vertical motion remains uncertain, but will have to monitor closely thunderstorm clusters over the eastern Great Lks and northern Mid-Atlantic as they could track across the area.

Today appears to be the hottest day of this week as westerly downslope flow results in compressional warming and drying. Thunderstorm chances this afternoon look almost NIL, however, guidance indicate a cluster of storms arriving this evening across northeast Maryland from southeast Pennsylvania. The timing suggests that convection will be weakening or probably sub-severe.

Wednesday's forecast seems to be the most uncertain with respect to thunderstorm chances. The late Tue night convection will leave a boundary across the area where it will stall as it fights the strong ridge to the south. Some thunderstorm development is possible across central PA and into northern MD. Timing seems like the biggest uncertainty, but some guidance suggest an early day complex rolling through the area.

By Thursday, cold front crossing the eastern Great Lks will likely ignite thunderstorm clusters over much of Pennsylvania that will likely track further south into the area at some point during the day or night with potential for severe wx given strengthening mid-level flow.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Record high minimum temperatures likely this week, but record high maximum temperatures appear unlikely now.

Guidance has had a high bias the past several days with respect to daytime highs. In addition, a slight cooling trend has also been seen which would make any record high maximum temperatures very unlikely, but the high humidity will keep minimum temperatures on the very warm side. Some record high minimums are possible or even likely this week. See Climate section below for actual numbers.

While it will be hot and humid this week, forecast heat indices appear will remain shy of heat advisory criteria.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Heat & thunderstorms begin to decrease towards the start of the weekend.

Beginning on Friday, temperatures decrease back to the lower 90s as the midweek cold front pushes to the south. Meanwhile, a strong surface high forming over Quebec will move into New England towards the start of the weekend. Associated with this will be signficant dry mid-level air moving across the Mid-Atlantic. As this feature continues to track south, subsidence across the East Coast combined with the dry mid-level air will stabilize conditions and reduce thunderstorm chances going into the weekend. As dewpoints drop, expect cooler, drier conditions closer to September normals, especially between Saturday and Sunday as temperatures continue to drop into the low-to-mid 80s during the day. A few spotty showers are not completely out of the question as low-level moisture persists over the mountains during this period, but overall expect progressively drier and cooler conditions across the Mid-Atlantic beginning Friday and into the holiday weekend.
s.avn:
Drying trend noted today, so kept TSRA out of the TAF forecast. A few evening showers are possible over northeast Maryland tonight, so added a TEMPO group for BWI and MTN.

Wednesday's forecast seem pretty uncertain at this time, but thunderstorm chances seem to increase late Wednesday afternoon through the end of work week.

Periods of sub-VFR conditions could persist through Friday as showers and thunderstorms track across the area primarily in the afternoon & evening hours. Some of these storms could become severe. Beginning Saturday, thunderstorm potential decreases overall, bringing conditions to terminals back to primarily VFR through the weekend. Westerly winds shift northerly on Saturday.
s.mar:
Winds below 10kt most of the time, but higher winds and waves can be expected near thunderstorms.

Winds remain below SCA thresholds on Friday before potentially increasing to marginal SCA conditions on Saturday. Northwest winds shift northerly early Saturday.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Daily severe weather threat through the end of the week.

Aloft, upper level ridging over the Ohio River Valley slowly shifts eastward this afternoon as a shortwave trough pivots over the forecast area. At the surface, a strong low pressure system tracks east across Canada through the end of the week with the associated fronts lingering near the forecast area. On Friday, the associated cold front tracks across the forecast area. Daily shower and thunderstorm chances continue through the end of the week across the forecast area with a hot and humid airmass yielding ample CAPE (1500-2500 J/kg)each afternoon.

For this afternoon, highest chances remain in NE Maryland where the Storm Prediction Center has a slight risk for severe weather. Primary hazard types are damaging wind gusts and large hail. The forecast for Wednesday through Friday remains uncertain regarding timing and thunderstorm coverage. Should thunderstorm development coincide with peak daytime heating, instability will yield strong to severe thunderstorms across the forecast area. The best chance for severe weather is on Thursday as the aforementioned cold front approaches the forecast area.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Hot and humid conditions yield possible record high minimum temperatures this week

A hot and humid airmass builds overhead this week with heat indices soaring into the upper 90s to low 100s each afternoon. Heat indices remain below criteria today and Wednesday, maxing out at around 100-103 along the metros. Coverage of heat indices exceeding criteria remains isolated and brief for tomorrow, so refrained from issuing a Heat Advisory for Wednesday. However, Thursday has the potential to be the warmest day of the week with heat indices forecast to exceed 100 in the valleys west of the Blue Ridge and 105 along the I-95 corridor. There remains some uncertainty regarding cloud coverage and convection on Thursday and how that effects the high temperatures. Should severe weather occur during the day, heat indices will struggle to reach criteria in the afternoon. However, if severe weather occurs later in the afternoon/evening, peak daytime heating will have high temperatures nearing the mid to upper 90s. Humid conditions continue overnight, with near record high minimum temperatures possible.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Decreasing heat & thunderstorm chances leading into Labor Day weekend.

On Saturday, high pressure builds at the surface over the Great Lakes further advancing a cold front south across our region. Drier air trailing behind this boundary will stabilize conditions and reduce thunderstorm chances through the weekend. Brief showers or thunderstorms remain possible as a few disturbances round the base of the upper-level trough, but overall, no hazardous weather is expected through the beginning of next week. Through the long weekend, day time temperatures continue to drop back into seasonable conditions for early September. With dew-points in the low to mid 60s, seasonable temperatures, and relatively low precipitation chances, Labor Day weekend is shaping up to be a pleasant September weekend.

Aloft, upper level ridging over the Ohio River Valley slowly shifts eastward this afternoon as a shortwave trough pivots over the forecast area. At the surface, a strong low pressure system tracks east across Canada through the end of the week with the associated fronts lingering near the forecast area. On Friday, the associated cold front tracks across the forecast area. Daily shower and thunderstorm chances continue through the end of the week across the forecast area with a hot and humid airmass yielding ample CAPE (1500-2500 J/kg)each afternoon.

The forecast for Wednesday through Friday remains uncertain regarding timing and thunderstorm coverage. Should thunderstorm development coincide with peak daytime heating, instability will yield strong to severe thunderstorms across the forecast area. The best chance for severe weather is on Thursday as the aforementioned cold front approaches the forecast area.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Hot and humid conditions yield possible record high minimum temperatures this week

A hot and humid airmass builds overhead this week with heat indices soaring into the upper 90s to low 100s each afternoon. Uncertainty with max heat index tomorrow due to potential convection and cloudcover. May end up with some advisories. However, Thursday has the potential to be the warmest day of the week with heat indices forecast to exceed 100 in the valleys west of the Blue Ridge and 105 along the I-95 corridor. Humid conditions continue overnight, with near record high minimum temperatures possible.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Decreasing heat & thunderstorm chances leading into Labor Day weekend.

On Saturday, high pressure builds at the surface over the Great Lakes further advancing a cold front south across our region. Drier air trailing behind this boundary will stabilize conditions and reduce thunderstorm chances through the weekend. Brief showers or thunderstorms remain possible as a few disturbances round the base of the upper-level trough, but overall, no hazardous weather is expected through the beginning of next week. Through the long weekend, day time temperatures continue to drop back into seasonable conditions for early September. With dew-points in the low to mid 60s, seasonable temperatures, and relatively low precipitation chances, Labor Day weekend is shaping up to be a pleasant September weekend.
s.avn:
Light winds and prevailing VFR conditions are expected across the terminals through Thursday. Showers and thunderstorms are possible in NE Maryland this evening, so have a PROB30 for KMTN and KBWI. For Wednesday and Thursday, daily shower and thunderstorm chances yield periods of sub-VFR conditions. Currently have a PROB30 for KIAD and KDCA for tomorrow evening for -TSRA. Convection will move into the TAF periods this evening and will be added at surrounding terminals.

Periods of sub-VFR conditions could persist Friday as showers and thunderstorms track across the area primarily in the afternoon & evening hours. Some of these storms could become severe. On Saturday afternoon and evening, terminals west of I-95 could experience sub- VFR conditions as thunderstorm and shower chances return in the afternoon and evening. Westerly winds shift north to northeasterly on Saturday with gusts below 20 kts.
s.mar:
SMWs possible this evening across upper Chesapeake Bay. Otherwise, light winds are expected over the waters through Thursday. Chances for strong to severe storms over the waters increases each day with SMWs possible. For Wednesday and Thursday, convection chances cover all waters.


On Friday and Saturday, winds below 15kts most of the time, but higher winds and waves could during afternoon and evening showers or thunderstorms. Westerly winds shift north to northeasterly on Saturday.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Daily severe weather threat through the end of the week.

Multiple rounds of thunderstorms, some likely severe with damaging winds, are likely today through Friday as upper level disturbances move from the Great Lks into the Mid Atlantic states. Already seen a small cluster of thunderstorms over south central Pennsylvania that will move through the area later this morning. Two additional rounds of thunderstorms seem likely today, one this afternoon, and a second one late this evening into the overnight hours tonight into Thursday. Thunderstorms will ride southeast along and north of a backdoor front currently pushing south through northern VA and southern MD as seen on TDWRs and wind shifts to the NE at IAD and DCA a couple of hours ago. The severe threat will not be necessarily tied to the afternoon and evening hours as record warm nighttime temperatures and high humidity yield strong instability and keep thunderstorms going strong well into the overnight hours.

By Friday, cold front should have cleared much of the forecast area causing a stabilizing effect limiting the risk of severe weather, but showers and thunderstorms will still be possible north of the sfc front.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Hot and humid conditions yield likely record high minimum temperatures this week.

Decent model agreement that areas south of US-33 and US-211 will see heat indices meet heat advisory criteria this afternoon. Based on yesterday's high temperature readings and greater confidence, issued Heat Advisories for the southern half of the fcst area.

Thursday's max temperature forecast has a lot more uncertainty due to potential for more convection. If convection doesn't materialize, more record high minimums are possible again today, but that doesn't seem likely at this time, except only at Charlottesville.

Record high minimum temperatures were set yesterday at IAD, DCA, and HGR. RERs were issued earlier.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Heat & thunderstorms begin to decrease heading into Labor Day weekend.

High pressure tracks southeast from the Great Lakes on Saturday, pushing a cold front further south of the region. This should bring a drop in heat & humidity across the Mid-Atlantic, with afternoon highs ranging in the mid-80s on Saturday. As mid-level dry air continues to track across the area, temperatures should continue to decrease as the weekened goes on. By the Labor Day holiday, it should feel relatively mild & dry, with dewpoints ranging in the upper-50s across the region.

Thunderstorm chances also begin to decrease past Friday once the cold front tracks to the south. A few showers & thunderstorms remain possible along the Blue Ridge as low-level moisture persists Saturday evening, but overall conditions should gradually clear as the weekend progresses. Surface high pressure tracks overhead by Monday, further reducing precipitation chances over the holiday.

Wind gusts stay below 15 knots Saturday night and Sunday, with northerly winds shifting northeast by Sunday.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Daily severe weather threat through the end of the week.

The original Mesoscale Convective Complex that moved out of Pennsylvania into our CWA late this morning has now bowed well south and east out over the Delmarva and central Chesapeake Bay and is aligned to the west and northwest into northeastern Virginia and northwest into eastern West Virginia. Winds have gusted between 45 to 65 mph within this complex, while isolated supercell thunderstorms that have become severe from Hampshire County to Fauquier County are producing large hail with damaging winds. Round two of thunderstorm clusters could develop somewhere over western or northwest Pennsylvania later this afternoon before racing east and southeast again toward our area. Confidence in timing and initiation of such thunderstorms are uncertain. We almost need to wait until storms start developing then we can track it and time better. This particular setup of transferring from Round 1 to Round 2 may be similar should be get Round 3 or 4 overnight tonight through Thursday night. By Friday, cold front should clear much of the forecast area causing a stabilizing effect limiting the risk of severe weather, but showers and thunderstorms will still be possible north of the sfc front. Timing seems to slow with later model runs of this outcome.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Hot temperatures, high humidity, and severe thunderstorm chances look to continue through Friday.

The severe weather threat continues to decrease this evening as the the remnant outflow/backdoor front washes out over the region. A leftover shower or two has been noted across up across Washington/Frederick counties, but this activity has gradually decreased in coverage given the stability in the lower levels. Scattered to broken mid and high level clouds will remain, especially points east of I-81 given the washed out boundary nearby.

Overall expecting a lull in any activity through at least 2-3am with the potential for a secondary round storms dropping south from PA heading into early Thursday morning. This activity is currently located up across the Twin Tiers of New York/northeast PA where numerous severe thunderstorm warnings are in effect. Hi-res guidance pushes this activity slowly south into areas along and north of I- 66/US-50 between 2am-6am Thursday morning. Guidance varies on coverage with a focus across northern and central MD compared to locations further south into Washington DC, southern MD, and northern VA. At this rate, not looking at any widespread severe weather with this batch of storms although locally gusty winds, heavy rainfall, and frequent lightning cannot be ruled out.

The big question is to how this round of morning convection (if it occurs) plays into what will happen in the afternoon. Current guidance suggest a scattering of storms originating in and around the Alleghenies working east as another wave of energy pulses through. Some of guidance has limited activity east of the mountains while others have more. General consensus is for convection to pop toward the mountains and west of US-15 between 11am-2pm before working east into the metros between 3-9pm. Coverage remains uncertain given any convective debris from the morning. Even with that said, expect some organization given 30-35 kts of shear aloft. Damaging winds will be the primary threat with storms given increased DCAPE values on the order of 1000-1400 j/kg. Large hail also cannot be ruled out due to decent lapse rates in the 6-7.5 degree C/km range. As for flooding, an isolated instance or two cannot be ruled out, especially in urban areas or in the event a cell backbuilds/trains over a given area. Modeling continues to hold additional thunderstorm threats Thursday night into Friday although confidence in this is low pending the timing and placement of the incumbent cold frontal boundary.

Right now, most of the guidance has a front dropping through the area either Friday morning into Friday afternoon or Friday afternoon into Friday night. This would spell continue concerns for severe weather in locations along and south of I-70/I-68 where instability may be maximized. The added lift from the front should help with better coverage and organization of t-storms Friday afternoon and evening. Damaging winds will once again be the main threat with storms along with frequent lightning, locally heavy rainfall, and large hail as secondary concerns.

Storms will have plenty of fuel to work with as highs pushing back into the low to mid 90s Thursday afternoon. Locations south of I- 66/US-50 and along/east of I-95 could see highs in the mid to upper 90s. Heat indices will range from 100 to 105 degrees for locations east of the Blue Ridge. Heat Advisories have been hoisted for portions of northern and central VA, southern MD and the eastern WV Panhandle where criteria will be met. Baltimore/Washington DC Metros will be just shy with heat indices likely hovering in the 100-104 degree range. Temperatures will cool a bit Friday with highs in the upper 80s and low 90s. Heat indices will decrease due to the incumbent front, added convection, and increased cloud cover across the region.

KEY MESSAGE 2... Mostly dry conditions and lowering humidity for the Labor Day holiday weekend ahead.

High pressure tracks southeast from the Great Lakes on Saturday, pushing a cold front through region throughout the day. Some uncertainty still exists regarding how far south this front will advance south before stalling, but most ensemble members depict this boundary south of our region by Saturday afternoon. This should bring a drop in heat & humidity across the Mid-Atlantic, with afternoon highs ranging in the mid-80s on Saturday. As mid-level dry air continues to track across the area, temperatures should continue to decrease as the weekend goes on. By the Labor Day holiday, it should feel relatively mild & dry, with dewpoints ranging in the upper-50s across the region.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Slight Risk of severe thunderstorms today and Friday.

Multiple thunderstorm clusters will move from Pennsylvania east southeast into northern.northeast Maryland today through tonight along a frontal zone well defined on surface observations and recent NUCAPS data. Given hot and unstable air mass south of this frontal zone and moderately strong flow aloft, thunderstorms will be capable of producing damaging wind gusts. However, the forecast for today isn't clear cut with satellite imagery showing strong upper level ridging over much of the area as per warm/dry water vapor signature on all three GOES WV channels.

The signal for convection is much stronger for Friday than it is for today with large scale height falls forecast, stronger low- level convergence, and strengthening/stronger mid-level flow. Believe the severe wx risk is greater tomorrow than it is today.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Hot and humid conditions will persist through Friday.

Deterministing and ensemble trends indicate MaxT today will be a couple of degrees hotter than yesterday, but show a spread of 2-3 degrees. Mid 90s seem likely and stayed away from any guidance showing upper 90s. Without any appreciable change in air mass, dewpoints should be in the low to mid 70s (72-73 degrees), which is what has been observed the past couple of days and stayed away from any guidance that was showing 75-77 dewpoints. Plugging 94 over 73 dewpoints yields max heat indices of 103.6F degrees. This is just shy of the heat advisory criteria of 105, so heat indices of 100-105 is the most likely range that we are going to experience today. Given the uncertainty in the MaxT range, will not make any changes to the Heat Advisory in effect. It will still be hot and humid nonetheless. Similar heat indices are expected Friday.

KEY MESSAGE 3...

As the cold front from earlier in the week tracks south of the region, surface high pressure begins to move across the Great Lakes Saturday. Mid-level dry air settles over the Mid-Atlantic between Saturday and Sunday, allowing for heat & humidity to drop through the weekend. Highs for Sunday range in the low 80s across much of the area, with dewpoints ranging in the 50s and low-60s. Overall, it should feel relatively mild & dry over the Labor Day holiday.

Thunderstorm chances drop during this period as well with increasingly stable conditions. Looking towards early next week, upper-level ridging will begin to build over the Appalachians, allowing for relatively dry conditions to continue as temperatures start to increase again by Tuesday. Thunderstorm chances remain low as this ridging builds overhead into next week.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Slight Risk of severe thunderstorms today and Friday.

Clouds have readily thinned in the wake of morning shower and thunderstorm activity. This is allowing for temperatures to rise quickly through the 80s to near 90. This heating will play an important role in the potential for severe weather through the evening hours.

As of 2:30 PM, a few discrete (transient supercell) thunderstorms had developed over the Shenandoah Valley, and had a history of producing large hail and wind damage. These storms are developing in an area that has been clear since daybreak, and in an area of enhanced low-level convergence due to residual outflow from morning convection to the north, a washed out front, and terrain circulations. Anticipate this activity to continue into the late afternoon hours with a risk of localized damaging wind gusts and large hail.

Meanwhile, upstream over the lower Great Lakes and Ohio Valley, a large reservoir of MLCAPE 3000-4000+ J/kg exists. The north end of this CAPE pool lies along the southern edge of the westerlies, with a 100+ kt 300 hPa jet streak and mid-level shortwave impulse located just to the north. This setup is favorable for the development of a Mesoscale Convective Complex (MCS), which is an organized line of thunderstorms that persists for several hours.

Locally, mid-level lapse rates of 6.5-7 C/km (per latest mesoanalysis and the KIAD 12Z RAOB) atop a very moist boundary layer with surface dew points well into the 70s F will lead to increasing CAPE despite the late start at surface heating. The question then becomes just how organized upstream storms become, and how stable the boundary layer is heading further into the evening. A more organized and potent line of storms a bit earlier in the evening would result in a notably higher risk for more numerous damaging wind gusts, especially focused along the residual baroclinic zone/theta-e gradient which should lie near the Potomac River/US-50/I-66 this evening. A somewhat slower and/or more disorganized line would result in a lower risk for severe surface gusts, though some isolated damaging winds would still be possible given high CAPE/DCAPE and the shallow nature of the stable layer near the surface. Areas of western Maryland and perhaps into the eastern West Virginia panhandle are most likely to see the storms prior to the onset of appreciable nocturnal boundary layer stability.

The area remains in a Slight Risk (level 2 out of 5) for severe weather from SPC as of the midday outlook update, driven mostly by the threat of damaging wind gusts. There is a threat for large hail in stronger cores, though mid-level lapse rates will gradually become less steep tonight. A linear storm mode would tend to be less favorable for large hail production (as opposed to discrete/individual cells), as well. A few discrete cells are possible this evening in weak low-level WAA, however, independent of any linear system that may affect the region. These storms would be most likely to develop over northern and central Virginia into central Maryland along a weak surface trough and the aforementioned moisture/instability gradient.

Additional showers and thunderstorms, possibly strong to severe, are anticipated again on Friday. Timing is a bit uncertain given the subtle waves aloft, but increasing low-level convergence paired with another upper impulse may very well result in another round or two of storms with a damaging wind risk. The latest guidance has nudged the threat a bit further north, encompassing areas as far north as I-70 or the Mason-Dixon line (as opposed to I-66/US-50). This will depend on any residual early day clouds or convection, of course.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Hot and humid conditions will persist through Friday.

Temperatures in the upper 80s to lower 90s and dew points in the lower to middle 70s will result in heat indices in the upper 90s to lower 100s each afternoon through Friday, just shy of Heat Advisory criteria for most (except around Charlottesville and surrounding Albemarle/Nelson Counties). The potential for early day clouds to offset heating precludes enough confidence to issue any further heat headlines at this time, though it will be unusually hot and humid for early September regardless.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Drier conditions expected for the Labor Day weekend through early next week.

A high pressure system over the Great Lakes continues to track southeastward towards our forecast region through Tuesday. Over this time period, condtions remain predominantly dry, apart from an isolated shower in the Appalachian mountains.

Temperatures remain seasonable for early September this weekend, with temperatures rising above normal by Tuesday. Moist and warmer conditions return as we head into the middle of next week. Warm, moist air at the surface could lead to unstable conditions, with chances for showers and thunderstorms returning by late Wednesday.
s.avn:
Have shifted PROB30s to this evening for most TAF sites (slightly earlier at KMRB but still mainly this evening). This appears to be the highest chance for storms, though some lead activity to develop especially near KCHO a bit earlier).

Winds will vary between W and SW as a surface trough develops overhead with speeds generally AOB 10 kts. Guidance is not keen on low clouds or fog overnight into early Friday, though the pattern would suggest at least some conditional potential.

Additional storms with somewhat uncertain timing are possible Friday. Was too low on confidence in timing for 18Z TAFs, but PROB30s are likely to be included in subsequent updates, focused probably on the typical peak diurnal window (~19Z-01Z). Winds will shift to NW by late Friday through Saturday.

This weekend, prevailing VFR conditions are expected across all terminals and are expected to continue into early next week. Light northeasterly winds on Sunday shift easterly by Monday.
s.mar:
Special Marine Warnings may be needed this evening as storms develop and track towards the waters. Additional storms are anticipated on Friday, most likely late afternoon and evening. Otherwise, generally light flow is expected into the upcoming weekend, though NW gusts could approach SCA levels Friday night into Saturday.

On Sunday and Monday, wind gusts remain below SCA-criteria with highest chances for approaching SCA thresholds Sunday afternoon or evening. Light northeasterly winds on Sunday shift easterly by Monday.

Locally, mid- level lapse rates of 6.5-7 C/km (per latest mesoanalysis and the KIAD 00Z RAOB) atop a very moist boundary layer with surface dew points well into the 70s F will lead to increasing CAPE despite the late start at surface heating. The question then becomes just how organized upstream storms become, and how stable the boundary layer is heading further into the evening. A more organized and potent line of storms a bit earlier in the evening would result in a notably higher risk for more numerous damaging wind gusts, especially focused along the residual baroclinic zone/theta-e gradient which should lie near the Potomac River/US- 50/I-66 this evening. A somewhat slower and/or more disorganized line would result in a lower risk for severe surface gusts, though some isolated damaging winds would still be possible given high CAPE/DCAPE and the shallow nature of the stable layer near the surface. Areas of western Maryland and perhaps into the eastern West Virginia panhandle are most likely to see the storms prior to the onset of appreciable nocturnal boundary layer stability.

The area remains in a Slight Risk (level 2 out of 5) for severe weather from SPC as of the 20z/4pm outlook update, driven mostly by the threat of damaging wind gusts. There is a threat for large hail in stronger cores, though mid-level lapse rates will gradually become less steep tonight. A linear storm mode would tend to be less favorable for large hail production (as opposed to discrete/individual cells), as well. A few discrete cells are possible this evening in weak low-level WAA, however, independent of any linear system that may affect the region. These storms would be most likely to develop over northern and central Virginia into central Maryland along a weak surface trough and the aforementioned moisture/instability gradient.

Current timing has this initial round of storms into western MD and eastern WV between 7-9pm gradually advancing east toward northern and central MD and northern VA between 9pm-midnight. The secondary complex of storms will push south and east mostly likely after 10pm- 2am. Pending how much energy the first complex of storms zaps away combined with the nocturnal stable layer will determine how of the secondary complex survives. The severity may drop off although gusty winds, frequent lightning, and locally heavy rainfall will remain the primary concerns.

Additional showers and thunderstorms, possibly strong to severe, are anticipated again on Friday. Timing is a bit uncertain given the subtle waves aloft, but increasing low-level convergence paired with another upper impulse may very well result in another round or two of storms with a damaging wind risk. The latest guidance has nudged the threat a bit further north, encompassing areas as far north as I- 70 or the Mason-Dixon line (as opposed to I-66/US-50). This will depend on any residual early day clouds or convection, of course.

Lows tonight will fall into the upper 60s and mid 70s with heat index values in the mid 70s and low 80s. Highs Friday will range from the upper 80s to lower 90s with dew points in the lower to middle 70s resulting in heat indices in the upper 90s to lower 100s. This will be just shy of heat headline criteria (except in Charlottesville and surrounding Albemarle/Nelson Counties). The potential for early day clouds to offset heating precludes enough confidence to issue any further heat headlines at this time, though it will be unusually hot and humid for early September regardless.

The MCS that we had been tracking in the OH Valley earlier this morning has arrived into our western areas a couple hours earlier than expected, as the system sped up this morning. Seeing a few 40+ mph gusts in the strongest cores so far this morning, so nothing severe at this time, but that threat does still exist into the afternoon. This MCS is moving into an environment with at least modest CAPE values around 1000 J/kg and wind shear around 20-30 knots. It isn't the most favorable environment for organized severe weather, but there is just enough of a combination of ingredients to yield a non-zero severe threat through the afternoon, hence the marginal risk (level 1 out of 5) from SPC. The slight does clip Nelson county, but is focused primarily south. This checks out, as the environment will become increasingly favorable for some more organized damaging gusts the further south and east you go, where there is more instability. For storms that do manage to get severe today, damaging winds will be the main threat, along with frequent lightning and locally heavy rain rates. Areas north of I-66 should stay clear of the severe threat today, though a pop up shower or storm can't be ruled out into the early afternoon hours.

This leads to high temperatures in the mid to upper 80s Tuesday, perhaps near 90 Wednesday (slightly cooler in the mountains). Low temperatures (and dew points) will generally be in the 50s and 60s during this time. Some river valley fog is likely each morning.

The upper-level ridge will begin to flatten out Wednesday before breaking down and pushing south and east into Thursday. Several pieces of upper-level energy rotating around an upper low centered over the Hudson Bay will slowly push a cold front south towards our region by Thursday. At the surface, high pressure pushing offshore will bring increasingly warm and humid conditions to the area, with highs in the 80s to near 90 with dew points in the upper 60s to low 70s, with the highest values being Thursday.

Model guidance over the past 24 hours has come into better agreement in regards to the progression of the front on Thursday, as well as the upper-level pattern in association with it. The front really looks like it will flatten out as it moves southward, and really loses the upper-level support. The timing of peak heating and the highest shear just doesn't look to line up at this point. There may be some jet-induced showers and storms late Thursday as we move into the right entrance of the upper jet centered over New England, but not necessarily expecting those to be severe at that point, as the front should be largely through the region. At this point, the severe weather threat looks very limited, but any storm that develops on the warm side of the boundary could bring some gusty winds along with it, but the lack of a substantial wind field will really make that more difficult with southward extent.
