s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry through mid week.

Conditions will remain tranquil as high pressure persists over the Mid-Atlantic through Wednesday before gradually moving offshore. Large scale subsidence and dry air lead to a precipitation-free forecast with temperatures rising to several degrees above normal as the high pulls offshore. This leads to high temperatures in the mid to upper 80s today, perhaps near 90 Wednesday (slightly cooler in the mountains). Low temperatures (and dew points) will generally be in the 50s and 60s during this time. Some river valley fog is likely each morning.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Shower and thunderstorm chances return Thursday.

The upper-level ridge will begin to flatten out Wednesday before breaking down and pushing south and east into Thursday. Several pieces of upper-level energy rotating around an upper low centered over the Hudson Bay will slowly push a cold front south towards our region by Thursday. At the surface, high pressure pushing offshore will bring increasingly warm and humid conditions to the area, with highs in the 80s to near 90 with dew points in the upper 60s to low 70s, with the highest values being Thursday.

Model guidance over the past 24 hours has come into better agreement in regards to the progression of the front on Thursday, as well as the upper-level pattern in association with it. The front really looks like it will flatten out as it moves southward, and really loses the upper-level support. The timing of peak heating and the highest shear just doesn't look to line up at this point. There may be some jet-induced showers and storms late Thursday as we move into the right entrance of the upper jet centered over New England, but not necessarily expecting those to be severe at that point, as the front should be largely through the region. At this point, the severe weather threat looks very limited, but any storm that develops on the warm side of the boundary could bring some gusty winds along with it, but the lack of a substantial wind field will really make that more difficult with southward extent.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Cooler and less humid conditions are expected on Friday, before humidity builds back in next weekend.

High pressure will build to our north on Friday in the wake of Thursday's frontal passage. Cooler and drier air will advect into the region from the north in advance of the approaching high. Mostly sunny skies are expected, with high temperatures in the upper 70s and lower 80s. It will also feel considerably less humid, with dewpoints dropping into the upper 50s and lower 60s.

High pressure will move offshore and a strong area of low pressure will track across Hudson Bay on Saturday, causing winds to turn out of the south in response. Southerly winds will advect a more humid airmass back into the area, with dewpoints climbing into the upper 60s and lower 70s. Chances for afternoon showers and thunderstorms will accompany the more humid airmass. Both instability and shear values are forecast to remain low, so any storms that do form are expected to stay on the weaker side.

Model guidance begins to diverge a bit by Sunday and Monday, but most solutions favor continued above average temperatures, with highs in the mid to upper 80s. Ensemble guidance suggests that chances for afternoon showers and thunderstorms should trend downward as Saturday's system tracks further east across Canada within zonal flow, but there are a few solutions (such as the 12z Canadian) that favor a more amplified longwave pattern and greater chances for showers and thunderstorms.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Mostly dry through mid week.

Conditions will remain tranquil as high pressure persists over the Mid-Atlantic through Wednesday before gradually moving offshore. Large scale subsidence and dry air lead to a mostly precipitation-free forecast with temperatures rising to several degrees above normal as the high pulls offshore.

A weak surface trough in the wake of gradually departing high pressure may be enough to produce a few showers mainly over the Shenandoah Valley/I-81 corridor into the eastern WV panhandle from late Wednesday morning through late Wednesday afternoon.

High temperatures may approach 90 Wednesday (slightly cooler in the mountains). Low temperatures (and dew points) will be in the 50s and 60s during this time. Some river valley fog is likely each morning.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Shower and thunderstorm chances return Thursday.

Mid- level moisture will be increasing on westerly flow, but that introduces a downsloping component in the lower levels. This reduces the amount of CAPE/DCAPE, especially when given anticipated cloud cover over the northern half of the area, for any potential severe weather. Still, a few clusters particularly from central VA to southern MD could contain gusty winds and heavy downpours Thursday, mainly in the afternoon and evening.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Cooler and less humid conditions are expected on Friday, before humidity builds back in this weekend.

Some shower or thunderstorm activity is possible near and south of I-64 as the front stalls just off to the south.

High pressure will move offshore and a strong area of low pressure will track across Hudson Bay on Saturday, causing winds to turn out of the south in response. Southerly winds will advect a more humid airmass back into the area, with dewpoints climbing into the upper 60s and lower 70s. Chances for showers and thunderstorms will accompany the more humid airmass. Both instability and shear values are forecast to remain relatively modest, so any storms that do form likely stay on the weaker side.

There is still some model divergence for Sunday. What we do know is that the humidity will stick around, bringing chances for showers and thunderstorms. However, there is still some uncertainty as to whether or not the marine layer will mix out. If not, temperatures will be cooler with plenty of clouds. If so, there will be some breaks of sunshine and it will be warmer. Guidance leans slightly toward the second scenario, but this will have to be monitored as it gets closer.

High pressure may return behind a weak cold front for Monday and Tuesday, bringing drier conditions, but temperatures will most likely still be above climo.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and warmer today.

High pressure over the Mid- Atlantic today and a southerly flow will allow for temperatures to be about 5 to 7 degrees above average this afternoon. Although we can't rule out a shower in spots between the Appalachian Front and the Shenandoah Valley this afternoon, most areas will remain dry. High temperatures may approach 90.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Showers and a few thunderstorms late tonight through Thursday night.

As the high breaks down and continues to slide to the east tonight into early Thursday, a cold front will approach the region from the northwest. It will be relatively slow in movement to the south and east. A couple of showers or a rumble of thunder could develop along the front and move into western Maryland overnight tonight shortly after midnight and continue to propagate southeastward throughout the night. Due to the lack of daytime heating, the convection should be mainly due to low level moisture and gradual lift from an approaching cold front. Some upper level energy and a jet streak aloft could add additional lift to showers and a couple of thunderstorms across the region during the day Thursday and into Thursday night. However, a westerly component to the wind in the lower levels could act as a downsloping effect and squash some of this convection in a few places. Highs Thursday could reach the upper 80s to near 90 and dewpoint temperatures could reach the upper 60s to low 70s. The front should be slow to move to the south and east that showers and thunderstorms could linger well into the night Thursday night. Showers and any thunderstorms should become more spotty or isolated Friday morning with the front nearly stalling across the Virginia Piedmont. Highs Friday should be a couple of degrees cooler due to cloud cover, convection and a northerly component to the wind on the north side of the front.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Daily shower and thunderstorm chances continue this weekend and into early next week.

On Saturday, surface high pressure over New England shifts offshore as a cold front approaches from the northwest. Surface winds shift to southerly, ushering in a more humid airmass. With increased humidity, showers and thunderstorms are possible Saturday and Sunday although are expected to remain below severe criteria.

Going into next week, precipitation chances linger but remain low (less than 20%). A low pressure system is currently forecast to track across the Great Lakes with the associated cold fronts impacting the mid-atlantic. Temperatures will be in the 70s and 80s each day with high humidity values yielding heat indices in the low 90s for some.

A couple of weak surface troughs were draped across the area as of mid afternoon - one from near Baltimore MD to Charlottesville VA, and another near I-81. Subsidence closer to high pressure offshore was suppressing cumulus development east of the Blue Ridge in association with the eastern trough. To the west, increasing moisture and modest CAPE were resulting in an expanding cumulus field. Lift overall is weak and instability is modest, with several lingering stable inversions and weak lapse rates aloft. This should keep convective activity isolated and shallow (probably not producing much if any lightning), and limited to in the vicinity of the western surface trough near/west of the Blue Ridge back to the Appalachians.

Mid/upper jet forcing increases tonight through Thursday as a surface cold front approaches from PA and WV. Thunderstorms that develop over the OH Valley this afternoon are expected to approach the Appalachian crest in weakening form after midnight. This activity should continue to readily weaken as it runs out of instability and forcing as it moves eastward toward daybreak, though a couple of showers can't be ruled out as far east as the metros Thursday morning.

A strong but flattening mid/upper jet will swing by to the north Thursday into Thursday night, with broad ascent in the right entrance region overhead. Increasing fgen and an associated frontal wave look to pivot west to east across north-central VA late Thursday afternoon into Thursday evening, then move east of the Chesapeake Bay overnight. Limited heating through abundant clouds as well as poor lapse rates, high mid-level moisture and modest moisture in the low levels due in part to downsloping flow will all keep instability limited. The greatest CAPE will likely be around 1000-1500 J/kg across central VA where the most heating and highest low-level moisture content is anticipated.

Some storms may tend to cluster heading into tomorrow evening given forcing along the front and increased flow aloft, but the modest CAPE/DCAPE should keep any severe weather threat rather limited for wind and hail. Still, can't rule out a briefly stronger, more organized rotating storm in the vicinity of the front/wave in the evening across central VA to southern MD.

The front will slowly but steadily drop southward heading into Friday. Some shower activity may linger or redevelop in the vicinity of the front near the I-64 corridor, but most of the time/area should be dry Friday unless the front slows down much more significantly.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Intermittent showers & thunderstorms possible between Thursday evening and Saturday as a slow moving cold front tracks through the region. So far any shower and thunderstorm activity has been pretty meager east of the mountains early this afternoon given a subtle stable layer aloft. It's a mashup of SCT-OVC cloud cover as a result of a cold front dropping south from Lake Erie and multiple pieces of shortwave energy ejecting east northeast from central WV and the south-central Ohio River Valley. Expect this activity to gradually drift east and northeast this evening as the shortwave shunts eastward and cold front drops south. The bulk of any shower activity should hold off until near midnight and continue through the pre- dawn hours of Friday morning. Shower activity will be relatively light to moderate with even a few embedded thunderstorms mixed in.

The severe weather threat appears low, but not zero given CAPE values hovering between 500-1500 j/kg and shear values around 30-40 kts. With a stronger piece of shortwave energy set to kick east out of WV expect an uptick in thunderstorm chances mainly across central VA and southern MD this evening where instability will be maximized due to more sunshine. These areas could see spotty clusters of thunderstorms with gusty winds as the primary threat along with frequent lightning and locally heavy rainfall. Not everyone will see the rain this afternoon and evening with more scattered to widespread showers expected later this evening and pre-dawn Friday morning as the front drops through.

Highs today will range from the mid 80s along the PA/MD line to low 90s over southern MD and central VA (70S mountains). Lows tonight will fall back into the low to mid 60s with upper 60s over central VA and southern MD. Some fog is possible west of the Blue Ridge although low clouds may be a bit more prevalent given the front nearby.

Additional rain showers could track east through the region Friday morning as the front sags to the south. Behind the front, instability lingers as a shortwave trough builds over the Ohio River Valley and begins to move through the region. This could bring additional intermittent showers and thunderstorms through the region late Friday and into Saturday as this system moves through. All told, total rainfall accumulation over the next 48-72 hours could range between 0.5 inches to greater than 1 inch in areas that receive multiple rounds of these intermittent showers/storms.

Highs through the weekend range in the mid-80s across most of the area, with humidity remaining elevated as the cold front slowly meanders to the south.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Above normal temperatures and dry conditions expected Monday and Tuesday; showers possible along a cold front by the middle of next week.

An upper level ridge is expected build overhead during the first half of next week supporting warmer than normal temperatures and dry conditions. The ridge starts breaking down during the second half of the week as a shortwave-trough digs across the Great Lakes. A cold front is forecast to cross the area next Thursday and will likely bring a few showers or possible thunderstorms, but the probability of severe wx remains too low.

VFR conditions are expected amongst the terminals through this evening. Temporary reductions are possible at times (21-02z/5-9pm) this evening due to spotty showers and thunderstorms. Highest confidence for afternoon showers and storms appears to be from a line south of CBE/MRB/IAD/DCA to BWI/MTN.

The coverage of showers and embedded thunderstorms likely increases later this evening and overnight as the a ripple of energy ejects east from the Ohio River Valley and cold front drops south from PA. Expect showers to move in from the west between 3-6z/10pm-2am before becoming more scattered to widespread across all terminals from 7z- 15/3am-11am Friday. Went will prevailing showers instead of Prob30s based on consistency amongst the hi-res guidance along with radar trends. Cigs will continue to bounce around with SCT-OVC mid and high level cloud decks expected well into the overnight hours.

Beyond the showers and thunderstorms, not looking at a whole lot of low clouds nor fog outside the mountains. MAV/MET guidance continues to hold a high likelihood of low cigs/vsbys mainly west of Blue Ridge heading into Friday morning. This will be something to monitor in subsequent TAF cycles. FOr now opted in for low clouds and even a little fog at both MRB/CHO although confidence is low. Any temporary restrictions this evening into early Friday morning will give way to VFR conditions Friday afternoon as brief dry air moves into the region. A leftover shower or thunderstorm is possible from KCHO south Friday afternoon and evening as the front stalls nearby.

Additional scattered showers and thunderstorms are possible during the afternoon/evening hours this weekend. This will lead to temporary reductions amongst the terminals at times otherwise VFR conditions will prevail. South to southeast winds Saturday will switch to the west and southwest winds Sunday at less than 15 kts. Fair weather conditions expected during the first half of next week. Winds turn to the north and northwest Monday and Tuesday as VFR conditions continue.
s.mar:
Showers and a few thunderstorms are anticipated later this evening into tonight. A few Special Marine Warnings are possible, especially toward southern MD. Winds shift to the west and northwest tonight as a cold front crosses, then shift to north and east through Friday as the front stalls to the south. Winds shift to south and southeast on Saturday with southerly channeling yielding Small Craft Advisory criteria winds in the afternoon.

West winds on Sunday shift to northerly on Monday, remaining below SCA criteria each day. Showers and an isolated thunderstorm are possible over the waters on both Saturday and Sunday, although SMWs are not likely.

SCA conditions expected Monday into Tuesday on northerly winds.
s.tide: Tide levels remain normal over the next couple of days as prevailing winds remain light. Looking towards late Saturday, levels increase again ahead of a warm front moving through the region on Sunday.

s.chg: Adjusted PoPs through the night to account for radar and model trends.
s.key:
- 1) Intermittent showers & thunderstorms possible between Thursday evening and Saturday as a slow moving cold front tracks through the region.

- 2) Above normal temperatures and dry conditions expected Monday and Tuesday; showers possible along a cold front by the middle of next week.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Intermittent showers & thunderstorms possible between Thursday evening and Saturday as a slow moving cold front tracks through the region.

The surface cold front appears to stretch across northern PA and OH this evening. The front will slide southward tonight while a shortwave trough approaches from the Great Lakes and a jet streak slides to the north. Diurnal convection largely formed south of the CWA late this afternoon/evening, so there are only some isolated showers/sprinkles around at 9 PM. More numerous showers are located across the Ohio Valley ahead of the approaching forcing. Models have been inconsistent on whether only scattered showers survive across the mountains or if there is a more organized area of rain. Higher rain chances, as well as precipitation amounts, will likely be focused closer to the Alleghenies. A lot of models don't have any showers reaching the Blue Ridge until 3-5 AM, although trajectories of current activity could place some showers that far east by midnight or so. Little lightning is being observed in the Ohio Valley, and would expect that to be the case locally overnight as well given little change to the minimal instability values in place. However, with precipitable water values of 1.75-2 inches, some locally heavy rain could occur with any convective elements.

Lows tonight will fall back into the low to mid 60s with upper 60s over central VA and southern MD. Some fog is possible west of the Blue Ridge although low clouds may be a bit more prevalent given the front nearby with clouds, showers, and drizzle.

Rain showers will gradually end Friday morning as the front sags to the south. Behind the front, instability lingers as a shortwave trough builds over the Ohio River Valley and begins to move through the region. This could bring additional intermittent showers and thunderstorms through the region late Friday and into Saturday as this system moves through. The highest rain (and possible thunderstorm) chances on Friday afternoon and evening will be across central Virginia. Rain will spread north Friday night and Saturday coincident with the shortwave trough and the surface front lifting back northward. All told, total rainfall accumulation over the next 48-72 hours could range between 0.5 inches to greater than 1 inch in areas that receive multiple rounds of these intermittent showers/storms.

Highs through the weekend range in the mid-80s across most of the area, with humidity remaining elevated as the cold front slowly meanders to the south.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Above normal temperatures and dry conditions expected Monday and Tuesday; showers possible along a cold front by the middle of next week.

An upper level ridge is expected build overhead during the first half of next week supporting warmer than normal temperatures and dry conditions. The ridge starts breaking down during the second half of the week as a shortwave-trough digs across the Great Lakes. A cold front is forecast to cross the area next Thursday and will likely bring a few showers or possible thunderstorms, but the probability of severe wx remains too low.
s.avn:
VFR conditions are expected amongst the terminals through this evening with light west winds. Shower coverage will increase overnight as a cold front approaches, although there is uncertainty in both timing and coverage. Most models have the highest rain chances arriving in the 06-10Z window from west to east, although upstream radar trends suggest some showers could arrive a few hours sooner than that if they don't fall apart. Went will prevailing showers instead of Prob30s based on long term model trends along with upstream radar. A few thunderstorms can't be ruled out, but little lightning is being observed upstream with little change to the environment expected. However, there could be some localized convective downpours that reduce visibility...this chance is currently too low to include in the TAF. As the front slides through toward daybreak, winds will shift more northerly and ceilings will lower some. Guidance backed off on MVFR/IFR ceilings and visibilities compared to the previous forecast, confining these closer to the mountains. At this time, CHO has the highest chance of MVFR ceilings, which could last from around daybreak Friday into the afternoon before lifting.

Elsewhere, any temporary restrictions give way to VFR conditions later Friday morning as brief dry air moves into the region. A leftover shower or thunderstorm is possible near KCHO Friday afternoon and evening as the front stalls nearby. Winds will shift to the east or southeast by Friday evening. Sub-VFR ceilings and visibilities may return northward, along with some rain, Friday night.

Additional scattered showers and thunderstorms are possible during the afternoon/evening hours this weekend. This will lead to temporary reductions amongst the terminals at times otherwise VFR conditions will prevail. South to southeast winds Saturday will switch to the west and southwest winds Sunday at less than 15 kts. Fair weather conditions expected during the first half of next week. Winds turn to the north and northwest Monday and Tuesday as VFR conditions continue.

Winds will become easterly Friday evening as the front stalls to the south. Winds shift to south and southeast on Saturday with southerly channeling yielding Small Craft Advisory criteria winds in the afternoon. West winds on Sunday shift to northerly on Monday, remaining below SCA criteria each day.

Showers and an isolated thunderstorm are possible over the waters on both Saturday and Sunday, although SMWs are unlikely.

SCA conditions expected Monday into Tuesday on northerly winds.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Storm chances linger through at least Saturday, with a possibly drier finish to the weekend.

The latest surface analysis places a cold front across southern Pennsylvania back across southeastern Ohio into the middle of Kentucky. Within the warm sector, numerous showers have begun to press eastward across the region. Although much of this activity is on the lighter side, recent radar returns are a bit heftier south of I-66/U.S. 50. Such elements will bring moderate intensity showers to areas south of the Washington, D.C. metro down into southern Maryland. The more regional-scale radar imagery shows a bit of a lull behind this wave, but with additional activity back over West Virginia. Most areas see shower chances diminish toward midday, but with some additional afternoon to evening development over the Potomac Highlands into the central Virginia Piedmont region. Overall conditions today will yield more clouds than sun. This is accompanied by high temperatures in the mid 70s to low 80s, locally a bit cooler across the mountains.

The cold front initially north of the Mason-Dixon Line is forecast to settle toward the Virginia-North Carolina border by tonight. Despite the frontal passage, its more diffuse nature will only bring a limited drop in temperatures and humidity levels. Saturday morning will start off in the 60s which comes with further shower and thunderstorm chances throughout the day. The focus is driven by an elongated trough currently crossing the Arklatex states. As this array of embedded shortwaves lift across the Tennessee Valley toward the southern Mid-Atlantic, storm chances increase in earnest. The 00Z high-resolution model suite shows an uptick in rainfall amounts, some of which are on the higher end (1 to 2 inches in 24 hours). With precipitable water values in the 1.75 to 2.00 inch range and deep warm cloud layers, some fairly efficient storms are possible in this environment. As such, the Weather Prediction Center supports a Slight risk for excessive rainfall on Saturday, especially across the I-95 urban corridor. Will continue to monitor the situation as new mesoscale guidance arrives.

Coming off temperatures similar to today, expect a slight warm up into Sunday with highs returning to the mid 80s. Some residual shower activity is possible to start the day. However, the local area will be in the wake of the passing shortwave trough. Expect some increase in humidity as the boundary to the south returns northward as a warm front. Unlike previous days, a fair amount of sunshine is possible, particularly for the second half of the day. Sunday night's low temperatures will fall into the 60s to low 70s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Seasonably warm ahead of a mid-week cold front.

H5 ridging builds Mon through Wed, before weakening as sw trofs and associated sfc cold front move through midweek. Some spread on exactly what day this happens, but overall consensus around Thu. This could bring showers and thunderstorms, but probability of svr wx remains low.
s.avn:
VFR conditions should prevail despite shower activity this morning. However, cannot rule out a brief restriction through daybreak if a locally more intense shower moves through. Will maintain shower chances through the late morning before conditions turn drier behind the passing cold front. The one exception would be at KCHO which may see a few afternoon thunderstorms in the 4-8 PM timeframe. Overall winds today will shift many times, but should remain around 5 knots or less.

Models have shown the potential for lower ceilings late tonight into Saturday morning. Some terminals could move over to MVFR at that point. Shower and thunderstorm chances increase on Saturday which will favor sub-VFR conditions at times, particularly during the afternoon/evening hours. With the frontal zone off to the south, prevailing winds will be out of the east to southeast. Restrictions may persist into Saturday night, while drier weather returns for Sunday amidst mainly west to northwesterly winds.

VFR conditions Mon and Tue with light N'ly winds Mon veering E'ly Mon night and S'ly Tue.
s.mar:
As a cold front crosses the waters, winds shift to northerly late this morning. Some channeling effects could yield wind gusts to around 15 knots or so, particularly over the upper to middle Chesapeake Bay. Overall winds turn more east to southeasterly by Saturday as the front pushes off to the south. This brings an increase in winds that may near advisory criteria on Saturday. Afternoon/evening convection may also support some hazardous marine conditions which would include lightning activity. Gradients weaken into Sunday with gusts in the 5 to 10 knot range.

SCAs expected Mon with brisk N'ly winds. Winds veer out of E Mon night and then S Tue, but remain below SCA levels by Tue afternoon.
s.tide: Tidal levels remain normal as anomalies sit near 0 feet early this morning. Initial light winds will shift to northwesterly later today which would support no coastal flooding issues. Looking towards late Saturday, water levels increase again ahead of a warm front moving through the region. This should persist into Sunday before a cold front eventually crosses the area by Monday morning.

s.chg: Heavier showers over the DC Metro have now pushed east. Additional showers continue through early afternoon, though mostly from DC northward. A few thunderstorms possible in Central VA late this afternoon.

- 1) A few Central Virginia thunderstorms today, then likely widespread convection Saturday into Saturday night.

- 2) Dry conditions expected early next week ahead of a midweek cold front.

KEY MESSAGE 1...A few Central Virginia thunderstorms today, then likely widespread convection Saturday into Saturday night.

The slow moving frontal boundary is now across Central VA, with a few showers and thunderstorms noted along the I-64 corridor. SPC has a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) along the far southern CWA centered in Nelson County. This is where low-level convergence and better instability could result in a strong storm or two. The time window for impacts in our area are limited as the front continues to push south. Most of the convection pushes south of our area by around 4- 5PM. After that, conditions should be mostly dry through this evening. Cloud cover has kept temps in the 70s for most of the area, and even those north of the frontal boundary are also in the mid to upper 70s.

Surface high pressure over southern New England slides offshore Saturday causing southeasterly flow to develop/strengthen over the Mid-Atlantic. The synoptic pattern gets messy into the weekend as an elongated trough stretches from the Deep South to Mid-Atlantic. The stalled boundary over southern VA lifts north as a warm front Saturday morning, bringing a possibly first round of showers to the area. As the boundary lifts north of the MD/PA border, warm sector showers are possible at time Saturday afternoon, though the bulk of convection is set to arrive toward the evening hours.

Numerous embedded shortwaves lift across the Tennessee Valley toward the southern Mid-Atlantic, helping produce ample lift and shear across the region. A surge of tropical moisture brings PWATs to around 2" Saturday afternoon into Saturday night. A wave of surface low pressure may try to develop somewhere in lee of the Alleghenies Saturday evening as the strongest shortwave traverses the region. A subtle jet streak develops ahead of the upper trough, and while not overly impressive it will be enough to aid in widespread showers and thunderstorm development. Locally heavy rain is likely in some areas, though the 12Z high res guidance does not point to any one specific location. Later analysis on areas of low-level convergence that set up will be key to determine where a flash flood threat could develop. But for now, have not issued any Flood Watches due to uncertainty in location of heaviest rain. WPC has expanded the Slight Risk area for excessive rainfall to include the Alleghenies where soils are more saturated from rain over the past month. Will continue to monitor the situation as new mesoscale guidance arrives.

A cold front associated with the upper trough finally swings through the area Sunday morning to afternoon, bringing an end to any lingering showers. This front won't bring much of an airmass change as temps still reach the 80s and humidity lingers.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry conditions expected early next week ahead of a midweek cold front.

Upper-level ridging begins to build over the Southeast beginning Monday and into Tuesday as the cold front transitions offshore. Humidity & temperatures decrease in the wake of the cold front on Monday, with dewpoints ranging in the 50s and low 60s as mid-level dry air transitions overhead. Monday night might be the first fall night of widespread lows in the 50s.

Overall, anticipate seasonal, dry conditions to persist over the following days as this ridging continues to build into the midweek period. Beginning Wednesday, this ridging begins to transition into more of a zonal flow overhead as a trough further north forms over Quebec and Nova Scotia. An associated cold front could begin to track across the East Coast sometime during this period, although current guidance shows some spread in the timing of this frontal passage. This front could bring some showers and thunderstorms to the region, but probability of severe weather remains low at this time.
s.avn:
A few thunderstorms are possible around CHO through late this afternoon. A front that is moving south of the area today is going to stall tonight, then lift north as a warm front Saturday. Expect sub-VFR conditions to overspread the area from south to north Saturday morning. There is uncertainty as to how far north the sub- VFR CIGs are, but likely impact most of the terminals. Widespread showers and scattered thunderstorms are expected areawide Saturday afternoon into late Saturday evening. TEMPO groups are likely to be needed, but are just beyond the current TAF period.

A couple of reinforcing cold fronts move through the region Sunday into Sunday night, with VFR conditions returning in WNW/NW winds.

Prevailing VFR conditions are anticipated across terminals Monday through Wednesday. A few lingering showers could temporarily bring reduced conditions near KCHO on Monday, but otherwise conditions remain mostly clear throughout Tuesday & Wednesday. Northerly winds shift southeasterly by Tuesday night.
s.mar: A slow moving front continues to slide south through the waters. The brief surge of winds earlier this morning has now abated, with overall north winds around 10 knots. The front stalls south of the waters tonight, then lifts north as a warm front Saturday night. An increase in winds over the waters Saturday could be near SCA levels. Late afternoon to late evening thunderstorms could lead to hazardous marine conditions, with Special Marine Warnings possibly needed. A secondary front moves through Sunday, then a stronger cold front on Monday. Wind gusts could increase to near marginal SCA thresholds on Monday before diminishing throughout the day Tuesday. Winds stay below SCA criteria through Wednesday. Northeasterly winds shift southeasterly in the wake of a cold front by Tuesday night.
s.tide: Strengthening onshore flow Saturday will bring tide levels up across the area. Some locations could reach Action Stage by Saturday night to early Sunday high tides. A cold front moves through Sunday, and again Monday, which should bring an end to any coastal flooding potential.

s.chg: Hourly trends have been touched up, but there are no major changes to the forecast at this time.

Looking out to Monday night, strong Canadian high pressure could easily yield colder overnight temperatures than shown. Recent guidance has been slow to show the rapid drying of the air mass.

- 2) Seasonably warm and dry ahead of a mid-week cold front.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Widespread convection expected through tonight, while turning cooler and drier into early next week.

The current setup features a stalled surface boundary sitting just south of the Virginia-North Carolina border. This is bounded by a modest area of high pressure stretching across much of New England into the Mid-Atlantic states. At the same time, a broad upper trough currently swirling across the Mid-South. As this trough axis pushes off toward the east, models show a low level response of enhanced moisture/theta-e advection. With surface to 850-mb winds shifting to mainly south to southeasterly, precipitable water values will further rise in time. Increasing isentropic lift atop the poleward advancing boundary should set the stages for a more active day of convection.

At the moment, fairly tranquil weather remains amidst a thickening area of low clouds. Over the last hour, there has been a notable moistening of the boundary layer with stratus expanding from the central Virginia Piedmont up across the Shenandoah Valley. This should eventually yield a fairly extensive stratus deck across the area this morning. Temperatures largely sit in the mid 60s to low 70s, with dew points in the 60s. Given increasing moisture advection, widely scattered showers are expected to pop through the morning hours. With upstream forcing from the trough still off to the west, any activity should stay fairly disorganized in nature. However, storm-scale organization should improve in time heading into the late afternoon to evening/overnight period.

The 00Z high-resolution model suite shows two possible areas of more widespread convective development. (1) As depicted in the 00Z HREF 40-dBZ paintball plots, the more pronounced activity forms across West Virginia up into western Pennsylvania, mainly in the 4 to 8 PM timeframe. As these cells encroach on the Allegheny Front, the slow moving nature of such storm elements coupled with saturated soils (per satellite) would afford a non- zero flash flood risk. (2) Additionally, the warm conveyor belt along the I-95 corridor will likely be an additional focus area for storm genesis. This may occur more into the evening hours as this activity is driven by instablity along/south of the warm front. How this convection interacts with development coming off the Alleghenies will determine the risk of flash flood potential along the I-95 corridor. High-resolution model depictions of this evolution feature quite a bit of spread, but the signal bears watching. Flood Watches may be needed at some point during subsequent shifts.

Depending on instability and storm evolution, the mentioned convective complexes could fester into tonight. A preponderance of solutions favor shifting this activity into northeastern Maryland by around 3-5 AM (early Sunday). Patchy fog could materialize in the wake, particularly for areas seeing some of the heavier rainfall.

Locally heavier rainfall this evening into the night could lower conditions to IFR at times. Once showers exit into northeastern Maryland, a mixture of MVFR to IFR ceilings are expected for all sites.

Northwesterly winds increase on Monday behind a strong cold front with afternoon gusts possibly reaching 25 knots.

Prevailing VFR conditions are expected to continue at terminals Tuesday through Thursday. A few showers forming ahead of a cold front on Thursday evening could bring temporary reductions. Winds generally flow between 5-10 knots southerly to southeasterly.

Small Craft Advisories may need to be expanded up the bay/extended into the late evening. Additionally, showers increase in coverage toward the evening and especially the overnight hours. The most likely area to see thunderstorms would be south of U.S. 50. It remains to be seen how far north instability can reach.

Sub-advisory winds are expected for Sunday before a stronger surge of northwesterlies ensue behind a cold front on Monday. Widespread advisory-caliber wind gusts are likely which will necessitate Small Craft Advisories.

Winds likely remain below SCA thresholds Tuesday through Thursday, shifting NE Tuesday to SE Wednesday, then S by Thursday.
s.tide: Strengthening onshore flow will bring tide levels up across the area through tonight. Some locations could reach Action Stage tonight/early Sunday. Annapolis could near Minor. A cold front moves through by early Monday which should bring an end to any coastal flooding potential.

- 2) Seasonably warm & dry conditions anticipated early next week ahead of a cold front.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Widespread convection expected through tonight, while turning cooler and drier into early next week.

The current setup features a surface boundary located near the Virginia-North Carolina border this evening. This boundary will lift northward as a warm front overnight. At the same time, a shortwave trough is swinging into the upper Ohio Valley. As this trough axis pushes off toward the east, models continue to show a low- level response of enhanced moisture/theta-e advection. With surface to 850-mb winds shifting to mainly south to southeasterly, precipitable water values will further rise in time. Increasing isentropic lift atop the poleward advancing warm front should set the stage for convection through tonight.

Current radar imagery shows two areas of ongoing showers and storms. The first is located near and west of the Allegheny Front. This area of showers and storms is expected to continue to gradually progress toward the north and east through the night, following a zone of large scale ascent associated with the aforementioned shortwave trough. A second area of showers and a few thunderstorms is ongoing across much of the Virginia Piedmont. This activity is associated with warm/moist advection to the north of the front, and is expected to gradually, Havre de Grace, and Annapolis lift northward through the night. Embedded areas of higher rainfall rates have occurred with some of the showers and storms in what is a high PWAT environment. A Flood Watch remains in effect for extreme Western Allegany and Garrett Counties through 2 AM. Current radar trends suggest that the flood threat there may have peaked, but a few of the recent runs of the HRRR try to build heavier rain back in from the west next over the next few hours. For that reason, we'll keep the Watch going. Further east, an isolated instance or two of flooding can't be ruled out overnight, but confidence is too low for a Watch. The back edge of the precipitation should clear the area by mid-morning tomorrow.

For Sunday into Monday, multiple temperature swings are expected. Ahead of the approaching cold front, some weak downslope component to the wind fields should steer highs well into the 80s on Sunday. As this front crosses during the diurnal minimum in heating (i.e., overnight Sunday/early Monday), storm chances will be rather limited. Will maintain showers and a few rumbles of thunder along the Alleghenies, with lower (but not quite zero) probabilities further east across the piedmont. Monday's forecast features prevailing northwesterlies with afternoon gusts up to 15 to 25 mph. High temperatures should range from the mid 70s to low 80s, while being locally cooler in the mountains. This also comes with falling humidity and cool temperatures on Monday night. Robust surface high pressure crossing the northeastern U.S. will support widespread 50s overnight. Even some upper 40s are likely in spots that can fully decouple and remain cloud-free.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Seasonably warm and dry ahead of a mid-week cold front.

High pressure will continue to build on Tuesday as mid-level dry air moves in from the Great Lakes. Expect seasonable and dry conditions to persist during this time as highs reach into the lower 80s with dewpoints potentially dipping into the upper 40s on Tuesday morning.

Strong upper-level ridging builds toward the area Tuesday into Wednesday, then begins to break down by late in the week as a retrograding low tracks south into the Florida Peninsula from the Atlantic. Humidity likely begins to increase again on Wednesday as any lingering dry air is driven east out of the region. Meanwhile, a trough will begin to develop over the Northern Plains with a stemming cold front tracking east through the Mid-Atlantic sometime in the mid-to-late week period. Updated model guidance has delayed the arrival of this front potentially to Thursday & into Friday, with showers & potentially a few thunderstorms accompanying the front. However, significant uncertainty remains in the time of arrival here as models continue to grasp this synoptic setup. Regardless, severe probabilities continue to look low as we begin to transition out of the summertime thunderstorm season.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Some lingering showers this morning before turning cooler with less humidity on Monday and Tuesday.

Early morning local radar imagery shows multiple areas of light to moderate shower activity. A bulk of this is emerging off the Allegheny Front and tracking across the Shenandoah Valley. Despite the somewhat lackluster appearance of these showers, quasi-tropical rain rates are being observed. Based on upstream trends, 3-hour precipitation totals are generally around 0.25 to 0.50 inches, locally approaching an inch in spots. Despite the 06Z RAP objective analysis depicting most unstable CAPE values in the 500-750 J/kg range, this has not been enough to produce any recent lightning activity. The lone exception is approaching Highland County from the south as storms lift away from Hot Springs, Virginia. With most hydrographs featuring current water levels well below any pre-defined stages, any flooding risk appears low at this time.

The array of showers will progress eastward to the I-95 corridor by 4-6 AM timeframe before exiting off into northeastern Maryland by just after sunrise. While much of the remainder of the day will be dry, a warm front just south of the Richmond metro area is forecast to cross the region later this morning. This may help induce a few additional showers, but these should be rather disorganized in nature. By the afternoon, expect more sun than clouds which will help crank temperatures back well into the 80s. This is aided by a weak downslope component to the winds as they shift to northwesterly. Despite the wind shift, humidity levels do remain elevated with dew points in the upper 60s to low 70s.

Heading into tonight, an approaching cold front from the Great Lakes may induce additional showers along and west of the Allegheny Front. Otherwise, this is largely a drier frontal passage which will also lead to cool temperatures and lower humidity to start off the work week. Gradients are rather tight for mid-September as a broad 1024-mb surface high approaches from the Great Lakes. This will favor a breezy northwesterly wind for Monday, with afternoon gusts up to 20 to 25 mph at times. Forecast highs are in the mid 70s to low 80s (5 to 15 degrees cooler for mountain locales). As the seasonably strong dome of high pressure settles over the northeastern U.S. on Monday night, low temperatures plunge into the upper 40s to 50s. The autumnal feel to the air lingers into Tuesday before an eventual warm up by mid-week. Plenty of sunshine can be expected each day, but with decreasing winds on Tuesday with the ridge along the Eastern Seaboard. This all comes with dew points in the upper 40s to mid 50s which is certainly a change from recent days.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Warm and dry conditions through the end of the week; showers possible along a cold front next weekend.

A strong upper ridge builds over the region during the middle portion of the week supporting very warm and dry conditions. Not looking at any record highs since records are in the mid 90s. The ridge begins to flatten at the end of the week as it starts feeling pressure from a deepening trough over Hudson Bay. A front eventually sinks southward at the end of the week possibly bringing few-sct showers. Overall, very warm and dry this week, turning cooler and potentially wetter for late September.
s.avn:
Low ceilings are commonplace early this morning as a warm front slowly approaches from central Virginia. Most terminals are seeing borderline IFR conditions. This comes wth an array of light to moderate showers tracking eastward from the Shenandoah Valley. The forecast calls for such activity to impact downstream TAF sites in Washington, D.C. and Baltimore through just after daybreak. MVFR ceilings persist through the mid/late morning before improvements to VFR take shape by midday. Thereafter, clouds should continue to erode which allows for some sun to break out.

VFR conditions continue through Tuesday as well. Winds remain weak today, generally out of the west to northwest. A seasonably strong cold front tracks through early Monday which yields post-frontal northwesterlies with gusts to around 20 to perhaps 25 knots. Winds eventually weaken into Tuesday as high pressure builds over the region.

Fair weather conditions expected through Thursday.
s.mar:

Some showers will cross the waters early this morning, but the threat for lightning is quite low. A cold front arriving early Monday is forecast to yield increasing northwesterly winds with gusts up to 20 to 25 knots. Small Craft Advisories look quite likely on Monday into portions of Monday night. Multiple wind shifts take place on Tuesday as high pressure passes by to the north. However, gusts drop off back into the 5 to 10 knot range.

Sub-advisory conditions continue into Wednesday and Thursday with gusts to around 5 to 10 knots.
s.tide: Tidal anomalies remain elevated, generally sitting in the 0.75 to 1 foot range. This is enough to put a number of locations into Action stage, especially during the higher of the two astronomical high tides. At this point, no site is forecast to reach Minor flood stage through tonight. A cold front moves through by early Monday which should bring an end to any coastal flooding potential.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Canadian high pressure will bring dry conditions with low humidity to start the work week.

What remains of showers that tracked across western Maryland have since fallen apart in the last few hours. Scattered mid to high clouds remain in the wake across locations east of the Blue Ridge. Although drier air aloft has begun to move in, the GOES-19 nighttime microphysics channel and surface observations show stratus clouds developing along/west of the Alleghenies. This will likely persist during the next few hours before drier air across the Ohio Valley tracks into the local area. Until this occurs, a seasonably mild and humid air mass remains over the region early this morning. Current temperatures range from the mid 60s to mid 70s, with dew points sitting in the mid 60s to low 70s. The near saturated boundary layer has fostered the development of some patchy fog, particularly around Fauquier and Prince William counties. However, expect this to erode ahead of sunrise.

A cold front currently nearing the Allegheny Front is forecast to quickly sweep through the region early this morning. By mid- morning, this boundary should be down around the Virginia Tidewater area. In the wake, a rather strong dome of Canadian high pressure works its way eastward from the Great Lakes. Over the next couple of days, this frontal zone is to settle along the southeastern U.S. coast while a 1028-mb ridge tracks through New England. This will favor abundant sunshine, dry weather, cooler temperatures, as well as much less humidity. In fact, dew points temperatures are likely to drop into the mid/upper 40s. Daily highs through Tuesday should be in the mid 70s to low 80s (60s to low 70s across the mountains). The dry nature of the air mass will support cool overnight periods, particularly tonight. With the ridge axis right over the northeastern U.S., forecast lows tonight will fall into the upper 40s to mid 50s. The I-95 urban corridor could stay slightly milder being in the upper 50s.

Among the days ahead, today should prove to be the breeziest given the tight gradient formed by the departing front and Great Lakes high pressure. Northwesterly gusts up to 20 to 25 mph are expected this afternoon, possibly to near 30 mph in a few spots. Expect winds to drop off after dark with the decrease in boundary layer mixing. Winds turn lighter by Tuesday with high pressure in place. By mid-week, this ridge eventually begins to shift off the Atlantic coast. This will support a gradual warm up as winds return to southerly. Wednesday's forecast highs push back into the mid/upper 80s, with mainly 70s for the mountains. Despite an uptick in humidity, the pattern does remain dry.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Warm and dry conditions expected through Thursday; showers possible along a cold front at the end of the week.

A strong upper ridge builds over the region during the middle portion of the week supporting very warm and dry conditions. Not looking at any record highs since records are in the mid 90s. The ridge begins to flatten during the second half of the week as it starts feeling pressure from a deepening trough over Hudson Bay. A front is expected to progress southward at the end of the week and bring chances of showers and thunderstorms. While we should start seeing a cooling trend next weekend, temperatures still look to be above normal. However, there has been noticeable model run-to-run changes and large spread seen in temperatures for next weekend which decreases confidence in the temperature forecast.
s.avn:
Aside from a few hours of patchy fog around KCHO early this morning, VFR conditions are expected the next few days. Behind a cold front that pushes through shortly, winds will shift over to northwesterly while increasing in strength. Late morning to afternoon gusts should reach 20 to 25 knots which comes with a marked decrease in clouds. Such gusts gradually drop off into the evening to overnight hours. Winds turn lighter by Tuesday with Canadian high pressure centered across New England. A dry forecast persists into Wednesday while this ridge slowly pulls away from the coast which favors a return to southerly flow.

Fair weather conditions expected through Thursday and Friday.
s.mar:

In the wake of a cold frontal passage this morning, a rather strong dome of Canadian high pressure works its way eastward from the Great Lakes. Over the next couple of days, this frontal zone is to settle along the southeastern U.S. coast while a 1028-mb ridge tracks through New England. This will favor abundant sunshine, dry weather, cooler temperatures, as well as much less humidity. In fact, dew points temperatures are likely to drop into the mid/upper 40s. Daily highs through Tuesday should be in the mid 70s to low 80s (60s to low 70s across the mountains). The dry nature of the air mass will support cool overnight periods, particularly tonight. With the ridge axis right over the northeastern U.S., forecast lows tonight will fall into the upper 40s to mid 50s. The I-95 urban corridor could stay slightly milder being in the upper 50s.

Among the days ahead, today should prove to be the breeziest given the tight gradient formed by the departing front and Great Lakes high pressure. Northwesterly gusts up to 20 to 25 mph are expected this afternoon, possibly to near 30 mph in a few spots. Expect winds to drop off after dark with the decrease in boundary layer mixing. Winds turn lighter by Tuesday with high pressure in place. By mid-week, this ridge eventually begins to shift off the Atlantic coast. This will support a gradual warm up as winds return to southerly. Wednesday's forecast highs push back into the mid/upper 80s, with mainly 70s for the mountains. Despite an uptick in humidity, the pattern does remain dry.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Warm and dry conditions expected through Thursday; showers possible along a cold front at the end of the week.

A strong upper ridge builds over the region during the middle portion of the week supporting very warm and dry conditions. Not looking at any record highs since records are in the mid 90s. The ridge begins to flatten during the second half of the week as it starts feeling pressure from a deepening trough over Hudson Bay. A front is expected to progress southward at the end of the week and bring chances of showers and thunderstorms. While we should start seeing a cooling trend next weekend, temperatures still look to be above normal. However, there has been noticeable model run-to-run changes and large spread seen in temperatures for next weekend which decreases confidence in the temperature forecast.
s.avn:

Behind a cold front that pushes through shortly, winds will shift over to northwesterly while increasing in strength. Late morning to afternoon gusts should reach 20 to 25 knots which comes with a marked decrease in clouds. Such gusts gradually drop off into the evening to overnight hours. Winds turn lighter by Tuesday with Canadian high pressure centered across New England. A dry forecast persists into Wednesday while this ridge slowly pulls away from the coast which favors a return to southerly flow.

Fair weather conditions expected through Thursday and Friday.

High pressure building over the region tonight promotes light to calm winds and clear skies. A great setup for radiative cooling that will drop temps to the 50s east of the Blue Ridge, and 40s to the west. The highest locations in the Alleghenies could drop to the upper 30s.

Light east to southeast winds Tuesday and Wednesday as the high pressure shifts offshore. Expect a gradual warm up with Wednesday's forecast highs back into the mid/upper 80s, with mainly 70s for the mountains. Despite higher humidity, the pattern does remain dry.

Upper level ridging shifts eastward offshore throughout the day on Thursday as a cold front drops southeast from the Great Lakes. Primarily dry conditions are expected on Thursday with only a slight chances of showers and thunderstorms west of I-81 in the afternoon. High temperatures will be in the upper 70s to 80s across the forecast area with RH values expected to increase through the afternoon.

The approaching cold front brings a good bit of uncertainty with the forecast for Friday through the weekend. The main impact will be on temperature forecast with the high temperature spread ranging from the upper 60s to upper 90s depending on the placement of the front this weekend. The first possible solution will be the cooler of the two with the front passing through the forecast area before stalling near the VA/NC border. The second solution involves the front stalling overhead with warmer temperatures expected.

Either way, expect the return of daily shower and thunderstorm chances later this week and into the weekend as the front approaches and impacts the forecast area. The best chance for storms will be Friday as the initial front moves into the Mid-Atlantic and then again on Sunday as an additional front approaches from the northwest.

The influence of Canadian high pressure is well underway with a marked fall in temperatures and dew points over the region. Relative to 24 hours ago, most locations have seen such readings fall by around 10 to 15 degrees. This translates to early morning temperatures that will start off in the upper 40s to 50s, locally into the mid 40s along the Allegheny Front. With low-level moisture being trapped within nocturnal radiation inversions, some patchy fog may materialize before daybreak. This would occur around the usual vulnerable locations like river valleys and other low-lying areas.

With a broad 1026-mb surface anticyclone anchored over the northeastern U.S., expect conditions to be fairly similar to yesterday/Monday. The one major difference will be the marked reduction in winds given weak gradients within the influence of this dome of high pressure. Today's high temperatures are forecast to reach the mid 70s to low 80s (upper 60s to low 70s in the mountains). This comes with continued low humidity with dew points mainly in the upper 40s to low 50s. Aside from some passing high cirrus, abundant sunshine is expected throughout the day. Light southeasterly gradients will favor an uptick in overnight temperatures. While still cooler than recent days, most can anticipate lows in the mid 50s to low 60s (mildest along the I-95 urban areas as well as near the Potomac River and Chesapeake Bay shorelines).

Behind an exiting longwave trough that pushes into the Canadian Maritimes, mid/upper heights begin to build in earnest. An expansive 594-dm mid-level ridge initially over the southern U.S. will flex northward in time. These above average heights remain a fixture in the forecast through Thursday. This supports a return of warmer temperatures along with building humidity levels. Daily highs push back into the mid/upper 80s, locally reaching the low 90s in the warm spots. The return of the humidity also favors milder nights with widespread lows in the 60s. Any shower and thunderstorm chances should hold off until Thursday given the stout ridge aloft quelling most precipitation chances. Most models keep such a threat mainly west of the Shenandoah Valley, especially closer to the Alleghenies.

A high latitude trough digging across southeastern Canada should be enough to nudge the upper ridge back toward the south-central U.S. This allows a cold front to push through early Friday which again brings a gradual cool down with decreasing humidity into Saturday. However, this reprieve is somewhat brief as additional disturbances in the atmosphere track toward the area late in the weekend. The overall jet pattern turns a bit more complex as an array of features enter the picture. A broad upper low retrogrades across the Gulf of America. At the same time, a myriad of shortwaves will eject across the central U.S. toward the Mississippi Valley. How these impulses behave along with where surface features reside will dictate any local weather impacts. However, all signs point toward a more active pattern on Sunday into early next week.

Canadian high pressure will support VFR conditions through mid- week. Weak gradients keep lighter winds than yesterday/Monday, with winds gradually shifting from east to southeasterly today. This ridge eventually edges toward the Atlantic coastline which will support mainly southerly winds on Wednesday into Thursday. Some storm chances emerge by Thursday, but these are currently expected to stay west of the area terminals.

A cold front moves through early Friday which results in some uptick in shower chances. This may come with a few restrictions if convection becomes more pronounced. In the wake of this frontal passage, winds turn more northerly with afternoon gusts to around 15 knots or so. High pressure building to the north results in a east to southeasterly wind for Saturday. This comes with likely VFR conditions.

Small Craft Advisories continue over the southern waters through 7 AM with gusts to around 20 to 25 knots. Across the middle Chesapeake Bay, gusts occasionally approach 20 knots, but these are more sporadic and infrequent in nature. However, gradients weaken through the day with gusts around 5 to 10 knots.

Thereafter, high pressure slowly pushes away toward the coast which results in a south to southeasterly wind for Wednesday and Thursday. Some southerly channeling effects may necessitate Small Craft Advisories for parts of Thursday, especially across southern sections of the Chesapeake Bay. A cold front tracks across the waters on Friday morning which favors a shift to north to northeasterly winds. These could near advisory criteria, but confidence is low. High pressure passing by to the north will result in a shift to east-southeasterlies for Saturday. Gusts up to 15 to perhaps 20 knots are possible.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Turning warmer with a return of shower and thunderstorm chances for the second half of the work week.

Today will provide one more day of dry weather before the pattern turns more active for latter portions of the work week. Canadian high pressure remains over the Eastern Seaboard but has continued to advance closer to the Atlantic coastline. Given the ridge axis is not directly bisecting the local area, some weak onshore gradients have allowed for light winds overnight. As of 07Z/3 AM, most locations are sitting in the upper 50s to low 60s. This does come with some pockets of mid 60s across Washington, D.C. and Baltimore, as well as near river/bay influences along and east of I-95. Skies do remain clear given the presence of high pressure. A few areas of patchy fog may develop ahead of daybreak, especially across mountain valleys and other low-lying spots.

Relative to early in the week, temperatures will return to above average for mid-September. This is in response to the building of mid/upper heights as southern U.S. ridging flexes northward. An expansive mid-level 594-dm ridge is forecast to extend from the Southern Plains and Gulf Coast region up to the Mid-Atlantic states. Some ensemble guidance even show the development of a 600-dm contour over the Mid-South. These positive height anomalies will run around 2 to 2.5 sigma above climatology. Although there is tremendous warming aloft, this does not fully reflect at the surface. While conditions will be warm, high temperatures should be confined to the mid/upper 80s, with a few low 90s across the Allegheny mountain valleys. A shift to southerly gradients also aids in increasing humidity, but certainly not oppressive by any means. The forecast does stay dry with subsidence aloft keeping skies mostly sunny.

Canadian high pressure becomes centered just off the Atlantic coast tonight. At the same time, an approaching cold front is expected to briefly stall over the Ohio Valley through Thursday morning/afternoon. Tonight will yield a gradual increase in clouds, particularly north of I-66/U.S. 50. The added clouds and continued southerly winds carries overnight lows in the low/mid 60s. Thursday also offers the next opportunity for showers and thunderstorms. This largely focused west of U.S. 15, and especially toward the Shenandoah Valley and points westward. Some erosion of this strong upper ridge will allow diurnal heating and terrain circulations to fire off some scattered storms. As convection presses eastward, the influence of the stout ridge aloft should yield a weakening trend of such activity. High temperatures are forecast to return to near 90 degrees, with the cool spot being in the mountains where mid 70s to low 80s will be more commonplace. Above average temperatures continue into the night with lows in the mid 60s to low 70s.

The mentioned cold front should track across the local area early Friday as another dome of strong high pressure approaches from southern Ontario. Post-frontal northerly winds pick up in earnest with afternoon gusts to around 15 to 20 mph. It will not be a completely dry forecast as showers form around the eastern periphery of the retreating upper ridge. s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Warm and humid, with thunderstorm chances today before turning cooler into the first half of the weekend.

As Canadian high pressure has edged toward the Atlantic coastline, return flow around the west side of this anticyclone has yielded a milder and more moisture-laden air mass. Relative to 24 hours, current temperatures and dew points have increased by about 8 to 12 degrees. Consequently, this places 07Z/3 AM temperatures in the mid 60s to low 70s, with dew points mainly ranging between 62 and 68 degrees. A southeasterly onshore component to the wind fields has led to the development of a mid-level cloud deck along/east of I-95. Off to the west, scattered showers continue to churn eastward across eastern Ohio into western Pennsylvania. Like much of the last 3 to 6 hours, any approaching showers quickly weaken given the notable convective inhibition (CIN) at around 50 to 100 J/kg. As a result, will keep only isolated showers in the forecast through daybreak across western Maryland.

Unlike previous days, diurnal showers and thunderstorms return to the picture. The current players are: (1) An expansive and anomalous mid/upper ridge stretching across southern U.S./Gulf Coast up into the Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic states, (2) A sharpening trough crossing western Ontario, and (3) An area of disturbed weather just north of the Bahamas. In time, the high- latitude trough is expected to erode the northern extent of the ridge. Although height anomalies remain around 1.5 to 2 sigma above mid-September climatology, the subtle height falls should be enough to support increased lift this afternoon. This shift in the synoptic pattern allows a stalled front along I-70 in Ohio/Indiana to push southeastward later today. The cold front is not expected to cross the entire region until late tonight into early Friday morning. Thus, the pre-frontal air mass will support scattered convection this afternoon and evening.

With high temperatures rising into the mid 80s to low 90s, coupled with dew points reaching the upper 60s, around 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg of surface-based CAPE develops. Deep-layer shear is somewhat meager, generally averaging around 15 to 20 knots. However, forecast soundings do show some modest downdraft CAPE around 500 to 700 J/kg. This would be enough to produce spotty gusty winds in any more robust thunderstorm. Although low-level lapse rates sit in the 8 to 8.5 C/km range, mid-level lapse rates are weak which casts a doubt on how tall any storm will get. Convection is expected to form off the higher terrain before pushing toward the I-95 corridor during the 4-9 PM timeframe. Shower chances should diminish by a couple hours after dark given the loss of instability.

The cold front sweeps through overnight before reaching the Northern Neck of Virginia by midday Friday. With some residual forcing crossing the central Virginia Piedmont back into the Potomac Highlands, some afternoon showers and thunderstorms are possible. Overall, forecast highs will be in the upper 70s to mid 80s, with low/mid 70s for mountain locales. Winds will mainly be out of the north with gusts up to 15 to 20 mph. A cooler night lies ahead as high pressure crosses southern Quebec into New England. Friday night's lows should be in the upper 50s to mid 60s. The influence of this ridge favors near average temperatures to start the weekend on Saturday. Although skies should be mostly cloudy, it is a mainly dry forecast with highs in the 70s to low 80s with a reduction in humidity.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Unsettled weather conditions return again Sunday and into next week.

From Sunday and into next week, model guidence points to more unsettled weather, as a persistent upper ridge axis pushes towards the deep South. This allows multiple upper-level disturbances to move across the Mid-Atlantic from the Great Plains, driving daily chances for showers and thunderstorms. Long-term enemble models show a wide range of possibilities reguarding the timing and location of these disturbances. While widespread chances for showers and thunderstorms exist, the exact timing, coverage, and nature of these storms remains quite uncertain. It will interesting to watch the evolution of these disturbances in the coming model runs.

Height falls amidst a humid airmass resulted in showers and thunderstorms expanding in coverage from northwest to southeast over the past several hours. Poor mid level lapse rates and weak shear have prevented the convection from becoming too deep/strong. The weak shear and sufficient (but generally modest) DCAPE has allow the storms to become outflow dominant, with some observed gusts of 30-40 mph. At this point the probability of severe thunderstorms is low. Instability decreases east of the I-95 corridor, and so far, convection has been weakening as it approaches this threshold. The main question now is whether there is another round of showers later this afternoon and evening closer to the approach cold front. This would likely originate from the activity in the upper Ohio Valley to northern Pennsylvania. Given the diurnal timing and an airmass which has already been cooled from the previous convection and lingering clouds, thunder appears less likely with this round.

While the cold front drops in later tonight, guidance indicates some patchy fog could develop before the wind shift occurs. This would most likely occur along rivers and low lying areas, although low clouds may move into the Allegheny and Potomac Highlands which could also reduce visibility.

While the wind shift portion of the cold front likely pushes south of the area Friday morning, the moisture gradient may hang back across central Virginia up to the Potomac Highlands. As a shortwave trough swings through during the afternoon, some additional showers and thunderstorms may develop in these areas. Temperatures will fall back into the lower to mid 80s with northerly gusts up to 20 mph at times. There may also be a fair amount of stratocumulus at times as well. A cooler night lies ahead as high pressure crosses southern Quebec into New England. Friday night's lows should be in the upper 50s to mid 60s.

High pressure to the northeast on Saturday should provide enough dry air to keep rain at bay. One exception may be along the Allegheny Front due to convergence in an inverted surface trough. Warm advection aloft and mid level perturbations will likely provide cloud cover areawide. Temperatures will be closer to climatology, ranging from the mid 70s to lower 80s. Low pressure moving into the Ohio Valley may increase rain chances Saturday night.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Shower and thunderstorm chances shift southward in the wake of a cold front today. Slightly cooler and drier conditions are forecast for Saturday, before shower and thunderstorm chances return on Sunday.

A cold front will move southward across the area this morning. As winds shift to out of the north, slightly cooler and drier air will gradually filter in from the north over the course of the day. Dewpoints will drop from the lower 70s currently into the 60s by later this afternoon, and temperatures will still climb into the 80s at lower elevations beneath a mix of sun and clouds. As the drier air advects in from the north, instability will be confined to far southwestern portions of the forecast area by peak heating this afternoon. As a result, any thunderstorms are expected to form across Central Virginia before eventually tracking off to the south and east out of our forecast area. Forecast soundings show less than 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE, DCAPE values of 600 J/kg or less, and relatively weak wind fields, so any storms that form aren't expected to turn severe. A few showers may be possible further north, but coverage of showers is expected to be isolated at best.

A secondary surge of cold/dry advection will occur tonight within north to northeasterly flow as high pressure builds to our north. Dry conditions are expected across the entire forecast area on Saturday within the drier airmass. Temperatures are forecast to climb into the 70s to near 80 beneath a mix of sun and clouds.

High pressure will shift offshore on Sunday, causing winds to turn back out of the south. In response, a warmer, more humid airmass will work back in from the south and west over the course of the day, with dewpoints climbing back into the lower 70s and temperatures reaching into the lower 80s. A deep upper trough will track well to our north across Ontario and Quebec during this time, with an unseasonably strong area of high pressure building in the zone of subsidence in its wake across Ontario. This anomalously strong high building to our northwest will encourage a cold front to approach from the north. While the front will likely remain off to our north during the daylight hours, gradually falling heights aloft combined with increasing heat/humidity at low-levels will likely lead to the development of showers and a few thunderstorms Sunday afternoon. Showers could then continue on and off through the night as the cold front drops southward through the area.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Daily chances for showers persist through much of next week, with temperatures likely falling below normal

Overall, nearby disturbances bring unsettled weather to the region persisting through midweek.
s.avn:
Other than some patchy fog this morning, prevailing VFR conditions are expected at the terminals through the day today. A few MVFR clouds can't be completely ruled out for a brief time late this morning into early this afternoon, but for now have kept just a mention of FEW030 in the TAFs. Winds today will be out of the north, and may gust to around 15-20 knots. Winds remain out of the north to northeast tonight as a secondary surge of cold advection moves through. Most guidance keeps conditions VFR, but a few solutions show some MVFR clouds later tonight through the day Saturday. For now we're favoring VFR conditions through that period. Winds shift to out of the east by Saturday afternoon, and then south on Sunday, with continued prevailing VFR conditions. Temporary drops to sub-VFR conditions may be possible in any thunderstorms that form Sunday afternoon, but coverage of storms isn't expected to be high.

Winds shift to north/northeasterly on Monday in the wake of the front persisting through late next week. Showers are possible each day, with restrictions expected during heaviest precipitation. Gusts begin light and strengthen moderately as the week continues.
s.mar:
Winds shift to out of the north today in the wake of a cold front, but are expected to remain just below SCA levels. A secondary surge of cold advection will move through tonight, with winds potentially reaching low-end SCA levels for a time as they shift to out of the north-northeast. Confidence was still too low to issue an SCA at this time, but the potential will need to monitored through the day. Winds gradually shift to out of the east on Saturday, and then south on Sunday. Low-end SCA conditions may be possible at times throughout the weekend within both easterly and southerly flow. SMWs could also be possible Sunday afternoon if thunderstorms track toward the waters.

Winds shift to north/northeasterly on Monday in the wake of the front persisting through late next week. After the weekend, gusts could approach or surpass SCA criteria, potentially strengthening as the week continues. While there's still a lot of forecast uncertainty at this juncture, some of the stronger solutions show Gale force winds within east to northeasterly flow during the middle of the week. Showers are possible each day, and SMWs could be plausible, even if prevailing Gale conditions aren't realized.
s.tide: Water levels are forecast to drop behind a cold front within northerly flow today through tonight. Anomalies start to climb again Saturday into Sunday as winds turn to out of the east on Saturday and then south on Sunday. Model guidance suggests that Minor flooding may possible Saturday night into Sunday. Water levels may drop again briefly on Monday as winds shift to out of the northeast. Persistent east to northeasterly flow during the middle of next week will likely lead to rising anomalies and potential coastal flooding issues, although uncertainty is high this far out, and it's far too early to get into details.

Cdfnt will continue to push south of the area this afternoon with isolated light showers ending from north to south, but could linger through mid evening in central VA. Surface ridging builds in for Saturday supporting fair weather conditions. Warm air and moisture advection atop a shallow cool layer will support scattered showers across the northern half of the fcst area late Sat night into Sunday. Then, additional showers and thunderstorms are expected Sunday afternoon and evening along a retreating warm front. The front will sink south Sunday night as low pressure passes by and high pressure starts building south again.
