Upper-level ridging breaks down early next week, with multiple shortwave disurbances moving across the Mid-Atlantic in the days following. Mid-level moisture brought in from the south will continue overhead as winds flow northeasterly. As a result, daily showers remain a possibility into late next week as these disturbances slowly track across the region. Temperatures drop on Tuesday in the wake of one of these disturbances, with highs generally ranging in the upper 50s and 60s. This cooler- than- average weather persists at least through midweek as nearby disturbances continue to bring rain showers to the area. Towards the bay & coastlines, wind gusts could remain elevated mid-to- late week as these disturbances begin to track offshore. Overall, coastal flooding could become something to watch out for next week as these elevated winds combined with persistent rain stretches on.

High pressure currently centered across southern Quebec will continue to build southeastward over the course of the day today, eventually reaching the Gulf of Maine by this evening. As the high shifts further east, winds will gradually shift from out of the north/northeast this morning to out of the east and then southeast this afternoon. Persistent cool/dry advection has enabled dewpoints to drop into the upper 50s to mid 60s as of early this morning. With this somewhat drier airmass in place, zonal flow aloft, and the influence of the high building to our north, conditions are expected to remain dry through the day today. Temperatures are forecast to climb into the 70s to near 80 beneath mostly cloudy skies.

High pressure will shift further offshore tomorrow while a shortwave disturbance tracks eastward across southern Ontario and Quebec. Winds at the surface will turn southerly in response to the high moving further offshore, while winds aloft turn westerly in response to the shortwave passing to our north. The net effect of these wind shifts will be to draw a warmer, more humid airmass back into the area from the south and west. Temperatures are forecast to climb well into the 80s with dewpoints jumping back into the lower 70s. This cold front will eventually move through the area Sunday night, causing winds to shift to out of the north to northeast.

Persistent cool/dry advection has enabled dewpoints to drop into the upper 50s to mid 60s as of early this morning. With this somewhat drier airmass in place, zonal flow aloft, and the influence of the high building to our north, conditions are expected to remain dry through the day today. Temperatures are forecast to climb into the 70s to near 80 beneath mostly cloudy skies.

Winds at the surface will turn southerly in response to the high moving further offshore, while winds aloft turn westerly in response to the shortwave passing to our north. Temperatures are forecast to climb well into the 80s with dewpoints jumping back into the lower 70s. Showers will continue into the evening along a frontal zone before dissipating or shifting south late Sunday night.

Light rain or off and on showers will persist through Tue morning, particularly along and west of the Blue Ridge Mountains in areas of onshore flow. Expect a noticeable cooling trend beginning Monday in the wake of the cold front late Sunday night.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Scattered showers and perhaps a few thunderstorms look to finish out the weekend as a front passes through.

Added some light showers and sprinkles in across central and western MD this evening as spotty activity drops south from central and western PA. Outside of these showers and sprinkles, is increased low and mid level cloudiness. This is in association with a squeeze play between fronts with moisture advection increasing from the south and east and a cold front slowly dropping down from the Great Lakes region. Low and mid level clouds will remain abundant overnight with some filtered breaks the further south you get toward the I-64 corridor. Most will remain dry overnight, but with moisture advection increasing over a shallow cool layer aloft expect humidity values to gradually climb and spotty showers likely developing over the mountains heading into Sunday morning. This shower activity will be scattered in nature and in association with the warm front and lead piece of shortwave energy ahead of the front that is currently located back across the eastern Great Lakes and Ohio River Valley. The first round of showers should exit the area around midday with a secondary area of showers and perhaps a few thunderstorms working through the region Sunday afternoon and evening as the cold front drops through. Current hi-res guidance has slowed the front up a bit while dissipating/washing it out over the region Sunday evening into Sunday night. Deterministic synoptic guidance has a similar solution while keeping a ripple of low pressure riding along the boundary Sunday evening into Sunday night forcing it south. With that said, severe weather does not appear to be a concern although a few thunderstorm cannot be ruled out over central VA, southern MD, and the northern neck of VA where some breaks of sun may filter through. Any of these storms will be capable of locally gusty winds, heavy rainfall, and lightning.

The front will eventually shunt southward heading into Monday morning although on and off shower activity will persists into the new workweek given increased onshore flow. Expect a noticeable cooling trend beginning Monday in the wake of the cold front late Sunday night. Highs Sunday will push into the upper 70s and low 80s (low 70s mountains) with overnight lows in the upper 50s and mid 60s. Highs Monday will struggle to get out of the upper 60s and low 70s as more of a wedging pattern sets up with increasing onshore flow.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Daily shower chances and cooler temperatures persists through midweek with drier conditions for the upcoming weekend.

VFR conditions look to continue through at least 02z/10pm with MVFR cigs settling in overnight as low and mid level clouds thicken. Low and mid level clouds will persists through Sunday afternoon as a result of increased moisture advection ahead of a series of fronts pushing through. Most locations will remain dry tonight outside of a passing shower or sprinkle for terminals west of MRB. Shower coverage will increase early to mid Sunday morning between 10- 16z/6am-12pm as a result of a warm front lifting into the region. Moisture advection with this front combined with a leading piece of shortwave energy will yield scattered light to moderate showers mainly at terminals north of KCHO. Expect a lull in the showers midday with an additional round of scattered showers and perhaps a few thunderstorms Sunday afternoon beyond 19z-23z/3-7pm. Greatest opportunity for a thunderstorm would be south of the corridor from DCA down to CHO/RIC where breaks of sun will be more prevalent. Severe weather is not expected although locally gusty winds and brief heavy rain cannot be ruled out with any thunderstorms that form. CIGS become more scattered to broken Sunday evening into Sunday night before restrictions return Monday as onshore east to northeast flow increases.

Expect a mashup of MVFR to perhaps periods of IFR cigs on both Monday and Tuesday as a result of increased onshore flow. Low and mid level cloudiness will be persistent through midweek along with daily chances for showers. Sub-VFR conditions could persist through Thursday as scattered showers continue throughout the region. Gusty winds between 20-25 knots are possible on Thursday. Winds flow from northeasterly to northerly by Friday.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Scattered showers and perhaps a few thunderstorms are expected today.

As of 330 AM, radar imagery shows numerous showers and thunderstorms ongoing across much of southern Ohio and northern West Virginia. This activity will continue to track eastward toward our area over the next several hours, but is expected to weaken as it moves east of the Appalachians into an environment characterized by lesser instability. However, it's likely that at least some showers and maybe an embedded thunderstorms or two will track eastward across the area this morning. This activity is expected to eventually dissipate entirely, but it does cast some uncertainty regarding whether additional thunderstorm activity will be able to form in its wake this afternoon.

On the synoptic scale, a warm front will be lifting northward through the forecast area today, with higher dewpoint air streaming in from the south and west. Most guidance does show at least some destabilization today as the deeper moisture works in and limited surface heating occurs through a broken cloud deck. Temperatures are forecast to climb into the low to mid 80s this afternoon, with dewpoints reaching into the lower 70s. This yields around 500-1000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Model guidance also shows a weak shortwave disturbance moving through around peak heating. The best forcing for ascent associated with this feature and the greatest instability are both forecast to be across the southern half of the forecast area. While an afternoon thunderstorm can't be ruled out anywhere, the greatest chance for a storm appears to be roughly south of I-66 and east of the Blue Ridge. However, forecast uncertainty remains high with the activity from WV/OH moving through this morning, which isn't being handled particularly well by model guidance. Even if storms do form, the background environment doesn't look favorable for severe storms.

A cold front will move through the area tonight, causing winds to shift around to out of the north. Low clouds will build in overnight, with low temperatures forecast to be in the upper 50s to mid 60s.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Cool and wet conditions continue through the end of the week.

Continuing northeasterly flow, strong high pressure to our north, and a developing low pressure system trailing up the eastern seaboard sets up a classic cold air damming environment across the Mid- Atlantic through much of the week. Temperatures remain well- below late-September averages due to persistent cloud cover and a stable cool airmass remaining trapped against the Blue Ridge. Several short- wave disturbances tracking across the Mid- Atlantic sustain on and off showers through the end of the week. Substantial cloud cover Thursday and Friday reduce instability and thunderstorm potential.

This coastal low pressure system offshore continues to move northward coinciding with a strengthening high pressure system lingering in Quebec. Tightening pressure gradients over our region particularly across our Coastal Plains, could lead to breezier winds late Thursday and Friday. Continued onshore flow combined with stronger tidal influence could increase coastal flood risk during this period. Refer to the coastal flooding section below for more details.

As this system tracks to the north of our region by the weekend, windier conditions fade. Shifting northwesterly wind ushers in drier conditions and decreasing shower potential to start of the weekend.
s.avn:
Prevailing VFR conditions are expected today, although a few MVFR clouds may briefly be possible this morning. As of 330 AM we continue to monitor ongoing thunderstorms across West Virginia and Ohio. These storms should tend to weaken as they cross the Appalachians and move into an environment characterized by lesser instability, but a few showers may persist. A major forecast question for today is whether storms form again this afternoon in the wake of this morning shower activity/cloud cover. PROB30 groups for -TSRA have been introduced at many of the terminals this afternoon to account for the potential of thunderstorm development, but confidence remains low. Winds today will start out of the south, before shifting to the southwest this afternoon. A cold front will move through tonight, causing winds to shift around to out of the north. Ceilings should gradually lower tonight in northerly flow, but there's disagreement in model guidance with respect to just how low ceilings get. Some solutions show MVFR conditions later tonight through the day Monday, while others show IFR. For now have MVFR ceilings in the TAFs, but have hinted at the potential for IFR. IFR conditions appear even more likely on Tuesday within northeasterly flow. Showers will be possible on and off through both Monday and Tuesday.

Increasing low and mid-level clouds and potential off and on showers could lead to sub-VFR conditions through the end of the week due to onshore flow. Gusty winds remain a possibility mid to late next week with winds continuing to flow out of the north and northeast before the weekend.
s.mar:
Small Craft Advisories continue for the Bay and Lower Tidal Potomac within southerly flow through 1 PM. Winds decrease slightly and shift to out of the southwest this afternoon. A cold front moves over the waters tonight, with winds shifting to out of the north. Winds are expected to stay just below SCA criteria tonight. Winds shift to out of the northeast and gradually pick up in magnitude for Monday and Tuesday. SCA conditions appear likely Monday into Tuesday, with gusts potentially nearing 30 knots by Tuesday afternoon.

North to northeasterly wind gusts remain elevated through Thursday as an area of low pressure travels along the East Coast, with showers possible over the waters during this period. As this system begins to track past our coastline late in the week, winds could decrease heading into the weekend.
s.tide: A Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect for Annapolis through 5 AM. Anomalies are expected to decrease within northerly flow behind a cold frontal passage tonight, but Annapolis may come close to Minor Flood stage again tonight. No coastal flooding is anticipated on Monday, but tidal anomalies will increase again within onshore flow for Tuesday and Wednesday. With flow more out of the northeast than east, anomalies should be higher the further south you go in the Bay. At least Minor flooding appears likely at some locations on Tuesday and Wednesday. Moderate flooding looks less likely, but can't be completely ruled out at this point.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Numerous showers expected through this evening. Turning much cooler Monday and through the rest of the week.

Extensive cloudiness has limited instability all day with VIS imagery and NUCAPS data showing only southern MD having received enough sunshine for thunderstorms to potentially develop later this afternoon or evening. Otherwise, a weak area of low pressure will pass through the area early this evening and should bring a round of light showers to most areas through mid evening, except in the south. The front will sink south overnight with showers ending, with clouds lowering.

More showers will arrive in the west toward daybreak as the next shortwave-trough and weak area of low pressure approaches the area. These showers will slowly progress east during the afternoon Monday. The period of heaviest rainfall looks to be Monday night/early Tuesday when onshore flow/moisture advection is strongest combines with a weak low to mid-level low pressure.

High pressure then builds south from the Northeast Tue setting up a strong cold air damming event supporting well below normal temperatures and cloudy conditions.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Cool & wet conditions persist through the end of the week, with drier conditions heading into the weekend.

Intermittent showers remain possible mid-to-late week as a lingering frontal boundary sags to the south. Additionally, a strong coastal low begins to track north close to the Maryland coast Thursday and into Friday, which will bring gusty conditions to the region. This strong onshore flow could bring minor coastal flooding to sites along the Chesapeake Bay. See the coastal flooding section below for more information.

As this coastal low tracks to the north, dry mid-level air from the upper Midwest moves in overhead. This will create somewhat drier conditions heading into the weekend, although there is a bit of model discrepancy on how slow the coastal low will be moving out of the area. Winds could stay elevated until this system is well north of the Mid-Atlantic. Temperatures stay slightly cooler-than-average during this time, although gradually increase near the end of the week as any lingering shortwave disturbances track offshore.
s.avn:
A cold front will drop south this evening supporting numerous showers. Winds shift to the north tonight with IFR conditions developing. IFR cigs persist through mid week.

Intermittent sub-VFR conditions likely continue through Thursday as additional showers move through the Mid-Atlantic, reducing CIGs and VSBYs. Conditions potentially improve somewhat on Friday as a trough moves north out of the region. Gusty winds remain a possibility through the end of the week due to onshore flow, with gusts between 15-25 knots possible. Winds flow north to northeasterly.
s.mar:
Winds have relaxed a bit this afternoon, but are expected to strengthen Monday night through early Thursday. Additional SCAs will be needed.

Wind gusts will be strongest on Thursday over the Bay as a coastal storm tracks to the north off the East Coast. Sustained winds between 20-25 knots are possible with as winds flow northeasterly. Winds stay elevated on Friday, flowing due north. On and off showers are possible over the waters as multiple shortwave disturbances move through.
s.tide: Water levels remain elevated as onshore flow has developed. Stronger NNE winds Monday afternoon will push the water south into the mouth of Chesapeake Bay. This excess water is expected to slosh back mid week resulting in widespread minor coastal flooding, perhaps moderate at Annapolis.

s.chg: Hourly trends have been updated through the night based on latest radar and model data. Portions of the Small Craft Advisory now start at 3 AM.

- 1) Rounds of showers and decreasing temperatures through Tuesday.

- 2) Cool & wet conditions persist through the end of the week, with drier conditions heading into the weekend.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Rounds of showers and decreasing temperatures through Tuesday.

Showers have been much less common than earlier CAM runs suggested. This is changing as of mid evening, with showers along the surface cold front sinking southward from Pennsylvania, and a few additional showers near the bay where there is increasing convergence and slightly higher instability. Most of these showers should dissipate or exit around midnight to 2 AM. Additional showers and thunderstorms currently over the Ohio Valley will move toward the area the second half of the night. The highest chance of rain will obviously be along the Allegheny Mountains, with some uncertainty how well and showers hold together farther east. In between the rounds of showers and lower clouds advecting from the north, some patchy fog could develop where there is clearing.

More showers may arrive in the west toward daybreak as the next shortwave-trough and weak area of low pressure approaches the area. However, there is considerable model spread on the timing and coverage of any rain during the daylight hours of Monday. The period of heaviest rainfall looks to be Monday night/early Tuesday when onshore flow/moisture advection is strongest combines with a weak low to mid-level low pressure.

High pressure then builds south from the Northeast Tue setting up a strong cold air damming event supporting well below normal temperatures, cloudy conditions, and additional periods of rain.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Cool & wet conditions persist through the end of the week, with drier conditions heading into the weekend.

Intermittent showers remain possible mid-to-late week as a lingering frontal boundary sags to the south. Additionally, a strong coastal low begins to track north close to the Maryland coast Thursday and into Friday, which will bring gusty conditions to the region. This strong onshore flow could bring minor coastal flooding to sites along the Chesapeake Bay. See the coastal flooding section below for more information.

As this coastal low tracks to the north, dry mid-level air from the upper Midwest moves in overhead. This will create somewhat drier conditions heading into the weekend, although there is a bit of model discrepancy on how slow the coastal low will be moving out of the area. Winds could stay elevated until this system is well north of the Mid-Atlantic. Temperatures stay slightly cooler-than-average during this time, although gradually increase near the end of the week as any lingering shortwave disturbances track offshore.
s.avn:
Some notable changes were made to the 00Z TAFs. First, showers have been less common early this evening, though a more concentrated ribbon of showers along a cold front is approaching from the north. Confidence in rain is highest at MRB/BWI/MTN, with decreasing chances to the south. This will also bring a wind shift to the NW to N. The second change was to be more conservative with the ceiling forecast through Monday. This is largely based on BUFKIT moisture profiles. In fact, the period of MVFR ceilings behind the front overnight into early Monday could actually be pretty brief, except at CHO. Before these ceilings arrive, some fog may develop at CHO, but this is uncertain and dependent on cloud breaks. Believe the metro terminals should improve to VFR by late Monday morning if not earlier. The one caveat is if more widespread rain moves into the area Monday. That could reduce ceilings and visibilities, with the greatest chance of that happening at MRB. Some models maintain dry conditions through the day, which is why PROB30 groups were utilized in the metro areas and at CHO. There does appear to be greater consensus on rain and IFR conditions moving into the area at some point Monday evening.

Once IFR cigs develop Monday night, there will likely be little break through mid week as a cold air damming pattern develops. Rounds of rain and drizzle will reduce visibility at times.

Intermittent sub-VFR conditions likely continue through Thursday as additional showers move through the Mid-Atlantic, reducing CIGs and VSBYs. Conditions potentially improve somewhat on Friday as a trough moves north out of the region. Gusty winds remain a possibility through the end of the week due to onshore flow, with gusts between 15-25 knots possible. Winds flow north to northeasterly.
s.mar:
Gusty outflows from a ribbon of showers are possible over mainly the northern part of the bay this evening. These showers mark a cold frontal passage, which will bring a wind shift to the north. A bit of a pressure surge arrives the second half of the night, so started the Small Craft Advisory at 3 AM for the portion north of Drum Point. Overall this advisory looks marginal though, with wind gusts above 20 kt unlikely. Winds are expected to subside briefly Monday afternoon but then strengthen Monday night through early Thursday. Additional SCAs will be needed. High end SCA to near gale conditions are possible by Wednesday as low pressure develops off the coast.

Wind gusts will be strongest on Thursday over the Bay as a coastal storm tracks to the north off the East Coast. Sustained winds between 20-25 knots are possible with as winds flow northeasterly. Winds stay elevated on Friday, flowing due north. On and off showers are possible over the waters as multiple shortwave disturbances move through.
s.tide: Water levels remain elevated this evening but are starting to drop slightly. This may mean any minor flooding at Annapolis overnight is only near the threshold at most. Stronger NNE winds Monday afternoon will push the water south into the mouth of Chesapeake Bay. This excess water is expected to slosh back mid week resulting in widespread minor coastal flooding, perhaps moderate at Annapolis.

s.chg: A Small Craft Advisory was issued for tonight through Tuesday night.

- 2) Daily shower chances, abundant cloud cover, and cool temperatures continue through Thursday. Drier this weekend.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Cloudy and cooler conditions are expected through mid-week, along with daily chances for showers.

As of 330 AM, current radar imagery shows a weakening MCS approaching from central West Virginia. Cloud tops have shown substantial warming over the last couple hours. This complex of storms is expected to continue weakening into showers as it tracks eastward into our area, where northerly flow behind a cold front is gradually advecting more stable air in. It's plausible that at least showers will persist into locations to the west of the Blue Ridge this morning. Questions remain regarding whether these showers will hold together further east. Regardless, conditions will be mostly cloudy today. Temperatures will be cooler than previous days, and conditions will also be less humid, with dewpoints dropping into the 60s. There could be a substantial gradient in temperatures from northwest to southeast today. Western Maryland and the West Virginia Panhandle will likely struggle to climb out of the 60s with thick cloud cover and higher coverage of showers. Locations along and east of I-95 may make it into the upper 70s to near 80 with lower coverage of showers and a few more breaks in the cloud cover.

High pressure already in place to our north across southern Quebec will rapidly strengthen from the upper 1020s hPa today to near 1040 hPa by tomorrow night. As this occurs, northeasterly flow will strengthen and the CAD wedge in place to the east of the Appalachians will strengthen. Large scale forcing for ascent will also gradually increase from west to east tonight into tomorrow as a shortwave trough and embedded upper low approach from the Ohio Valley. As large scale forcing for ascent increases, the relatively low coverage of showers today will increase substantially heading into tonight, and persist through tomorrow, tomorrow night, and Wednesday morning. At times the precipitation may even resemble more of a continuous stratiform rain shield as opposed to showers.

The flow pattern across the CONUS over the next couple days will be extremely complex, with a split flow pattern and a closed upper level ridge building to the north of the upper low over the Ohio Valley. So while the big picture of the forecast tonight through Wednesday has high confidence (low clouds, cool, and rainy), there is still some forecast uncertainty regarding the finer scale details. A few model solutions attempt to produce several inches of rainfall over localized areas as we become positioned in the right entrance region of a strong jet streak developing off to our north and east, but there is lots of model to model inconsistency as to if that will occur and where. As of now, the most likely scenario appears to be for most of the region to receive 1-2 inches of rainfall spread out a prolonged period time period tonight through Wednesday morning. If this were to occur, the rainfall would be beneficial in nature given the ongoing drought conditions. However, if the solutions that produce isolated totals of 3-6 inches were to play out, there could be localized issues with flooding. Even if the solution with higher end totals plays out, instantaneous rainfall rates won't be overly high given the lack of instability, so it would be more of a prolonged soaking rainfall leading to areal flooding, as opposed to thunderstorms producing flash flooding. We'll continue to monitor this potential as we move forward.

Either way, Tuesday and Wednesday will feature low clouds, gusty northeasterly winds, and well below normal temperatures. Temperatures likely hold in the 60s on Tuesday, and may even struggle to get out of the 50s on Wednesday as the CAD wedge reaches its peak strength.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Daily shower chances, abundant cloud cover, and cool temperatures continue through Thursday. Drier this weekend.

A persistent wedge-like pattern will remain through at least Thursday as wedging/blocking high pressure remains up across eastern Canada and coastal low pressure strengthens off the Mid-Atlantic coast. This will lead to persistent onshore flow as a series of shortwave disturbances pivot around the coastal low offshore and the remnant stalled frontal boundary south/east of the region. The persistent northeast/east fetch off the Atlantic will yield continued cloudiness, minor to (potentially moderate) coastal flooding (along the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay), cool temperatures, and widespread shower chances to the region.

With a persistent wedge in place expect highs to struggle to get out of the upper 50s and mid 60s through at least Friday. Overnight lows will fall into the 40s and 50s given the cool maritime airmass overhead.

Coastal low pressure will track northward toward the NJ/Long Island coast Friday into Saturday putting more subsidence over the region. This will allow for decreasing precipitation chances and rising temperatures with highs in the upper 60s and mid 70s. Even with that said, model discrepancies remain beyond Saturday as the coastal low looks to retrograde in the vicinity of the Mid-Atlantic coast. Current 00z members have the low meandering up toward the Jersey Shore Saturday before dropping is back south toward the Delmarva Sunday into the early part of next week. This would lead to abundant cloud cover in place along with continued chances for showers ,especially in locations east of the Blue Ridge/closest to the low pressure system. It's not until the middle of next week (i.e September 30th) when the pattern looks to flip again as a stronger front looks to cross the region. Temperatures will remain near normal through the remainder of the extended period with above normal precipitation expected.
s.avn:
A challenging ceiling forecast today. MVFR ceilings have streamed in from the north behind a cold front and are slowly making southward progress early this morning. There are conflicting signals regarding whether ceilings will lift back up to VFR near peak heating today. Locations further north and east should have the greatest chance of returning back to VFR for a few hours this afternoon. For now, that is in the TAF at BWI and MTN, but it can't be ruled out at DCA or IAD as well. For now have maintained continued MVFR conditions at those sites. Showers may be possible on and off through the day. The greater the coverage of those showers, the lesser the likelihood that conditions return back to VFR. Winds today will generally be out of the north to northeast at around 5-10 knots.

Guidance is in better agreement that ceilings will lower to IFR tonight as showers increase in coverage across the area. IFR ceilings and on and off showers then continue through the day Wednesday. Winds will be out of the northeast tonight through Wednesday, and should gust to around 15-25 knots on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Sub-VFR conditions look to continue at times through at least Friday as shower chances persists due to coastal low pressure offshore. Conditions look to slowly improve Friday afternoon and night as coastal low pressure lifts north of the region. VFR conditions should prevail through the weekend although intermittent periods of sub-vfr remain possible Sunday into early next week for terminals mainly along and east of I-95 as coastal low pressure remains nearby. Increase north to northeasterly flow is expected through Friday. Gusts of 15 to 25 kts are possible, especially at terminals near the waters.
s.mar:
Small Craft Advisories remain in effect in the main stem of the Bay through noon within northerly flow. There will likely be a small lull in the winds this afternoon, before they pick up again in earnest within northeasterly flow later tonight into tomorrow as high pressure strengthens to our north. A prolonged period of northeasterly winds is expected through Wednesday with that area of high pressure in place. Small Craft Advisories have been issued again starting tonight and continuing through Tuesday night. At least high-end Small Craft Advisory gusts will continue within northeasterly flow through at least Wednesday. Low- end Gale gusts can't be ruled out late Tuesday night into Wednesday across the widest waters of the Bay, but confidence in that occurring was too low for Gale Watches at the moment.

High end small craft conditions will continue through Friday due to increased onshore north to northeasterly flow. Expect gusts between 20-25 kts with 30 kt gusts sporadically sprinkled over the middle and open waters. On and off showers are also possible at times as multiple shortwave disturbances pivot through. SCA conditions will likely continue through the weekend as low pressure remains off the Mid-Atalntic coast. Strongest gusts will be over the bay and lower tidal Potomac.
s.tide: A cold front will pass south of the waters today. North to northeasterly flow will lead to decreasing anomalies today, with no coastal flooding anticipated. That will be short-lived, however, as tides are expected to snap back to the north, with anomalies rapidly rising again later tonight through the day tomorrow. Elevated tide levels are then expected through much of the week as a strong area of high pressure builds to our north, leading to persistent onshore flow. The wind direction will be closer to northeasterly rather than easterly, so the tidal levels are expected to increase with southward extent in the Bay. Many locations will likely reach Minor Flood Stage on Tuesday and Wednesday, and Annapolis could come close to flooding tonight as well. Moderate flooding can't be ruled out at some locations, but appears to be a less likely outcome at this juncture. A coastal low is expected to develop offshore later this week, potentially prolonging coastal flood concerns.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry conditions return later this week and into the weekend.

Surface high pressure builds northwest of the forecast area beginning on Friday as a surface low pressure tracks northward off the East Coast. Primarily dry conditions are expected, although a nearby low pressure system brings increased precipitation chances to the eastern portions of the forecast area.

Uncertainty remains on the track and timing of the low pressure system, but recent guidance has it tracking north towards the Northeast away from the Mid-Atlantic, possibly making a cyclonic loop near Long Island. The most likely impact from the nearby system will be increased winds due to the tight pressure gradient overhead. North/northwest winds blow around 15-20 mph Friday and Saturday before decreasing Sunday and into the workweek.

Ceilings will vary between MVFR and VFR into this evening before dropping more readily to IFR. An area of rain showers will move across through about 22Z, with embedded TSRA near KCHO.

Guidance is in better agreement that ceilings will lower to IFR tonight as showers increase in coverage across the area. IFR ceilings and on and off showers then continue through the day Wednesday. Winds will be out of the northeast through Wednesday, and should gust to around 15-25 knots on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Northeast winds on Thursday shift to north/northwesterly on Friday, gusting 15 to 20 knots each afternoon. On Friday, metro terminals gust 20 to 25 knots. VFR conditions are expected both days under dry conditions.

East to northeast winds increase through mid week, with gales possibly mainly around southern Maryland Wednesday into Thursday. Periods of rain are also expected, which will reduce visibility. Persistent onshore flow may result in waves as high as 3 to 6 feet in the wider waters of the Chesapeake Bay off southern Maryland by mid week.

Northeast winds on Thursday blow 15 to 25 knots over the waters with gusts up to 35 knots possible. A Gale Watch is in effect until Thursday afternoon for the middle portions of the Chesapeake Bay off southern Maryland. On Friday, north/northwest winds blow 20 to 30 knots over the waters with gusts up to 35 knots possible. Gale conditions are possible over the southern portions of the waters with additional watches possible.

s.avn:
Ceilings will continue to drop this evening as onshore flow increases with the strengthened high wedging in from the north, stalled front nearby, and area of low pressure approaching from the Ohio River Valley. As of 00z/8pm it's a smattering of MVFR to IFR cigs with LIFR cigs back towards the mountains. FOr now, we remain in a lull with lingering showers over northeast MD and the southern Shenandaoh Valley. Expect this lull through 2-4z/10pm-midnight with shower coverage likely increasing overnight into Tuesday morning. IFR conditions will be the theme of the valid TAF period and really through the middle of the workweek as the onshore flow increases. Periods of light to moderate showers will continue as well likely lingering through at least Thursday morning as a series of low pressure systems push through. Winds will remain out of the northeast through Wednesday, and should gust to around 15-25 knots on Tuesday and Wednesday. Gusts will begin to increase at the corridor terminals prior to 9z/5am Tuesday morning as the gradient tightens.

Northeast winds on Thursday shift to north/northwesterly on Friday, gusting 15 to 20 knots each afternoon. On Friday, metro terminals gust 20 to 25 knots. VFR conditions are expected both days under dry conditions.
s.mar:
Expect a lull in the shower activity over the waters the next few hours before an increase heading into early Tuesday morning. Small Craft Advisories are now in effect with east to northeast winds increasing heading into midweek. Gale Watches are in effect for the waters around southern MD Wednesday into Thursday. We'll see if we need to expand or upgrade this watch to a warning in the subsequent shift given better agreement amongst the guidance potentially kicking in gale conditions as early as Tuesday night over the aforementioned areas. Periods of rain are also expected, which will reduce visibility. Persistent onshore flow may result in waves as high as 3 to 6 feet in the wider waters of the Chesapeake Bay off southern Maryland by mid week.

Northeast winds on Thursday blow 15 to 25 knots over the waters with gusts up to 35 knots possible. A Gale Watch is in effect until Thursday afternoon for the middle portions of the Chesapeake Bay off southern Maryland. On Friday, north/northwest winds blow 20 to 30 knots over the waters with gusts up to 35 knots possible. Gale conditions are possible over the southern portions of the waters with additional watches possible.
s.tide: Tides are expected to snap back to the north, with anomalies rapidly rising again later tonight through the day Tuesday. Elevated tide levels are then expected through much of the week as a strong area of high pressure builds to our north, leading to persistent onshore flow. The wind direction will be closer to northeasterly rather than easterly, so the tidal levels are expected to increase with southward extent in the Chesapeake Bay. Many locations will likely reach Minor Flood Stage on Tuesday and Wednesday, and Annapolis could come close to flooding tonight as well. Moderate flooding can't be ruled out at some locations, especially at Annapolis by mid week. A coastal low is expected to develop offshore later this week, potentially prolonging coastal flood concerns.

Shower activity will continue through the day today as large scale forcing for ascent continues to increase downstream of an approaching shortwave disturbance/closed low over the Ohio Valley and within the right entrance region of a developing jet streak to our north. An already well developed CAD wedge will continue to be reinforced by the rainfall and northeasterly flow to the south of an unseasonably strong area of high pressure centered to our north across southern Quebec.

Cloudy skies, on and off showers, and well below normal temperatures will continue through the day tomorrow. By the time all is said and done, most locations should receive around 1-2 inches of rainfall, which should be beneficial in nature given the ongoing drought conditions. Temperatures will run well below normal, with highs both today and tomorrow in the upper 50s to mid 60s. Northeasterly winds gusting to around 15-30 mph will make it feel even cooler.

Rain should come to an end first tomorrow morning across far northeast Maryland, with the drier air making slow progress toward the southwest tomorrow afternoon through tomorrow night. Drier conditions are expected for all on Thursday beneath mostly cloudy skies. Temperatures will remain well below normal, with highs only in the 60s, and winds will stay gusty out of the northeast as a coastal low starts to deepen offshore.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier conditions and a gradual warming trend can be expected through the weekend.

A Rex block during the second half of the week transitions to more of an Omega block over the weekend as a trough moving across the Canadian Rockies results in ridge building across the Great Lakes. At this time, it appears this subtle shift allows the closed upper low to drift a bit to the east, somewhere near or just off the New England or Mid Atlantic coast. This likely keeps any coastal low threat and rainfall threats off to the northeast from Friday through the weekend. However, with inherently less predictability with blocky patterns, the end of the week still bears watching for any retrogression of the pattern. While some areas could see some sun Thursday, greater chances for reduced cloud cover arrive areawide on Friday. Breezy winds will continue through Saturday, if not Sunday, due to the pressure gradient between the coastal low near New England and surface high across the Great Lakes. The wind direction between northeast and northwest will help keep temperatures below normal into the weekend, though gradually warming. Temperatures will be closer to normal by Monday, as the low likely starts drifting away and the ridge builds overhead.

s.tide: A long duration coastal flood event is expected over the next several days within persistent onshore flow as high pressure remains centered to our north and a coastal low eventually takes shape offshore. Anomalies remain on the rise today, with levels forecast to be very close to the Action Stage/Minor Flood Stage line with the tide cycle this afternoon. As of now, water levels are forecast to stay just below Minor Flood Stage today at Annapolis, Solomons Island, Dahlgren, and Alexandria, but it will be close. At least Minor Flooding appears likely with the tide cycle tonight for most sites on the Tidal Potomac, and from Annapolis southward on the Bay. Minor Flooding appears likely each successive tide cycle at those locations through at least Thursday, and potentially even into Friday. With winds out of the northeast, the highest anomalies will be to the south, so locations like Baltimore, Havre de Grace, and Chesapeake City likely won't experience flooding. A few locations could potentially approach Moderate Flood stage later Wednesday into Thursday (Annapolis and Straits Point being the most likely), but confidence was still too low for Watches. Numerous coastal flood headlines will likely need to be issued today.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1... Damp and dreary conditions continue through Wednesday afternoon with drier weather returning Thursday.

Not a whole lot has changed in the synoptic pattern with strong/broad wedging high pressure over southeast Quebec and a stalled boundary over the VA/NC border. Ripples of low pressure continue to traverse this boundary to the south sending on and off showers to the region.

Expect a steady supply of abundant low cloud cover, showers/drizzle, and cool temperatures to continue through at least Wednesday afternoon. This is due largely in part to a series of low pressure systems passing along the stalled front to the south and a delay of mid level dry air from the north as wedging high pressure strengthens over southeast Canada. Conditions will slowly improve from north to south late Wednesday morning into Wednesday evening.

The wedging high pressure system should allow for the drainage of more dry air to the south shunting the front into the Carolinas while also developing a coastal low pressure system off the Delmarva/NC coast. This coastal low feature will supply extra subsidence Wednesday night into Thursday allowing for widespread drying conditions across the region. Unfortunately, with the low nearby breezy conditions will remain along with coastal flooding woes over sensitive locations within the bay/tidal Potomac (see tides discussion).

Given increased northeast flow expect steady temperatures in the upper 50s and mid 60s to continue through Wednesday with a warming trend Thursday as some sunshine returns. Northeasterly winds will gusts 15-30 mph at times with the highest gusts over the bay and higher ridges, especially Wednesday through Friday as coastal low pressure strengthens. The wind will give us more of a raw late Fall feel heading into Wednesday afternoon. Highs get back into the low to mid 60s with even few spots hitting 70 Thursday afternoon.

Rainfall wise most locations should see 1-3 inches of rainfall (includes what has fallen since Monday, and what is yet to fall through Wednesday afternoon). This should be beneficial in nature given the ongoing drought conditions.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Turning breezy and drier with a gradual warming trend Friday into the upcoming weekend.

High pressure will start weakening on Thu as low pressure forms a couple hundred miles off the coast and begins to track north and then west toward the coast. Global models show the low pressure making its closest approach to our area Sunday afternoon. Ensemble guidance show most of the rain staying to our east, but there is a small chance that it could make it as far west as I-95. The northeast flow should start weakening Thu, but there is still a chance that the winds may strengthen again Fri night into the weekend as low pressure approaches the coast. At this time, there isn't a definite clear trend of what winds will do this weekend as the track of the low and how close it gets to the coast remains highly uncertain.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1... Cloudy, showery, and cool conditions continue through much of the day today, with drier conditions building back in for Thursday and Friday.

As of 330 AM, radar imagery shows steady rain in place for most locations east of the Blue Ridge/south of I-70. Conditions have largely dried out to the west of the Blue Ridge, other than some spotty drizzle. To the north of I-70/east of the Blue Ridge the precipitation shield is a bit more broken up/showery in nature.

A strong cold-air damming (CAD) wedge remains in place across the entire area along with the aforementioned rain, cloudy skies, and cool temperatures. An unseasonably strong area of high pressure centered to our north across southern Quebec will reach peak strength today. As this occurs, drier air will slowly start to filter into the area from the northeast. This drier air will slowly start to break down the precipitation shield, with rain gradually coming to an end from northeast to southwest over the course of the day. Locations in central Virginia will be the last to see the precipitation/low clouds break up later tonight. Even after the precipitation comes to an end, it will still be a cool day with cloudy skies in place. Temperatures are only forecast to make it into the 50s to near 60 to the west of the Blue Ridge, and then low to mid 60s to the east of the Blue Ridge. Winds will remain gusty out of the northeast, with gusts to around 20-30 mph possible at times to the east of the Blue Ridge.

Drier conditions are forecast for Thursday and Friday as the upper trough axis that has been stalled out to our west finally starts to make some eastward progress. This trough axis will pass overhead tomorrow, and then progress offshore on Friday. As this occurs, a coastal low will deepen off to our east in response. The pressure gradient between the high to our north and the developing coastal low will keep winds gusty out of the north to northeast. Temperatures will stay below normal as a result, with highs in the 60s tomorrow, and then upper 60s to near 70 on Friday.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Breezy and warmer this weekend, but forecast remains uncertain as Nor'easter impacts Northeast U.S.

Anomalously strong surface ridge (by late September standards) begins to weaken this weekend as a strong Nor'easter develops off the coast of Southern New England/LI. Ensemble members still show quite a bit of spread regarding the exact track of the Nor'easter. A few members show the possibility the low tracks closer to the NJ / Delmarva coast this weekend. Regardless of exact position, we are likely to be on the drier side of the system with northwest winds bringing in breezy, warmer, and mostly dry conditions. If the Nor'easter tracks closer to our area that could bring some rain chances to the area, especially along/east of I-95, along with the potential for increasing winds. Safe to say that there isn't a definite trend for this weekend, so be sure to keep track of the forecast for any changes in the coming days.

The Nor'easter is eventually pushed offshore at the start of next week as high pressure builds in from the OH Valley and Great Lakes. Mid-level ridging builds over much of the eastern CONUS during the middle of next week, marking the return of much warmer temperatures and continued dry conditions.
s.avn:
As of 330 AM, many locations have actually improved back to MVFR/VFR, with only CHO observing IFR at the moment. Any locations that have improved back to VFR are expected to drop back to MVFR after sunrise. Thereafter, dry air is expected to make very slow southwestward progress throughout the day. Showers likely come to an end at most terminals mid- late morning or early afternoon. VFR ceilings are expected to reach the DC Metro terminals by late afternoon. Winds today will be gusty out of the northeast. VFR conditions are expected for all on Thursday and Friday, along with gusty north to northeasterly winds.

A strong Nor'easter off the coast near Southern New England to NJ will bring breezy northwest winds this weekend (gusts around 20-25 knots possible). Some showers are possible, but highly uncertain as it will depend how close the low pressure gets to our area. Continue to monitor for any additional impacts.
s.mar:

Gale Warnings go into effect for the waters surrounding Southern Maryland this morning, with high end SCAs (gusts to near 30 kt) in effect elsewhere. Small Craft Advisories have been issued for all waters Thursday through Thursday night, for continued gusty northeasterly winds. SCAs will likely be needed again in northerly flow on Friday.

High-end SCA conditions to Gales are possible this weekend over the waters, especially in the Chesapeake Bay due to the strong Nor'easter that will be off the coast. If the low tracks closer to our area, expect higher gusts over the waters. However, there remains a lot of uncertainty in the forecast, so be sure to check back as conditions become more certain through the week.

The upper trough axis that has lingered to our west for several days now will finally progress off to our east today. Dry conditions are expected locally, but winds will remain gusty out of the north as high pressure remains in place to our north and a coastal low starts to develop offshore. There will be enough remnant low-level moisture around for a stratocumulus deck to form in response to daytime heating. Temperatures will run well below normal, with highs in the 60s at lower elevations, and 50s in the mountains.

Skies are expected to clear out tonight as drier air works in from the north. The pressure gradient may weaken just enough tonight for some of the more sheltered valleys in the Alleghenies to decouple. If this occurs, some of the highest mountain valleys may get a little frost, with temperatures dropping back into the 30s. Current thinking is that coverage of the frost will be low enough to preclude the issuance of a Frost Advisory for those locations, but we'll continue to monitor the situation. Further east, we'll likely maintain enough of a pressure gradient for winds to persist. Overnight lows are generally forecast to be in the 40s to the west of I-95, and lower 50s to the east of I-95.

Sunnier skies are forecast tomorrow, along with slightly warmer temperatures. Winds will remain gusty out of the north (gusts to around 20-25 mph possible), and temperatures are forecast to reach into the lower 70s at lower elevations, with 60s in the mountains.

s.mar: Gale Warnings for the waters surrounding Southern Maryland drop back to Small Craft Advisories at 6 AM. SCAs are then in effect for all waters in north to northeasterly flow through 6 AM Friday. Forecast uncertainty increases substantially later Friday through the weekend as a coastal low strengthens and then potentially retrogrades westward toward the Mid- Atlantic coast. Coastal Flood Advisories are in effect for Alexandria, DC, Dahlgren, and Solomons Island through Thursday night. Further north along the Bay (Baltimore northward) anomalies are forecast to be lower due to a significant northerly component of the wind.

The forecast gets very complicated later Friday into Saturday as a coastal low strengthens and potentially retrogrades westward toward the area. Model guidance shows an extreme amount of forecast spread with respect to tidal levels Friday afternoon through the weekend. This uncertainty is tied to uncertainty in the placement of the aforementioned coastal low, and whether its associated wind field will allow water to be able to start to drain out of the mouth of the Bay. Further coastal flood headlines may be needed during this time period, but it's also possible that water levels begin to decrease significantly starting Friday night.

s.chg: Gale Warnings and Small Craft Advisories have been issued through Saturday. Coastal Flood Advisories have been extended through early Saturday morning for some locations. Patchy dense river valley fog is occurring west of the Blue Ridge this morning. Confidence is increasing on some rain moving inland this weekend, and the potential track spread of the Nor'easter seems to be narrowing.
s.key:
- 1) A Nor'easter brings below normal temperatures, breezy conditions, and possibly some rain at times through this weekend.

- 2) Patchy dense fog is possible along the river valleys west of the Blue Ridge Mountains this morning, with some frost possible in the higher elevation valleys.

- 3) Warm and calm conditions next week before rainfall chances return by late next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...A Nor'easter brings below normal temperatures, breezy conditions, and possibly some rain at times through this weekend.

A closed upper low stretches along the Mid Atlantic and Carolina coasts this morning, with a strengthening low pressure center east of Cape Hatteras. This Nor'easter will impact the area through the weekend, as the northern stream wave pattern will result in a blocking ridge building north of the closed low. 500 mb cluster analysis shows mainly subtle differences in the depth and position of the upper low, but these small differences could have notable impacts at the surface. With that said, both AI and physics-based 00Z ensemble runs showed some consistency with the surface low behavior... generally drifting northward and strengthening through Saturday before drifting westward toward the New Jersey coast, then becoming occluded and weakening while drifting slowly northeastward early next week as a shortwave trough in central Canada weakens the blocking ridge.

Sensible impacts will of course be greater with eastward extent in the area. Below normal temperatures (highs in the upper 60s to mid 70s) and gusty winds will continue for most of the area. In a worst case scenario (stronger low closer to the coast), locations near the Chesapeake Bay could need a Wind Advisory, but currently gusts between 20 and 40 mph are expected, strongest Saturday and possibly continuing Sunday. The cirrus shield will hug mainly eastern portions of the area today, but expect more extensive cloud cover Saturday and Sunday. The current track forecast also has more guidance spreading some rain into the area, particularly along the I-95 corridor, but potentially as far west as the Potomac Highlands. This rain could start as early as tonight but becomes more probable Saturday and Sunday. At this time, heavier rain is expected to remain east of the area. Coastal flooding, mostly minor in nature, will also be an issue...see separate section below.

While rain chances and wind gusts will likely start declining by Monday, cloud cover may remain stubbornly in place.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Patchy dense fog is possible along the river valleys west of the Blue Ridge Mountains this morning, with some frost possible in the higher elevation valleys.

Clear skies, calm winds, and temperatures dropping into lower 40s have resulted in fog forming along the river valleys west of the Blue Ridge this morning. The valleys in the Potomac Highlands are most filled in, but the immediate Shenandoah River also has fairly continuous coverage. Some observations indicate dense fog of a quarter mile or less, but it is unlikely it becomes widespread enough to warrant an advisory.

A Frost Advisory continues until 9 AM for portions of the higher Allegheny Mountains. Given current temperature trends, frost will likely be limited to the most sheltered cold air sinks.

Both threats will quickly end after sunrise.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Warm and calm conditions next week before rainfall chances return by late next week.

The Nor'easter near the area at the start of next week is going to quickly weaken, then push offshore Monday into Tuesday. Brief high pressure builds in behind the departing Nor'easter, with mostly dry conditions to begin next week. A gradual warming trend is expected as highs go from low to mid 70s on Monday to around 80F Wednesday and Thursday. Mid-level ridging might develop across much of the eastern CONUS at some point during the middle to late part of next week. There's still a lot of variance in the model guidance, but if that were to happen we could see highs reach well into the 80s at some point. A clipper passing by to our north could bring a few showers Wednesday. Otherwise, the next best chance for rain looks to be at the end of next week when a stronger cold front approaches from the west.
s.avn:
Patchy fog at CHO earlier seemed to be brief as there is now a light wind. Some valley fog could also roll into MRB before sunrise, although this remains somewhat uncertain.

Otherwise, VFR condtions are expected to continue through tonight. The biggest impact to terminals will be gusty winds as a slow moving Nor'easter drifts northward along the coast this weekend. Gusty north/northeast winds are expected today, before shifting to north/northwesterly on Saturday and Sunday. Each afternoon, wind gusts between 15 and 25 knots are expected across the terminals, with some gusts to 30 knots possible at BWI, DCA, and MTN. There is increasing confidence in lower ceilings and occasional rain Saturday into Sunday, particularly at those same terminals. Rain chances and wind gusts will start declining Monday, but sub-VFR ceilings may persist. Improving conditions are more likely Tuesday as high pressure builds toward the area.
s.mar:
Small Craft Advisories are in effect for all waters today, although the wider portions of the bay near southern Maryland could have some gusts that near gale force at times. Northerly winds will gradually increase tonight into Saturday as a Nor'easter strengthens off the coast. Gale Warnings go into effect south of North Beach tonight, then expand to Sandy Point and the adjacent estuaries Saturday. Small Craft Advisories were extended elsewhere. Warnings were issued where confidence is currently highest, but it's possible they may need to be extended for most of the Chesapeake Saturday. In a worst case scenario (low stronger and closer to the coast), gusts could approach storm force. Uncertainty increases Saturday night into Sunday as the Nor'easter pivots near the New Jersey coast. At a minimum, Small Craft Advisory conditions will continue, but gale force winds remain possible, especially along the Chesapeake.

SCA conditions could continue over most of the waters through Monday as the Nor'easter impacting the region finally weakens and begins to push offshore. Sub-SCA winds return Monday night through mid week.
s.tide:
Coastal flooding will continue to be an issue through the weekend due to a Nor'easter off the coast and high astronomical tides. There has been a slight downward trend in water levels this morning, so previous warnings were converted to advisories.

The forecast gets very complicated tonight through Sunday as the Nor'easter strengthens and potentially retrogrades westward toward the area Sunday. Model guidance shows an extreme amount of forecast spread with respect to tidal levels starting this afternoon through the weekend. This uncertainty is tied to the placement of the aforementioned coastal low, and whether its associated wind field will allow water to be able to start to drain out of the mouth of the Bay (or at least fully pushed to the southern end of the bay). Advisories were extended through early Saturday morning for the more southern locations, but only through this evening at Annapolis due to some potential for water starting to be shoved to the south. Points north of Annapolis are much less likely to see flooding due to the steady north wind.

Even with this decrease in water levels from the north, guidance is indicating there could be a snapback at some point over the weekend (likely the second half) which could reintroduce some flooding with northward extent. Another round of locally moderate flooding can't be ruled out. While the Nor'easter will pull away early next week, extended range guidance suggests water levels will remain elevated.

s.chg: Track of Nor'easter continues to trend westward increasing the likelihood of rain to areas as far west as I-81. Uncertainty remains with respect to onset of gale force winds and when the strongest winds will occur. Risk of moderate coastal flooding seems to be decreasing with blowout tides becoming a bigger concern for areas north of Annapolis, although minor coastal flooding is still expected through this weekend. Some changes to the Gale Warnings were made earlier.

- 2) Patchy dense fog is possible along the river valleys west of the Blue Ridge Mountains this morning, with some frost possible in the higher elevation valleys.

- 3) Warm and calm conditions next week before rainfall chances return by late next week.

No fresh water flooding is anticipated, but minor coastal flooding is still expected along the lower Potomac River and St. Marys County. Blowout tides are expected elsewhere starting Saturday. Winds will strengthen tonight and peak Saturday afternoon.

s.avn:
Some LLWS is possible at western terminals as winds decouple and winds aloft strengthen.

Main impact will be the gusty N or NNW winds up to 25 kt Saturday. Winds should start gradually diminishing Sat night into Sunday, but still a little breezy. Rain is now likely at all airports starting Sat afternoon and continuing through Sunday.

On Monday, VFR conditions are expected across all terminals through the middle of next week. Northeasterly winds persist, but reduce in magnitude sometime on Monday.
s.mar:
Winds are expected to strengthen tonight through Saturday with gale force winds likely south of Pooles Island. Gale Warnings were expanded further north earlier today.

Northerly winds continue to weaken below SCA criteria on Monday and into the middle of next week.
s.tide: Minor coastal flooding will continue for one or two more high tide cycles for Anne Arundel, Calvert, and Alexandria, but as winds strengthen from the N expect blowout tides through the weekend at those locations and locations further north on the Chesapeake Bay. Minor coastal flooding will persist at Dahlgren and St. Marys County for several high tide cycles. As Nor'easter departs early next week, a snap back event may occur with renewd minor coastal flooding possible.

s.chg: Have increased the sky cover forecast for along and east of I-95 given current satellite trends. Additionally, with the westward shift in the precipitation forecast, measurable rainfall chances have been raised for the second half of Saturday. For the tidal forecast, outside of Dahlgren, water levels have been a bit lower than anticipated. Tidal flooding does appear likely where Coastal Flood Advisories have been issued.

KEY MESSAGE 1...A Nor'easter brings below normal temperatures, breezy conditions, and some rain at times through this weekend.

The center of the circulation of the Nor'easter remains well off the Delmarva coast this evening. Despite its offshore position, the western edge of the high cirrus shield continues to pivot slowly toward the west in time. Aside from that, the atmospheric profile is quite dry owing to the prevailing northerly winds in the column. With the loss of daytime heating, most locations have seen the breezy factor to the winds dropping off after dark. Tonight's lows will eventually fall into the 50s east of the Blue Ridge, with mainly mid/upper 40s off to the west. The one exception would be the Alleghenies which could fall into the low 40s.

On Monday, VFR conditions are expected across all terminals through the middle of next week. Northeasterly winds persist, but reduce in magnitude sometime on Monday.

Northerly winds continue to weaken below SCA criteria on Monday and into the middle of next week.

s.chg: The Gale Warning was expanded to include north of Pooles Island. Dry air may tend to erode the westward expansion of rain today. Some uncertainty lingers in the track of the Nor'easter, which will affect rain coverage and winds Sunday.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...A Nor'easter brings below normal temperatures, breezy conditions, and some rain at times through this weekend.

The strong Nor'easter is located east of the Delmarva peninsula this morning, nearly collocated with the upper level low. Dry air/subsidence is evident on water vapor west of the low, encompassing much of the forecast area. The northerly winds are supplying mid 40s dew points into the area. A shortwave trough in central Canada will cause a blocking ridge to build north of the low tonight into Sunday, resulting in slight retrogression to the west. The low will occlude, and shortwaves in the northern stream will weaken the blocking ridge, allowing the remnant low to eventually drift off to the northeast Monday.

Moisture will advect westward today, but it will likely take some time to saturate the column, and eventually the low level dry air will win out with westward extent. Some light rain will move into areas along and east of I-95 this morning, likely holding off anywhere to the west until afternoon. There's still some spread in the westward extent, but measurable rain becomes much more unlikely west of the Blue Ridge.

There may be a break in the rain this evening as the low reaches its (temporary) northern most position. After that, there is still notable spread in where the low will track. The ECMWF and its ensembles are clustered slightly southward, closer to Cape May, while the GFS and Canadian ensembles allow a more northward position, although it is worth noting some models take the low as far north as Long Island before looping it southwestward across New Jersey. As the pivot occurs, more rain will spread into the area late tonight into Sunday. Chances will be highest across the northern half of the area, and this period has the highest chance for rain to reach as far west as the Alleghenies. But the ultimate latitude of the low will have an impact on rain amounts. While north central/northeast Maryland will likely see the most rain regardless of the track, probabilities for 0.5 inch are much higher in the EC ensemble compared to the other two ensembles.

Wind gusts will be 20-35 mph today, and up to 40 mph near the Chesapeake Bay. Winds any higher than that are becoming less likely. Similar or slightly lower winds are likely on Sunday, with the highest values resulting from a farther southwest and/or stronger low.

The warmest temperatures today (mid 70s) will be across the Potomac Highlands and central Virginia as thicker clouds move in from the east. On Sunday, clouds will envelop most of the area, limiting highs to the 60s with 70s confined to central Virginia.

Coastal flooding, mostly minor in nature, will also be an issue...see separate section below.

While rain chances and wind gusts will likely start declining by Monday, cloud cover will likely remain stubbornly in place. The current forecast calls for upper 60s and lower 70s, but would not be surprised if they are a bit lower if clouds are thick. As winds shift more northwesterly, some upslope showers or drizzle will be possible in the Alleghenies.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Warm and calm conditions next week before rainfall chances return by late next week.

Generally benign weather conditions for the middle to late part of next week for our area. Upper troughing over the Northeast moves offshore Tuesday night into Wednesday, then a fast moving Clipper system passes by to our north Wednesday night into Thursday. Given all of the forcing remains to the north and moisture return ahead of the system is weak, not expecting any precip. Deep ridging develops over the southwest Atlantic at the end of next week, which brings in some warmer temperatures, but still not much in the way of moisture. The next chance for rain looks to be Friday into next weekend as a cold front approaches. Highs in the 70s for most of next week, though low 80s are possible in the middle to late part of the week.
s.avn:
A strong Nor'easter off the coast will bring gusty north to northwest winds today and Sunday, with perhaps a modest decrease in gusts tonight. Gusts of 25-30 kt will be common each day, perhaps slightly lower at MRB and CHO.

Low levels have been trending drier through tonight, so while some light rain will likely move from east to west today, it may not reduce visibility very much, and will likely fail to reach MRB and CHO. MVFR ceilings may be brief at best for BWI, DCA, and MTN. Additional rain will likely move into the area late tonight or Sunday as the low pivots near New Jersey. There's still some uncertainty with the extent of this rain, with CHO least likely to see any rain. MVFR ceilings will slowly spread into the area as well, but this may not occur until Sunday afternoon and evening.

Wind gusts and rain chances will decrease Sunday night into Monday, although MVFR ceilings will likely continue through Monday night.

VFR conditions are forecast to prevail Tuesday and Wednesday, with no precipitation chances.
s.mar:
As the Nor'easter churns offshore of the Delmarva coast, winds are expected to strengthen today. The Gale Warning has been expanded to include the entire Chesapeake. While the western waters will be farther removed from the wind fields, drier air will promote deeper mixing, and some gale force gusts can't be ruled out this afternoon. This situation will be monitored. Winds should decrease slightly tonight, with Gale Warnings ending at 10 PM this evening.

Exactly where the Nor'easter pivots near New Jersey could impact winds on Sunday. While Small Craft Advisories are a sure bet, a stronger/southwestward solution could result in another period of gale conditions.

The Nor'easter will slowly pull away Monday, although Small Craft Advisories may be needed before winds fully subside Monday night.

Favorable marine conditions expected through the middle of next week. Southerly channeling is possible over the open waters of the Chesapeake Bay on Wednesday, though still uncertain if those winds will be near SCA strength.
s.tide: Northerly winds are slowly leading to declining anomalies. It's possible the high tide cycle today will see no flooding, but left the advisories for Dahlgren and Straits Point since it will be close. As the Nor'easter lifts northward tonight and Sunday, some guidance has water sloshing back northward. This will extended the flood threat for the lower Potomac at a minimum, but additional locations could also see some minor flooding. Uncertainty continues into early next week, as some guidance has water levels dropping as the system departs, while others keep the levels elevated.

s.chg: A Coastal Flood Advisory was issued for Calvert County until 5 AM Monday.

A strong Nor'easter off the coast will bring gusty north to northwest winds today and Sunday, with perhaps a modest decrease in gusts tonight. Gusts of 25-30 kt will be common each day, perhaps slightly lower at MRB and CHO.

Low levels have been trending drier through tonight, so while some light rain will likely move from east to west today, it may not reduce visibility very much, and will likely fail to reach MRB and CHO. MVFR ceilings may be brief at best for BWI, DCA, and MTN. Additional rain will likely move into the area late tonight or Sunday as the low pivots near New Jersey. There's still some uncertainty with the extent of this rain, with CHO least likely to see any rain. MVFR ceilings will slowly spread into the area as well, but this may not occur until Sunday afternoon and evening.

Wind gusts and rain chances will decrease Sunday night into Monday, although MVFR ceilings will likely continue through Monday night.

VFR conditions are forecast to prevail Tuesday and Wednesday, with no precipitation chances.
s.mar:
As the Nor'easter churns offshore of the Delmarva coast, winds are expected to strengthen today. The Gale Warning has been expanded to include the entire Chesapeake. While the western waters will be farther removed from the wind fields, drier air will promote deeper mixing, and some gale force gusts can't be ruled out this afternoon. This situation will be monitored. Winds should decrease slightly tonight, with Gale Warnings ending at 10 PM this evening.

Exactly where the Nor'easter pivots near New Jersey could impact winds on Sunday. While Small Craft Advisories are a sure bet, a stronger/southwestward solution could result in another period of gale conditions.

The Nor'easter will slowly pull away Monday, although Small Craft Advisories may be needed before winds fully subside Monday night.

Favorable marine conditions expected through the middle of next week. Southerly channeling is possible over the open waters of the Chesapeake Bay on Wednesday, though still uncertain if those winds will be near SCA strength.
s.tide:
A Coastal Flood Advisory was issued for Calvert County.

Northerly winds are slowly leading to declining anomalies. It's possible the high tide cycle today will see no flooding, but left the advisories for Dahlgren and Straits Point since it will be close. As the Nor'easter lifts northward tonight and Sunday, some guidance has water sloshing back northward. This will extended the flood threat for the lower Potomac at a minimum, but additional locations could also see some minor flooding. Uncertainty continues into early next week, as some guidance has water levels dropping as the system departs, while others keep the levels elevated.

s.chg: New Coastal Flood Advisories have been issued for Alexandria and Annapolis.
