- 2) Warm and tranquil weather is expected for the middle of the week before rain chances return by late in the work week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...A Nor'easter brings below normal temperatures, breezy conditions, and some rain at times through this weekend.

A Nor'easter is positioned east of New Jersey early this morning beneath a closed upper low. These features will drift west or southwest today as an upper level ridge passes across eastern Canada. Showers along the Chesapeake Bay will continue to expand westward through the day. There remains some uncertainty with just how far south and west the rain will reach due to relatively drier air. Winds are also a bit more northwesterly today, so some downsloping could help erode the western edge as well. Rain amounts will be light, generally less than a quarter inch for most, although locations in northeastern Maryland could see up to an additional inch of rain. Expect wind gusts to increase again after sunrise as the gradient wind field rotates over the area. Peak gusts will again be in the 25-35 mph range for much of the area. The advancing rain and lower clouds will limit temperatures for the northern two thirds of the area in the 60s. Locations in central Virginia will likely rise into the lower to mid 70s. Tidal flooding will continue to be an issue through tonight...see separate section below.

The Nor'easter will start weakening tonight as it pivots near the Delaware Bay. This will lead to decreasing rain chances tonight, although some patches of light rain or drizzle may persist. Lows will be in the 50s.

As the blocking ridge departs, the low will be able to start progressing northeastward Monday while continuing to weaken. Winds gusts will be much lower than the weekend, and most locations should remain dry. However, cloud cover will likely remain stubbornly in place in a broad moisture shield left behind by the upper low. The current forecast calls for highs in the upper 60s and lower 70s, but would not be surprised if they are a bit lower if clouds are thick. As winds shift more northwesterly, some upslope showers or drizzle will be possible in the Alleghenies.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Warm and tranquil weather is expected for the middle of the week before rain chances return by late in the work week.

As the Nor'easter and accompanying longwave trough continue to pull away from the Atlantic coast Tuesday and Wednesday, mid/upper heights begin to build in earnest. These above average 500-mb heights are forecast to run around 585-588 dm as the transient upper ridge swings eastward toward the Atlantic Seaboard. Subsidence accompanying this regime favors dry conditions. However, the moisture left behind by the low may become trapped beneath the subsidence inversion, so Tuesday will likely feature more clouds than sun. More sun is likely Wednesday as surface winds turn southerly. Some fair weather cumulus likely develop Wednesday and Thursday as instability increases a bit through the day. However, the forecast is dry through at least Thursday.

The peak in the warming trend is likely to occur in the mid/late week period. Global ensemble box-and-whisker plots show fairly low spread on Wednesday and Thursday and high temperatures return to the low to perhaps mid 80s. Much of the late week uncertainty revolves around the increase in shower and cloud coverage. There is some uncertainty whether the front pushes southward rather quickly or stalls out nearby. Once this system does push southward, temperatures are expected to return to more seasonable numbers for next weekend.
s.avn:
Additional rain showers will continue to move in from the northeast through today as a Nor'easter pivots near New Jersey. The steadiest rain will be at BWI/MTN, where visibility may be reduced at times, but rain will be lighter elsewhere and may not reach CHO at all. Lower ceilings will also migrate westward through the day. They should largely be MVFR, although IFR is possible later this afternoon and evening at BWI/MTN. NNW winds will increase again after sunrise, with gusts of 20 to 30 kt through the day before subsiding this evening.

MVFR ceilings will likely linger through Monday except at CHO, where any such lower ceilings will likely be brief. Northwest winds will be much lighter Monday. Stratocumulus ceilings may persist Tuesday but will likely be VFR as high pressure builds into the area.

A broad area of surface high pressure remains along the Atlantic coast on Wednesday into Thursday. This will favor VFR conditions along with mainly south to southwesterly winds each day.
s.mar:
Winds have subsided to SCA levels (or less) early this morning as the Nor'easter has lifted a bit to the north. It will pivot back to the southwest today but will also start weakening. Some models show the greatest chance of winds near gale force in the far northern Bay (near the low) while others show the strongest winds in the mid bay (longer fetch). However, did not feel either of these scenarios was worth holding onto a Gale Warning at this time. The Nor'easter will start weakening tonight and gradually lift northeastward Monday. Winds will start diminishing as a result. Extended the Small Craft Advisories for portions or all of tonight depending on location. Advisories may need to be extended into Monday, but such conditions would be much more marginal. Lighter winds are expected Monday night and Tuesday as high pressure starts building into the area.

With high pressure edging off the coast, marine winds will mainly be out of the south to southwesterly direction. Gusts should stay below advisory thresholds on Wednesday. However, some uptick is possible by Thursday as southerly channeling ensues. This could near Small Craft Advisory levels, particularly over southern portions of the Chesapeake Bay.
s.tide: Water levels are rather erratic, rising quickly in the northern part of the bay while remaining steady farther south. Surge guidance has had a hard time figuring out what happens to water levels through the day, leading to much lower confidence in the tidal forecast. Did think trends were evident enough that St. Marys County will not experience moderate flooding, so downgraded the warning to an advisory. Left the watch for Annapolis this afternoon/evening due to the large amount of uncertainty, although only the spread in the Stevens ensemble suggests that moderate would be possible. As the Nor'easter weakens tonight and begins pulling away Monday, water levels should start declining, with the threat of flooding ending by Monday morning.

Think that most of the showers should be gone by 10 PM and, in some locations, much sooner than that. Still a healthy band of showers on the east side of the circulation that may try to make into Cecil County this evening or overnight.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Warm, tranquil weather through midweek before chances for showers return Friday and into next weekend.

As the Nor'easter and accompanying longwave trough continue to pull away from the Atlantic coast Tuesday and Wednesday, mid/upper heights begin to build in earnest. These above average 500-mb heights coincide with a transient upper ridge swinging eastward toward the Atlantic Seaboard. Subsidence accompanying this regime favors dry and warming conditions. However, the moisture left behind by the low may become trapped beneath the subsidence inversion, so Tuesday will likely feature more clouds than sun. Likely more sunshine on Wednesday as surface winds turn southerly. Some fair weather cumulus likely develop Wednesday and Thursday as instability increases a bit through the day with dry conditions through this period. More sunshine brings warming daytime temperatures through the work week. Global ensembles show fairly high agreement on high temperatures rising into the 70s Wednesday and perhaps the mid 80s on Thursday.

Heading into the weekend, temperatures and the potential for rain remains somewhat uncertain, mainly revolving around how far south and how quickly a cold front can push into the Mid-Atlantic. Currently, global ensemble members favor a later arrival with rain chances and daytime temperatures rising Friday and through the beginning of the weekend. However, temperatures are generally dependent on shower and cloud coverage associated with this front. As winds shift more northwesterly, some upslope showers or drizzle will be possible in the Alleghenies.

As the Nor'easter and accompanying longwave trough continue to pull away from the Atlantic coast Tuesday and Wednesday, mid/upper heights begin to build in earnest. These above average 500-mb heights coincide with a transient upper ridge swinging eastward toward the Atlantic Seaboard. Subsidence accompanying this regime favors dry and warming conditions. However, the moisture left behind by the low may become trapped beneath the subsidence inversion, so Tuesday will likely feature more clouds than sun. Likely more sunshine on Wednesday as surface winds turn southerly. Some fair weather cumulus likely develop Wednesday and Thursday as instability increases a bit through the day with dry conditions through this period. More sunshine brings warming daytime temperatures through the work week. Global ensembles show fairly high agreement on high temperatures rising into the 70s Wednesday and perhaps the mid 80s on Thursday.

Heading into the weekend, temperatures and the potential for rain remains somewhat uncertain, mainly revolving around how far south and how quickly a cold front can push into the Mid-Atlantic. Currently, global ensemble members favor a later arrival with rain chances and daytime temperatures rising Friday and through the beginning of the weekend. However, temperatures are generally dependent on shower and cloud coverage associated with this front. Overall, the farther and sooner this front pushes southward into our region, the quicker we could see temperatures returning to seasonable next weekend.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Tranquil weather is expected through the middle of the week with climbing temperatures.

The weakening Nor'easter is beginning to move away from the New Jersey coast and will continue to progress northeastward today as a blocking ridge to the north translates eastward. Before it does so, a few light showers/patches of drizzle continue across mainly north central and northeastern Maryland. It appears the risk for rain will start declining by mid morning. Some CAM reflectivity forecasts try to spit out a few sprinkles this afternoon from the residual shallow moisture layer, but have left the forecast dry for now. That moisture will result in persistent clouds through the day, especially across the northern half of the area. Clouds will hold temperatures in the upper 60s to lower 70s, except mid 70s in central Virginia where there may be more breaks of sun. Winds will be lighter than the weekend as the pressure gradient relaxes.

Some clouds likely linger through tonight. Some fog may develop west of the Blue Ridge, if there are breaks. Lows will largely be in the 50s.

Ridging at the surface and aloft will build toward the eastern US for the middle of the week, leading to a steady warming trend. Residual moisture may remain trapped beneath the subsidence inversion with weak gradients on Tuesday, although deeper mixing will likely support more breaks of sun. While dry conditions are most likely, it's worth noting some guidance indicates there may be a brief shower or sprinkle as the mid/upper level trough axis will still be overhead. Highs will be closer to normal in the 70s.

Temperatures will climb further Wednesday and Thursday, with more locations reaching the 80s. Some spots could even reach the upper 80s by Thursday. Developing southerly flow will lead to more sunshine. Dry weather is expected both days. With light winds and elevated dew points, some patchy fog could form during the overnight hours.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A cold front will approach on Friday, leading to cooler and potentially unsettled weather for the weekend.

Expect continued warm conditions Friday in response to the above average heights across the region. Unlike many ridges that stagnate during the summertime, this feature is forecast to be more transient in nature while edging off the Atlantic coast by Friday. Amplifying flow in the northern stream will allow a longwave trough to graze the area by Friday into Saturday. Given the height falls are rather weak, the accompanying cold front which reaches the area on Friday likely stalls just off to the south through the weekend. The pattern turns a bit more unpredictable by Sunday into early next week. An elongated area of vorticity spinning initially around the Southern Plains may begin to edge northeastward in time. Enhanced vertical motions plus increasing moisture fluxes would support a risk for more concentrated rainfall. However, uncertainty is rather high given the mesoscale nature of these features.

As the weak surface boundary nears the area, rain chances return to the forecast for Friday. Given the weak nature of the front and limited upper- level support, such chances are largely capped around 20 to 40 percent. As mentioned above, this frontal system is likely to linger just off to the south for the weekend. This will maintain a continued threat for rain along with cooler temperatures. At this point, daily highs are forecast to be in the 60s, with 50s at night given the abundant clouds and further rain chances.

Some models are printing spotty light QPF this afternoon as instability increases beneath the trough axis. However, moisture will be shallow, likely limiting any precipitation to sprinkles.

Skies should clear some tonight as ridging builds in at the surface and aloft. This set up could be favorable for fog to develop, although the coverage remains somewhat uncertain at this time. Lows will be close to the dew points in the 50s.

The surface high will move off the coast late Wednesday into Thursday while heights continue to increase. Temperatures will climb further, with more locations reaching the 80s. Some spots could even approach 90 by Thursday. Developing southerly flow will lead to more sunshine. Dry weather is expected both days. While nightly fog is possible, increasing southwesterly flow just above the surface may limit low level saturation.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Well above normal normal temperatures continue through Friday, but forecast confidence decreases moving into the weekend as rain chances increase.

Another day of well above normal temperatures is expected on Friday. 850 hPa temperatures of around 16-18C should yield high temperatures in the mid 80s to near 90 at lower elevations, and 70s in the mountains. Clouds will be on the increase through the day, and a few showers can't be ruled out in western Maryland or the West Virginia Panhandle during the afternoon as a cold front approaches from the northwest. Guidance varies substantially from model to model and ensemble member to ensemble member regarding the positioning of this front through the upcoming weekend. With the frontal boundary in the vicinity, there will be at least some chance for showers either day this weekend, with ensemble guidance favoring higher chances on Sunday. Forecast uncertainty remains high however, with ensemble members showing high temperature solutions ranging from the upper 50s to low 90s Saturday, with cooler temperatures more likely by Sunday. The frontal zone is likely to clear the area by Monday, leaving below normal temperatures in its wake.
s.avn:
Moisture wrapping around what's left of the Nor'easter will continue to bring ceilings through today, although they will most likely remain VFR. The overcast is widespread enough that fog appears unlikely this morning, although a few patches could develop if there are any breaks before sunrise. Light northwest winds continue through the day. Added in a MVFR TEMPO at KMRB until 15Z with patchy drizzle bringing in lower ceilings.

Clouds should break tonight with light winds forecast. That could result in fog, although coverage is uncertain. MRB and CHO would have higher chances of lower visibilities, but will play TAFs conservatively now until confidence increases.

VFR conditions will continue Wednesday and Thursday as high pressure passes, with light winds turning southerly. Fog looks a little less likely Wednesday and Thursday nights but can't be ruled out.

VFR conditions and southwesterly winds are expected on Friday. Depending on the positioning of a front, sub-VFR conditions could be possible on Saturday, but forecast confidence during that time period remains low.
s.mar:
High pressure moving toward the area will provide light winds through Wednesday. A northwesterly direction today will turn southerly on Wednesday.

Southerly winds begin to pick up in strength on Thursday, with some channeling effects possibly bringing gusts to near 20 knots over the Chesapeake Thursday night.

Sub-SCA level winds are expected on Friday in south to southwesterly flow. Winds are currently forecast to shift to out of the northeast on Saturday, but forecast confidence remains low with a frontal boundary nearby. SCA conditions are possible depending on the frontal position.
s.tide: Some uncertainty exists for the remainder of the week as tide levels remain elevated. Any subtle shifts upward could result in minor flooding, particularly at Annapolis. However, Alexandria, Dahlgren, and Havre de Grace may also be close at times. Minor flooding could occur as soon as this evening's high tide. Evening tides would be favored going forward as well since they are astronomically higher.

s.chg: Increased precipitation chances this afternoon to accommodate light rain/drizzle moving across portions of the forecast area. Additionally, Coastal Flood Advisories were issued for Annapolis and Havre de Grace.

- 2) A stalling cold front and wave of low pressure may affect the area this weekend.

- 3) High pressure likely returns early next week.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Tranquil weather is expected through Thursday with climbing temperatures.

Moisture associated with the departing Nor'Easter remains over the Mid-Atlantic through this afternoon, yielding increased cloud cover and perhaps some light drizzle/rain showers. Upper level ridging slowly builds overhead beginning tonight with surface high pressure remaining overhead through Thursday.

With upper level ridging and surface high pressure overhead, dry conditions and warming temperatures are expected through the end of the week. High temperatures today will rise into the 60s and 70s with highs by Thursday rising in the 90s for portions of the area. On Friday, surface high pressure shifts offshore as a cold front approaches from the northwest. Dry conditions and warming temperatures continue for most with the exception of afternoon rain showers in the western portions of the Alleghenies.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A stalling cold front and wave of low pressure may affect the area this weekend.

Upper troughing shears out toward the Great Lakes, eventually becoming absorbed in a larger cyclonic gyre near Hudson Bay this weekend. At the surface, this pattern sends a cold front southward into Virginia. There is some lingering uncertainty as to where the front stalls, with a sharp temperature gradient across the frontal zone (60s on the north/cool side, 80s on the south/warm side). The temperature forecast for Saturday may be subject to large changes of 10 or more degrees as a result, with the current forecast splitting the difference and calling for widespread 60s and 70s given at least some broad consensus that the front ends up to the south placing the Mid-Atlantic on its cooler and cloudier side. Shower activity may accompany the stalling front, with uncertainty in coverage (though anything severe or particularly heavy seems unlikely at this point).

A wave of low pressure, infused with tropical moisture from the remnants of multiple East Pacific systems, treks toward the OH/TN Valleys Saturday into Saturday night. The track of the low beyond this point will depend on (1) where exactly the stalled front is, and (2) the strength of a transient blocking high pressure to the north. Rain or showers become increasingly likely for much of the region Saturday night into Sunday, with a soaking rain possible if the wave of low pressure is a bit more organized/closer to the area.

KEY MESSAGE 3...High pressure likely returns early next week.

Following the weekend system, a large area of high pressure will likely build from the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes to the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic early next week. This sets the stage for much drier weather and below normal temperatures for the first half of next week. Daytime highs on Monday and Tuesday likely stay in the 60s (50s in the mountains), with overnight lows in the 40s to near 50 (30s in the mountains and sheltered valleys west of the Blue Ridge with perhaps some frost potential in the coldest spots).
s.avn:
VFR conditions continue this afternoon across eastern terminals with near MVFR ceilings lingering at KMRB. Winds remain light out of the northwest this afternoon before becoming light and variable overnight. With light winds, cloud cover diminishes tonight which could lead to fog developing mainly over MRB and CHO.

Surface high pressure remains overhead Wednesday and Thursday with VFR conditions expected both days. Winds shift to southerly on Wednesday, blowing 10 knots or less. Winds remain light out of the south/southwest on Thursday.

Lower CIGs are possible in the wake of a stalling cold front Saturday. Rain showers become increasingly likely Saturday night into Sunday with sub-VFR CIGs/VSBYs possible at times. The wind forecast is somewhat uncertain and contingent on where exactly a front stalls Saturday, and where a wave of low pressure tracks Sunday, but generally north to east flow is expected. Some gusts of 15 to 20 knots are plausible each day.
s.mar:
Light winds remain out of the north/northwest this afternoon before becoming light and variable overnight. Winds shift to southerly Wednesday and remain out of the south on Thursday. With southerly channeling, winds increase over the waters although are expected to remain below SCA criteria. That being said, a brief period of near SCA criteria winds are possible on Thursday afternoon and can likely be covered with an MWS.

North to northeast winds may gust to around 20 knots in the wake of a stalling front Saturday, though the wind forecast is a bit uncertain and depends on exactly where the front stalls. A wave of low pressure passes by on Sunday, which depending on its exact track and strength could result in additional gustiness and SCAs. Rain showers are most likely Saturday night into Sunday; thunder potential seems very low, but not zero during this time.
s.tide: Some uncertainty exists for the remainder of the week as tide levels remain elevated. Coastal Flood Advisories have been issued for Annapolis and Havre de Grace with tidal anomalies forecast to reach minor flood stage. Any subtle shifts upward could result in additional minor flooding, particularly at Dahlgren, Alexandria, and Baltimore where high tide will near minor flood stage. Minor flooding will occur as soon as this evening's high tide. Evening tides would be favored going forward as well since they are astronomically higher.

- 1) After locally dense morning fog, temperatures will climb above normal today through Friday.

- 2) A cold front will bring rain showers and cooler temperatures to the area this weekend.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...After locally dense morning fog, temperatures will climb above normal today through Friday.

Surface high pressure is nearly overhead this morning. The residual mid/upper level trough axis is starting to depart, which has allowed the more expansive stratus deck to steadily shrink. However, some low level moisture still exists, and some more clouds have filled in across the central Shenandoah Valley and central Virginia. These clouds have been limiting fog development, but have seen river valley and ground fog in areas that are clear. It's still a bit uncertain if fog can become more widespread, but at least locally dense fog will be possible through sunrise.

A shortwave ridge aloft will crest the area today while the surface high starts moving off the coast. The ensuing southerly flow will result in temperatures rising above normal, with highs in the upper 70s and lower 80s expected for much of the area. Stratocumulus clouds should scatter out through the day. However, a shortwave passing through the Great Lakes will bring increasing high level clouds later this afternoon into tonight. Those clouds, combined with a light southwesterly flow, will make any fog development much more localized tonight. Lows will be in the upper 50s and lower 60s.

After the departure of the Great Lakes shortwave Thursday morning, a large ridge will build over the southeastern CONUS. Temperatures will rise further, with most of the lower elevations in the 80s on Thursday, and perhaps even nearing 90 in a few spots. The ridge will break down on Friday as a trough moves across the northern Great Lakes, but temperatures could squeak a couple degrees higher. The exception will be west of I-81 where clouds will be thickening, but it will still be a very warm day.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A cold front will bring rain showers and cooler temperatures to the area this weekend.

Upper-level troughing develops over the northern Plains before tracking east late in the week, with a stemming cold front forming ahead of it. Infused with tropical moisture from the Southwest, this front will move into the Mid-Atlantic between late Friday and Saturday before stalling to the south. Showers will become likely along the Allegheny Mountains by Friday afternoon, but there is some uncertainty how well the showers hold together farther east moving into Friday night. As the front stalls, additional rain showers will be possible throughout the weekend, although timing and total QPF remains uncertain as models deviate on where exactly the front will stall and the development of a wave of low pressure. Many of the 00Z models have shown a decidedly southern shift to the frontal zone, as strong high pressure crossing the Great Lakes exerts influence. Both the ECMWF and GFS AI ensembles still show relatively high rain chances across the southern half of the CWA though, so the coverage of rain is far from solidified. Regardless, temperatures drop on Saturday in the wake of this front, potentially failing to reach 70 degrees depending on the amount of cloud cover.

A wave of low pressure to the north and trailing secondary cold front will push the stalled front offshore by early next week, with high pressure building behind the front as upper-level zonal flow develops overhead. Conditions look to be much drier during this period, with temperatures remaining cooler overall. By Tuesday morning, temperatures over the mountains could reach the 30s with perhaps some frost potential in the coldest spots.
s.avn:
Fog will be the main issue this morning, although its development is hinging on several areas of (VFR) stratocumulus clouds. Based on guidance available for the 06Z TAFs, CHO was most likely to experience IFR conditions (and did very briefly earlier), but clouds have now moved in there. That may leave IAD, MRB, and perhaps BWI as the next best candidates for fog.

Surface high pressure will remain nearby today and Thursday with VFR conditions expected both days. Southerly winds generally less than 10 kt are expected both days. Fog is less probable Thursday and Friday mornings.

An approaching cold front could bring some showers late Friday afternoon and into the night, although they don't appear particularly heavy and ceilings may remain VFR. Lower CIGs are possible at terminals Saturday and into Sunday as the front stalls to the south. Intermittent rain showers Saturday night and into Sunday could temporarily reduce VSBYs. However, these impacts will be dependent on the frontal position, which has trended south in recent guidance. Winds generally flow north to northwesterly, with gusts between 15-20 knots possible during then as the front tracks southeast.
s.mar:
Winds will become southerly today as high pressure drifts off the coast. There could be a brief increase in winds this evening on the wider waters of the middle Bay, but the potential for a Small Craft Advisory is minimal. There may be a greater chance of southerly channeling warranting an advisory Thursday night into Friday.

A cold front will press southward Friday night, and the ensuing northerly wind shift could result in advisory conditions. North to northwest winds may remain within SCA thresholds on Saturday in the wake of the cold front before diminishing some overnight. Scattered showers are possible throughout the weekend as the front moves through and potentially stalls for a bit, but timing remains uncertain as model guidance still shows some spread in where the front will linger.
s.tide: Some uncertainty continues to exist for the remainder of the week as tide levels remain elevated and subtly fluctuating. These small changes will make the difference in whether there is additional minor flooding. Alexandria, Dahlgren, Annapolis, and Havre de Grace have the greatest chance of reaching flood stage. The evening high tides are favored for any flooding since they are astronomically higher. A cold frontal passage should lead to declining water levels Friday night.

High clouds associated with a passing shortwave-trough to the north tonight should prevent widespread fog development, but some river valley fog is still possible west of I-81. Otherwise, fair weather will continue through Fri morning along with rising temperatures. Temps should climb into the mid 80s Thursday under abundant sunshine and approach 90 on Friday under high clouds before showers arrive in the afternoon.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A pair of cold fronts will move across the area in the next five days, one Friday evening, and a second one Monday.

The first front will cross the area Fri evening. Expect scattered to numerous showers and perhaps a thunderstorm as the front crosses the area. Not a lot of upper support with this front and neither a lot of instability, so only light to moderate rainfall amounts are expected. The front will stall across the southern Mid-Atlantic states Saturday while high pressure builds to the north. This will provide for a cooler, dry day Saturday.

A wave of low pressure develops along the front in the southern Appalachians Sunday bringing the threat of showers again to the area Sunday into Sunday evening.

A second stronger cold front associated with a deepening trof south of James Bay will cross the area Monday morning. This appears to be a dry frontal passage, but bring a significant cool down for the first full week of October.

KEY MESSAGE 3...A strong area of Canadian high pressure brings frost and freeze conditions beginning Monday night.

While overnight temperatures east of the Blue Ridge stay in the 40s overnight, lows along and west of the Blue Ridge will drop into the upper 20s and 30s. Frost and freeze conditions are possible both Monday and Tuesday nights, mainly along the Alleghenies although could extend into the Shenandoah Valley. Low temperatures in the Alleghenies will be in the upper 20s to low 30s with the Shenandoah valley dipping into the mid 30s.

With high pressure overhead, dry conditions are expected both days with weakening winds. High temperatures on Monday will be in the 60s for most with those at higher elevations staying in the 50s. Tuesday will be noticeably cooler during the day with highs in the 50s and 60s.

KEY MESSAGE 1...After patchy morning fog, temperatures will remain above normal through Friday.

A shortwave trough is passing from the eastern Great Lakes to New England this morning. Only some high level clouds have been affecting our area, but now the thickest cloud shield is departing to the east. In its wake, some patchy fog is developing, mainly in the typical valleys and other rural areas. Some locally dense fog is possible, but it appears unlikely it will become widespread.

An upper level ridge will build over the area today while surface high pressure remains offshore. Temperatures will climb further today, with most of the lower elevations reaching the lower 80s. Increasing low level winds will prevent full decoupling tonight, resulting in most locations remaining in the 60s for lows. Even with increasing high level clouds Friday, another day with highs in the 80s is expected.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A stalling cold front may bring rain at times from Friday through Sunday.

A cold front will approach from the northwest Friday afternoon, eventually pushing south of the area Friday night. Showers will likely reach western Maryland by midday, progresses southeastward during the afternoon and into the night. Despite the warm temperatures, poor lapse rates aloft will limit instability, so few if any thunderstorms are expected. A westerly component to the flow could also result in downslope drying, and many models show showers becoming more scattered in nature with eastward extent. Rainfall amounts with this round will likely be less than a quarter inch for most locations.

Strong high pressure will pass north of the area Saturday while the front stalls across the southeastern states. Southern stream moisture will likely overrun the boundary fairly far to the north, but there remains some uncertainty in the dividing line between rain and no rain. Overall, Saturday probably has a better chance of being dry with the high to the north. A wave of low pressure will likely ride along the boundary Saturday night into Sunday, and this may provide a higher chance of rain spreading northward into the area. In a reversal of last night, the latest guidance has shifted back northward with rainfall coverage during this period. In the end, the details are far from solidified. However, any rain that does occur will likely exit the area Sunday evening.

Being north of the boundary and potentially having a lot of cloud cover, high temperatures will likely remain in the 60s for most areas over the weekend.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Cooler and drier weather early next week with potential for frost and freeze west of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

A second stronger cold front associated with a deepening trof south of James Bay will cross the area Monday morning. This appears to be a dry frontal passage, and temperatures could rebound back into the 70s as skies clear.

A large area of high pressure will build from the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes to the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic in the wake of the front. This will bring at least a few days of dry weather and below normal temperatures. Highs will likely be in the 60s (50s mountains), with lows in the 40s to near 50 (30s mountains).

As high pressure moves overhead Monday night through Tuesday night, winds will be light and skies will be clear. Given the cooler air in place during this time and the favorable setup for radiational cooling, sheltered valleys and higher elevations near and west of the Blue Ridge may be cold enough for frost formation. Some of the typical cold sinks could drop to near freezing, as well. This is roughly 1 to 2 weeks earlier than average.
s.avn:
Patchy fog is developing this morning, and has already been affecting CHO and MRB. It appears unlikely the other terminals are affected. Otherwise VFR conditions are expected into midday Friday with light southerly winds.

A cold front will enter the area late Friday afternoon or evening. Some showers are possible along the front, but they will likely be fairly light. A brief period of MVFR conditions is possible Friday night.

The front will stall to the south over the weekend, but its position remains uncertain. Saturday has the greater chance of being dry, with a wave of low pressure potentially bringing rain on Sunday. Any sub-VFR conditions would likely be limited to CHO Saturday, but could spread northward Sunday.

VFR conditions are expected to prevail Monday into Tuesday, though some early morning river valley fog is possible. Winds will be north with an increase for a time in the wake of the weekend system. The timing is a bit uncertain, but favors late Monday or early Tuesday when gusts of 20-25 kts are possible.
s.mar:
Southerly winds will uptick a little today into Friday. A Small Craft Advisory may be needed on the wider waters of the middle bay tonight into Friday morning, but confidence is lower since a southwesterly component to the flow would limit channeling effects. A cold front will push southward Friday night, with advisories possible in the ensuing northerly flow through parts of Saturday. After that, winds may be relatively lighter until a second cold front pushes through on Monday.

Strong northerly winds in the wake of this front will likely prompt SCAs Monday into Tuesday. A few gusts near gale force are possible if the stronger solutions verify.
s.tide: Some uncertainty continues to exist through Friday as tide levels remain elevated and subtly fluctuating. These small changes will make the difference in whether there is additional minor flooding. Alexandria, Dahlgren, Annapolis, and Havre de Grace have the greatest chance of reaching flood stage, although based on current trends, Annapolis has the highest chance. The evening high tides are favored for any flooding since they are astronomically higher. A cold frontal passage should lead to declining water levels Friday night.

Showers will likely reach western Maryland by the afternoon, progressing southeastward during the evening and overnight. Thunderstorms will be few, if any, despite temperatures becoming 15 degrees above average for early October. A right entrance jet streak later today and a mid-level elongated trough could be enough for a few places to encounter a thunderstorm or two. Otherwise, a westerly component could result in downslope drying. Showers could become more scattered the further east we look later today. Rainfall amounts will be generally less than a quarter inch for most locations.

Strong high pressure will pass north of the area Saturday while the front stalls across the southeastern states. Southern stream moisture will likely overrun the boundary fairly far to the north, but there remains some uncertainty in the dividing line between rain and no rain. Overall, Saturday probably has a better chance of being dry, especially the further north you go with strong high pressure set up to the north.

A wave of low pressure will likely ride along the boundary Saturday night into Sunday, and this may provide a higher chance of rain spreading northward into the area. Rain that does occur will likely exit the area Sunday evening.

Being north of the boundary and potentially having a lot of cloud cover, high temperatures will likely remain in the 60s for most areas over the weekend.


KEY MESSAGE 2... First widespread frost and freeze potential west of the Blue Ridge early next week.

The true Fall feel sets in next week with highs and lows near to below normal. Monday will feature broad 1025-1028 mb high pressure building east from the Upper Midwest/western Great Lakes behind a departing upper trof/secondary cold front exiting the Mid-Atlantic coast. The frontal passage itself appears mostly dry with perhaps a lingering shower/sprinkle if any moisture is leftover. Breezy west to northwest winds will accompany the front with gusts 20-30 mph and high temperatures in the upper 60s to mid 70s (upper 50s mountains).

High pressure moves overhead Monday night into Tuesday allowing the winds to lighten and skies to clear. This will yield a prime radiational cooling setup, especially west of the Blue Ridge where widespread frost and freeze conditions are possible. Of particular concern is the high elevations and sheltered valleys (cold sinks) which could drop down to around freezing. Elsewhere, expect lows in the upper 30s to mid 40s. Locations near the water will be in the low 50s. Similar conditions are expected Tuesday night with widespread mid to upper 30s west of the Blue Ridge and north/west of the I-95 metro areas. These chilly conditions (concern for frost) are roughly 1 to 2 weeks earlier than average.

Outside of the frost and freeze potential, dry conditions will prevail for much of the week with broad high pressure overhead. A cold front looks to cross the region Thursday into Friday, perhaps bringing a few showers to the mountains. Low pressure lurking off the Southeast coast bears monitoring, but may stay southeast of the area. Otherwise, another large area of high pressure returns for the weekend with warming temperatures heading into the following workweek. Highs Tuesday through Wednesday will likely be in the 60s (50s mountains), with lows in the 40s to near 50 (30s mountains). Thursday and Friday, highs warm back into the upper 60s to mid 70s (low 60s mountains) with lows in the 40s and 50s.

VFR conditions are expected through midday today with light southerly winds. Some marginal LLWS is possible overnight.

A cold front will enter the area later this afternoon or evening. Some showers are possible along the front, but they will likely be fairly light. A brief period of MVFR conditions is possible tonight.

The front will stall to the south over the weekend, but its position remains uncertain. Saturday has the greater chance of being dry, with a wave of low pressure potentially bringing rain on Sunday. Any sub-VFR conditions would likely be limited to CHO Saturday, but could spread northward Sunday.

VFR conditions are expected to prevail Monday through Thursday, although river valley fog is possible each morning. Winds will be out of the north and northwest Monday with gusts around 20 to 25 kts. s.mar:
Southerly winds will uptick a little through today ahead of an approaching cold front. The cold front will then push southward tonight, brining a surge of gusty northerly winds. Small Craft Advisories are in effect for this threat through early Saturday afternoon.

After that, winds may be relatively lighter until a second cold front pushes through on Monday.

High end SCA conditions are possible Monday into Tuesday in the wake of a departing cold frontal boundary. Northerly winds will gust 25 to 30 kts before dropping off Tuesday morning. Winds will switch from the north back to the south by the middle of next week.
s.tide:
Tidal anomalies have been on the decrease over the past few cycles. No tidal flooding is expected today as a result, while the typical more sensitive locations will reach action stage in the evening cycle. A cold front then pushes through tonight, and will lead to declining water levels over at least the next 24 to 36 hours.

Another tidal surge is possible going into early next week ahead of the next frontal system. Lots of uncertainty at this time, but some minor tidal flooding looks possible.

Current surface analysis depicts an area of low pressure over far eastern Canada with a cold front draped south through New England and into the Ohio Valley. Mostly light showers are currently located along this boundary, which will drift southeast through tonight. Ahead of this, we are well above average in terms of temperatures, with readings in the mid to upper 80s for most. Dew points are in the mid 60s, which combined with the warmth should yield at least some minimal CAPE values this afternoon/evening. As the front drops southward, expect showers to increase in coverage and perhaps pop off a few thunderstorms as they move into the slightly unstable air mass. They will also be aided by the right entrance region of an approaching jet streak, which should help to overcome the mid- level drying that is ongoing now in westerly flow. Rainfall amounts will be generally less than a quarter inch for most locations.

Strong high pressure will pass north of the area Saturday while the front stalls just to our south. Southern stream moisture will likely overrun the boundary fairly far to the north, but there remains some uncertainty in the dividing line between rain and no rain. The trend has been for a further north track, so have shifted rain chances about 20 to 30 miles north with the latest forecast package.

A wave of low pressure will ride along this stalled boundary Saturday night into Sunday, and this may provide a higher chance of some heavier rain spreading northward into the area. The Weather Prediction Center does have our eastern areas in a Marginal Excessive Rainfall Outlook, and this seems plausible given the potential for a surge of 2"+ PWATs. Rain that does occur will likely exit the area Sunday evening.

Being north of the boundary and potentially having a lot of cloud cover, high temperatures will likely remain in the 60s for most areas over the weekend.


KEY MESSAGE 2...First widespread frost and freeze potential west of the Blue Ridge early next week.

A distinct pattern shift unfolds into the first full week of October. A highly amplified trough characterized by mid-level heights around 531-dm is expected to cross through Quebec and New Brunswick on Monday. While the core of the forcing remains across New England and points northward, the main impact will come with the cold air arriving in the wake of this trough. A robust area of Canadian high pressure moves into the area Monday night through mid- week. Consequently, this is forecast to bring a true autumnal feel to the air with daily temperatures well below average. For Tuesday and Wednesday, forecast highs will generally range from the upper 50s to 60s, with mountain locales mainly in the 50s. Looking at overnight conditions, the dry nature of the air mass allows temperatures to plummet at night. Areas west of the Blue Ridge can expect widespread mid/upper 30s on Monday and Tuesday nights. This will also include some pockets of upper 20s to near the freezing mark. Given the growing season continues across the region, there will be a threat of some frost/freeze conditions both of those nights. For those with sensitive outdoor vegetation, plans should be made to ensure their safety in these conditions.

Although Canadian high pressure moves off the coast toward the mid/late week period, the overall pattern will remain dry throughout next week. Temperatures slowly rebound through the week as forecast highs return to the low/mid 70s. Nighttime lows remain chilly, but the threat for frost/freeze conditions should diminish beyond Wednesday morning.

The latest surface analysis places a cold front across North Carolina which stretches southwestward to the Lower Mississippi Valley. As stout high pressure sits across the Great Lakes, a cold air damming (CAD) wedge signature is evident across the local area. In response, mainly northerly flow is occurring which coupled with ample cloud cover is keeping temperatures in the mid 50s to mid 60s. The warmer side of this range is occurring closer to the Mason-Dixon Line where a few cloud breaks are evident on visible satellite imagery. Looking on radar, light rain continues to overrun the surface front. Despite the anomalous moisture in place, the stable nature of the air mass coupled with some low-level dry air has limited rainfall amounts. Hourly totals are not amounting to much more than a trace to 0.05 inches. For those south of I-66, such activity will likely impact these areas through the rest of the afternoon and into the early evening.

For tonight, a thick stratus deck remains overhead which will hold overnight lows in the 50s. Some patchy fog is possible, particularly in the more rural low-lying areas. Rain chances do remain just before daybreak Sunday as the next impulse traverses the quasi-stationary front. A band of light rain, perhaps locally moderate in nature, will track northeastward across the region through at least the first half of Sunday. A persistent northeasterly wind should again hold temperatures down in the 60s. Any rain chances should largely come to an end just before sundown Sunday. Overnight conditions should be fairly similar to tonight with lows again in the 50s.

As a deep upper trough tracks across far eastern Canada, a more potent cold front sweeps through the northeastern U.S. on Monday. This will favor increasing sunshine, but also a large uptick in northwesterly winds. Afternoon gusts up to 20 to 25 mph are possible, but with highs returning to the upper 60s to mid 70s (upper 50s to 60s in the mountains).


KEY MESSAGE 2...Frost and freezing temperatures are possible to the west of the Blue Ridge early next week.

A strong area of high pressure will build over the area next week, leading to an extended period of dry conditions. As a cooler airmass works in and high pressure builds overhead, frost and freezing temperatures may be possible to the west of the Blue Ridge both Monday night and Tuesday night. We'll start to see slightly warmer air build in from the south and west later in the week. High temperatures at lower elevations are forecast to be in the 60s (upper 50s/low 60s mountains) on Tuesday, upper 60s to low 70s on Wednesday (60s mountains), and mid 70s (mid-upper 60s mountains) on Wednesday and Thursday. Low temperatures will gradually moderate from the 30s/40s early in the week, to the upper 40s/low 50s later in the week.

A thick area of cloud cover remains over the region this afternoon. However, outside of KCHO, low-level dry air is keeping cloud ceilings high enough to avoid any restrictions. Light rain and drizzle moving through central Virginia is favoring some lower cloud heights around KCHO. Heading into tonight, low-level moistening will favor a return to MVFR to even IFR ceilings at most TAF sites. This does come with increasing rain chances just before daybreak on Sunday. Rain likely continues through the first half of the day before a drying trend before dark. Low ceilings likely persist into Sunday night given persistent northeasterly flow. However, VFR conditions return for Monday behind a strong cold front. Gusts up to 20 to 25 knots are possible during the afternoon hours.

VFR conditions are expected on both Tuesday and Wednesday. Winds are forecast to be out of the north on Tuesday, and then south on Wednesday.

Expect this to persist into Sunday with prevailing north to northeasterly flow given the CAD wedge in place. The true ramp up in wind fields comes for the second half of Monday behind a cold front. Small Craft Advisories will likely be needed midday Monday through the night.

Sub-SCA level northerly winds are expected on Tuesday. Wind shift to out of the south on Wednesday, and are expected to remain sub-SCA in nature.

A cold air damming (CAD) wedge remains in place across the Mid- Atlantic region. The persistent low-level north to northeasterly winds have maintained a stratus deck with some areas of drizzle. However, any of the more concentrated rainfall remains well to the south around the Virginia Tidewater region. While the mid- level water vapor channel and earlier IAD sounding showed a dry mid-level layer, immense moisture remains trapped in the stable lower atmosphere. For the remainder of the day, expect temperatures to hold steady in the 60s. With some cloud breaks across the Allegheny Front, spotty low 70s are possible across the mountain valleys. Overnight conditions stay cloudy, accompanied by some patchy fog development.

Any residual cloud cover should erode as a cold front sweeps through the area early Monday morning. This yields a mostly sunny day with temperatures warming back into the upper 60s to mid 70s, with 60s across the mountains. Northwesterly winds pick up behind the frontal system with afternoon gusts to around 20 to 25 mph. A strong area of Canadian high pressure pushes in from the Midwest on Monday before settling over the local area by the overnight period. This sets the stages for the first widespread frost event, mainly west of the Blue Ridge. The Allegheny ridgetops could even near the freezing mark. For east of the Blue Ridge, forecast lows will be in the 40s.

High pressure maintains its influence over the area on Tuesday which brings cool temperatures, lighter winds, and sunny skies. Most can expect highs in the 60s, with mid/upper 50s across mountain locales. Tuesday night also looks chilly, but forecast temperatures have come up a tad given light southerly flow around the departing high pressure center. At this point temperatures would be just mild enough to avoid another frost event. For most, the forecast lows are in the low/mid 40s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry conditions and warmer temperatures are forecast for Wednesday through Saturday.

High pressure will remain in control locally through much of the upcoming week. Dry conditions are forecast for Wednesday through Saturday, along with warmer temperatures. Highs each day will generally be in the 70s, with lows in the upper 40s to lower 50s.

There are signs that the stretch of dry weather will come to an end on Sunday as an area of low pressure tracks northward out of the Gulf toward the Ohio Valley. If this occurs, rain will likely move into the area from the south. However, there's still a lot of variability in model guidance with respect to what will occur with this system, and if/when we'll get rain.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Frost is expected in the Alleghenies tonight. Quiet weather conditions are anticipated thereafter.

Post frontal northwesterly flow continues to advect drier and cooler air into the region. Skies are mostly sunny this afternoon, with just a few fair weather cumulus scattered about the area. Temperatures are near their highs for the day in the upper 60s to mid 70s (upper 50s/60s mountains), and dewpoints have dropped into the 30s/40s (west) and 50s (east). Dewpoints will continue to drop, eventually reaching the 30s and lower 40s later tonight.

High pressure currently centered over the Great Lakes will build southeastward overnight, eventually becoming centered over the Alleghenies by late in the night. Winds are expected to go calm in locations to the west of the Blue Ridge as the pressure gradient weakens. Locations further east will likely maintain a light northerly wind through much of the night. The combination of low dewpoints, clear skies, and calm winds will set the stage for a near ideal radiational cooling night to the west of the Blue Ridge. Most locations there will drop into the 30s or lower 40s, with higher elevation valleys in the Alleghenies likely dropping into the low to mid 30s. Frost is expected to form there as a result, and Frost Advisories are in effect from Midnight to 9 AM. Locations in the Central Shenandoah Valley will also get close to having frost form, and it wouldn't be shocking to see some patchy frost here and there, but confidence wasn't high enough at this point to extend the Frost Advisory further east. To the east of the Blue Ridge, overnight lows are forecast to be in the 40s.

Quiet weather conditions are expected locally for Tuesday and Wednesday, with high pressure building directly overhead tomorrow, and then moving just offshore on Wednesday. Sunny skies are expected both days. Tuesday looks to be the coolest day of the week, with highs in the 60s for most. Tuesday night will be another cool night, but with the high a bit further east, locations east of the Blue Ridge will have the greatest chance to decouple. Lows Tuesday night are forecast to be in the upper 30s to mid 40s. Temperatures warm a bit on Wednesday in southerly flow, with high temperatures forecast to be in the 70s for most.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Remaining dry through the first half of the weekend before rain chances return by Sunday.

The northern latitude pattern will remain amplified during the mid/late week period. An embedded shortwave trough passes by to the north on Thursday which ushers in the next cold front. Like the early week system, this frontal passage will also be a dry one. Thus, the peak in warmth during the period is likely on Thursday with highs reaching the upper 70s to low 80s. Another dome of surface high pressure builds in for Friday and into the upcoming weekend. This supports a slow but steady cooling trend as highs return to the upper 60s to low 70s by Sunday. Overnight conditions will be seasonable as lows drop into the mid 40s to mid 50s. At this point, it does not appear any frost/freeze concerns will exist.

One area to monitor will be the southwestern Gulf of America/Bay of Campeche. As of 2 PM, the National Hurricane Center continues to raise the probabilities of development (60%) within the next 48 hours. Whatever does materialize and lifts toward the Gulf Coast features a lot of forecast uncertainty. Global ensembles show an area of weakening low centers scattered about the Tennessee Valley to southeastern U.S. Depending on track and quality of tropical moisture, heavier rainfall may impact some area east of the Mississippi River. Will continue to monitor and keep precipitation chances around 30 to 50 percent for Sunday into next Monday.

Another dome of surface high pressure builds in for Friday and into the upcoming weekend. This supports a slow but steady cooling trend as highs return to the upper 60s to low 70s by Sunday. Overnight conditions will be seasonable as lows drop into the mid 40s to mid 50s. At this point, it does not appear any frost/freeze concerns will exist.

One area to monitor will be the southwestern Gulf of America/Bay of Campeche. As of 2 PM, the National Hurricane Center continues to raise the probabilities of development (60%) within the next 48 hours. Whatever does materialize and lifts toward the Gulf Coast features a lot of forecast uncertainty. Global ensembles show an area of weakening low centers scattered about the Tennessee Valley to southeastern U.S. Depending on track and quality of tropical moisture, heavier rainfall may impact some area east of the Mississippi River. Will continue to monitor and keep precipitation chances around 30 to 50 percent for Sunday into next Monday.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Frost is expected in the Alleghenies this morning. Quiet weather conditions are anticipated thereafter.

High pressure will be centered over the Alleghenies this morning yielding calm winds and favorable conditions for radiational cooling/frost formation.

Otherwise, dry and sunny weather conditions are expected locally through midweek. High pressure will build directly overhead today, and then move just offshore Wed. Today will be the coolest day of the week, with highs in the 60s for most. Tonight will be another cool night, but with the high a bit further east, locations east of the Blue Ridge will have the greatest chance to decouple. Lows tonight are forecast to be in the upper 30s to mid 40s. Temps warm a bit on Wed in S'ly flow, with high temps forecast to be in the 70s for most.

An embedded shortwave trough passes by to the north on Thu which ushers in the next cold front. Like the early week system, this frontal passage will also be a dry one. Thus, the peak in warmth during the period is likely on Thu with highs reaching the upper 70s to low 80s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Remaining dry through the first half of the weekend before rain chances return by Sunday.

The weather during the second half of the upcoming weekend into early next week will be dictated at least in part to an area of low pressure currently in the Bay of Campeche.

Synoptically, a large longwave trough will be lifting out of the Northeast to start the weekend. Meanwhile, the aforementioned low pressure area will drift generally northward to the east/southeast side of an upper-level low over Texas. Ridging pivoting across the Upper Midwest will attempt to merge with ridging building over the southwest Atlantic from near Bermuda to the Bahamas. The main uncertainty appears to stem from the depth and forward speed of low pressure as it approaches the Gulf Coast, which will determine how it navigates around the areas of ridging.

At this juncture, several scenarios appear possible:

(1) Quick-moving low pressure moves onshore of the Gulf Coast, and threads the needle between high pressure over the Southwest Atlantic and the Upper Midwest, allowing it to move further north toward the OH Valley, central Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic, delivering notably higher rain potential and amounts locally.

(2) A very quick-moving low pressure system is forced to make an eastward turn sooner across the Southeast prior to the western extent of SW Atlantic ridging exiting the coast. This would keep a majority of moisture and rain chances to the south, though some moisture could still be drawn northward along a passing front.

(3) A slow-moving low pressure system is forced to make that eastward turn sooner, blocked in this scenario by the second area of high pressure in the Upper Midwest building in before it can trek too far to the north. This would keep nearly all precipitation and moisture associated with the low suppressed to the south.

(4) A very slow-moving area of low pressure would not only get caught beneath ridging building over the Upper Midwest, but could then remain cutoff from the large scale steering pattern. This would leave low pressure meandering somewhere well to our south for a time, before an uncertain exit beyond the current forecast period.

At the moment, deterministic and ensemble medium range guidance exhibits very large spread, falling into (but not necessarily favoring) any one of the four scenarios listed above.

Otherwise, temps should generally trend cooler or stay relatively steady, but will depend highly on the extent of cloud cover or any precip (or lack thereof).

Temps warm up to near 80 Thu before the passage of another dry cold front. Temps cool off slightly for the end of the week as weak high pressure of Canadian origin builds in.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Increased rain potential late this weekend into early next week.

The main feature to watch in the extended portion of the forecast will be what becomes of Tropical Depression 9. Key steering features will be a ridge in the western Atlantic, a trough/closed low over Texas, and eventually a trough ejecting from the northern Rockies. The NHC forecast has the remnants of this system moving into the Tennessee and Ohio Valleys over the weekend, although there still remains considerable uncertainty on the track and especially forward speed of the system. Even despite this westward position of the cyclone, moisture from both the Gulf of America and Atlantic will likely be transported northward into the Mid Atlantic. Rain will become increasingly likely Sun, although as mentioned, this timing could vary a bit. The remnant low could then move eastward, potentially extending rain chances into Monday. At this juncture, the rain will be the main impact from this system, but we will continue to monitor any changing trends.

It will be important to stay tuned to the forecast over the next few days, and monitor hurricanes.gov for updated details on Tropical Depression 9.

Daytime temperatures will likely be seasonal through the weekend and early next week but will take a dip when rain is the most widespread. Meanwhile overnight lows will be mild thanks to increasing clouds and dew points.

Cooler weather to end the week as high pressure of Canadian origin builds in. High pressure center settles in by Saturday morning with low temps in the 40s and 50s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Remnants of Tropical Storm Isaias arrive late this weekend.

As of today, the National Hurricane Center is now issuing advisories on Tropical Storm Isaias down in the Bay of Campeche. This Tropical cyclone will need to be monitored closely in the coming days in regards to potential impacts to our region late this weekend. There remains a great deal of uncertainty, owing to a complex upper-level pattern ahead of it. A cutoff low over the southern Plains and an area of high pressure over Florida will act as the primary steering mechanisms in the coming days. The big questions are going to be... where does it go, and how fast does does it get there? A track directly over our area is highly unlikely at this time. However, it does seem likely to track somewhere up into the MS River Valley and then eventually up towards the Great Lakes as it transitions into a non-tropical low.

At present, the most likely impacts to our region will be rain. However, there isn't a great concern for flooding at this time, as the system should be progressive and much of the region could use a good soaking rain to help with drought relief. That being said, this system is still several days out, so we will be monitoring any rainfall trends closely as the time draws closer. There is also a non-zero, but very small, chance that some severe weather could occur as a result of the remnants of Isaias. However, again, this will greatly depend on how the upper-level pattern evolves and interacts with Isaias as it moves into our region. Main threat, if it materializes would be the non-zero threat of a quick tornado on Sunday afternoon/evening.

All of this to say, we just simply don't know if Isaias will bring any significant impacts our way. However, as is the case with any tropical cyclone, it will be important to stay tuned to the forecast over the next few days. Monitor hurricanes.gov for details on Isaias.

KEY MESSAGE 1...Sunny & mild conditions continue through the end of the week.

Current surface analysis depicts that the cold front has largely pushed through the region this morning. In its wake, dry air builds in from the west as high pressure moves in overhead. A few wind gusts could reach around 20 knots late this afternoon before diminishing overnight as the front fully transitions out of the region. Temperatures remain in the mid-to-upper 70s today & tomorrow as upper-level ridging briefly builds over the Appalachians, with dewpoints ranging generally in the 30s across most areas. As most of CONUS remains quiet off to our west, clear skies and light winds should continue to dominate over the next 36-48 hours ahead of any potential remnants of Hurricane Isaias.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Remnants of Hurricane Isaias to arrive Saturday night.


Latest guidance show rain associated with remnants of Isaias arriving in central VA Saturday evening, a little quicker than what it was shown yesterday, and spreading northeast across the rest of the fcst area late Saturday night, reaching the Susquehanna River by 12Z Sunday. The rain will be moderately intense during the overnight hours Sat night through Sunday morning, and begin to diminish in intensity mid afternoon Sunday as mid-level dry slot begins to move in from the southwest. Ensemble guidance shows generally one to two inches of rain falling, with the heaviest/most intense rainfall falling in a roughly 12-hr period from 06Z-18Z Sun. Given the long duration and stratiform type, no flooding is expected. As for the risk of severe wx, if it were to occur, it would be Sunday night, with the greatest risk south of Point Lookout into the VA Tidewater region. Some showers could linger into Monday morning as the mid- level circulation crosses the area.

A strong cold front associated with a deepening northern stream trough is then fcst to cross the area Tue night bringing autumn chill for the middle and second half of next week.

Winds should strengthen Saturday night into Sunday as pressure gradient tightens. Wouldn't rule out some LLWS if a strong inversion develops. Showers should end by midday Monday. Expect IFR conditions late Sunday night through Sunday night with conditions improving Monday.

s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Remnants of Hurricane Isaias to bring rain, breezy conditions Sunday into Sunday night.

The main weather impact to the region over the next week is going to be from the remnants of what is now Hurricane Isaias. Model guidance is in generally good agreement that Hurricane Isaias' surface low weakens and broadens as the system moves into the TN Valley Saturday night into Sunday. The mid-level circulation amplifies and becomes a strong cutoff low over KY/TN that moves slowly east across the Mid- Atlantic Sunday into Monday. Periods of rain are likely across the area at times Saturday evening through Sunday night. Rainfall amounts of 1-2 inches are expected across the area. Higher rain totals are certainly possible, but will depend on a few other smaller scale features.

Tropical moisture surges north into our area Saturday night into Sunday, with the highest PWAT values at or above 2" (most likely east of the Blue Ridge). While the main cutoff low associated with the remnants of Isaias remain west of the Appalachians on Saturday, expect light rain to move in from south to north in the evening. Forcing for ascent increases Saturday night, and especially Sunday morning into Sunday afternoon as mid-level heights fall with the approach of the cutoff low. There is going to be enhanced low-level convergence somewhere over the region as the surface high to the east and cutoff low to the west interact. Easterly flow into the Blue Ridge could also produce enhanced rain amounts due to orographic effects. Additionally, an inverted trough or wave of low pressure tries to develop in lee of the Appalachians Sunday as it crosses Virginia to the Delmarva.

Uncertainty remains regarding the exact evolution and timing of these features, which will ultimately determine where / if any locally heavy rain occurs. s.key:
- 1) Remnants of Hurricane Isaias to bring rain, breezy to windy conditions, and the threat of tornadoes Sunday.

- 2) Above normal temperatures Tuesday will fall the second half of the week as moisture starved fronts move through.
s.disc:
KEY MESSAGE 1...Remnants of Hurricane Isaias to bring rain, breezy to windy conditions, and the threat of tornadoes Sunday.

Hurricane Isaias is forecast to move north toward the TN Valley today as it weakens and eventually loses all of its tropical characteristics. The mid-level circulation strengthens and becomes a large cutoff low later tonight. To the east, surface high pressure over the Northeast today moves offshore off southern New England tonight.

The interaction of Isaias' remnants to the west and surface high to the east will create a large area of convergence / broad frontal zone over the Mid-Atlantic. There is good model agreement that rain steadily moves from south to north this evening into tonight as forcing for ascent increases with some mid-level height falls in response to the approaching cutoff low. It'll take a bit of time for the surface to truly saturate, so any rain late afternoon to this evening in Central Virginia is going to be light. Eventually, tropical moisture with PWATs at or above 2" surges in after midnight.

It is worth mentioning again that conditions are favorable for a widespread soaking rain, and 00Z models have responded with more QPF across the region. Forcing for ascent increases tonight, and especially Sunday morning into Sunday afternoon as mid-level heights fall with the approach of the cutoff low. Enhanced low-level convergence and moisture transport will peak Sunday morning into early Sunday afternoon. Strengthening easterly flow into the Blue Ridge could also produce enhanced rain amounts due to orographic effects. As a result, forecast rain amounts have increased to 1.5- 2.5", with locally higher amounts of 3-4" possible. No Flood Watch issued with this forecast update as the heaviest rain is forecast to occur in areas that can handle it, but will continue to monitor the latest guidance today.

Another noticeable trend in the 00Z guidance is the higher probabilities for severe weather Sunday afternoon. The main synoptically forced rain moves north of the area early Sunday afternoon. Rapid height-falls and increasing low-level winds provide a few hour window where some breaks in the clouds area possible, leading to pockets of instability. A surface wave of low pressure moves right through our area Sunday afternoon. Forecast soundings indicate large, swooping hodographs, with ample shear in place to support organized severe convection. Clusters of thunderstorms develop along the leading edge of the surface low pressure, with tornadoes and damaging wind gusts as the main threats (looks mostly to be east of the Blue Ridge). The NAM12, RRFS, and 06Z HRRR all show this scenario. The big question still remains how much instability actually develops. SPC has introduced a Slight Risk for Sunday just to our south, with a Marginal Risk north to the MD/PA border.

The strong mid-level circulation is going to bring windy conditions to the Alleghenies and Blue Ridge, starting late tonight into Sunday morning. Wind Advisories have been issued for downsloping easterly winds in the Alleghenies (western Garrett, western Grant, and western Pendleton Counties), and the Blue Ridge. The current forecast for peak wind gusts is 40-50 mph in the Alleghenies/Blue Ridge and 20-30 mph elsewhere.

The remnants of Isaias push offshore Monday, bringing an end to any lingering showers. While conditions return humid and warm Monday, there likely won't be much in the way of shower activity due to subsidence behind the departing trough.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Above normal temperatures Tuesday will fall the second half of the week as moisture starved fronts move through.

Brief ridging in the wake of the tropical remnants may bring high temperatures Tuesday to near 80 degrees. Low pressure passing north of the area will send a cold front southward Tuesday night. Most of the rain likely remains across Pennsylvania, although some showers may sneak southward. Showers will also be possible along the Allegheny Front. There's still some significant model spread on the progression of this front during the middle of the week, with a large spread of temperatures possible on Wednesday. However, the general trend will be downward for the second half of the week. A wave of low pressure or cold front may approach toward the end of the week which could bring some rain, but model spread remains high on the details.
s.avn:
VFR conditions prevail through this evening, then conditions deteriorate tonight into Sunday as the remnants of Hurricane Isaias impact the region. IFR conditions are likely to overspread all terminals late tonight through Sunday afternoon, as periods of rain and gusty winds cross the region. There could be a few hour period of thunderstorms Sunday afternoon, some of which could be severe, though this threat is greatest east of the Blue Ridge. Conditions improve Monday morning, with the return of VFR conditions. Northwest winds gusting around 20-25 knots possible Monday afternoon.

VFR conditions are most likely Tuesday and Wednesday. A dry cold frontal passage Tuesday night may be followed by gusty northwest winds Wednesday.
s.mar:
Marine conditions are expected to deteriorate tonight through Sunday night as the remnants of Hurricane Isaias move across the Mid- Atlantic. SCA conditions develop this evening in the central Chesapeake Bay, then across all the waters tonight. The strongest winds, gusts around 30 knots, will occur Sunday morning. Special Marine Warnings may be needed Sunday afternoon for thunderstorms capable of producing strong wind gusts and waterspouts. The remnants of Isaias move offshore Monday morning, but SCA conditions continue through Monday evening due to gusty northwest winds in its wake.

Sub-SCA conditions are likely Tuesday with brief high pressure. SCA conditions are possible in southerly flow Tuesday night and northwesterly flow on Wednesday as a cold front pushes through.
s.tide: Widespread tidal flooding is likely during the Sunday afternoon to evening high tide cycle. Several conditions are coming together to produce a surge of water up the Chesapeake Bay and Potomac River. Strong onshore winds coming during the highest of the daily tides, which happens to coincide with the New Moon are going to produce minor tidal flooding at most forecast locations. A Coastal Flood Watch has been issued for Annapolis where Moderate tidal flooding is possible. Water levels quickly decrease Monday morning as offshore winds follow.
